parts.answer: A zero error: the pointer or ruler is not at zero when there is no load, so every extension is shifted by 0.4 cm; this is a systematic error.
parts.working: B1 zero error (pointer or ruler not at zero with no load); B1 systematic, so every reading is offset by the same amount.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the student should correct the data.
parts.answer: Subtract 0.4 cm from each extension (or re-zero the ruler) before plotting or finding the gradient.
parts.working: B1 subtract the zero error from each extension.

practice.stem: A student tests whether R is proportional to L for a wire: (L = 0.50 m, R = 2.4 Ω), (L = 1.00 m, R = 4.9 Ω), (L = 1.50 m, R = 7.1 Ω), (L = 2.00 m, R = 9.8 Ω).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate R/L for each reading, to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a conclusion, commenting on the third reading.
parts.answer: The data support R ∝ L, with R/L about 4.8 Ω/m; the 1.50 m reading is about 2 % below the others, which may be random error in the reading.
parts.working: B1 R proportional to L (R/L roughly constant); B1 the 1.50 m reading is an outlier from random error, not a clear departure from proportionality.

practice.stem: A radioactive source gives these counts in successive 10-minute intervals: 800 (at t = 0), 400 (at 10 min), 200 (at 20 min), 100 (at 30 min).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of each count to the previous one.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the data support the halving of the count every 10 min, and state the half-life.
parts.answer: Yes: the count halves every 10 min, so the half-life is 10 min.
parts.working: B1 yes, constant ratio 0.50; B1 half-life 10 min.

practice.stem: A ball rolls down a ramp from height h and leaves the bench horizontally, landing a distance d from the bench. Readings: h = 0.100 m, d = 0.316 m; h = 0.400 m, d = 0.620 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate k = d/h for each set of readings and state whether the results support d ∝ h, using the criterion that the two values of k should differ by less than 10 % (difference ÷ smaller value).
parts.answer: k₁ = 3.16, k₂ = 1.55; they differ by about 100 %, so d ∝ h is not supported
parts.working: k₁ = 0.316/0.100 = 3.16, k₂ = 0.620/0.400 = 1.55 (B1); differ by far more than 10 % so not supported (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate K = d/√h for each set of readings and comment on the suggestion that d ∝ √h.
parts.answer: K₁ = 0.999 m¹ᐟ², K₂ = 0.980 m¹ᐟ²; difference 1.9 % < 10 %, so d ∝ √h is supported

practice.stem: A student measures the power P of a lamp at four voltages: (V = 2.0 V, P = 0.40 W), (V = 4.0 V, P = 1.60 W), (V = 6.0 V, P = 3.60 W), (V = 8.0 V, P = 6.40 W). The hypothesis is P ∝ V².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate P/V² for each reading.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State your conclusion and explain why the test covers only a limited range.
parts.answer: The ratio is constant, so P ∝ V² is supported over 2–8 V; but the test covers only that range, and a real filament warms up at higher voltage, so its resistance changes and the law may not hold beyond it.
parts.working: B1 supported (constant P/V²); B1 limit of range, and real filament resistance changes with temperature.

practice.stem: A student tests the relationship between the period T of a simple pendulum and its length L, using T = kLⁿ. The readings are (L = 0.40 m, T = 1.27 s) and (L = 1.60 m, T = 2.54 s).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate n from n = ln(T₂/T₁) ÷ ln(L₂/L₁), to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the data support T ∝ √L.
parts.answer: Yes: n = 0.50, which equals the power for T ∝ √L.
parts.working: B1 n is 0.50; B1 matches T ∝ L^½, i.e. T ∝ √L.

practice.stem: A student tests I = k/dⁿ for light from a lamp. Readings: (d = 1.0 m, I = 8.0 W/m²), (d = 2.0 m, I = 2.1 W/m²), (d = 3.0 m, I = 0.9 W/m²).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate n from the readings at d = 1.0 m and d = 3.0 m, to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the data support the inverse square law, referring to I × d².
parts.answer: Yes: n = 1.99 is close to 2, and I × d² is about 8 W at each distance (8.0, 8.4, 8.1), within the scatter.
parts.working: B1 n close to 2; B1 I × d² roughly constant, so the inverse square law is supported.

practice.stem: A radioactive source gives these corrected counts: N = 800 at t = 0, N = 449 at t = 10 min, N = 252 at t = 20 min, N = 141 at t = 30 min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio N(t + 10 min) ÷ N(t) for each pair of readings, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the half-life implied by this ratio and whether the data support exponential decay.
parts.answer: The constant ratio supports exponential decay; from 0.561 = (½)^(10/T½), T½ = 12 min.
parts.working: C1 0.561 = 2^(−10/T½); B1 T½ = 12.0 min; B1 constant ratio supports exponential decay.

practice.stem: On a wet road in Lahore, a car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 15 m s⁻¹ runs into the back of a stationary car of mass 900 kg. The two cars lock together and move off along the same line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define linear momentum.
parts.answer: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the two cars immediately after the collision.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the loss of kinetic energy in the collision.
parts.working: C1: initial KE = ½ × 1200 × 15² = 135 kJ. C1: final KE = ½ × 2100 × 8.57² = 77.1 kJ. A1: loss = 57.9 kJ.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is a correct unit for impulse?
A kg m s⁻²
B kg m s⁻¹
C kg m² s⁻¹
D N s⁻¹
parts.working: Impulse = force × time, so N s = (kg m s⁻²)(s) = kg m s⁻¹, the same unit as momentum. A is the unit of force, not impulse.

practice.stem: A cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg is bowled at 32 m s⁻¹ towards a batter. It is hit straight back along the same line at 41 m s⁻¹. The bat is in contact with the ball for 1.2 ms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State Newton's second law of motion in terms of momentum.
parts.answer: The resultant force on a body is proportional to (equal to) its rate of change of momentum.
parts.working: B1: resultant force ∝ / = rate of change of momentum (and in the same direction).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the change in momentum of the ball.
parts.working: C1: take towards the batter as positive: Δp = 0.16 × (−41) − 0.16 × 32. A1: |Δp| = 0.16 × 73 = 11.7 N s (kg m s⁻¹).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the average force exerted on the ball by the bat.
parts.working: C1: F = Δp/Δt = 11.7 / 1.2 × 10⁻³. A1: F = 9730 N (opposite to the ball's original direction).

practice.stem: A football of mass 0.43 kg is at rest. During a kick, the force on the ball rises steadily from zero to 1800 N in 4.0 ms and then falls steadily back to zero in a further 6.0 ms. The force always acts in the same direction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is represented by the area under a force–time graph.
parts.answer: The impulse of the force (the change in momentum).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the impulse given to the ball.
parts.working: C1: area of triangle = ½ × 1800 × 0.010. A1: 9.00 N s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the ball as it leaves the foot.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two spheres collide head-on in a perfectly elastic collision. No external forces act. Which quantity is NOT necessarily the same before and after the collision?
A the total momentum of the two spheres
B the total kinetic energy of the two spheres
C the relative speed of the two spheres
D the momentum of each individual sphere
parts.answer: D the momentum of each individual sphere
parts.working: Total momentum is always conserved; in an elastic collision total KE is conserved and the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation. Momentum is transferred between the spheres, so each sphere's momentum changes. B is conserved here because the collision is elastic.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A trolley of mass 2.0 kg moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary trolley of mass 1.0 kg and sticks to it. What is the speed of the combined trolleys immediately after the collision?
A 6.0 m s⁻¹
B 3.0 m s⁻¹
C 2.0 m s⁻¹
D 1.0 m s⁻¹
parts.working: Momentum is conserved: 2.0×3.0 = (2.0+1.0)v, so v = 2.0 m s⁻¹. 6.0 m s⁻¹ forgets to divide by the total mass; 3.0 m s⁻¹ assumes the first trolley keeps its speed; 1.0 m s⁻¹ is wrong arithmetic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A golf ball of mass 46 g is struck. Its velocity changes from rest to 62 m s⁻¹ and the ball is in contact with the club for 1.5 ms. Calculate the impulse given to the ball.
parts.working: Impulse = change in momentum = 0.046 × 62 = 2.85 N s (2.9 N s to 2 s.f.).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average force exerted by the club on the ball during contact.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The weight of the ball is about 0.45 N. Explain why the weight can be neglected during the contact.
parts.answer: The contact force (about 1900 N) is thousands of times greater than the weight (about 0.45 N), so the weight makes a negligible contribution to the impulse during the short contact.
parts.working: 1 mark for comparing the forces with numbers; 1 mark for the conclusion that the net impulse is effectively due to the contact force.

practice.stem: On a horizontal frictionless air track, trolley A of mass 0.50 kg moves at 0.60 m s⁻¹ towards trolley B of mass 0.30 kg, which is at rest. The trolleys collide head-on and the collision is perfectly elastic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a perfectly elastic collision.
parts.answer: A collision in which the total kinetic energy is conserved.
parts.working: B1: total kinetic energy is the same before and after (momentum is always conserved).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use conservation of momentum and the relative speeds of the trolleys to calculate the velocity of each trolley after the collision.
parts.answer: A: 0.150 m s⁻¹, B: 0.750 m s⁻¹, both in the original direction of A
parts.working: C1: 0.50 × 0.60 = 0.50 vA + 0.30 vB. C1: relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation: 0.60 = vB − vA. M1: solve: 0.30 = 0.50 vA + 0.30(vA + 0.60) → 0.80 vA = 0.12. A1: vA = 0.150 m s⁻¹, vB = 0.750 m s⁻¹ (same direction as A's initial motion).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that your answers to (b) are consistent with the collision being perfectly elastic.
parts.answer: KE before = 0.0900 J; KE after = 0.0900 J, so KE is conserved

practice.stem: A radon-222 nucleus, initially at rest, decays by emitting an α-particle of kinetic energy 5.49 MeV. The daughter nucleus is polonium-218. Take the mass of the α-particle as 4u and of the daughter nucleus as 218u, where u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the daughter nucleus and the α-particle move off in exactly opposite directions.
parts.answer: Total momentum before is zero, so the momenta after must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
parts.working: B1: initial momentum is zero (nucleus at rest) and momentum is conserved. B1: so the two momenta must cancel: equal and opposite.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the α-particle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the daughter nucleus.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the daughter nucleus, in MeV.
parts.working: A1: KE ∝ p²/m with equal p, so KE_d = (4/218) × 5.49 = 0.101 MeV (or ½mv² with values from (c)).

practice.stem: On smooth ice, puck A of mass 0.17 kg moving at 6.0 m s⁻¹ strikes an identical puck B at rest. After the collision, A moves at 3.0 m s⁻¹ in a direction at 60° to its original direction. Friction is negligible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the components of the velocity of puck B after the collision, parallel and perpendicular to the original direction of A.
parts.answer: 4.5 m s⁻¹ parallel; 2.6 m s⁻¹ perpendicular (on the opposite side of the line from A)
parts.working: C1: parallel: 0.17 × 6.0 = 0.17 × 3.0 cos 60° + 0.17 vx → vx = 4.5 m s⁻¹. C1: perpendicular: 0 = 0.17 × 3.0 sin 60° + 0.17 vy. A1: vy = −2.6 m s⁻¹ (opposite side).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the speed of B and the angle its path makes with the original direction of A.
parts.answer: 5.20 m s⁻¹ at 30° to the original direction
parts.working: A1: v = √(4.5² + 2.60²) = 5.20 m s⁻¹. A1: tan θ = 2.60/4.5, θ = 30° (on the other side of the line from A).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine whether the collision is elastic.
parts.answer: Yes: total KE before = 3.06 J = total KE after
parts.working: M1: KE before = ½ × 0.17 × 6.0² = 3.06 J; after = ½ × 0.17 × (3.0² + 5.20²) = 0.765 + 2.30 = 3.06 J. A1: KE conserved so elastic.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A ball of mass 0.20 kg falls vertically and hits the floor at 5.0 m s⁻¹. It rebounds vertically at 3.0 m s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the change in momentum of the ball?
A 0.40 N s
B 1.0 N s
C 1.6 N s
D 3.4 N s
parts.working: Velocity reverses, so Δp = 0.20 × (3.0 − (−5.0)) = 1.6 N s. A (0.40 N s) comes from subtracting speeds and ignoring the change of direction.

practice.stem: A rifle of mass 4.2 kg fires a bullet of mass 12 g horizontally at 750 m s⁻¹. The rifle is initially at rest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the recoil speed of the rifle, assuming it is free to move.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rifle is brought to rest over a distance of 0.15 m. Calculate the average force needed.
parts.working: C1: KE of rifle = ½ × 4.2 × 2.14² = 9.64 J. C1: work done = F × 0.15. A1: F = 64.3 N.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the bullet and rifle have equal magnitudes of momentum but very different kinetic energies.
parts.answer: Momenta are equal and opposite (total zero); KE = p²/2m, so the much smaller mass of the bullet gives it far more KE (3380 J compared with 9.64 J).
parts.working: B1: momentum conserved from zero, so equal magnitudes. B1: KE = p²/2m, smaller mass → larger KE (bullet ≈ 3400 J).

practice.stem: A fire-fighter in Karachi directs a horizontal jet of water at a wall. Water leaves the hose at 18 m s⁻¹ and the mass of water leaving per second is 2.5 kg s⁻¹. The water hits the wall at right angles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the force exerted by the water on the wall when the water does not rebound.
parts.working: C1: F = rate of change of momentum = (mass per second) × Δv. A1: F = 2.5 × 18 = 45.0 N.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The wall is replaced by a surface from which the water splashes straight back at 4.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the new force.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use Newton's third law to explain why the person holding the hose feels a force.
parts.answer: The hose exerts a forward force on the water to accelerate it; the water exerts an equal and opposite (backward) force on the hose.
parts.working: B1: hose pushes water forwards (increasing its momentum). B1: water pushes the hose backwards with an equal force (third-law pair, same type of force).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A hockey puck of mass 0.16 kg slides at 12 m s⁻¹ into a rigid barrier and rebounds horizontally at 8.0 m s⁻¹ in the opposite direction. What is the magnitude of the impulse on the puck?
A 0.64 N s
B 1.9 N s
C 3.2 N s
D 6.4 N s
parts.working: Take the initial direction as positive. Δp = m(v − u) = 0.16 × (−8.0 − 12) = −3.2 kg m s⁻¹, so the impulse has magnitude 3.2 N s. 0.64 N s uses 12 − 8 and ignores the change of direction; 1.9 N s is the initial momentum (0.16 × 12) with the rebound ignored; 6.4 N s is double the correct answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A stationary object of mass 0.80 kg explodes into two pieces of masses 0.30 kg and 0.50 kg moving along a straight line. The 0.30 kg piece moves at 12 m s⁻¹ east. Calculate the velocity of the 0.50 kg piece.
parts.working: Total momentum is zero: 0.30 × 12 + 0.50 × v = 0, so v = −7.2 m s⁻¹ (7.2 m s⁻¹ west).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total kinetic energy released in the explosion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where the energy released in the explosion comes from.
parts.answer: The energy comes from the internal (chemical or stored) energy of the object before it exploded.
parts.working: Energy is conserved; kinetic energy is gained from internal energy store.

practice.stem: A ballistic pendulum is used to measure the speed of an air-gun pellet. A pellet of mass 5.0 g is fired horizontally into a wooden block of mass 1.200 kg hanging from long strings. The pellet stays in the block, and the block rises through a vertical height of 8.5 cm. Air resistance is negligible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the block and pellet immediately after the impact.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the pellet just before it hits the block.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the percentage of the pellet's initial kinetic energy that is converted to other forms in the impact is more than 99%, and state two of these other forms.
parts.answer: 99.6% is lost, as thermal energy (heating) and sound / work deforming the block
parts.working: M1: fraction of KE remaining = m/(M + m) (or calculate both KEs: 242 J and 1.01 J). A1: lost = 99.6%. B1: any two of: internal (thermal) energy, sound, work done in plastic deformation.

practice.stem: Two gliders of masses 0.40 kg and 0.60 kg are held at rest on a level air track with a compressed spring between them. When released, the spring transfers 0.30 J of elastic potential energy to the kinetic energy of the gliders. The spring has negligible mass and falls away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the gliders move off in opposite directions with equal magnitudes of momentum.
parts.answer: Total momentum is zero before release and is conserved (no external horizontal force), so the momenta are equal and opposite.
parts.working: B1: initial total momentum zero. B1: momentum conserved so p₁ = −p₂.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of each glider after they separate.
parts.answer: 0.40 kg glider: 0.949 m s⁻¹; 0.60 kg glider: 0.632 m s⁻¹

practice.stem: A firework shell is momentarily at rest at the top of its flight when it explodes into three fragments that all move horizontally. A fragment of mass 0.20 kg moves east at 30 m s⁻¹ and a fragment of mass 0.30 kg moves north at 20 m s⁻¹. The third fragment has mass 0.25 kg. Ignore gravity during the very short explosion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the third fragment and state its direction.
parts.answer: 33.9 m s⁻¹ towards the south-west (45° south of west)
parts.working: C1: momenta of first two: 6.0 N s east and 6.0 N s north. C1: third must cancel: magnitude √(6.0² + 6.0²) = 8.49 N s. A1: v = 8.49/0.25 = 33.9 m s⁻¹. B1: direction south-west, at 45° to both west and south.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total kinetic energy released by the explosion.

practice.stem: In a nuclear reactor, fast neutrons are slowed down by collisions with carbon-12 nuclei. Consider a neutron (mass 1u) moving at speed u that makes a head-on, perfectly elastic collision with a stationary carbon-12 nucleus (mass 12u).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using conservation of momentum and the fact that relative speed of approach equals relative speed of separation, show that the neutron rebounds with a speed of (11/13)u.
parts.answer: Neutron rebounds at 11u/13 (carbon moves forward at 2u/13).
parts.working: M1: 1 × u = 1 × v_n + 12 × v_C. M1: u = v_C − v_n. A1: substitute: u = v_n + 12(u + v_n) → 13v_n = −11u, so speed 11u/13 (direction reversed).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of its kinetic energy that the neutron keeps in one such collision.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A neutron starts with kinetic energy 2.0 MeV. Calculate the minimum number of such head-on collisions needed to reduce its kinetic energy below 1.0 keV.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A ball A of mass m moving at speed u collides head-on and elastically with ball B of mass 3m, which is at rest. What fraction of the initial kinetic energy of A is transferred to B?
A 0.25
B 0.50
C 0.75
D 0.90
parts.working: For an elastic collision with B at rest, v_B = 2m u/(m + 3m) = u/2. KE of B afterwards = ½(3m)(u/2)² = 3mu²/8; initial KE of A = ½mu², so the fraction is (3/8)/(1/2) = 0.75. 0.50 wrongly uses the velocity ratio of the masses; 0.25 uses the velocity of A only.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A skydiver falls vertically at a constant (terminal) velocity. Which statement is correct?
A The air resistance is zero and the acceleration is g.
B The air resistance is less than the weight and the acceleration is decreasing.
C The resultant force is zero and the acceleration is zero.
D The resultant force is equal to the weight and the acceleration is zero.
parts.answer: C The resultant force is zero and the acceleration is zero.
parts.working: At terminal velocity drag equals weight, so the resultant force and the acceleration are both zero. B describes the motion before terminal velocity is reached.

practice.stem: A steel ball bearing is released from rest just below the surface of a tall cylinder of oil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the three forces acting on the ball bearing as it falls through the oil.
parts.working: B1: all three named (weight downwards, upthrust and drag upwards).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the acceleration of the ball bearing decreases as it falls.
parts.answer: As speed increases the drag increases; the resultant downward force (weight − upthrust − drag) decreases, so acceleration decreases.
parts.working: B1: drag increases with speed. B1: resultant force decreases (weight and upthrust constant), so a = F/m decreases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain what happens to the ball bearing's speed once the acceleration becomes zero.
parts.answer: It stays constant (terminal velocity) because drag + upthrust = weight, so the resultant force is zero.
parts.working: B1: constant speed / terminal velocity. B1: forces balanced, resultant force zero.

practice.stem: A skydiver of total mass 75 kg falls vertically before opening her parachute. At one instant her speed is 30 m s⁻¹ and the air resistance on her is 410 N.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the skydiver at this instant.
parts.working: C1: resultant force = 75 × 9.81 − 410 = 326 N. A1: a = 326/75 = 4.34 m s⁻² (downwards).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the air resistance on the skydiver when she reaches terminal velocity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The air resistance is proportional to the square of the speed. Calculate the terminal speed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A small sphere of mass 0.30 kg falls through air and reaches a constant terminal velocity. What is the magnitude of the air resistance (drag) force on the sphere at terminal velocity?
A 0.031 N
B 2.9 N
C 8.0 N
D 24 N
parts.working: At terminal velocity the net force is zero, so drag = weight = mg = 0.30 × 9.81 = 2.94 N. 0.031 N is far too small; 8.0 N and 24 N treat the terminal speed (or a multiple of it) as if it were a force.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A steel ball of mass 25 g falls through a liquid. Its upthrust is 0.080 N. List the three forces acting on the ball and state whether each acts upwards or downwards.
parts.answer: Weight 0.245 N downwards; upthrust 0.080 N upwards; drag (viscous resistance) 0.165 N upwards while the ball is falling.
parts.working: 1 mark for weight down and upthrust up; 1 mark for drag acting up (opposing the motion).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The ball reaches a terminal velocity of 0.40 m s⁻¹. Calculate the drag force at this velocity.
parts.working: At terminal velocity the forces balance: drag = weight − upthrust = 0.2453 − 0.080 = 0.165 N.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the ball does not keep accelerating once it reaches terminal velocity.
parts.answer: As the speed increases the drag force increases until it equals weight minus upthrust; the net force then becomes zero, so the acceleration is zero and the speed stays constant.
parts.working: 1 mark for drag increasing with speed; 1 mark for net force zero so acceleration zero.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ball of mass 0.12 kg is released from rest and falls vertically. At an instant when its speed is 4.0 m s⁻¹ its acceleration is 6.0 m s⁻¹ downwards. Calculate its weight.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the air resistance (drag) on the ball at this instant. Assume the upthrust from air is negligible.
parts.working: Resultant force = ma = 0.12 × 6.0 = 0.72 N downwards. Drag = weight − resultant = 1.177 − 0.72 = 0.46 N (upwards).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain what happens to the acceleration of the ball as its speed increases towards its terminal velocity.
parts.answer: The acceleration decreases to zero: the drag increases with speed, so the resultant force falls until drag equals weight.
parts.working: 1 mark for decrease to zero; 1 mark for drag increasing with speed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a flat sheet of paper falls more slowly than a tightly crumpled ball of paper of the same mass.
parts.answer: The flat sheet has a larger cross-sectional area, so for the same speed it experiences a larger drag force. Drag increases with speed, so the sheet reaches a lower speed at which drag equals weight (its terminal velocity is lower). The crumpled ball has a smaller area and reaches a higher terminal velocity.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: larger area of the sheet; greater drag for the same speed; drag increases with speed; terminal velocity reached when drag equals weight, so the sheet has a lower terminal velocity.

practice.stem: On the Lahore–Islamabad motorway, the air resistance F on a car is given by F = kv², where v is the speed of the car and k = 0.42 in SI units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express the unit of k in SI base units.
parts.working: B1: k = F/v² → kg m s⁻² / (m² s⁻²) = kg m⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the drag force at 25 m s⁻¹ and the power needed just to overcome it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that increasing the speed from 25 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹ multiplies this power by about 1.7.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A parachutist is falling at a high terminal velocity. She opens her parachute at time t₀. Which describes her motion just after t₀?
A She accelerates upwards with an acceleration of constant magnitude until she stops.
B She decelerates, with a deceleration that decreases in magnitude, until she reaches a lower terminal velocity.
C She decelerates, with a deceleration that increases in magnitude, until she reaches a lower terminal velocity.
D She continues at the same terminal velocity because her weight has not changed.
parts.answer: B She decelerates, with a deceleration that decreases in magnitude, until she reaches a lower terminal velocity.
parts.working: Opening the parachute makes drag greater than weight, so she decelerates; as she slows the drag falls, so the deceleration gets smaller until drag = weight again at a lower speed. She does not move upwards (A); she is still moving down.

practice.stem:
A student drops steel spheres of different radius r into a tall tube of glycerol. She times each sphere between two marks 0.300 m apart, the upper mark being 15 cm below the surface.
Results (r / mm, t / s): 1.0, 15.2; 1.5, 6.6; 2.0, 3.8; 2.5, 2.4; 3.0, 1.7.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the terminal velocity v for each sphere. Give your values to an appropriate number of significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: It is suggested that v = Kr², where K is a constant. Plot a suitable graph (describe the axes) and use it to estimate K in m s⁻¹ mm⁻².
parts.answer: v against r² gives a straight line through the origin; K ≈ 0.020 m s⁻¹ mm⁻² (accept 0.019–0.021)
parts.working: B1: plot v (y-axis) against r² (x-axis). M1: gradient from a large triangle on the line. A1: K = gradient ≈ 0.020 m s⁻¹ mm⁻².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the value of t for the largest sphere is the least reliable reading, and one improvement to deal with it.
parts.answer: Time is short (≈1.7 s) so reaction time gives a large percentage uncertainty; use a longer fall distance / video with a timer / light gates.
parts.working: B1: short time → large percentage uncertainty from reaction time. B1: specific improvement: longer distance between marks, or video the fall with a stopwatch in view, or light gates.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the upper mark is placed well below the surface of the glycerol.
parts.answer: So that the sphere has reached terminal velocity before timing starts.
parts.working: B1: sphere must already be at constant (terminal) speed when it passes the first mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sphere falls through air with a drag force proportional to the square of its speed and reaches a terminal speed of 6.0 m s⁻¹. The sphere is replaced by one with the same size and shape but four times the mass. What is the new terminal speed?
A 3.0 m s⁻¹
B 6.0 m s⁻¹
C 12 m s⁻¹
D 24 m s⁻¹
parts.working: At terminal speed mg = kv². With the same k, v ∝ √m, so quadrupling m doubles v: 2 × 6.0 = 12 m s⁻¹. 24 m s⁻¹ would follow from a linear dependence on mass, which is not the case here; 3.0 m s⁻¹ inverts the relationship.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cyclist of total mass 90 kg rides on a level road. The air resistance is F = 0.25v², where F is in newtons and v in m s⁻¹. Calculate the air resistance when v = 10 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The cyclist pedals with a constant driving force of 40 N on the level road and reaches a steady speed. Calculate this steady speed.
parts.working: At a steady speed the driving force equals air resistance: 0.25v² = 40, so v = √160 = 12.6 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the power the cyclist must supply at this steady speed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ball is dropped from rest. The table gives its speed v at times t after release. t/s: 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0. v/m s⁻¹: 0.0, 6.0, 9.5, 11.0. Use the trapezium rule to estimate the distance fallen in the first 3.0 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the area under a speed–time graph represents.
parts.answer: The distance travelled (displacement for motion in one direction).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether the trapezium-rule estimate is an underestimate or an overestimate of the true distance.
parts.answer: The speed–time curve is concave downwards (the increase in speed each second gets smaller), so the straight chords lie below the curve: the estimate is an underestimate.
parts.working: 1 mark for the shape of the curve (slope decreasing); 1 mark for chords below curve, hence underestimate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A steel ball bearing is released from rest in a tall tube of glycerol. The table gives its speed v at time t. t/s: 0.00, 0.20, 0.40, 0.60, 0.80, 1.00. v/m s⁻¹: 0.00, 0.85, 1.36, 1.62, 1.75, 1.80. Estimate the acceleration between t = 0 and t = 0.20 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the terminal velocity from the data.
parts.working: The speed levels off at about 1.80 m s⁻¹ (the last two readings are almost equal).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the acceleration becomes very small at t = 0.80 s.
parts.answer: The drag force on the ball increases with its speed, so the resultant force decreases; the acceleration approaches zero as drag approaches weight minus upthrust.
parts.working: 1 mark for drag increasing with speed; 1 mark for resultant force and acceleration tending to zero.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small object of mass 0.25 kg falls through a fluid. The upthrust is 1.2 N and the drag force is 2.0v (in N, with v in m s⁻¹). Calculate its terminal velocity.
parts.working: At terminal velocity: mg = U + 2.0v, so 2.4525 − 1.2 = 2.0v and v = 0.63 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resultant force on the object when its speed is 0.30 m s⁻¹.
parts.working: Weight 2.4525 N down; upthrust 1.2 N up; drag 2.0 × 0.30 = 0.60 N up. Resultant = 2.4525 − 1.2 − 0.60 = 0.65 N down.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the object at this speed.

practice.stem: A spherical raindrop of radius 0.50 mm falls through still air. The density of water is 1000 kg m⁻³. The air resistance is kv², where v is the speed and k is a constant for this drop. The terminal speed of the drop is 4.0 m s⁻¹. Ignore upthrust.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the constant k.
parts.working: C1: m = (4/3)π(0.50 × 10⁻³)³ × 1000 = 5.24 × 10⁻⁷ kg. C1: at terminal velocity kv_t² = mg. A1: k = mg/4.0² = 3.21 × 10⁻⁷ kg m⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the drop when its speed is 2.0 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For drops of different radius r, k is proportional to r². Show that the terminal speed is proportional to √r, and calculate the terminal speed of a drop of radius 1.0 mm.
parts.working: M1: mg ∝ r³, so v_t² = mg/k ∝ r³/r² = r. M1: v_t ∝ √r. A1: v_t = 4.0 × √2 = 5.66 m s⁻¹.

practice.stem: A ball of mass 0.15 kg is thrown vertically upwards on a playing field in Peshawar. Air resistance acts on it at all times while it is moving. When it is moving upwards at 12 m s⁻¹ the air resistance is 0.60 N. When it is moving downwards at 8.0 m s⁻¹ the air resistance is 0.27 N.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the ball at the instant it is moving upwards at 12 m s⁻¹.
parts.working: C1: weight and drag both act downwards: F = 1.47 + 0.60 = 2.07 N. A1: a = 13.8 m s⁻² downwards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the ball at the instant it is moving downwards at 8.0 m s⁻¹.
parts.working: C1: drag now acts upwards: F = 1.47 − 0.27 = 1.20 N. A1: a = 8.01 m s⁻² downwards.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the acceleration of the ball at the top of its path.
parts.working: B1: speed is zero so drag is zero; a = g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the ball takes longer to fall back to the thrower than it took to rise.
parts.answer: Air resistance removes energy, so at each height the ball is slower on the way down; also the downward acceleration is less than g on the way down but greater than g on the way up.
parts.working: B1: work done against drag, so speed at any height lower on the way down. B1: same distance covered at lower average speed (acceleration < g down, > g up) → longer time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small object of mass 0.80 kg falls through a viscous fluid. The drag force is F = bv with b = 0.40 kg s⁻¹. Show that the terminal velocity is about 19.6 m s⁻¹.
parts.answer: At terminal velocity mg = bv, so v = mg/b = 0.80 × 9.81/0.40 = 19.62 m s⁻¹ ≈ 19.6 m s⁻¹.
parts.working: 1 mark for mg = bv at terminal velocity; 1 mark for substitution giving 19.6 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The speed of the object is given by v = v_T(1 − e^(−t/τ)), where τ = m/b. Show that τ = 2.0 s and calculate the speed at t = 2.0 s.
parts.working: 1 mark for τ = m/b = 2.0 s; 1 mark for the exponential form with e⁻¹; 1 mark for 12.4 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the acceleration of the object at t = 0 is equal to g.
parts.answer: At t = 0 the speed is zero, so there is no drag force; the only force is weight, giving acceleration g.
parts.working: Drag is proportional to v, which is zero at t = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A base-jumper of mass 80 kg falls with air resistance F = kv², where k = 0.25 kg m⁻¹. Show that the terminal velocity is about 56 m s⁻¹.
parts.answer: At terminal velocity mg = kv², so v = √(mg/k) = √(80 × 9.81/0.25) = 56.0 m s⁻¹ ≈ 56 m s⁻¹.
parts.working: 1 mark for mg = kv²; 1 mark for 56 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed at which the acceleration of the jumper is g/2 (about 4.9 m s⁻²) downwards.
parts.working: Acceleration a = g − kv²/m = g(1 − v²/v_T²). For a = g/2, v² = v_T²/2, so v = 56.0/√2 = 39.6 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A larger parachute increases k by a factor of 100. Estimate the new terminal velocity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car of mass 1200 kg coasts along a level road in neutral. It experiences a constant rolling resistance of 180 N and an air resistance of 0.45v² N (v in m s⁻¹). Calculate the total resistive force when v = 25 m s⁻¹.
parts.working: Air resistance = 0.45 × 25² = 281.25 N. Total = 180 + 281.25 = 461.25 N, about 461 N.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the deceleration of the car at 25 m s⁻¹.
parts.working: Deceleration = resultant force/m = 461.25/1200 = 0.384 m s⁻² (about 0.38 m s⁻²).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed at which the air resistance equals the rolling resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A book rests on a horizontal table. The weight of the book is one force of a Newton's third law pair. What is the other force of the pair?
A the normal contact force of the table on the book
B the normal contact force of the book on the table
C the gravitational force of the book on the Earth
D the gravitational force of the Earth on the table
parts.answer: C the gravitational force of the book on the Earth
parts.working: Third-law pairs act on different bodies and are the same type of force: the Earth pulls the book, so the book pulls the Earth (gravitational). A is equal and opposite to the weight but acts on the same body and is a different type of force.

practice.stem: A passenger of mass 62 kg stands in a lift in an office tower in Islamabad. The lift starts from rest and accelerates upwards at 1.5 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between mass and weight.
parts.answer: Mass is the property of a body that resists change in motion (quantity of matter), measured in kg; weight is the gravitational force on it, measured in N.
parts.working: B1: mass: property resisting changes in motion / amount of matter, scalar, kg. B1: weight: force due to a gravitational field on the mass (W = mg), vector, N.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the force exerted on the passenger by the floor of the lift.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the force exerted by the floor when the lift moves upwards at constant speed. Explain your answer.
parts.working: B1: 62 × 9.81 = 608 N. B1: constant velocity so resultant force zero (Newton's first law).

practice.stem: On a farm near Multan, a tractor of mass 3200 kg pulls a loaded trolley of mass 1800 kg along a straight level track using a light tow bar. The driving force on the tractor is 7500 N. Resistive forces of 900 N act on the tractor and 600 N act on the trolley.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the tractor and trolley.
parts.working: C1: resultant force on whole system = 7500 − 900 − 600 = 6000 N. A1: a = 6000/5000 = 1.20 m s⁻².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the tension in the tow bar.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the force exerted by the trolley on the tractor through the tow bar.
parts.working: B1: equal and opposite (Newton's third law): 2760 N towards the back.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg. On the Moon the gravitational field strength is 1.6 N kg⁻¹. What is the astronaut's weight on the Moon?
A 8.0 N
B 50 N
C 128 N
D 785 N
parts.working: Weight = mass × g = 80 × 1.6 = 128 N. Mass does not change between planets. 785 N is the weight on Earth (80 × 9.81); 50 N comes from dividing 80 by 1.6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the mass of an object and distinguish it from its weight.
parts.answer: Mass is the amount of matter in an object (a scalar, measured in kg); weight is the gravitational force on the object (a vector, measured in N, W = mg).
parts.working: 1 mark each for mass as amount of matter and weight as gravitational force.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A 0.60 kg mass hangs from a spring balance inside a model rocket that is accelerating vertically upwards at 15 m s⁻². Calculate the reading on the spring balance in newtons.
parts.working: Tension in the spring = m(g + a) = 0.60 × (9.81 + 15) = 14.89 N ≈ 14.9 N.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the reading would be if the rocket were at rest on the ground.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two blocks A (mass 3.0 kg) and B (mass 5.0 kg) lie on a smooth horizontal table. A horizontal force of 24 N pulls A, which is connected to B by a light string. Calculate the acceleration of the system.
parts.working: Total mass 8.0 kg; a = F/m = 24/8.0 = 3.0 m s⁻².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the tension in the string.
parts.working: Consider B only: T = m_B a = 5.0 × 3.0 = 15 N.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the tension is less than 24 N.
parts.answer: Part of the applied force is used to accelerate block A itself (the string transmits only the force needed to accelerate B), so the tension is less than the applied force.
parts.working: 1 mark for the force on A: F − T = m_A a; 1 mark for the conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the mass and the weight of a bag of rice.
parts.answer: Mass is the quantity of matter in the bag and does not change with location; weight is the gravitational force on it, which depends on the gravitational field strength.
parts.working: 1 mark for mass as the quantity of matter, unchanged by location; 1 mark for weight = mg, which depends on g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A bag of rice has mass 2.5 kg. Calculate its weight on Earth and on Mars, where the gravitational field strength is 3.7 N kg⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the mass of the bag on Mars.
parts.working: Mass does not change with location.

practice.stem: A block of mass 2.0 kg rests on a smooth horizontal bench. It is attached by a light inextensible string, passing over a frictionless pulley at the edge of the bench, to a block of mass 0.50 kg hanging freely. The system is released from rest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the blocks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the tension in the string.
parts.working: C1: T = 2.0 × a (only force on the block on the table). A1: T = 3.92 N (less than 4.9 N, the weight of the hanging block).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the block on the table to move 0.80 m from rest.

practice.stem: A box of mass 30 kg is released on a ramp inclined at 25° to the horizontal at a warehouse loading bay. A constant frictional force of 60 N acts up the ramp while the box slides down.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the component of the weight of the box acting down the ramp.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the box.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The box starts from rest. Calculate its speed after sliding 4.0 m down the ramp.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A rocket of mass 500 kg expels exhaust gas at a steady rate of 2.0 kg s⁻¹, with the gas leaving at 300 m s⁻¹ relative to the rocket. What is the thrust on the rocket?
A 0.0067 N
B 150 N
C 600 N
D 1.5 × 10⁵ N
parts.working: Thrust = rate of change of momentum of the exhaust = (mass per second) × (exhaust speed) = 2.0 × 300 = 600 N. 150 N comes from dividing 300 by 2.0 instead of multiplying; 0.0067 N is 2.0 ÷ 300; 1.5 × 10⁵ N multiplies the rocket mass by the exhaust speed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 12 kg crate is released from rest on a slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal. A friction force of 18 N acts up the slope. Calculate the component of the weight acting down the slope.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the crate down the slope.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the normal contact force on the crate is not equal to its weight, and calculate it.
parts.answer: N = mg cos30° = 12 × 9.81 × 0.866 = 102 N, which is less than the weight (118 N) because the weight has a component along the slope.
parts.working: 1 mark for the component of weight perpendicular to the slope being the normal force; 1 mark for the value 102 N.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A crane lifts a load of mass 1500 kg vertically upwards with an acceleration of 0.80 m s⁻². Calculate the tension in the cable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The load is then lowered at a constant velocity. Calculate the tension in the cable.
parts.working: At constant velocity the tension equals the weight: 1500 × 9.81 = 14715 N.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The load is now moving downwards and speeding up at 0.80 m s⁻². Calculate the tension in the cable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In free space an astronaut of mass 65 kg pushes a satellite of mass 120 kg with a force of 40 N. State the magnitude and direction of the force the satellite exerts on the astronaut.
parts.answer: 40 N, directed away from the satellite (opposite to the push on the satellite).
parts.working: Newton's third law: equal and opposite forces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the astronaut and of the satellite.
parts.answer: astronaut 0.62 m s⁻²; satellite 0.33 m s⁻²
parts.working: a = F/m: astronaut 40/65 = 0.62 m s⁻²; satellite 40/120 = 0.33 m s⁻².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two accelerations are different although the forces are equal.
parts.answer: The forces are equal and opposite, but the masses are different; acceleration is inversely proportional to mass (Newton's second law), so the lighter astronaut accelerates more.
parts.working: 1 mark for equal forces; 1 mark for a = F/m with different masses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A trolley of mass 0.90 kg is pulled along a horizontal bench by a string. The tension is 6.0 N at 20° above the horizontal. A friction force of 3.0 N opposes the motion. Calculate the horizontal component of the tension.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the trolley.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the normal contact force exerted by the bench on the trolley.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A drone of mass 1.2 kg hovers in still air by pushing air downwards. Calculate its weight.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rate of change of momentum of the air pushed downwards must equal the weight of the drone. The drone pushes air at a rate of 0.40 kg s⁻¹. State the rate of change of momentum of this air and explain why it must equal the weight.
parts.working: By Newton's second law the net force on the air equals its rate of change of momentum; by Newton's third law the air pushes the drone up with an equal force, which must balance its weight.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed at which the air must be pushed downwards.
parts.working: F = (mass per second) × v, so v = 11.77/0.40 = 29.4 m s⁻¹.

practice.stem:
A student stands on bathroom scales (which measure the normal contact force in newtons) in a lift. The lift starts from rest and makes one journey. The readings are:
stage 1 (at rest): 588 N
stage 2 (speeding up): 650 N
stage 3 (constant speed): 588 N
stage 4 (slowing down): 540 N
stage 5 (at rest): 588 N

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of the student.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration during stages 2 and 4.
parts.answer: stage 2: 1.03 m s⁻² upwards; stage 4: 0.801 m s⁻² downwards

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the readings show that the lift travelled upwards rather than downwards.
parts.answer: Starting from rest, the reading rose above the weight, so the acceleration while speeding up was upwards; speeding up from rest means the velocity is in the direction of the acceleration, i.e. upwards. In stage 4 the downward acceleration then slows this upward motion.
parts.working: B1: stage 2 reading > weight → upward resultant force/acceleration. B1: lift speeds up from rest, so velocity is in the same direction as this acceleration: upwards (a downward journey would have given a reading below 588 N at the start).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the reading on the scales if the lift were in free fall.

practice.stem: At a cement plant, sand falls vertically onto a horizontal conveyor belt at a steady rate of 15 kg s⁻¹. The belt moves at a constant speed of 2.0 m s⁻¹. The sand lands with no horizontal velocity and is quickly carried along at the speed of the belt.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use Newton's second law in terms of momentum to calculate the horizontal force the motor must apply to the belt to keep its speed constant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the power supplied by this force.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate at which the sand gains kinetic energy and explain why it differs from your answer to (b).
parts.answer: 30.0 W; the other half is transferred to thermal energy (and sound) by friction as the sand slips on the belt before reaching belt speed
parts.working: C1: ½ × 15 × 2.0² per second. A1: 30.0 W. B1: the remaining 30.0 W is dissipated as heat/internal energy by friction while sand slides relative to the belt.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 4.0 kg block rests on a smooth slope inclined at 30°. A light string passes over a smooth pulley at the top of the slope and holds a 2.5 kg mass hanging freely. The system is released from rest. Calculate the acceleration of the system.
parts.working: For the whole system: (m_hang g − m_block g sin30°) = (m_block + m_hang) a, so a = (24.53 − 19.62)/6.5 = 0.75 m s⁻².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the tension in the string.
parts.working: For the hanging mass: m_hang(g − a) = 2.5 × (9.81 − 0.755) = 22.6 N.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the tension is less than the weight of the hanging mass.
parts.answer: The hanging mass accelerates downwards, so the net downward force on it is its weight minus the tension, which must be positive.
parts.working: 1 mark: the hanging mass has a resultant downwards force, so T < mg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 3.0 kg object lies on a smooth horizontal surface. Two horizontal forces act on it: 12 N due east and 9.0 N due north. Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration.
parts.working: Resultant force = √(12² + 9²) = 15 N, so a = 15/3.0 = 5.0 m s⁻².

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction of the acceleration, as an angle measured from east.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The object starts from rest. Calculate its speed after 4.0 s.
parts.working: v = u + at = 0 + 5.0 × 4.0 = 20 m s⁻¹ (in the same direction).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A block rests on a rough slope. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the slope is 0.40. Calculate the angle of the slope at which the block just starts to slide.
parts.working: At the point of slipping mg sinθ = μ_s mg cosθ, so tanθ = 0.40 and θ = 21.8°.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The slope is now set at 25° and the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.30. The block slides down the slope from rest. Calculate its acceleration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.
parts.answer: The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is proportional to (equal to) the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage.
parts.working: M1: induced e.m.f. ∝ / = rate of change of A1: magnetic flux linkage (not just 'flux').

parts.label: b
parts.text: State Lenz's law.
parts.answer: The direction of the induced e.m.f. is such that it tends to produce effects (a current) that oppose the change producing it.
parts.working: M1: direction of induced e.m.f./current. A1: opposes the change (in flux linkage) that causes it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how Lenz's law is a consequence of the principle of conservation of energy.
parts.answer: Because the induced current opposes the change, work must be done (e.g. pushing a magnet against a repulsive force) to produce it; this work is the source of the electrical energy. If it aided the change, energy would be created from nothing.
parts.working: B1: work has to be done against the opposing force. B1: this work becomes the electrical energy; otherwise energy would be created.

practice.stem: A flat coil of 200 turns and area 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is placed with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.15 T.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnetic flux linkage of the coil.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The coil is pulled out of the field in 0.050 s. Calculate the average e.m.f. induced.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the unit of magnetic flux in SI base units.
parts.working: B1: Wb = T m² = (kg s⁻² A⁻¹)(m²).

practice.stem: A bar magnet is dropped vertically, north pole first, through the centre of a fixed coil connected to a data logger that records the induced e.m.f.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the e.m.f. varies with time as the magnet falls through the coil.
parts.answer: A pulse of e.m.f. as the magnet enters, falling to zero when it is at the centre, then a pulse of opposite sign as it leaves; the second pulse has a larger peak and a shorter duration.
parts.working: B1: e.m.f. as the magnet enters, (near) zero in the middle. B1: opposite polarity as it leaves. B1: second peak larger and narrower (magnet moving faster).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the second pulse has a larger peak value.
parts.answer: The magnet is accelerating, so it moves faster as it leaves; the flux linkage changes at a greater rate, so by Faraday's law the e.m.f. is larger.
parts.working: B1: greater speed when leaving. B1: greater rate of change of flux linkage → larger e.m.f.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The coil is connected to a resistor. Explain why the magnet then has a slightly smaller acceleration than g while it is near the coil.
parts.answer: An induced current flows; by Lenz's law it creates a magnetic field that opposes the motion of the magnet (repels it on entry, attracts it on exit), so there is an upward force on the magnet.
parts.working: B1: induced current produces magnetic field. B1: force on magnet opposes its motion (upward force).

practice.stem: A passenger aircraft with a wingspan of 35 m flies horizontally at 240 m s⁻¹ over northern Pakistan, where the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic flux density is 4.5 × 10⁻⁵ T.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the e.m.f. induced between the wing tips.
parts.working: C1: E = BLv (wings cut the vertical component of the field). A1: E = 4.5 × 10⁻⁵ × 35 × 240 = 0.378 V.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this e.m.f. cannot be used to light a lamp on board by connecting wires between the wing tips.
parts.answer: The connecting wires inside the aircraft move through the same field at the same velocity, so an equal e.m.f. is induced in them, cancelling the e.m.f. around the circuit; no current flows.
parts.working: B1: the wires also cut the field / have an equal e.m.f. induced. B1: e.m.f.s cancel around the circuit, so no net e.m.f./current.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A coil of 200 turns is placed in a magnetic field. The magnetic flux through each turn changes from 0.50 mWb to 0.10 mWb in 0.20 s. Calculate the average e.m.f. induced in the coil.
parts.working: 1 mark for ε = NΔΦ/Δt with ΔΦ = 0.40 mWb; 1 mark for 0.40 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards a closed coil. Explain the direction of the induced current in the coil.
parts.answer: The induced current flows in the direction that produces a magnetic field opposing the increase in flux linkage (Lenz's law). The face of the coil nearer the magnet becomes a north pole, repelling the approaching magnet.
parts.working: 1 mark for Lenz's law (induced effect opposes the change); 1 mark for the induced field opposing the approach of the north pole; 1 mark for the resulting direction of current (as seen from the magnet).

practice.stem: A rectangular coil of 150 turns measures 5.0 cm × 3.0 cm. It lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.080 T. The coil is rotated through 90° in 0.12 s so that its plane becomes parallel to the field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in magnetic flux linkage of the coil.
parts.working: C1: initial NBA = 150 × 0.080 × (0.050 × 0.030); final zero (plane parallel to B). A1: change = 0.0180 Wb.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average e.m.f. induced.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The coil is then rotated through a further 90° in the same direction in the same time. State and explain the average e.m.f. during this rotation.
parts.answer: 0.150 V again, with the same polarity: the flux linkage changes from zero to NBA through the opposite face, a change of the same magnitude and sign in the same time.
parts.working: B1: same magnitude (0.15 V). B1: change of flux linkage has the same magnitude (0 → NBA through the opposite face) in the same time.

practice.stem:
A small coil of 500 turns and area 2.0 cm² is placed inside an electromagnet with its plane perpendicular to the field. The flux density B changes as follows:
stage 1: B increases uniformly from 0 to 0.30 T in 0.20 s
stage 2: B stays at 0.30 T for 0.30 s
stage 3: B decreases uniformly from 0.30 T to 0 in 0.10 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the e.m.f. induced in the coil during each of the three stages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain how the polarity of the e.m.f. in stage 3 compares with that in stage 1.
parts.answer: Opposite: in stage 1 the flux linkage increases, in stage 3 it decreases, so the induced e.m.f. (opposing the change, Lenz's law) is reversed.
parts.working: B1: opposite polarity. B1: flux increasing in one stage, decreasing in the other.

practice.stem: A flat aluminium plate hangs from a pivot as a pendulum. It swings through the gap between the poles of a strong permanent magnet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the oscillations of the aluminium plate die away quickly when it swings between the poles of the magnet.
parts.answer: As the plate moves through the field, the flux through parts of it changes, inducing e.m.f.s and hence eddy currents in the plate; by Lenz's law these currents produce forces that oppose the motion; the plate's kinetic energy is converted to thermal energy in the plate.
parts.working: B1: changing flux / plate cuts field lines → e.m.f. induced, eddy currents flow. B1: forces on currents oppose the motion (Lenz). B1: kinetic energy → thermal energy (I²R heating).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Several narrow slots are cut into the plate. Explain why the plate now swings for much longer.
parts.answer: The slots break up the paths for the eddy currents, so the currents (and the opposing forces) are much smaller, and less energy is dissipated each swing.
parts.working: B1: slots increase resistance / reduce eddy current loops. B1: smaller opposing force / less energy dissipated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one practical use of this effect.
parts.answer: Magnetic braking (e.g. in trains or roller-coasters) or damping the needle of a meter/balance.
parts.working: B1: any valid application, e.g. eddy-current brakes, damping a balance.

practice.stem: A metal rod of length 0.25 m slides at a constant speed of 3.0 m s⁻¹ along two horizontal parallel rails that are 0.25 m apart. The rails are joined at one end by a resistor; the total resistance of the circuit is 1.5 Ω. A uniform vertical magnetic field of flux density 0.60 T acts over the whole region.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the e.m.f. induced in the rod and the current in the circuit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the force on the rod due to the current and state its direction.
parts.answer: 0.0450 N, opposite to the direction of motion
parts.working: C1: F = BIL = 0.60 × 0.300 × 0.25. A1: 0.0450 N, opposing the motion (Lenz's law).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the mechanical power needed to keep the rod moving at constant speed equals the electrical power dissipated in the resistor.
parts.working: M1: mechanical power = Fv = 0.135 W. A1: electrical power = I²R (or EI) = 0.135 W, equal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rectangular coil of 80 turns and area 5.0 × 10⁻³ m² rotates at a constant angular speed of 50 rad s⁻¹ in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.25 T. Calculate the peak e.m.f. induced in the coil.
parts.working: 1 mark for ε₀ = NBAω; 1 mark for 5.0 V.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum flux linkage of the coil.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the flux linkage when the induced e.m.f. is at its peak, and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Zero. The rate of change of flux linkage is greatest when the flux linkage is zero (coil plane parallel to field), so the induced e.m.f. is greatest then.
parts.working: 1 mark for zero flux linkage; 1 mark for the rate of change of flux linkage (dΦ/dt) being maximum at that instant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An aluminium ring is placed over the iron core of a solenoid carrying an alternating current. The ring is pushed upwards and jumps off the core. Explain this observation using Faraday's and Lenz's laws.
parts.answer: The alternating current in the solenoid produces a changing flux through the ring, inducing an e.m.f. and a current in the ring. By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the change, so the ring's field repels the solenoid's field and the ring is pushed upwards.
parts.working: 1 mark for a changing flux inducing an e.m.f. and current in the ring; 1 mark for the induced current opposing the change (Lenz); 1 mark for the repulsion that pushes the ring upwards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A coil of 30 turns and area 12 cm² is placed with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. The flux density increases uniformly from 0 to 0.80 T in 4.0 ms. Calculate the e.m.f. induced in the coil.
parts.working: 1 mark for the area in m² and the change in flux; 1 mark for 7.2 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A coil has a total resistance of 2.5 Ω. An induced e.m.f. of 0.40 V is produced in it. Calculate the current in the coil and the power dissipated in the coil.
parts.working: 1 mark for I = ε/R; 1 mark for P = I²R or P = εI; 1 mark for 0.064 W.

practice.stem: A long solenoid has 2000 turns per metre. A small coil of 50 turns and cross-sectional area 3.0 cm² is placed inside the solenoid near its centre, with its plane perpendicular to the solenoid's axis. The current in the solenoid increases uniformly from 0 to 4.0 A in 25 ms. µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H m⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in magnetic flux density inside the solenoid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average e.m.f. induced in the small coil.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The current in the solenoid is now an alternating current. Explain why an alternating e.m.f. is induced in the small coil, and state when the induced e.m.f. is a maximum.
parts.answer: The alternating current produces a continually changing flux in the solenoid, so the flux linkage of the small coil keeps changing and an e.m.f. is induced that reverses as the rate of change reverses; the e.m.f. is greatest when the current is changing fastest, i.e. when the current is zero.
parts.working: B1: changing current → changing flux linkage in small coil. B1: e.m.f. ∝ rate of change, which alternates in sign. B1: maximum when current (flux) is zero / changing most rapidly.

practice.stem: A coil rotates at a steady rate in a uniform magnetic field. Its magnetic flux linkage NΦ varies with time t as a cosine curve: NΦ = 0.050 Wb at t = 0, falling to zero at t = 5.0 ms, reaching −0.050 Wb at t = 10 ms and returning to 0.050 Wb at t = 20 ms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the times during the first period at which the induced e.m.f. is zero, and explain your answer.
parts.working: B1: when flux linkage is a maximum (positive or negative). B1: gradient of the NΦ–t graph is zero there, so rate of change is zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the maximum e.m.f. is about 16 V.
parts.working: M1: NΦ = 0.050 cos(2πft); maximum gradient = 0.050 × 2πf. A1: 0.050 × 2π × 50 = 15.7 V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The speed of rotation is doubled. State the new maximum e.m.f. and the new period.
parts.working: B1: e.m.f. doubles to 31 V (both frequency and rate of change double). B1: period halves to 10 ms.

practice.stem: A student investigates electromagnetic induction. A small cylindrical magnet falls vertically through the centre of a coil. It is suggested that the maximum e.m.f. E₀ induced in the coil is directly proportional to the speed v of the magnet as it passes through the coil.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Design a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between E₀ and v. You should draw a diagram (describe it in words here), showing the arrangement of your equipment. In your account you should pay particular attention to:
• the procedure to be followed
• the measurements to be taken
• the control of variables
• the analysis of the data
• any safety precautions to be taken.
parts.answer: Drop the magnet from different measured heights h through a fixed coil connected to a data logger/oscilloscope; v = √(2gh) at the coil; record peak e.m.f. E₀; plot E₀ against √h (or v); a straight line through the origin confirms E₀ ∝ v.
parts.working:
Defining the problem (3): B1 v (or drop height h) is the independent variable; B1 E₀ is the dependent variable; B1 keep the same magnet, same coil (number of turns, area), magnet orientation and path through the coil constant.
Methods of data collection (5): B1 workable arrangement: vertical clear tube through the centre of a coil clamped in a stand, coil connected to a data logger or oscilloscope (not an ammeter); B1 measure h from the bottom of the magnet to the centre of the coil with a metre rule; B1 v found from v = √(2gh) or measured with a light gate just above the coil (length of magnet ÷ time); B1 record E₀ from the peak of the trace (data logger with high sampling rate / oscilloscope with suitable time-base, single sweep); B1 release from rest, magnet falling through the centre without touching (guide tube).
Method of analysis (2): B1 plot E₀ against v (or √h); B1 relationship valid if straight line through the origin.
Safety (1): B1 a soft cushion/sand tray to catch the magnet so it does not shatter or fly off; keep magnet away from feet.
Additional detail (4): any four, e.g. use a tube made of plastic (not metal, to avoid eddy currents); repeat each height and average the peak values; use a large range of heights (e.g. 0.10–1.00 m); use a coil with many turns / strong magnet to give a measurable e.m.f.; use the first peak (entering) consistently; check the trace is a single clean pulse; account for magnet length when measuring h; use the second (exit) peak with h measured to the coil's lower face.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A magnetic flux Φ = Φ₀ sin ωt passes through a 100-turn coil, with Φ₀ = 4.0 mWb and a period of 0.040 s. Show that the peak induced e.m.f. is about 63 V.
parts.working: 1 mark for differentiating to obtain NΦ₀ω; 1 mark for ω = 2π/T and the value 63 V.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the instantaneous e.m.f. at t = 0.005 s.
parts.working: 1 mark for the cosine form ε = ε₀ cos ωt; 1 mark for 44 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A straight conductor of length L moves at constant speed v perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B, with its ends in contact with a closed circuit. Show that the e.m.f. induced is ε = BLv.
parts.answer: In time t the conductor sweeps area Lvt, so the flux change is ΔΦ = BLvt. ε = ΔΦ/Δt = BLv.
parts.working: 1 mark for the area swept in time t being Lvt; 1 mark for ΔΦ = BLvt; 1 mark for ε = ΔΦ/Δt = BLv.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The conductor is 0.25 m long and moves at 1.5 m s⁻¹ in a field of 0.40 T, at 60° to the plane of its motion. Calculate the induced e.m.f.
parts.working: 1 mark for using the perpendicular component of B (or of v); 1 mark for 0.13 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an experiment to test whether the e.m.f. induced in a coil depends on the rate at which the magnet moves through it. State the apparatus, the variables, how you would control them, and how you would analyse your results.
parts.answer: Use a coil connected to a data logger or voltmeter, and a bar magnet dropped or pushed through at different speeds; measure the peak e.m.f. for each speed. Keep the magnet, coil and number of turns the same; vary speed only. Plot peak e.m.f. against speed; a straight line through the origin shows proportionality.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: independent variable (speed of the magnet); dependent variable (peak e.m.f.); controlled variables (magnet, coil, turns, orientation); apparatus (coil, voltage sensor/datalogger); repeats and a valid method of varying speed; analysis by graph of e.m.f. against speed.

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)
practice.stem: An electron moving at 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ enters a uniform magnetic field of flux density 2.5 mT at right angles to the field. Mass of electron = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the force on the electron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the radius of the electron's circular path.

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)
practice.stem: A proton enters a uniform magnetic field with its velocity perpendicular to the field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the path of the proton is a circle.
parts.answer: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does not change the speed; with constant speed and constant B the force has constant magnitude; a constant-magnitude force always perpendicular to the velocity provides a centripetal force, giving circular motion.
parts.working: B1: force perpendicular to velocity (and to field). B1: speed (and so force magnitude) constant. B1: provides the centripetal force → circle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain whether the magnetic field does work on the proton.
parts.answer: No: the force is perpendicular to the direction of motion, so there is no displacement in the direction of the force and the kinetic energy is unchanged.
parts.working: B1: no work done. B1: force ⟂ displacement / KE constant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect on the radius of the path if the speed of the proton were doubled.

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)
practice.stem: A Hall probe contains a thin slice of semiconductor 0.20 mm thick carrying a current of 40 mA. The number density of charge carriers is 2.5 × 10²² m⁻³, and each carrier has charge 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. The probe is placed in a magnetic field of flux density 0.25 T, oriented to give the maximum Hall voltage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Hall voltage across the slice.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the slice should be orientated to obtain the maximum Hall voltage.
parts.answer: With its flat face perpendicular to the magnetic field.
parts.working: B1: plane (face) of the slice normal to B (current at right angles to B).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two changes to the probe that would increase the Hall voltage for the same field.
parts.answer: Increase the current; use a thinner slice (or a material with a lower number density of charge carriers).
parts.working: B1 each for any two: larger I, smaller thickness t, smaller n (different semiconductor).

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A proton travelling at 3.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ enters a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.50 T at right angles to the field. Calculate the magnetic force on the proton.
parts.working: 1 mark for F = Bqv; 1 mark for 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ N.

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the magnetic force on a charged particle does no work on the particle, so that its kinetic energy remains constant.
parts.answer: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it has no component along the displacement and does no work. Its speed (and kinetic energy) therefore stays the same.
parts.working: 1 mark for force perpendicular to velocity (no component along displacement); 1 mark for speed and kinetic energy unchanged.

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron moves horizontally towards the north. The magnetic flux density is horizontal and points towards the east. Determine the direction of the magnetic force on the electron.
parts.answer: Vertically upwards. (For a positive charge moving north in a field pointing east, the force would be downwards; the electron, being negative, experiences a force upwards.)
parts.working: 1 mark for the force being perpendicular to both v and B; 1 mark for vertically upwards (reversed because the charge is negative).

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)
practice.stem: A velocity selector consists of two parallel metal plates 12 mm apart with a p.d. of 600 V between them. A uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.020 T acts perpendicular to both the electric field and the ion beam.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength between the plates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the ions that pass through undeflected have speed v = E/B, and calculate this speed.
parts.working: M1: undeflected when electric force = magnetic force: qE = Bqv. M1: q cancels, v = E/B. A1: v = 50000/0.020 = 2.50 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain what happens to an ion of the same charge moving faster than this speed.
parts.answer: It is deflected in the direction of the magnetic force, because Bqv now exceeds qE (the electric force does not depend on speed).
parts.working: B1: deflected towards the side of the magnetic force. B1: magnetic force increases with v, electric force does not.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the selected speed does not depend on the mass or charge of the ions.
parts.answer: Both forces are proportional to q, which cancels; neither force depends on mass (no acceleration if balanced).
parts.working: B1: q cancels and mass does not appear in qE = Bqv.

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)
practice.stem: In a mass spectrometer, singly charged neon ions all with speed 4.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ enter a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.30 T at right angles to the field. Neon-20 ions have mass 20u and neon-22 ions have mass 22u, where u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the radius of the path of each type of ion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The ions travel through a semicircle before hitting a detector plate. Calculate the separation of the two points where they land.
parts.working: C1: separation = difference in diameters = 2(r₂₂ − r₂₀). A1: 5.53 cm.

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)
practice.stem: A copper strip 0.10 mm thick carries a current of 3.0 A in a magnetic field of 0.50 T perpendicular to its face. The number density of free electrons in copper is 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Hall voltage across the copper strip.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A strip of an unknown material with the same thickness, carrying the same current in the same field, gives a Hall voltage of 12 mV. Calculate the number density of charge carriers in this material, assuming each carries charge e.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest whether the unknown material is a metal or a semiconductor.
parts.answer: A semiconductor — its carrier density is far smaller than that of a metal.

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)
practice.stem: A proton (mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the time for one complete orbit is T = 2πm/(Bq), and that it does not depend on the speed of the proton.
parts.answer: T = 2πr/v with r = mv/(Bq), so T = 2πm/(Bq)
parts.working: M1: Bqv = mv²/r → r = mv/(Bq). M1: T = 2πr/v. A1: T = 2πm/(Bq): v cancels, so T is independent of speed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the period and the frequency of the orbit for a proton in a field of 0.50 T.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this result allows an alternating voltage of fixed frequency to keep accelerating protons in a cyclotron as their orbits grow larger.
parts.answer: Faster protons move in larger circles but take the same time per orbit, so they always arrive at the accelerating gap in step with the fixed-frequency voltage.
parts.working: B1: time per half-orbit constant as speed and radius increase.

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron of mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a uniform field of flux density 0.010 T. Calculate the radius of its circular path.
parts.working: 1 mark for r = mv/(Bq); 1 mark for 1.14 × 10⁻³ m.

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)

parts.label: a
parts.text: An α-particle (mass 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge +2e) moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.25 T. Show that the period of its orbit is about 5.2 × 10⁻⁷ s, and explain why the period does not depend on its speed.
parts.answer: T = 2πr/v = 2πm/(Bq) = 2π × 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷/(0.25 × 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 5.2 × 10⁻⁷ s. The speed cancels because the radius is proportional to the speed, so the circumference and speed are both proportional to v.
parts.working: 1 mark for T = 2πr/v; 1 mark for substituting r = mv/(Bq) to get T = 2πm/(Bq); 1 mark for explaining that v cancels (r ∝ v so the orbit length ∝ v).

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)

parts.label: a
parts.text: An α-particle and a proton have the same speed and enter the same uniform magnetic field perpendicular to it. The mass of the α-particle is 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, the mass of the proton is 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, and the α-particle has charge +2e. Calculate the ratio r_α/r_p of their radii of path.
parts.working: 1 mark for r = mv/(qB) and the same v and B; 1 mark for the charge ratio of 2 in the denominator; 1 mark for 2.0.

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A proton moves in a circular path of radius 0.50 m in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T, with its velocity perpendicular to the field. Calculate the kinetic energy of the proton. (Mass of proton = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)
parts.working: 1 mark for v = Bqr/m; 1 mark for Ek = (Bqr)²/(2m); 1 mark for 7.66 × 10⁻¹⁴ J.

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A beam of electrons travelling at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force on each electron is 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. Calculate the flux density of the field.
parts.working: 1 mark for B = F/(qv); 1 mark for 0.10 T.

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)
practice.stem: Electrons are accelerated from rest through a potential difference V and then enter a uniform magnetic field of flux density B at right angles to the field. They move in a circle of radius r.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the specific charge of the electron is given by e/m = 2V/(B²r²).
parts.working: M1: eV = ½mv² → v² = 2eV/m. M1: Bev = mv²/r → v = Ber/m. A1: square and equate: B²e²r²/m² = 2eV/m → e/m = 2V/(B²r²).

parts.label: b
parts.text: In an experiment, V = 250 V, B = 1.8 mT and the measured radius is 2.96 cm. Calculate e/m.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The radius is measured with an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm and B with an uncertainty of ±1%. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in e/m (ignore the uncertainty in V).

practice.subtopic: Force on a moving charge (Hall effect, velocity selection)
