parts.label: a
parts.text:
The count rate from a radioactive source is not reduced at all by a sheet of paper but falls to background level after 3 mm of aluminium. Which radiation is emitted by the source?
A α-particles only
B β⁻ particles only
C γ-rays only
D a mixture of α-particles and γ-rays
parts.working: Paper stops α-particles, so the source emits no α. Aluminium of about 3 mm stops β particles, but γ-rays would not be reduced to background by this thickness. A and D are excluded by the paper result; C would not fall to background after 3 mm of aluminium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Thorium-232 (²³²₉₀Th) emits one α-particle. Identify the nuclide formed.
parts.working: 1 mark for the nucleon and proton numbers of the nuclide after α decay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The nuclide from (a) then emits two β⁻ particles in succession. Identify the final nuclide, giving its nucleon number and proton number.
parts.answer: Each β⁻ decay keeps the nucleon number and raises the proton number by 1. Final: ²²⁸₉₀Th (nucleon number 228, proton number 90)
parts.working: 1 mark for the proton number rising by 2 (88 → 90); 1 mark for the final nuclide ²²⁸₉₀Th.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Radon-222 (²²²₈₆Rn) emits an α-particle to form nuclide X. X then emits an α-particle to form nuclide Y. Identify X and Y, giving their nucleon and proton numbers.
parts.working: 1 mark for X with its nucleon and proton numbers; 1 mark for Y with its nucleon and proton numbers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Y then emits a β⁻ particle to form nuclide Z. Identify Z, giving its nucleon and proton numbers.
parts.answer: Z: ²¹⁴₈₃Bi (nucleon number unchanged at 214; proton number 82 + 1 = 83)
parts.working: 1 mark for the nucleon number staying 214; 1 mark for the proton number 83.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the charge on a strange antiquark (s̄)?
A −⅓e
B +⅓e
C −⅔e
D +⅔e
parts.working: The strange quark has charge −⅓e; its antiquark has the opposite charge, +⅓e. −⅓e is the strange quark itself.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a fundamental particle.
parts.answer: A particle that is not made of any smaller particles (has no internal structure).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the quark composition of (i) a proton, (ii) a neutron. Use the quark charges to show that each has the correct charge.
parts.answer: (i) uud: +⅔ + ⅔ − ⅓ = +1 (ii) udd: +⅔ − ⅓ − ⅓ = 0
parts.working: B1 uud; B1 charge sum shown = +e; B1 udd; B1 charge sum shown = 0

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two particles in the atom that are fundamental particles.
parts.answer: the electron and the quarks (up and down)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hadrons are divided into two groups. Name the groups and state the quark structure of each.
parts.answer: Baryons: three quarks (or three antiquarks). Mesons: one quark and one antiquark.
parts.working: B1 baryon – three quarks; B1 meson – quark + antiquark

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Classify each particle as a baryon, a meson or a lepton:
proton, π⁻ (d ū), electron, neutron, K⁺ (u s̄), electron neutrino.
parts.answer: baryons: proton, neutron; mesons: π⁻, K⁺; leptons: electron, electron neutrino

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two properties that are the same and one property that is different for an electron and a positron.
parts.answer: Same: mass (and magnitude of charge, spin); different: sign of charge (−e and +e).
parts.working: B1 same mass and same magnitude of charge; B1 opposite charge

parts.label: b
parts.text: An antiparticle has the quark composition ū d̄ d̄. Determine its charge and name the particle of which it is the antiparticle.
parts.answer: charge 0; it is the antineutron (antiparticle of the neutron, udd)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the antiparticle produced in β⁻ decay.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two leptons.
parts.answer: electron and electron neutrino (also positron, antineutrino)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two differences between leptons and hadrons.
parts.answer: Leptons are fundamental (not made of quarks); hadrons are made of quarks. Hadrons are affected by the strong force; leptons are not.
parts.working: B1 leptons fundamental / hadrons made of quarks; B1 strong force acts on hadrons, not leptons

parts.label: c
parts.text: A proton and an electron have charges of equal magnitude. State why the proton is not a fundamental particle but the electron is.
parts.answer: The proton is made of three quarks (uud); the electron is not made of smaller particles.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which particle is a meson?
A neutron (udd)
B electron
C π⁺ meson (u d̄)
D electron neutrino
parts.working: A meson is a quark–antiquark pair. The π⁺ is u d̄. A neutron is a baryon with three quarks; the electron and the electron neutrino are leptons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Ξ⁻ baryon has the quark composition dss. Determine its charge in terms of e.
parts.working: 1 mark for using −1/3 e for each d and s quark; 1 mark for −e.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the Ξ⁻ is a baryon or a meson, and give the reason.
parts.working: 1 mark for baryon with a reason (three quarks).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between a muon and a π⁺ meson.
parts.answer: A muon is a lepton with no quarks; a π⁺ is a meson made of a quark and an antiquark (u d̄). A muon has a lepton number but a π⁺ has none. A muon is not affected by the strong interaction, but a pion is.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct difference (any two of: lepton/meson; no quarks/made of quarks; lepton number; strong interaction).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a neutron is not considered to be a fundamental particle.
parts.answer: A neutron is made of three quarks (udd), so it has internal structure. Fundamental particles, such as quarks and leptons, have no known substructure.
parts.working: 1 mark for a neutron being made of quarks (a baryon); 1 mark for fundamental particles having no substructure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student claims that a particle with quark composition u d s has a charge of +e. Decide whether the claim is correct, showing your working.
parts.answer: Incorrect. Charge = (+2/3) + (−1/3) + (−1/3) = 0. This is the neutral Λ⁰ baryon.
parts.working: 1 mark for adding the quark charges (+2/3, −1/3, −1/3); 1 mark for the total of zero and the conclusion that the claim is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which quark combination could be a baryon with a charge of −e?
A d d s
B ū d
C u u s
D d s̄
parts.working: A baryon has three quarks: d d s gives −⅓ −⅓ −⅓ = −1. ū d has charge −1 but is a quark–antiquark pair (a meson); u u s has charge +1; d s̄ is a neutral meson.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the β⁻ decay of a free neutron, including all the particles produced.
parts.working: B1 proton and electron; B1 electron antineutrino

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the change in quark composition that takes place, and show that charge is conserved in this quark change.
parts.working: B1 udd → uud; B1 a down quark changes to an up quark; B1 charge check −⅓ = ⅔ − 1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of interaction responsible for β decay.

practice.stem: Some baryons contain strange quarks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Σ⁺ baryon has the quark composition u u s. Determine its charge in terms of e.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the quark composition and the charge of the antiparticle of the Σ⁺.
parts.working: B1 ū ū s̄; B1 −⅔ − ⅔ + ⅓ = −1

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Ξ⁰ baryon has zero charge and contains two strange quarks. Deduce its quark composition.
parts.working: M1 two s quarks give −⅔, so the third quark must have charge +⅔; A1 u s s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carbon-11, ¹¹₆C, used in PET scanners, decays by β⁺ emission to an isotope of boron (B). Write the nuclear equation, including all particles.
parts.working: B1 ¹¹₅B; B1 positron and electron neutrino

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the change in quark flavour that occurs.
parts.answer: an up quark changes to a down quark (u → d)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify which of the particles produced in (a) are leptons and which is an antiparticle.
parts.answer: Leptons: positron and neutrino; the positron is an antiparticle (of the electron).
parts.working: B1 positron and neutrino are leptons; B1 positron is the antiparticle

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the K⁰ meson, with quark composition d s̄, has zero charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the quark composition of the antiparticle of the K⁰.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a neutral particle such as the K⁰ can have an antiparticle that is a different particle from itself.
parts.answer: Its antiparticle is made of the antiquarks of its quarks (s d̄ instead of d s̄); the quark content is different even though both charges are zero.
parts.working: B1 antiparticle has each quark replaced by its antiquark; B1 d s̄ ≠ s d̄, so they are different particles

parts.label: d
parts.text: State whether the K⁰ is a hadron or a lepton, and give a reason.
parts.answer: A hadron (a meson), because it is made of quarks.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The K⁺ meson has quark composition u s̄. What is its charge?
A 0
B +e
C +2e
D −e
parts.working: Charge of u = +2/3 e and charge of s̄ = +1/3 e, so the total is +1e. A would be the answer for a neutral meson such as u ū; C adds two units; D has the wrong sign.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An antiproton has the quark composition ū ū d̄. Determine its charge in terms of e.
parts.working: 1 mark for the charges −2/3 e (ū) and +1/3 e (d̄); 1 mark for −e.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the baryon number of an antiproton.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A muon μ⁻ decays into an electron, an electron antineutrino and a muon neutrino: μ⁻ → e⁻ + ν̄ₑ + ν_μ. Show that charge is conserved.
parts.working: 1 mark for showing the charges on each side are equal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the electron lepton number is conserved in this decay.
parts.working: 1 mark for the left-hand total of 0; 1 mark for the right-hand total of +1 − 1 = 0.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the muon lepton number is conserved.
parts.working: 1 mark for the muon-type lepton number +1 on both sides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A π⁻ meson has quark composition d ū. Determine its charge in terms of e.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The π⁻ decays to a muon μ⁻ and an antineutrino ν̄_μ: π⁻ → μ⁻ + ν̄_μ. Show that charge is conserved and state the lepton number of each product.
parts.answer: Charge: −1 on the left, −1 + 0 on the right. The μ⁻ has muon lepton number +1 and the ν̄_μ has −1.
parts.working: 1 mark for the charge check; 1 mark for the two muon-type lepton numbers (+1 and −1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation for the decay of an antineutron (n̄) into an antiproton (p̄), including all the particles produced. This is the antimatter counterpart of the β⁻ decay of a neutron.
parts.working: 1 mark for p̄ + e⁺; 1 mark for the electron neutrino νₑ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the lepton number of the electron family is conserved in this decay.
parts.working: 1 mark for the zero total on each side.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the baryon number of the Σ⁻ baryon, of the neutron and of the π⁻ meson.
parts.working: 1 mark: baryons (three quarks) have baryon number +1, mesons have 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Σ⁻ baryon has quark composition dds. Show that charge is conserved in the decay Σ⁻ → n + π⁻, given that the neutron has zero charge.
parts.answer: Charge of Σ⁻ = 3 × (−1/3) = −1 e. Right: 0 (neutron) + (−1) (π⁻) = −1 e, so charge is conserved.
parts.working: 1 mark for the Σ⁻ charge from its quarks; 1 mark for the right-hand total equal to −1 e.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A proton in a nucleus changes into a neutron by β⁺ decay. Which describes the change at quark level and the leptons emitted?
A u → d + e⁺ + ν
B u → d + e⁺ + ν̄
C d → u + e⁺ + ν
D d → u + e⁻ + ν̄
parts.working: Proton uud → neutron udd, so an up quark becomes a down quark; charge +⅔ = −⅓ + 1 needs a positron, and β⁺ decay emits an electron neutrino (not an antineutrino). D is β⁻ decay.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Δ⁺⁺ baryon contains three quarks, all of the same flavour. Determine its quark composition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why no meson can have a charge of +2e.
parts.answer: A meson is one quark and one antiquark; the largest possible charge is +⅔ + ⅓ = +1 (e.g. u d̄), so +2e is impossible.
parts.working: B1 meson = quark + antiquark; B1 maximum charge +⅔ (quark) + ⅓ (antiquark) = +1

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the possible charges, in terms of e, of a meson.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A student claims that a baryon of charge +e could be made of two up quarks and one strange antiquark. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: u u s̄ has charge +⅔ + ⅔ + ⅓ = +5/3, which is not a whole number; also a baryon must be three quarks or three antiquarks, not a mixture.
parts.working: B1 charge would be +5/3 e; B1 baryons are qqq or q̄q̄q̄, not a mixture

practice.stem: Quarks come in six flavours: up (u), down (d), strange (s), charm (c), top (t) and bottom (b). The charm quark has charge +⅔e and the bottom quark has charge −⅓e.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine, in terms of e, the charge of each meson: (i) D⁰ (c ū), (ii) D_s⁺ (c s̄), (iii) B⁻ (b ū), (iv) B⁺ (u b̄).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the quark composition of the antiparticle of the D_s⁺ meson and give its charge.

practice.stem: Sodium-24 (proton number 11) decays by β⁻ emission to magnesium-24 (proton number 12). It is used to trace leaks in underground water pipes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the total numbers of up quarks and down quarks in a sodium-24 nucleus.
parts.working: M1 11 protons (uud) and 13 neutrons (udd); A1 up = 2 × 11 + 13 = 35, down = 11 + 2 × 13 = 37

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the numbers of up quarks and down quarks in the magnesium-24 nucleus formed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why the nucleon number does not change in β⁻ decay but the proton number increases by one.
parts.answer: The total number of quarks stays 72 (so 24 nucleons); one down quark becomes an up quark, turning one neutron (udd) into a proton (uud).
parts.working: B1 total quarks unchanged → nucleon number unchanged; B1 one d → u, so one neutron becomes a proton

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A neutron decays to a proton and an electron only: n → p + e⁻ (no antineutrino is produced). Which conservation law does this decay violate?
A charge
B baryon number
C lepton number
D number of quarks
parts.working: Charge: 0 → (+1) + (−1) = 0, so conserved. Baryon number: 1 → 1, conserved. Number of quarks: 3 → 3, conserved. Lepton number: 0 is required on the left but the electron gives +1 on the right, so the lepton number is not conserved. The antineutrino is needed to balance it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The K⁻ meson has quark composition s ū. Determine its charge in terms of e.
parts.working: 1 mark for the quark charges −1/3 e (s) and −2/3 e (ū); 1 mark for −e.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the K⁻ is a baryon or a meson, and give the reason.
parts.answer: Meson: it contains only two quarks, a quark and an antiquark (s ū), not three quarks.
parts.working: 1 mark for meson; 1 mark for a quark–antiquark pair (two quarks, not three).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A positron and an electron, both at rest, annihilate to produce two γ-photons of equal energy. Calculate the energy of each photon in joules. Take the rest energy of an electron to be 0.511 MeV. (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
parts.answer: Total energy = 2 × 0.511 MeV = 1.022 MeV; each photon = 0.511 MeV = 0.511 × 10⁶ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 8.18 × 10⁻¹⁴ J
parts.working: 1 mark for the total rest energy 1.022 MeV shared between two photons; 1 mark for 8.18 × 10⁻¹⁴ J.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one quantity that is conserved in this annihilation.
parts.answer: Total charge (zero before and after); or total energy; or total momentum; or lepton number
parts.working: 1 mark for any one conserved quantity (charge, energy, momentum or lepton number).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A neutron (udd) in a nucleus changes into a proton (uud) by β⁻ decay. Describe the change at the quark level, naming the particles emitted.
parts.answer: One down quark changes into an up quark: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ. The electron and electron antineutrino are emitted; the change is mediated by the weak interaction (a W⁻ boson).
parts.working: 1 mark for a down quark changing into an up quark; 1 mark for the electron (e⁻) and electron antineutrino (ν̄ₑ) being emitted; 1 mark for the weak interaction (W⁻ boson).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A Λ⁰ baryon (mass 1116 MeV c⁻²) decays to a proton (938 MeV c⁻²) and a π⁻ meson (140 MeV c⁻²). Calculate the energy released in this decay in joules. (1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J)
parts.answer: Energy released = (1116 − 938 − 140) MeV = 38 MeV = 38 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J = 6.1 × 10⁻¹² J
parts.working: 1 mark for subtracting the product masses from the Λ⁰ mass; 1 mark for 38 MeV; 1 mark for 6.1 × 10⁻¹² J.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A light-dependent resistor (LDR) and a fixed resistor are connected in series across a battery. The output voltage is taken across the fixed resistor. The light falling on the LDR becomes brighter. What happens?
A The resistance of the LDR increases and the output voltage increases.
B The resistance of the LDR increases and the output voltage decreases.
C The resistance of the LDR decreases and the output voltage increases.
D The resistance of the LDR decreases and the output voltage decreases.
parts.answer: C The resistance of the LDR decreases and the output voltage increases.
parts.working: An LDR's resistance falls as light intensity rises, so it takes a smaller share of the supply p.d. and the fixed resistor a larger share. D would be correct only if the output were across the LDR.

practice.stem: A negative temperature coefficient (NTC) thermistor and a 3.3 kΩ fixed resistor are connected in series across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The output voltage is taken across the fixed resistor. At 20 °C the resistance of the thermistor is 1.5 kΩ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output voltage at 20 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The temperature rises. State and explain the change in the output voltage.
parts.answer: The output voltage increases. The thermistor's resistance falls as temperature rises, so its share of the 6.0 V falls and the share across the fixed resistor rises.
parts.working: B1 increases; B1 thermistor resistance decreases so p.d. across it decreases

practice.stem: A variable resistor of range 0 to 10 kΩ is connected in series with a 5.0 kΩ fixed resistor across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The output voltage is taken across the fixed resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the largest output voltage.
parts.working: Variable resistor at 0 Ω: all 6.0 V across the 5.0 kΩ resistor (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the smallest output voltage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: This circuit cannot make the output smaller than 2.0 V. Describe how the variable resistor alone could be connected as a potentiometer (potential divider) so that the p.d. across the 5.0 kΩ resistor could be varied all the way from 0 to 6.0 V.
parts.answer: Connect the two ends of the variable resistor's track directly across the 6.0 V supply, and connect the 5.0 kΩ resistor between the sliding contact and one end of the track. Moving the slider varies the output from 0 V (slider at that end) to 6.0 V (slider at the other end).
parts.working: B1 whole track across the supply (all three terminals used); B1 output taken between slider and one end, giving 0 to 6.0 V

practice.stem: On a potentiometer wire, a cell X of e.m.f. 1.50 V gives a balance length of 72.0 cm. Without changing the driver circuit, cell X is replaced by cell Y, which balances at 55.2 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the e.m.f. of cell Y.
parts.working: C1 E ∝ balance length: E_Y = 1.50 × 55.2/72.0; A1 1.15 V

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the driver cell must have a larger e.m.f. than either cell being tested.
parts.answer: Otherwise the p.d. across the whole wire is less than the test e.m.f., and no balance point can be found.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A 4.0 kΩ resistor and a resistor of resistance R are connected in series across a 12 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The potential difference across R is 9.0 V. What is R?
A 3.0 kΩ
B 4.0 kΩ
C 9.0 kΩ
D 12 kΩ
parts.working: p.d. across 4.0 kΩ = 3.0 V, so current = 0.75 mA and R = 9.0/0.75 mA = 12 kΩ (p.d.s are in the ratio of resistances, 9 : 3). A comes from inverting the ratio of p.d.s.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A potentiometer is used to measure the e.m.f. of a cell. At the balance point the galvanometer reading is zero. Why is the balance length a measure of the e.m.f. of the cell rather than of a smaller terminal p.d.?
A There is no current in the cell, so there is no p.d. across its internal resistance.
B The driver cell has negligible internal resistance.
C The potentiometer wire has a uniform resistance per unit length.
D The galvanometer has a very small resistance.
parts.answer: A There is no current in the cell, so there is no p.d. across its internal resistance.
parts.working: With zero current, terminal p.d. = E − Ir = E. B and C are needed for the wire to give a steady, linear scale, but do not explain why the e.m.f. is measured.

practice.stem: A heat sensor for a fire alarm uses an NTC thermistor in series with a 2.2 kΩ fixed resistor across a 9.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The output voltage is taken across the fixed resistor. The resistance of the thermistor is 12 kΩ at 25 °C and 0.80 kΩ at 90 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output voltage at 25 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the output voltage at 90 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The alarm sounds when the output voltage reaches 4.5 V. State the resistance of the thermistor at that moment, with a reason.
parts.answer: 2.2 kΩ: the output is half the supply, so both resistors have equal resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Resistors of 2.2 kΩ and 6.8 kΩ are connected in series across a 9.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. What is the p.d. across the 6.8 kΩ resistor?
A 2.2 V
B 2.9 V
C 6.8 V
D 6.1 V
parts.working: V = 9.0 × 6.8/(2.2 + 6.8) = 6.8 V. A is the p.d. across the 2.2 kΩ resistor; B uses the wrong ratio 9.0 × 2.2/6.8.

practice.stem: A gardener in Murree builds a frost alarm. An NTC thermistor is connected in series with a fixed resistor across a 5.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The output is taken across the thermistor and must be 2.0 V when the thermistor's resistance is 800 Ω.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the fixed resistor needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When the soil is colder, the thermistor's resistance is higher. State whether the output voltage is then above or below 2.0 V, and explain.
parts.answer: Above 2.0 V: the thermistor has a larger share of the total resistance, so a larger share of the supply p.d.

practice.stem: A potentiometer consists of a uniform resistance wire of length 100.0 cm connected across a driver cell of e.m.f. 2.00 V and negligible internal resistance. A test cell is connected, in series with a galvanometer, between one end of the wire and a sliding contact. The galvanometer reads zero when the sliding contact is 64.5 cm from that end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the e.m.f. of the test cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this method measures the e.m.f. of the test cell rather than its terminal p.d. on load.
parts.answer: At balance the galvanometer shows zero, so no current flows through the test cell; with no current there is no p.d. across its internal resistance, so its terminal p.d. equals its e.m.f.
parts.working: B1 no current in test cell at balance; B1 no lost volts / terminal p.d. = e.m.f.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a longer potentiometer wire, with the same driver cell, would give a more precise result.
parts.answer: The balance length would be longer, so its percentage uncertainty would be smaller.

practice.stem: A street-light controller uses a light-dependent resistor (LDR) in series with a 10 kΩ fixed resistor across a 9.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The output is taken across the LDR. The LDR's resistance is 500 kΩ in the dark and 2.0 kΩ in bright daylight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output voltage in the dark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the output voltage in bright light.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The circuit switches on a street light when the output voltage rises above 6.0 V. Calculate the LDR resistance at which this happens.

practice.stem: The volume control of a radio is a 10 kΩ resistance track with a sliding contact. The two ends of the track are connected across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The output is taken between the lower end of the track and the slider, which is 30% of the way up the track.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output voltage when nothing is connected to the output.
parts.working: Lower section 3.0 kΩ of 10 kΩ: V = 6.0 × 3.0/10 = 1.8 V (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: An earphone of resistance 1.0 kΩ is now connected to the output. Calculate the new output voltage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the output voltage falls when the earphone is connected.
parts.answer: The earphone in parallel lowers the resistance of the lower section, so it takes a smaller share of the supply p.d.

practice.stem:
A student puts an NTC thermistor in a beaker of water and connects it in series with a 1.0 kΩ resistor across a 5.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. She records the voltage V across the fixed resistor at different water temperatures T.
T / °C: 20, 40, 60, 80
V / V: 0.71, 1.28, 2.00, 2.75

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the thermistor at 60 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the thermistor at 40 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how V varies with T.
parts.answer: V increases as T increases, but not linearly (not proportional).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one precaution to make sure that the recorded temperature is the temperature of the thermistor.
parts.answer: Stir the water and wait until the thermometer and voltmeter readings are steady before reading; keep the thermometer bulb next to the thermistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two 10 kΩ resistors are connected in series across a 12 V supply of negligible internal resistance. A voltmeter of resistance 10 kΩ is connected across one of the resistors. What does the voltmeter read?
A 3.0 V
B 4.0 V
C 6.0 V
D 8.0 V
parts.working: Voltmeter in parallel with 10 kΩ gives 5.0 kΩ; V = 12 × 5.0/15 = 4.0 V. C assumes an ideal (infinite-resistance) voltmeter; D is the p.d. across the other resistor.

practice.stem: A potentiometer wire of length 1.000 m and resistance 5.0 Ω is connected in series with a resistor R and a driver cell of e.m.f. 4.0 V and negligible internal resistance. A standard cell of e.m.f. 1.018 V balances at 80.0 cm along the wire.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the p.d. across the whole potentiometer wire.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current in the wire.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the resistance R.
parts.working: M1 total resistance = 4.0/0.255 = 15.7 Ω; A1 R = 10.7 Ω

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why adding the series resistor R makes the potentiometer more suitable for measuring small e.m.f.s.
parts.answer: It reduces the p.d. per unit length of the wire, so a small e.m.f. balances at a longer, more precisely measured length.

practice.stem: Two potential dividers are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply of negligible internal resistance. In the first, a 4.7 kΩ resistor is connected to the positive terminal and an NTC thermistor to the negative terminal; their junction is X. In the second, two 3.0 kΩ resistors are in series; their junction is Y. A high-resistance voltmeter is connected between X and Y.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the voltmeter reads zero when the thermistor's resistance is 4.7 kΩ.
parts.answer: Both junctions are then at 6.0 V (half of 12 V), so there is no p.d. between them.
parts.working: B1 X at 12 × 4.7/9.4 = 6.0 V; B1 Y at 6.0 V, so p.d. zero

parts.label: b
parts.text: At 40 °C the thermistor's resistance is 2.2 kΩ. Calculate the voltmeter reading and state which junction is at the higher potential.
parts.answer: 2.17 V; Y is at the higher potential

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of this arrangement over a single potential divider for measuring small changes of temperature near the balance temperature.
parts.answer: The reading starts from zero, so a sensitive (small-range) voltmeter can be used and small changes are easily seen.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plan an experiment to investigate how the output voltage V of a potential divider varies with the distance d between a light-dependent resistor (LDR) and a small lamp. The LDR is in series with a fixed resistor across a d.c. supply, and V is measured across the fixed resistor. It is suggested that V = V₀ d⁻ⁿ over a limited range, where V₀ and n are constants.
Your account should include: the procedure, the measurements and how they are made, the control of variables, how the data are analysed to test the relationship and find n, and any safety precautions.
parts.answer: A full plan: vary d, measure V, control lamp power and stray light, plot lg V against lg d; gradient = −n, intercept = lg V₀.
parts.working: Mark points (1 mark each, max 15): Defining the problem: d is the independent variable, V the dependent variable; keep lamp p.d./current (power), supply e.m.f. and fixed resistor constant. Method: circuit diagram described with LDR in series with fixed resistor and supply, voltmeter across fixed resistor; separate lamp circuit with ammeter/voltmeter to monitor lamp power; measure d from lamp filament to LDR face with a metre rule; align lamp and LDR at the same height facing each other (e.g. on an optical bench); range of at least 6 distances, e.g. 10 cm to 60 cm. Control: work in a darkened room or use a black tube/shield to exclude stray light; allow lamp to warm up and LDR to settle before reading; keep LDR temperature steady. Analysis: plot lg V against lg d; relationship valid if a straight line; gradient = −n; y-intercept = lg V₀. Additional detail: high-resistance voltmeter (or data logger) so it does not load the divider; choose fixed resistor of similar size to LDR resistance for a large change in V; repeat each reading and average; check d to filament not glass. Safety: lamp becomes hot – allow to cool/do not touch; do not look directly at a bright lamp. Bands: 13–15 detailed workable plan with analysis and control; 9–12 workable with minor gaps; 5–8 basic method; 1–4 fragments.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A light-dependent resistor (LDR) and an NTC thermistor are connected in series across a battery. The output voltage is taken across the thermistor. Which change is certain to increase the output voltage?
A brighter light and higher temperature
B brighter light and lower temperature
C dimmer light and higher temperature
D dimmer light and lower temperature
parts.answer: B brighter light and lower temperature
parts.working: Brighter light lowers the LDR resistance and lower temperature raises the thermistor resistance; both increase the thermistor's share of the e.m.f. In A and D the two changes act against each other, so the result is uncertain.

practice.stem: A potentiometer is used to find the internal resistance of a cell. With the cell on open circuit, the balance length is 75.0 cm. When a 10.0 Ω resistor is connected across the terminals of the cell, the balance length becomes 62.5 cm. The driver circuit is unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the balance length of 75.0 cm corresponds to the e.m.f. of the cell.
parts.answer: At balance there is no current in the cell, so there is no p.d. across its internal resistance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the internal resistance r is given by r = R(l₁ − l₂)/l₂, where l₁ and l₂ are the two balance lengths and R is the resistor.
parts.answer: E ∝ l₁ and V ∝ l₂; E/V = (R + r)/R = l₁/l₂, so r = R(l₁/l₂ − 1) = R(l₁ − l₂)/l₂.
parts.working: M1: E/V = l₁/l₂. M1: E/V = (R + r)/R and rearrangement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the internal resistance of the cell.

practice.stem: A potentiometer wire is 1.000 m long and has a resistance of 4.5 Ω. It is connected in series with a driver cell of e.m.f. 2.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current in the wire and the potential difference per metre along it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance length for a cell of e.m.f. 1.20 V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Over several weeks the internal resistance of the driver cell increases while its e.m.f. stays the same. State and explain the effect on the balance length for the 1.20 V cell.
parts.answer: The balance length increases: the current in the wire falls, so the p.d. per unit length falls and a longer length is needed to give 1.20 V.
parts.working: M1: smaller current / smaller p.d. per unit length. A1: balance length increases.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Kirchhoff's first law states that the sum of the currents into a junction equals the sum of the currents out of it. This law is a consequence of the conservation of
A energy
B charge
C potential difference
D power
parts.working: Charge cannot build up at or vanish from a junction. A (energy) is the basis of Kirchhoff's second law.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use Kirchhoff's laws to show that the combined resistance R of resistors R₁ and R₂ in parallel is given by 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.
parts.answer: Same p.d. V across each (second law); I = I₁ + I₂ (first law); V/R = V/R₁ + V/R₂, so 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.
parts.working: B1 same p.d. across parallel branches; B1 I = I₁ + I₂; B1 substitution I = V/R and cancel V

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the combined resistance of 10 Ω, 15 Ω and 30 Ω resistors connected in parallel.

practice.stem: A string of decorative lights for a wedding in Lahore consists of 40 identical filament lamps connected in series to a 230 V supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the p.d. across each lamp.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The current is 0.20 A. Calculate the resistance of each lamp.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State Kirchhoff's second law and explain how it applies to this string of lamps.
parts.answer: Around any closed loop, the sum of the e.m.f.s equals the sum of the p.d.s. Here the supply p.d. 230 V equals the sum of the 40 lamp p.d.s.

practice.stem: Resistors of 220 Ω, 330 Ω and 470 Ω are connected in series across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current in the circuit, in mA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the p.d. across the 470 Ω resistor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which resistor dissipates the most power and explain why.
parts.answer: The 470 Ω resistor: the current is the same in all, so P = I²R is largest for the largest R.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
At a junction in a circuit, currents of 2.5 A and 0.6 A flow into the junction and a current of 1.2 A flows out along one wire. One other wire is connected to the junction. What is the current in this wire?
A 0.7 A out of the junction
B 1.3 A out of the junction
C 1.9 A out of the junction
D 4.3 A into the junction
parts.answer: C 1.9 A out of the junction
parts.working: Kirchhoff's first law: total in = total out, so 2.5 + 0.6 = 1.2 + I and I = 1.9 A out. B ignores the 0.6 A.

practice.stem: A lamp rated 6.0 V, 0.30 A is to be run at its normal brightness from a 9.0 V battery of negligible internal resistance, using a resistor in series with it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State Kirchhoff's second law.
parts.answer: Around any closed loop, the sum of the e.m.f.s equals the sum of the potential differences.
parts.working: B1 (allow: is a consequence of conservation of energy).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the series resistor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the power dissipated in the resistor and the fraction of the battery's output power that the lamp uses.

practice.stem: Four identical lamps, each of resistance 12 Ω, are connected to a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. Lamps A and B are in series in one branch and lamps C and D are in series in a second branch; the two branches are in parallel across the supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total resistance of the lamps.
parts.working: Each branch 24 Ω (C1); two equal branches in parallel = 12 Ω (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current from the supply.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The filament of lamp A breaks. State which lamps stay lit and calculate the new current from the supply.
parts.answer: C and D stay lit (B goes out); 0.25 A
parts.working: B1: B goes out, C and D unaffected. A1: I = 6.0/24 = 0.25 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A 12 Ω resistor and a 4.0 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. This combination is connected in series with a 6.0 Ω resistor. What is the total resistance?
A 2.4 Ω
B 9.0 Ω
C 13 Ω
D 22 Ω
parts.working: 12 ∥ 4.0 = 48/16 = 3.0 Ω; total = 3.0 + 6.0 = 9.0 Ω. D adds all three in series; A treats all three as parallel.

practice.stem: A 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current from the battery.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current in the 6.0 Ω resistor and in the 12 Ω resistor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the power dissipated in the 4.0 Ω resistor.

practice.stem: In a camper van, three 12 V appliances are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance: lights rated 24 W, a fridge rated 60 W and a fan rated 36 W.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current in each appliance.
parts.answer: lights 2.0 A; fridge 5.0 A; fan 3.0 A
parts.working: C1 I = P/V; A1 all three

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total current from the battery and the combined resistance of the three appliances.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the appliances are connected in parallel rather than in series.
parts.answer: Each gets the full 12 V and can be switched on or off independently.

practice.stem: A 9.0 V battery of negligible internal resistance is connected to a resistor R in series with a parallel combination of a 30 Ω resistor and a lamp. The current in the 30 Ω resistor is 0.10 A and the current in the lamp is 0.25 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the p.d. across the lamp and its resistance.
parts.working: B1 p.d. across 30 Ω = 0.10 × 30 = 3.0 V = p.d. across lamp; B1 R = 3.0/0.25 = 12 Ω

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of R.
parts.working: M1 current in R = 0.35 A and p.d. = 6.0 V; A1 R = 17.1 Ω

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Three identical resistors each have resistance R. Which arrangement has a combined resistance of 2R/3?
A all three in parallel
B two in parallel, and this combination in series with the third
C two in series, and this combination in parallel with the third
D all three in series
parts.answer: C two in series, and this combination in parallel with the third
parts.working: (2R × R)/(2R + R) = 2R/3. A gives R/3, B gives 3R/2 and D gives 3R.

practice.stem: A cell of e.m.f. 12.0 V and a cell of e.m.f. 4.5 V, both of negligible internal resistance, are connected in a single loop with a 5.0 Ω resistor and a 10.0 Ω resistor in series. The positive terminal of the 12.0 V cell is connected (through the resistors) to the positive terminal of the 4.5 V cell, so the cells oppose each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use Kirchhoff's second law to calculate the current in the loop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference across the 10.0 Ω resistor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate at which energy is transferred to chemical energy in the 4.5 V cell, and show that energy is conserved in the circuit.

practice.stem: An extension board in a house in Multan is connected to the 230 V mains. The board is protected by a 13 A fuse. An electric kettle (2.0 kW), a room heater (1.2 kW) and a phone charger (10 W) are plugged into it at the same time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State Kirchhoff's first law and the quantity that it shows is conserved.
parts.answer: The sum of the currents into a junction equals the sum of the currents out; charge is conserved.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total current drawn through the board and state whether the fuse will melt.
parts.working: I = (2000 + 1200 + 10)/230 (M1) = 14.0 A, greater than 13 A so the fuse melts (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the kettle element when in use.

practice.stem:
Two points P (top) and Q (bottom) are joined by three parallel branches.
Branch 1: a cell of e.m.f. 9.0 V (positive terminal towards P) in series with a 3.0 Ω resistor.
Branch 2: a 6.0 Ω resistor.
Branch 3: a cell of e.m.f. 4.5 V (positive terminal towards P) in series with a 2.0 Ω resistor.
Both cells have negligible internal resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use Kirchhoff's laws to calculate the current in each branch. State the direction of the current in the cell of e.m.f. 4.5 V.
parts.answer: 9.0 V branch: 1.25 A (out of its positive terminal); 6.0 Ω branch: 0.875 A downwards; 4.5 V branch: 0.375 A, flowing into its positive terminal (the cell is being charged).
parts.working: Let I₁ = current up through the 9.0 V branch towards P, I₂ = current down through the 6.0 Ω resistor, I₃ = current up through the 4.5 V branch towards P. M1 first law at P: I₁ + I₃ = I₂; M1 loop with 9.0 V cell and 6.0 Ω: 9.0 = 3.0 I₁ + 6.0 I₂; M1 loop with 4.5 V cell and 6.0 Ω: 4.5 = 2.0 I₃ + 6.0 I₂; A1 I₁ = 1.25 A, I₂ = 0.875 A; A1 I₃ = −0.375 A, i.e. 0.375 A flows into the positive terminal of the 4.5 V cell

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference between P and Q.

practice.stem: A network has four outer resistors: 10 Ω from A to C, 10 Ω from C to B, 20 Ω from A to D and 20 Ω from D to B. A 15 Ω resistor connects C and D. A p.d. is applied between A and B.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that there is no current in the 15 Ω resistor.
parts.answer: C and D are both at the potential midway between A and B (10:10 and 20:20 are equal ratios), so the p.d. across CD is zero.
parts.working: B1 ratio 10/10 = 20/20; B1 C and D at same potential so no current

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the network between A and B.
parts.working: M1 ignore CD: 20 Ω path in parallel with 40 Ω path; A1 (20 × 40)/60 = 13.3 Ω

parts.label: c
parts.text: The 15 Ω resistor is replaced by a 100 Ω resistor. State, with a reason, whether the resistance between A and B changes.
parts.answer: No change: there is still no p.d. across CD, so no current flows whatever its resistance.

practice.stem: A uniform wire of total resistance 16 Ω is bent into a square ABCD and the ends are joined, so that each side has resistance 4.0 Ω.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance between two adjacent corners A and B.
parts.working: M1 4.0 Ω side in parallel with 12 Ω (other three sides); A1 3.0 Ω

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance between opposite corners A and C.
parts.working: M1 8.0 Ω in parallel with 8.0 Ω; A1 4.0 Ω

parts.label: c
parts.text: A 6.0 V cell of negligible internal resistance is connected between A and C. Calculate the current in side AB.

practice.stem: A ladder network is made of six 10 Ω resistors. From input terminal A, a 10 Ω resistor runs to point P. From P, one 10 Ω resistor runs to the return line and another runs to point Q. From Q, one 10 Ω resistor runs to the return line and another runs to point S. From S, a 10 Ω resistor runs to the return line. A p.d. of 13.0 V is applied between A and the return line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the resistance between A and the return line is 16.25 Ω.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current entering at A and the potential of P.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the current in the final 10 Ω resistor between S and the return line.

practice.stem: Two branches are connected in parallel across a 12.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. Branch 1: a 100 Ω resistor (from the positive terminal) in series with a 200 Ω resistor; their junction is M. Branch 2: a 150 Ω resistor (from the positive terminal) in series with an unknown resistor X; their junction is N. An ideal voltmeter connected between M and N reads 1.0 V, with M at the higher potential.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the potential of M above the negative terminal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the resistance of X.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the value of X for which the voltmeter would read zero.
parts.working: Same ratio as branch 1: 100/200 = 150/X, X = 300 Ω (B1).

practice.stem: Two resistors have a combined resistance of 25 Ω when connected in series and 4.0 Ω when connected in parallel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the resistance of each resistor.
parts.working: R₁ + R₂ = 25 and R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = 4.0, so R₁R₂ = 100 (M1); R² − 25R + 100 = 0 (M1); R = 20 Ω and 5.0 Ω (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The two resistors are connected in parallel across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. Calculate the current in each resistor and the total current.
parts.working: 0.30 A and 1.2 A (A1); total 1.5 A, which equals 6.0/4.0 (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement defines the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source?
A the energy transferred per unit charge from electrical to other forms in the external circuit
B the force that drives the current round the circuit
C the energy transferred per unit charge from other forms to electrical energy by the source
D the power supplied per unit current to the external resistor
parts.answer: C the energy transferred per unit charge from other forms to electrical energy by the source
parts.working: E.m.f. is energy converted into electrical energy per coulomb by the source. A defines potential difference; B is wrong because e.m.f. is not a force.

practice.stem: A car battery has an e.m.f. of 12.6 V and internal resistance 0.020 Ω. When the starter motor is switched on it draws a current of 150 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the terminal p.d. of the battery while the motor runs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate at which energy is dissipated inside the battery.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the car's headlights dim while the starter motor is turning.
parts.answer: The large current causes a large p.d. across the internal resistance, so the terminal p.d. available to the lamps falls.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A battery of e.m.f. 9.0 V has a terminal p.d. of 8.4 V when it supplies a current of 0.30 A. What is its internal resistance?
A 0.50 Ω
B 2.0 Ω
C 28 Ω
D 30 Ω
parts.working: Lost volts = 9.0 − 8.4 = 0.6 V; r = 0.6/0.30 = 2.0 Ω. C is the external resistance 8.4/0.30; D is 9.0/0.30.

practice.stem: A small solar cell has an e.m.f. of 0.60 V and an internal resistance of 1.5 Ω. It is connected to a 4.5 Ω resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between the e.m.f. of a source and the potential difference across a resistor, in terms of energy.
parts.answer: e.m.f.: energy transferred from other forms to electrical per unit charge (by the source); p.d.: energy transferred from electrical to other forms per unit charge (in the resistor).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current in the circuit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the terminal p.d. of the cell.

practice.stem: A school laboratory has an extra-high-tension (EHT) supply of e.m.f. 5.0 kV. It is designed to have an internal resistance of 50 MΩ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the largest current that the supply can deliver.
parts.working: Largest current with zero external resistance: I = E/r (M1) = 5.0 × 10³/50 × 10⁶ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ A (0.10 mA) (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the high internal resistance makes the supply safer to use.
parts.answer: It limits the current to a very small value even if the terminals are short-circuited (e.g. through a person).

practice.stem: A torch contains three cells in series. Each cell has an e.m.f. of 1.5 V and an internal resistance of 0.20 Ω. The lamp has a resistance of 4.0 Ω.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the current in the lamp.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the terminal p.d. of the battery of cells.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total power output of the cells that is delivered to the lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A cell of e.m.f. 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω is connected to a 2.5 Ω resistor. What is the terminal p.d. of the cell?
A 0.25 V
B 1.20 V
C 1.25 V
D 1.50 V
parts.working: I = 1.5/3.0 = 0.50 A; V = E − Ir = 1.5 − 0.25 = 1.25 V. A is the lost volts; D ignores internal resistance.

practice.stem:
A student connects a battery pack to a variable resistor and an ammeter in series, with a voltmeter across the battery terminals. She records the terminal p.d. V for different currents I.
I / A | V / V
0.20 | 4.27
0.50 | 3.89
0.80 | 3.56
1.10 | 3.18
1.40 | 2.80
1.70 | 2.47

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that V = E − Ir and state what the gradient and the V-intercept of a graph of V against I represent.
parts.answer: E = V + Ir so V = −rI + E; gradient = −r, intercept = E.
parts.working: B1 rearrangement; B1 gradient −r and intercept E

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the first and last rows (or a best-fit line), determine the e.m.f. E and internal resistance r of the battery pack.
parts.working: M1 gradient from widely separated points; A1 r; A1 E

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student switches off the circuit between readings.
parts.answer: To stop the battery and resistor heating up, which would change r (and R), and to save the battery.

practice.stem: When a torch cell delivers a current of 0.20 A its terminal p.d. is 1.42 V. When it delivers 0.50 A its terminal p.d. is 1.30 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the internal resistance of the cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the e.m.f. of the cell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the current when the terminals are short-circuited by a wire of negligible resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A battery with internal resistance is connected to a variable resistor. The resistance of the variable resistor is decreased. What happens to the terminal p.d. of the battery and to the 'lost volts' inside it?
A terminal p.d. increases, lost volts decrease
B terminal p.d. decreases, lost volts increase
C both increase
D terminal p.d. unchanged, lost volts increase
parts.answer: B terminal p.d. decreases, lost volts increase
parts.working: Smaller external resistance → larger current → larger Ir (lost volts), so V = E − Ir decreases. D would need zero internal resistance, but then the lost volts would not change either.

practice.stem: A phone power bank has an e.m.f. of 5.1 V. When it supplies a current of 2.0 A to a phone, its terminal p.d. is 4.8 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the internal resistance of the power bank.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the power wasted inside the power bank and its efficiency.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Two phones are charged at once and the total current is 3.0 A. Calculate the terminal p.d.

practice.stem: A car battery of e.m.f. 12.0 V and internal resistance 0.10 Ω is being recharged. It is connected to a charger of e.m.f. 14.0 V (negligible internal resistance) through leads of total resistance 0.40 Ω, positive terminal to positive terminal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charging current.
parts.working: Net e.m.f. = 2.0 V, total resistance 0.50 Ω (C1); I = 4.0 A (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate at which energy is stored as chemical energy in the battery and the rate at which energy is dissipated as heat.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the efficiency of the charging process.

practice.stem: A digital voltmeter of very high resistance reads 1.58 V when connected across a cell on its own. When a 10.0 Ω resistor is connected across the cell, the voltmeter reads 1.43 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the first reading is equal to the e.m.f. of the cell.
parts.answer: The voltmeter draws (almost) no current, so there is no p.d. across the internal resistance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current when the 10.0 Ω resistor is connected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the internal resistance of the cell.

practice.stem: A battery of unknown e.m.f. E and internal resistance r is connected to a 6.0 Ω resistor; the current is 0.80 A. A 3.0 Ω resistor is then connected in parallel with the 6.0 Ω resistor, and the current from the battery becomes 1.8 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the combined resistance of the two resistors in parallel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine E and r.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the terminal p.d. of the battery in the second case.

practice.stem: A power supply of e.m.f. E = 6.0 V and internal resistance r = 2.0 Ω is connected to a variable resistor of resistance R.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the power P dissipated in R is given by P = E²R/(R + r)².
parts.answer: I = E/(R + r); P = I²R = E²R/(R + r)².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the power in R when R = 4.0 Ω and when R = 2.0 Ω.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The maximum power in R occurs when R = r. Calculate the efficiency of the energy transfer (useful power in R ÷ total power from the source) when R = r and when R = 4.0 Ω, and comment.
parts.answer: 50 % when R = r; 67 % when R = 4.0 Ω. Maximum power transfer does not give maximum efficiency.
parts.working: M1 efficiency = R/(R + r); A1 50 % and 67 %; B1 comment

practice.stem: Four identical cells, each of e.m.f. 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.30 Ω, are connected as two series pairs, and the two pairs are then connected in parallel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the e.m.f. and internal resistance of the combination.
parts.working: B1 each series pair: 3.0 V, 0.60 Ω; B1 two pairs in parallel: 3.0 V, 0.30 Ω

parts.label: b
parts.text: The combination is connected to a 2.7 Ω lamp. Calculate the current in the lamp and the terminal p.d.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the current in each individual cell.
parts.working: Current divides equally between the two identical pairs (B1)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of this arrangement compared with all four cells in series, for this lamp.
parts.answer: The lamp gets a suitable p.d. of 2.7 V: four cells in series (6.0 V, 1.2 Ω) would drive about 1.5 A and put about 4.2 V across it, which could overheat it. Also each cell supplies only 0.50 A, so the cells last longer. (Either point.)
parts.working: B1 any one: suitable (lower) p.d./current for the lamp compared with series (≈4.2 V, 1.5 A); each cell supplies only half the current so lasts longer

practice.stem:
A student makes a cell by pushing a copper strip and a zinc strip into a lemon. She connects it to a resistance box of resistance R and a sensitive ammeter, and records the current I.
R / Ω: 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000
I / mA: 1.46, 1.12, 0.905, 0.760, 0.655
It is suggested that E = I(R + r), where E is the e.m.f. and r the internal resistance of the lemon cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a graph of 1/I against R should be a straight line, and state expressions for its gradient and its intercept on the 1/I axis.
parts.answer: 1/I = R/E + r/E, of the form y = mx + c; gradient = 1/E, intercept = r/E.
parts.working: M1: rearrangement. A1: gradient 1/E and intercept r/E.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the first and last readings to determine E and r.
parts.working: 1/I = 685 A⁻¹ and 1527 A⁻¹ (C1); gradient = 1.052 A⁻¹ Ω⁻¹ so E = 0.950 V (A1); intercept = 474 A⁻¹ so r = intercept × E ≈ 450 Ω (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the readings may not be reproducible, and one way to reduce its effect.
parts.answer: The e.m.f. and internal resistance of a fruit cell drift with time (the electrodes polarise / the juice changes); take readings quickly, disconnect between readings, and repeat with the readings in reverse order and average.

practice.stem: A car battery has an e.m.f. of 12.0 V and an internal resistance of 0.025 Ω. The headlights have a total resistance of 1.2 Ω. The starter motor, while turning the engine, behaves like a resistance of 0.070 Ω connected in parallel with the headlights.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the terminal p.d. and the power of the headlights when only the headlights are on.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the terminal p.d. when the starter motor is also operating.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the headlights dim while the engine is being started, and calculate their power at this time.
parts.answer: Large current → large p.d. across internal resistance → terminal p.d. falls; P = 63.2 W
parts.working: B1: large current gives large lost volts. A1: P = 8.71²/1.2 = 63.2 W.

practice.stem: Identical cells, each of e.m.f. 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.60 Ω, are to be connected in parallel to drive a current of at least 2.0 A through a 0.50 Ω resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the e.m.f. and the internal resistance of n such cells connected in parallel.
parts.working: B1: e.m.f. unchanged. B1: internal resistances in parallel, r/n.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the smallest number of cells needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the current with this number of cells.

practice.stem: A solar panel at a farm near Bahawalpur has an e.m.f. of 21 V and an internal resistance of 3.5 Ω under steady sunlight. It is connected to a load of resistance R.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the value of R for which the power delivered to the load is a maximum, and calculate this power.
parts.working: Maximum when R = r = 3.5 Ω (B1); P = E²/4r = 441/14 = 31.5 W (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the efficiency of the panel's electrical output at maximum power.
parts.working: Half of EI is dissipated in r (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The farmer wants 80% of the electrical power to be delivered to the load. Calculate the load resistance needed and the power then delivered.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement defines the torque of a couple?
A the sum of the two forces multiplied by the distance between them
B one of the forces multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the forces
C one of the forces multiplied by the distance from either force to the centre of the object
D the resultant force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot
parts.answer: B one of the forces multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the forces
parts.working: Torque of a couple = one force × perpendicular separation of the two lines of action. A doubles the torque by adding both forces; D is wrong because a couple has zero resultant force.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A rigid body is acted on by several coplanar forces. Which pair of conditions must both be true for the body to be in equilibrium?
A resultant force is zero and resultant torque is zero
B resultant force is zero and the body is at rest
C resultant torque is zero and the forces all pass through the centre of gravity
D the sum of clockwise forces equals the sum of anticlockwise forces
parts.answer: A resultant force is zero and resultant torque is zero
parts.working: Equilibrium needs no resultant force (no linear acceleration) and no resultant torque about any point (no angular acceleration). B is wrong: a body moving at constant velocity can be in equilibrium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the moment of a force about a point.
parts.answer: The force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A mechanic in a Faisalabad workshop pushes on the end of a spanner 0.25 m from the centre of a nut with a force of 80 N at right angles to the spanner. Calculate the moment about the centre of the nut.

parts.label: c
parts.text: He now pushes with the same 80 N force at 30° to the spanner, at the same point. Calculate the new moment and explain why it is smaller.
parts.answer: 10 N m; the perpendicular distance to the line of action is smaller (0.25 sin 30° = 0.125 m).
parts.working: M1 perpendicular distance 0.25 sin 30°; A1 10 N m

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the principle of moments.
parts.answer: For a body in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same point.
parts.working: B1 in equilibrium; B1 sum clockwise = sum anticlockwise about the same point

parts.label: b
parts.text: On a see-saw in a park in Karachi, Ali (mass 32 kg) sits 1.5 m from the pivot. His sister (mass 24 kg) sits on the other side. The see-saw is uniform and pivoted at its centre. Calculate how far from the pivot she must sit for the see-saw to balance.
parts.working: M1 32g × 1.5 = 24g × d; A1 d = 2.0 m (g cancels; the see-saw's weight acts at the pivot)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer lifts the handles of a wheelbarrow so that its legs are just off the ground. The wheel axle acts as the pivot. The load of soil has weight 600 N acting 0.40 m horizontally from the axle, the barrow's weight 150 N acts 0.60 m from the axle, and the farmer lifts vertically at the handles, 1.40 m from the axle. Calculate the vertical force the farmer applies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the upward force of the ground on the wheel.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A driver turns a steering wheel of diameter 0.38 m by pushing up on one side and down on the other side of the rim, each hand applying a force of 25 N tangential to the rim. What is the torque of this couple?
A 2.4 N m
B 4.8 N m
C 9.5 N m
D 19 N m
parts.working: Torque of couple = one force × perpendicular distance between the forces = 25 × 0.38 = 9.5 N m. B uses the radius only (one force × 0.19 m); D adds both forces and multiplies by the diameter.

practice.stem: A worker uses a straight crowbar of length 1.20 m to lift the edge of a heavy stone slab. The crowbar rests on a small brick that acts as a pivot 0.15 m from the end of the bar that is under the slab. The worker pushes down at the other end with a force of 250 N at right angles to the bar. Ignore the weight of the crowbar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the two conditions for a rigid object to be in equilibrium.
parts.answer: The resultant force on it is zero; the resultant torque (moment) about any point is zero.
parts.working: B1 resultant force zero; B1 resultant torque/moment zero (about any point)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the force exerted by the crowbar on the slab, assuming this force is at right angles to the bar.
parts.working: M1 moments about pivot: F × 0.15 = 250 × 1.05; A1 F = 1750 N

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the worker can lift the slab more easily if the brick is moved closer to the slab.
parts.answer: The distance from the pivot to the slab decreases and the distance to the worker's hand increases, so the same applied moment gives a larger force on the slab.
parts.working: B1 perpendicular distance of effort from pivot increases / of load decreases; B1 so greater force for same applied force (principle of moments)

practice.stem: A wheel brace used to undo a car's wheel nut has two handles. A mechanic pushes one handle up and the other down, with forces of 60 N each, perpendicular to the brace. The hands are 0.40 m apart, one on each side of the nut.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the torque applied to the nut.
parts.working: C1 torque = F × perpendicular separation; A1 24 N m

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the resultant force exerted on the brace by the two hands and explain why the nut is not pushed sideways.
parts.answer: Zero; the two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction (they form a couple), so they only produce turning.
parts.working: B1 zero; B1 equal and opposite / couple gives torque only

parts.label: c
parts.text: The mechanic now uses only one hand, 0.20 m from the centre of the nut. Calculate the force needed to give the same torque.

practice.stem: A girl holds a 40 N shopping bag in her hand with her forearm horizontal. The forearm pivots at the elbow. The biceps muscle pulls vertically upwards on the forearm at a point 4.0 cm from the elbow. The forearm has weight 15 N acting 15 cm from the elbow, and the bag hangs 33 cm from the elbow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the force exerted by the biceps muscle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the size of the force at the elbow joint and state its direction.
parts.working: C1 resultant vertical force zero: 386 − 15 − 40; A1 331 N downwards

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A uniform metre rule of mass 0.12 kg is balanced on a pivot at the 30.0 cm mark by hanging a mass from the 5.0 cm mark. What is the hung mass?
A 0.072 kg
B 0.096 kg
C 0.144 kg
D 0.48 kg
parts.working: The rule's weight acts at the 50.0 cm mark, 20.0 cm from the pivot; the hung mass is 25.0 cm from it. m × 25.0 = 0.12 × 20.0, m = 0.096 kg. C comes from inverting the ratio of distances.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A uniform wooden plank of length 4.0 m and weight 600 N rests horizontally across a small stream, supported at its ends A and B. A man of weight 750 N stands on the plank 1.2 m from A. Calculate the upward force on the plank at B.
parts.working: M1 moments about A: R_B × 4.0 = 600 × 2.0 + 750 × 1.2; A1 R_B = 525 N

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the upward force at A.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The man walks slowly from A to B. Describe how the force at A changes.
parts.answer: It decreases steadily (linearly), from 1050 N when he is at A to 300 N when he is at B.

practice.stem: A non-uniform log of length 5.0 m lies on level ground. A vertical force of 420 N is just enough to lift end A off the ground (end B stays on the ground). A vertical force of 280 N is just enough to lift end B off the ground (end A stays on the ground).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define centre of gravity.
parts.answer: The point through which the whole weight of the object may be considered to act.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the weight of the log.
parts.working: When either end is just lifted the other end is the pivot; adding: W = 420 + 280 = 700 N (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the distance of the centre of gravity of the log from end A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a couple.
parts.answer: A pair of equal and opposite forces whose lines of action are parallel but do not coincide (separated).

parts.label: b
parts.text: To open a water tap, a girl applies two equal and opposite forces of 6.0 N with her finger and thumb on opposite sides of the tap handle. The lines of action of the forces are 3.0 cm apart. Calculate the torque applied.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the couple turns the tap handle but gives it no linear acceleration.
parts.answer: The forces are equal and opposite so the resultant force is zero, but they produce a resultant torque.

practice.stem:
A student investigates a uniform metre rule of unknown mass M. A mass m is hung from the 10.0 cm mark and the rule is moved on a knife edge until it balances. The knife edge is then at the p cm mark. The centre of gravity of the rule is at the 50.0 cm mark.
m / kg | p / cm
0.050 | 37.1
0.080 | 32.7
0.120 | 28.7
0.160 | 25.8
0.200 | 23.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that m = M(50.0 − p)/(p − 10.0), where p is in cm. Hence state what graph to plot to obtain M from its gradient.
parts.answer: Moments about the pivot: m(p − 10.0) = M(50.0 − p). Plot m against (50.0 − p)/(p − 10.0); gradient = M (line through origin).
parts.working: B1 moments equation; B1 graph and gradient = M

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate (50.0 − p)/(p − 10.0) for each row of the table.
parts.working: B1 all values correct; B1 consistent 3 s.f. or 3 d.p.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the first and last rows (or a best-fit line) to determine M.
parts.working: M1 gradient = Δm/Δx using widely separated points; A1 M in range 0.100–0.110 kg

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one source of uncertainty in finding p and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: The balance point is hard to judge because the rule tips over a range of positions; mark the position with a pin/use a sharper knife edge and repeat to find the mean, or use larger masses so the balance is more sensitive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A uniform rectangular cabinet of height 1.20 m, depth (front to back) 0.40 m and weight 500 N stands on a rough floor. A horizontal force F, perpendicular to the back face, is applied at the top of the back face, pushing the cabinet forwards. Calculate the value of F needed to just start tipping the cabinet about its bottom front edge (assume it does not slide).
parts.working: B1 pivot at the bottom edge; weight acts 0.20 m from it; M1 F × 1.20 = 500 × 0.20; A1 F = 83.3 N

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why fitting heavy drawers low down makes the cabinet more stable.
parts.answer: The centre of gravity is lowered, so the cabinet must be tilted through a larger angle before the line of action of the weight passes outside the base.
parts.working: B1 lower centre of gravity; B1 weight's line of action stays within base for larger tilt / needs larger toppling moment

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A uniform beam of length 5.0 m and weight 400 N rests horizontally on two supports, P at one end and Q 4.0 m from P. A load of 200 N hangs from the other end of the beam, 1.0 m beyond Q. What is the upward force on the beam from support P?
A 100 N
B 150 N
C 300 N
D 500 N
parts.working: Moments about Q: R_P × 4.0 + 200 × 1.0 = 400 × 1.5 → R_P = (600 − 200)/4.0 = 100 N. D (500 N) is the force at Q (total 600 N − 100 N).

practice.stem: A market trader uses a steelyard to weigh sacks. It is a uniform rod AB of length 0.90 m and weight 6.0 N. The rod hangs from a pivot 0.10 m from end A, and the sack hangs from a hook at end A. A counterweight of 15 N can slide along the rod on the other side of the pivot. The rod is horizontal when balanced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance of the counterweight from the pivot when a sack of weight 120 N is balanced.
parts.working: C1 rod's weight acts at 0.45 m from A, i.e. 0.35 m from pivot; M1 120 × 0.10 = 6.0 × 0.35 + 15x; A1 x = 0.66 m

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the largest weight of sack that can be weighed.
parts.working: C1 counterweight at B, 0.80 m from pivot; A1 W × 0.10 = 2.1 + 12.0 → W = 141 N

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the weight of sack that is balanced when the counterweight is at the pivot, and explain why it is not zero.
parts.answer: 21 N; the rod's own weight has a moment about the pivot on the counterweight side
parts.working: A1 W × 0.10 = 6.0 × 0.35 → 21 N; B1 centre of gravity of the rod is not at the pivot, so its weight provides a moment

practice.stem: A small boat is pulled along a straight canal at constant velocity by two horizontal ropes, one from each bank. One rope makes an angle of 25° with the direction of motion and the other makes an angle of 35° with it, on the other side. The total resistive force of the water on the boat is 900 N, directly opposite to the motion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the resultant force on the boat is zero.
parts.answer: The boat moves at constant velocity, so its acceleration is zero (Newton's first law).
parts.working: B1 constant velocity → no acceleration → zero resultant force

parts.label: b
parts.text: By resolving forces perpendicular to the motion, show that T₁ sin 25° = T₂ sin 35°, where T₁ and T₂ are the tensions in the ropes at 25° and 35°.
parts.answer: There is no motion sideways, so the perpendicular components of the two tensions must be equal and opposite.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate T₁ and T₂.
parts.working: M1 T₁ cos 25° + T₂ cos 35° = 900; M1 substitute T₂ = T₁ sin 25°/sin 35° (or use triangle of forces/sine rule); A1 T₁ = 596 N, T₂ = 439 N

practice.stem: A uniform trapdoor of weight 150 N is hinged along one horizontal edge. The distance from the hinge to the opposite edge is 1.2 m. It is held open, at 50° above the horizontal, by a force F applied at the free edge at right angles to the door.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the moment of the weight of the trapdoor about the hinge.
parts.working: C1 perpendicular distance = 0.60 cos 50° = 0.386 m; A1 moment = 57.9 N m

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate F.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The door is raised further while F stays perpendicular to the door. State and explain how F changes.
parts.answer: F decreases, because the perpendicular distance from the hinge to the line of action of the weight gets smaller while F's distance stays 1.2 m.
parts.working: B1 decreases; B1 moment arm of weight (0.6 cos θ) decreases as θ increases

practice.stem:
A student hinges a metre rule at its 0.0 cm end so it can turn in a vertical plane. A spring balance hooked at the 90.0 cm mark pulls vertically upwards to hold the rule horizontal. A 2.00 N load is hung at distance x from the hinge and the balance reading F is recorded.
x / m: 0.200, 0.350, 0.500, 0.650, 0.800
F / N: 1.06, 1.39, 1.72, 2.06, 2.39

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that F × 0.900 = 2.00x + 0.500W, where W is the weight of the rule.
parts.answer: Moments about the hinge: F acts 0.900 m from the hinge; the load acts at x; the rule's weight acts at its centre, 0.500 m from the hinge.
parts.working: B1 clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments with the three distances identified

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plot F against x (or calculate) and determine the gradient and the intercept on the F axis of the best-fit line.
parts.working: B1 gradient 2.20–2.25 N m⁻¹ (theory 2.00/0.900 = 2.22); B1 intercept 0.60–0.62 N

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your intercept to determine W.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one source of error in the experiment and an improvement.
parts.answer: e.g. spring balance not exactly vertical / rule not exactly horizontal – use a set square or spirit level; or reading the balance – use a newton-meter with finer scale or a force sensor.
parts.working: B1 any valid matched error and improvement

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A light rod of length 0.50 m can turn about its centre. Two forces of 20 N act, one at each end, in opposite directions. Each force makes an angle of 60° with the rod. What is the torque of this couple?
A 5.0 N m
B 8.7 N m
C 10 N m
D 17 N m
parts.working: Perpendicular distance between the lines of action = 0.50 sin 60° = 0.433 m. Torque = one force × separation = 20 × 0.433 = 8.7 N m. C ignores the angle (20 × 0.50); D adds both forces (2 × 20 × 0.433); A uses cos 60° instead of sin 60°.

practice.stem: A uniform horizontal beam of length 2.40 m and weight 180 N is hinged to a wall at end H. Its other end E is held up by a straight cable attached to the wall above H; the cable makes an angle of 35° with the beam. A shop sign of weight 120 N hangs from the beam 2.00 m from H. The beam is in equilibrium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the tension in the cable.
parts.working: M1 moments about hinge; M1 T sin 35° × 2.4 = 180 × 1.2 + 120 × 2.0 = 456; A1 T = 331 N

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the force exerted by the hinge on the beam.
parts.answer: horizontal 271 N (away from the wall); vertical 110 N (upwards)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the magnitude of the force exerted by the hinge.

practice.stem: A uniform ladder of length 5.0 m and weight 220 N leans against a smooth vertical wall, making an angle of 65° with the rough horizontal ground. A painter of weight 700 N stands on the ladder 3.5 m from its foot (measured along the ladder). The ladder is in equilibrium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the force exerted by the wall on the ladder is horizontal.
parts.answer: The wall is smooth, so there is no friction: the only force is the normal contact force, perpendicular to the wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: By taking moments about the foot of the ladder, calculate the force exerted by the wall.
parts.working: M1 moments about foot; M1 R × 5.0 sin 65° = 220 × 2.5 cos 65° + 700 × 3.5 cos 65°; A1 R = 280 N

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the total force exerted by the ground on the ladder and its angle to the horizontal.
parts.working: B1 vertical component = 220 + 700 = 920 N; B1 friction = 280 N; A1 √(920² + 280²) = 962 N at tan⁻¹(920/280) = 73.1°

practice.stem: A decorative lamp of weight 36 N hangs at rest from two light strings fixed to a ceiling. One string makes an angle of 40° with the horizontal and the other makes an angle of 55° with the horizontal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the two conditions for the lamp to be in equilibrium.
parts.answer: Resultant force zero and resultant torque zero (the three forces are concurrent and form a closed triangle).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the tension in each string.
parts.answer: string at 40°: 20.7 N; string at 55°: 27.7 N
parts.working: M1 horizontal: T₁ cos 40° = T₂ cos 55°; M1 vertical: T₁ sin 40° + T₂ sin 55° = 36; A1 T₁ = 20.7 N; A1 T₂ = 27.7 N (or sine rule on the closed triangle: T₁ = 36 cos 55°/sin 95°)

practice.stem: A tower crane on a building site in Islamabad has a horizontal jib. On one side of the tower a load of weight 12 kN hangs 25 m from the tower; the weight of the jib, 30 kN, acts 6.0 m from the tower on the same side as the load. A concrete counterweight is fixed 8.0 m from the tower on the other side.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the weight of counterweight needed so that the resultant moment about the tower is zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The trolley now moves the 12 kN load in to 15 m from the tower, with the counterweight unchanged. Calculate the resultant moment about the tower and state its direction.
parts.answer: 1.2 × 10⁵ N m, turning towards the counterweight side
parts.working: M1 60 000 × 8.0 − (12 000 × 15 + 30 000 × 6.0); A1 1.2 × 10⁵ N m towards the counterweight

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why tower cranes are designed so that the tower itself can withstand a resultant moment in either direction.
parts.answer: The load and its position change during lifting (and the crane may be unloaded), so the moments cannot always balance.

practice.stem: A uniform rod of length 1.6 m and weight 40 N is freely hinged at its lower end to the ground. It is held at rest at 60° to the horizontal by a horizontal force F applied at its upper end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate F.
parts.working: M1 moments about hinge; M1 F × 1.6 sin 60° = 40 × 0.8 cos 60°; A1 F = 11.5 N

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude and direction of the force exerted on the rod by the hinge.
parts.working: B1 horizontal component 11.5 N (opposite to F); B1 vertical component 40 N; A1 41.6 N at 73.9° to horizontal

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the lines of action of F, the weight and the hinge force must all pass through one point.
