parts.text: Show that the work done in lifting a mass m from the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R to a height R above the surface is GMm/(2R).
parts.working: Potential at the surface V = −GM/R; at height R, V = −GM/(2R). W = m[V(2R) − V(R)] = m[−GM/(2R) + GM/R] = GMm/(2R). M1 correct potentials; M1 change in potential × m; A1 simplification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate this work for a 200 kg rover lifted from the surface of Mars to a height equal to Mars's radius. M(Mars) = 6.42 × 10²³ kg, R = 3.39 × 10⁶ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A probe is launched radially upwards from the surface of Mars. Its speed at the surface is v. It is to reach a distance 3R from the centre of Mars (where R is the radius of Mars) with zero speed. Show that v = √(4GM/(3R)).
parts.working: Energy conservation: ½v² − GM/R = 0 − GM/(3R), so ½v² = GM/R − GM/(3R) = 2GM/(3R) and v² = 4GM/(3R). M1 energy equation; A1 rearrangement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the launch speed for Mars, which has M = 6.42 × 10²³ kg and R = 3.39 × 10⁶ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The gravitational potential at the surface of a planet is −4.2 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹ and the gravitational field strength there is 6.0 N kg⁻¹. Show that the potential at the surface is V = −gR, where R is the radius of the planet.
parts.working: V = −GM/R and g = GM/R², so GM = gR² and V = −gR²/R = −gR. M1 substitution for GM; A1 result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence calculate the radius of the planet.
parts.working: R = V/g with the sign ignored: R = 4.2 × 10⁷/6.0 = 7.0 × 10⁶ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two masses lie on the same line: a planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and a moon of mass 7.0 × 10²² kg. The centres of the planet and moon are 3.84 × 10⁸ m apart. A point P lies on the line 3.0 × 10⁸ m from the planet's centre (on the side facing the moon). Calculate the gravitational potential at P. G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
parts.working: V = −G(M_p/r_p + M_m/r_m) with r_p = 3.0 × 10⁸ m and r_m = 0.84 × 10⁸ m. M1 both distances; M1 both terms; A1 V = −1.39 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the moon contributes significantly to the potential at P, and justify your answer with a calculation.
parts.answer: Only a small contribution: the Moon's term (about −5.6 × 10⁴ J kg⁻¹) is about 4% of the planet's term (about −1.33 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹), so it can be neglected in a rough estimate.
parts.working: Moon term: 7.0 × 10²² /0.84 × 10⁸ × G = 5.6 × 10⁴ J kg⁻¹, about 4% of the planet's term 1.33 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Small compared with the planet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the gravitational field strength at a point equals the negative of the gradient of the gravitational potential–distance graph at that point.
parts.answer: Field strength is the force per unit mass, and the work done per unit distance against the field equals the change in potential; so g = −dV/dr.
parts.working: 1 mark for force = −(change in potential energy per unit distance) or g = −dV/dr; 1 mark for the gradient giving the magnitude of the field.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The table gives the gravitational potential V of a planet at distances r from its centre, for a planet of mass 1.0 × 10²⁴ kg:
r / 10⁷ m: 1.0, 2.0, 3.0
V / 10⁶ J kg⁻¹: −6.67, −3.34, −2.22
Using the points at r = 1.8 × 10⁷ m and 2.2 × 10⁷ m on the curve (V = −3.71 × 10⁶ and −3.03 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹), estimate the field strength at r = 2.0 × 10⁷ m.
parts.working: Gradient ≈ (−3.03 × 10⁶ + 3.71 × 10⁶)/(4.0 × 10⁶) = 0.169 N kg⁻¹; so g ≈ 0.169 N kg⁻¹ (the field is attractive, so the magnitude is taken). Accept 0.16–0.17 with a sensible gradient estimate.

practice.stem: A meteoroid starts from rest at a distance of 4.0 × 10⁷ m from the centre of the Earth and falls directly towards it. G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Mass of the Earth = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg; radius of the Earth = 6.37 × 10⁶ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the meteoroid as it reaches the Earth's surface, ignoring air resistance.
parts.working: Loss of PE = gain in KE: GMm(1/R − 1/r) = ½mv² (M1); substitution with r = 4.0 × 10⁷ m (M1); v = 1.03 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate its kinetic energy at the surface if its mass is 2.0 × 10⁵ kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a meteoroid falling from rest at a very large distance would reach the surface with a speed equal to the escape speed.
parts.answer: It loses PE equal to GMm/R (from φ = 0 at infinity to −GM/R), which is the same energy needed to escape; so ½mv² = GMm/R gives v = √(2GM/R).
parts.working: B1 energy argument (reverse of escape); B1 identifies ½mv² = GMm/R.

practice.stem: Point P lies on the line joining the centres of the Earth and Moon, 3.46 × 10⁸ m from the centre of the Earth, where the resultant gravitational field is zero. Earth mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, Moon mass 7.35 × 10²² kg, separation 3.84 × 10⁸ m. G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gravitational potential at P.
parts.working: Potentials are scalars and add (M1); φ = −GMₑ/3.46 × 10⁸ − GMₘ/3.84 × 10⁷ (M1) = −1.28 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the potential at the Moon's surface (radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m) due to both bodies, treating the Earth's centre as 3.84 × 10⁸ m away.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the minimum energy needed to send a 10 kg capsule from the Moon's surface to P.

practice.stem: G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Mass of the Earth = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the total energy of a satellite of mass m in a circular orbit of radius r is −GMm/(2r).
parts.answer: GMm/r² = mv²/r gives KE = ½mv² = GMm/(2r); PE = −GMm/r; total = GMm/(2r) − GMm/r = −GMm/(2r).
parts.working: M1 gravitational force = centripetal force; A1 KE = GMm/2r; A1 adding PE = −GMm/r.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A satellite of mass 500 kg is moved from a circular orbit of radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m to one of radius 4.22 × 10⁷ m. Calculate the minimum energy needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A probe is launched from the surface of Mars at 4.0 km s⁻¹, directed radially away from the planet. Mars has mass 6.42 × 10²³ kg and radius 3.39 × 10⁶ m. Calculate the speed of the probe when it is at a distance 2R from the centre of Mars.
parts.working: Energy conservation: ½v₀² + V(R) = ½v₂² + V(2R). ½v₂² = ½v₀² − GM/R + GM/(2R) = 8.00 × 10⁶ − 6.32 × 10⁶ = 1.68 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. v₂ = 1.84 × 10³ m s⁻¹. M1 energy equation; M1 potentials at R and 2R; A1 1.68 × 10⁶; A1 speed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the greatest height above the surface that the probe reaches.
parts.working: ½v₀² − GM/R = −GM/r_max ⇒ GM/r_max = GM/R − ½v₀² = 1.263 × 10⁷ − 8.0 × 10⁶ = 4.63 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; r_max = 9.25 × 10⁶ m; height = r_max − R = 5.86 × 10⁶ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A capsule of mass 300 kg is released from rest at a distance 1.0 × 10⁸ m from the centre of a planet of mass 5.0 × 10²⁴ kg and falls freely towards it. Show that its speed v when it is at a distance r₂ from the centre is given by v = √(2GM(1/r₂ − 1/r₁)), where r₁ is the release distance.
parts.working: Energy conservation: 0 + (−GMm/r₁) = ½mv² − GMm/r₂ ⇒ ½v² = GM(1/r₂ − 1/r₁); v = √(2GM(1/r₂ − 1/r₁)). M1 energy equation; A1 rearrangement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the capsule at r₂ = 2.0 × 10⁷ m.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the capsule at this point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rock is launched from the surface of Venus (mass 4.87 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 6.05 × 10⁶ m) at a speed of 10.0 km s⁻¹ directed vertically upwards. Air resistance is negligible. Show that the greatest distance from the centre of Venus, r_max, satisfies ½v² − GM/R = −GM/r_max, and calculate the greatest height of the rock above the surface.
parts.working: Energy conservation between the surface and r_max: ½v² − GM/R = −GM/r_max. GM/R = 5.37 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹; GM/r_max = 5.37 × 10⁷ − 5.00 × 10⁷ = 3.69 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; r_max = 8.80 × 10⁷ m; height = 8.80 × 10⁷ − 6.05 × 10⁶ = 8.2 × 10⁷ m. Allocate 2 marks to the energy equation and 3 to the calculation.

practice.stem: Take one day to be 8.64 × 10⁴ s. G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Mass of the Earth = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg; radius of the Earth = 6.37 × 10⁶ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three features of the orbit of a geostationary satellite.
parts.answer: Period 24 hours; orbit above the equator; moves west to east (same direction as the Earth's rotation).
parts.working: 1 mark each (also accept: circular orbit; stays above the same point on the Earth).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the radius of a geostationary orbit.
parts.working: GMm/r² = mω²r with ω = 2π/T (M1); r³ = GMT²/4π² (M1); r = 4.22 × 10⁷ m (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence find the height of the satellite above the Earth's surface.

practice.stem: A space station orbits the Earth in a circular orbit 410 km above the surface. G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Mass of the Earth = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg; radius of the Earth = 6.37 × 10⁶ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that for a circular orbit T² = (4π²/GM) r³.
parts.answer: GMm/r² = mv²/r with v = 2πr/T gives GM/r = 4π²r²/T², so T² = 4π²r³/GM.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the orbital period of the space station in minutes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the orbital speed of the space station.

practice.stem: The Moon orbits the Earth in a circular orbit of radius 3.84 × 10⁸ m with a period of 27.3 days (1 day = 86 400 s). G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use these data to calculate the mass of the Earth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the orbital speed of the Moon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A satellite is in a circular orbit of radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m around the Earth, where GM = 3.98 × 10¹⁴ N m² kg⁻². Calculate the orbital speed of the satellite.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the orbital period of the satellite, in minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Astronauts inside an orbiting space station appear to float. Explain why they appear weightless even though gravity still acts on them.
parts.answer: The station and astronauts are in free fall together, both accelerating towards the Earth with the same centripetal acceleration; there is no contact force between the astronauts and the station.
parts.working: 1 mark for free fall / both falling with the same acceleration; 1 mark for no normal (contact) force so no apparent weight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the orbital speed v of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r around a planet of mass M is v = √(GM/r).
parts.working: Gravitational force provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v² = GM/r. M1 equating forces; A1 rearrangement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the orbital speed of a 500 kg satellite at a distance 4.2 × 10⁷ m from the centre of the Earth (GM = 3.98 × 10¹⁴ N m² kg⁻²).
parts.working: v = √(3.98 × 10¹⁴/4.2 × 10⁷) = 3.08 × 10³ m s⁻¹. The satellite's mass does not affect the speed.

practice.stem:
An astronomy student analyses the orbits of five moons of a ringed planet. r is the orbital radius and T the period.
r / 10⁸ m: 1.86, 2.38, 2.95, 3.77, 5.27
T / days: 0.948, 1.37, 1.89, 2.73, 4.52
lg (r / m): 8.270, 8.377, 8.470, 8.576, 8.722
lg (T / s): 4.913, 5.073, 5.213, 5.373, 5.592
G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that a graph of lg T against lg r should be a straight line of gradient 1.5.
parts.answer: T² = 4π²r³/GM gives lg T = 1.5 lg r + ½ lg(4π²/GM): straight line of gradient 1.5.
parts.working: M1 taking logs; A1 gradient 1.5 identified.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the first and last pairs of values to find the gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Taking the gradient as exactly 1.5, use the first pair of values to find the y-intercept and hence the mass of the planet.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the answer in (c) is very sensitive to small errors in the intercept.
parts.answer: M depends on 10^(−2c), so a small change in c (e.g. 0.01) changes M by about 5%; the intercept is also far from the data (long extrapolation to lg r = 0).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Satellite B orbits at four times the orbital radius of satellite A. Determine the ratio (period of B) ÷ (period of A).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the ratio (orbital speed of B) ÷ (orbital speed of A).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why satellites in the same orbit travel at the same speed regardless of their mass.
parts.answer: In GMm/r² = mv²/r the satellite mass m cancels, so v = √(GM/r) depends only on M and r.

practice.stem: Communication satellites serving Pakistan are placed in geostationary orbits. The speed of electromagnetic waves is 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a television dish receiving signals from a geostationary satellite does not need to move.
parts.answer: The satellite has the same angular velocity as the Earth (period 24 h, same direction, above the equator), so it stays above the same point and its direction from the dish is fixed.
parts.working: B1 same period/angular speed and direction; B1 so it appears stationary relative to the dish.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A signal is sent from a ground station directly below a geostationary satellite to the satellite and straight back. Calculate the time taken. Use orbital radius 4.22 × 10⁷ m and Earth radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of a low polar orbit compared with a geostationary orbit for a satellite photographing crops in Punjab.
parts.answer: It is much closer to the ground, so it gives higher-resolution images (and it passes over every part of the Earth).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A low-Earth-orbit satellite completes one orbit in 90 minutes (5.4 × 10³ s). Show that the orbital radius r satisfies r³ = GMT²/(4π²), and hence calculate the altitude of the satellite above the surface of the Earth. Take GM = 3.98 × 10¹⁴ N m² kg⁻² and the Earth's radius as 6.37 × 10⁶ m.
parts.working: GMm/r² = mω²r and ω = 2π/T, so r³ = GMT²/(4π²). r = (3.98 × 10¹⁴ × (5.4 × 10³)²/(4π²))^(1/3) = 6.65 × 10⁶ m; altitude = 6.65 × 10⁶ − 6.37 × 10⁶ ≈ 2.79 × 10⁵ m = 279 km. M1 force equation; M1 use of ω = 2π/T; M1 cube root; A1 altitude.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phobos is a moon of Mars that orbits in a circular path of radius 9.38 × 10⁶ m with a period of 0.319 days (1 day = 86 400 s). Show that the mass of Mars is given by M = 4π²r³/(GT²).
parts.working: GMm/r² = m(2π/T)²r ⇒ GM = 4π²r³/T² ⇒ M = 4π²r³/(GT²). M1 force equation with centripetal acceleration; A1 rearrangement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of Mars using these data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the period of a satellite in circular orbit does not depend on the mass of the satellite.
parts.answer: The gravitational force on the satellite is GMm/r², and the centripetal force needed is mv²/r; m cancels, giving v² = GM/r and T = 2πr/v, so the period depends only on the orbit radius and the mass of the planet.
parts.working: 1 mark for equating forces; 1 mark for the mass cancelling; 1 mark for the period depending on r and M only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the mass of a planet can be found from the period and radius of a moon's circular orbit, and state the equation used.
parts.answer: Use GMm/r² = m(4π²/T²)r, so M = 4π²r³/(GT²). Measure the orbital radius r and period T of the moon; substitute values of G, r and T to find M. 1 mark for force equation; 1 mark for rearrangement; 1 mark for measuring r and T.
parts.working: Award marks for the equation, the rearrangement and the description of measuring the period and orbital radius.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A satellite is in a circular orbit around the Earth at a radius of 6.8 × 10⁶ m. A navigation satellite orbits the Earth at a radius of 4.2 × 10⁷ m. Taking M(Earth) = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, calculate the orbital period of the navigation satellite, in hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio (period of the navigation satellite)/(period of the first satellite).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two satellites orbit the same planet. Satellite X is at radius 6.8 × 10⁶ m and satellite Y is at radius 1.2 × 10⁷ m. Calculate the ratio (period of Y)/(period of X). Explain your answer using the relationship between period and radius.
parts.working: T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2) and the ratio = (1.2 × 10⁷/6.8 × 10⁶)^(3/2) = 2.34. The higher satellite has the longer period because the gravitational force is weaker at larger radius so it moves more slowly.

practice.stem: An exoplanet orbits a distant star in a circular orbit of radius 6.8 × 10⁹ m with a period of 3.5 days (1 day = 86 400 s). G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of the star.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express this as a multiple of the Sun's mass (1.99 × 10³⁰ kg).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the orbital speed of the planet.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one assumption made in (a).
parts.answer: The orbit is circular / the planet's mass is negligible compared with the star's / the star is a point mass or uniform sphere.

practice.stem: A satellite of mass 800 kg slowly loses height because of air resistance in the upper atmosphere, moving from a circular orbit of radius 7.2 × 10⁶ m to one of radius 7.1 × 10⁶ m. G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Mass of the Earth = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in kinetic energy of the satellite.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in gravitational potential energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the energy dissipated by air resistance and explain why the satellite speeds up even though air resistance acts against its motion.
parts.answer: 3.12 × 10⁸ J; the loss of PE is twice the gain in KE, so half the PE lost becomes KE and half is dissipated
parts.working: Total energy change = ΔKE + ΔPE = −3.12 × 10⁸ J, which is dissipated (M1, A1); B1: in a lower orbit v = √(GM/r) is larger; gravity does more work than air resistance removes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A satellite of mass 2.0 × 10³ kg moves in a circular orbit of radius 6.8 × 10⁶ m around the Earth (M = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg). Show that its total mechanical energy is −GMm/(2r). Hence calculate its kinetic energy, its gravitational potential energy and its total energy.
parts.working: Ek = ½mv² = GMm/(2r) = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ × 2.0 × 10³)/(2 × 6.8 × 10⁶) = 5.86 × 10¹⁰ J. Ep = −GMm/r = −1.17 × 10¹¹ J. Total = −5.86 × 10¹⁰ J. M1 kinetic energy; M1 potential energy; A1 total; A1 explanation that Etot = −Ek.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mars has mass 6.42 × 10²³ kg and its sidereal rotation period is 88 642 s. Calculate the radius of a circular orbit around Mars in which a satellite has the same period as Mars's rotation (a synchronous orbit). G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
parts.working: r³ = GMT²/(4π²) = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.42 × 10²³ × 88 642²)/(4π²) = 8.52 × 10²¹ m³; r = 2.04 × 10⁷ m. M1 relationship; M1 substitution; A1 answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The moon Phobos orbits Mars at radius 9.38 × 10⁶ m with period 2.76 × 10⁴ s. State whether Phobos orbits faster or slower than Mars rotates, and explain with a comparison of periods.
parts.answer: Faster: Phobos's period (2.76 × 10⁴ s) is shorter than Mars's rotation period (8.86 × 10⁴ s), so it completes orbits more often than Mars turns.
parts.working: 1 mark for comparing the periods (orbit is shorter); 1 mark for 'faster'/ it lies inside the synchronous orbit radius.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A satellite of mass 800 kg is in a circular orbit of radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m around the Earth. Show that the escape speed at this radius is √2 times the orbital speed. Hence calculate the extra speed the satellite must gain (in the direction of its motion) to escape completely from the Earth. Take GM = 3.98 × 10¹⁴ N m² kg⁻².
parts.working: v_orb = √(GM/r); v_esc = √(2GM/r) = √2 v_orb. Extra speed Δv = (√2 − 1)v_orb = 0.414 × 7.54 × 10³ = 3.12 × 10³ m s⁻¹, i.e. the escape speed (1.07 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹) minus the orbital speed (7.54 × 10³ m s⁻¹). M1 escape speed expression; M1 ratio; A1 Δv.

practice.stem: Ripples on the surface of a fish pond in Faisalabad have a frequency of 2.5 Hz and a wavelength of 0.84 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the frequency of a wave.
parts.answer: The number of oscillations (wavelengths passing a point) per unit time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the definitions of speed, frequency and wavelength to show that v = fλ.
parts.answer: In one period T the wave travels one wavelength λ, so v = λ/T, and f = 1/T gives v = fλ.
parts.working: M1 distance λ in time T; A1 f = 1/T leading to v = fλ

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the waves and their period.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two points on a progressive wave of wavelength 1.20 m are 0.30 m apart along the direction of travel. What is the phase difference between the oscillations of the two points?
A 45°
B 90°
C 180°
D 270°
parts.working: Phase difference = (0.30/1.20) × 360° = 90°. 180° would need a separation of half a wavelength (0.60 m).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a progressive wave.
parts.answer: A wave that transfers energy from one place to another (without transferring matter).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Explain the meaning of
(i) displacement, (ii) amplitude, (iii) phase difference.
parts.answer: (i) distance (in a given direction) of a point from its equilibrium position; (ii) maximum displacement; (iii) the fraction of a cycle (in degrees or radians) by which one oscillation leads or lags another.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A progressive wave travels along a stretched spring. A displacement–time graph for one point on the spring shows a period of 4.0 ms. A displacement–distance graph of the spring at one instant shows a wavelength of 0.68 m. What is the speed of the wave?
A 0.17 m s⁻¹
B 2.7 m s⁻¹
C 170 m s⁻¹
D 680 m s⁻¹
parts.working: v = λ/T = 0.68 / (4.0 × 10⁻³) = 170 m s⁻¹. A comes from leaving the period in ms; B multiplies λ by T in ms.

practice.stem: A buoy floats on the sea near Gwadar harbour. As waves pass, the buoy makes 12 complete up-and-down oscillations in 60 s. The horizontal distance between adjacent wave crests is 18 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the motion of the buoy shows about the energy and the water carried by a progressive wave.
parts.answer: The wave transfers energy but the water (and buoy) only oscillates about a fixed position; no matter is transferred.
parts.working: B1: energy transferred without net transfer of the medium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency and the period of the waves.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the waves.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for a crest to travel 450 m towards the shore, assuming the speed stays constant.

practice.stem: A microphone connected to a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) detects a sound wave. The time-base is set at 2.0 ms per division and the Y-gain at 0.50 V per division. One complete cycle of the trace occupies 4.0 horizontal divisions and the vertical distance from a crest to a trough is 5.2 divisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the frequency of the sound.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the amplitude of the signal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹. Calculate the wavelength of the sound.

practice.stem: As a water wave spreads out from a boat on Keenjhar Lake its amplitude falls from 4.0 mm to 2.8 mm. The intensity at the first point is 0.80 W m⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the relationship between the intensity and the amplitude of a wave.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the intensity of the wave at the second point.

practice.stem: A transverse wave of frequency 15 Hz travels along a long rope at a speed of 6.0 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the wave.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Point X on the rope is 0.10 m from point Y and point Z is 0.20 m from Y, all along the direction of travel. Calculate the phase difference, in radians, between
(i) X and Y, (ii) Z and Y.

parts.label: c
parts.text: At one instant Y is at a crest. Describe the displacement and motion of Z at that instant.
parts.answer: Z is at a trough (maximum negative displacement) and momentarily at rest.
parts.working: B1 trough/maximum displacement in opposite direction; B1 instantaneously at rest

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The amplitude of a sound wave increases by 50 %. By what factor does its intensity increase?
A 1.5
B 2.25
C 3.0
D 4.5
parts.working: I ∝ A², so the factor is 1.5² = 2.25. 1.5 assumes intensity is proportional to amplitude.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A progressive wave of frequency 125 Hz passes two points X and Y. Point X reaches its maximum displacement 1.5 ms after point Y does. What is the phase difference between the oscillations of X and Y?
A 22.5°
B 67.5°
C 135°
D 188°
parts.working: T = 1/125 = 8.0 ms. Phase difference = (1.5/8.0) × 360° = 67.5°. D treats 0.1875 cycle as degrees ×1000; C uses half the period.

practice.stem: A signal generator drives a loudspeaker. Trace 1 of a two-beam CRO shows the signal-generator voltage and trace 2 shows the output of a microphone in front of the loudspeaker. The time-base is set at 0.10 ms per division and one cycle of each trace occupies 5.0 horizontal divisions. The microphone is moved slowly away from the loudspeaker along a straight line. Starting from a position where the two traces are in phase, it must be moved 0.170 m before the traces are next in phase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the sound.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the wavelength of the sound and calculate the speed of sound in the air.
parts.working: λ = distance between successive in-phase positions = 0.170 m (B1); v = fλ = 2000 × 0.170 = 340 m s⁻¹ (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: From an in-phase position the microphone is moved a further 0.0425 m away from the loudspeaker. Calculate the phase difference between the two traces.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a student should measure the distance moved through several successive in-phase positions rather than just one.
parts.answer: A larger distance gives a smaller percentage uncertainty in λ (divide by the number of wavelengths).

practice.stem: A small loudspeaker at an open-air event emits sound of power 0.60 W uniformly in all directions. Assume no energy is absorbed by the air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define intensity.
parts.answer: Power transmitted per unit area (perpendicular to the direction of travel).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the intensity of the sound at a distance of 5.0 m from the loudspeaker.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the distance from the loudspeaker at which the amplitude of the sound wave is half its value at 5.0 m.
parts.working: amplitude halved → intensity ÷ 4 (C1); I ∝ 1/r² so r doubles to 10 m (A1)

practice.stem: Two microphones A and B lie on a straight line from a loudspeaker, with B further from the speaker than A. Their signals are shown on a two-trace CRO with time-base 0.50 ms per division. One cycle of each trace occupies 6.0 divisions and the trace from B is shifted 1.5 divisions to the right (lagging) relative to that from A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the sound.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the phase difference between the two signals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Microphone B is moved slowly further from the source along the line from the source. Calculate the extra distance it must be moved, from its original position, before the two traces are next in phase. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹.
parts.working: λ = 340/333 = 1.02 m (C1); B lags by ¼ cycle, so it must move a further ¾λ to lag by a whole cycle (C1); 0.75 × 1.02 = 0.765 ≈ 0.77 m (A1)

practice.stem: A hospital ultrasound probe emits waves of frequency 2.5 MHz in short pulses. The speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the ultrasound in the tissue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time between emission of a pulse and detection of its echo from a boundary 6.0 cm below the probe.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each pulse contains 4 complete cycles. Calculate the length of one pulse in the tissue.

practice.stem: The intensity of sunlight just above the Earth's atmosphere is 1.36 kW m⁻². The mean distance from the Sun to the Earth is 1.50 × 10¹¹ m and from the Sun to Mars is 2.28 × 10¹¹ m. Assume that the Sun radiates uniformly in all directions and that no energy is absorbed between the planets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total power emitted by the Sun.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the intensity of sunlight at Mars.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A rover on Mars carries solar panels of total area 2.0 m² facing the Sun, with an efficiency of 22%. Calculate the electrical power produced.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the ratio (amplitude of the light wave at Mars)/(amplitude of the light wave at the Earth).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of wave cannot be polarised?
A light
B microwaves
C sound in air
D radio waves
parts.working: Only transverse waves can be polarised. Sound in air is longitudinal; the other three are electromagnetic (transverse) waves.

practice.stem: Unpolarised light of intensity 64 W m⁻² is incident on two polarising filters, one after the other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the intensity of the light after it has passed through the first polariser.
parts.working: Unpolarised light: half transmitted, 64/2 = 32 W m⁻² (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The transmission axis of the second polariser is at 30° to that of the first. Calculate the intensity of the light leaving the second polariser.
parts.working: I = I₀ cos²θ = 32 cos² 30° (C1) = 24 W m⁻² (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which observation gives evidence that light is a transverse wave?
A Light spreads out after passing through a narrow slit.
B Light can be plane-polarised by a polarising filter.
C Light changes direction when it passes from air into glass.
D Light from two slits produces bright and dark fringes.
parts.answer: B Light can be plane-polarised by a polarising filter.
parts.working: Only transverse waves can be polarised, because their oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of travel. Diffraction, refraction and interference happen with longitudinal waves too.

practice.stem: Sunlight reflected from the surface of Kinjhar Lake is partly plane-polarised. The polarised part has an intensity of 150 W m⁻² and its plane of polarisation is horizontal. A fisherman wears polarising sunglasses whose transmission axes are vertical when his head is upright.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the sunglasses reduce the glare from the lake.
parts.answer: The polarised reflected light oscillates horizontally; the vertical transmission axis is at 90° to it, so (by Malus's law, cos² 90° = 0) this light is (almost) completely absorbed.
parts.working: B1: reflected light polarised horizontally / perpendicular to axis. B1: component along the axis is zero so it is blocked.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The fisherman tilts his head sideways through 20°. Calculate the intensity of the polarised reflected light that now passes through the lenses.
parts.working: Angle between polarisation and axis = 90° − 20° = 70° (C1); I = 150 cos² 70° = 17.5 W m⁻² (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the intensity of the polarised reflected light transmitted when he tilts his head through 90°.
parts.working: Axis now parallel to plane of polarisation: cos² 0° = 1, all 150 W m⁻² passes (B1).

practice.stem: A beam of unpolarised light passes through a polarising filter P and then through a second polarising filter A (the analyser). The intensity of the light between P and A is 24 W m⁻². Filter A is rotated slowly through 360° about the direction of the beam.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the intensity of the light emerging from A varies as A is rotated through 360°.
parts.answer: It varies between a maximum (24 W m⁻²) and zero twice in each rotation: maxima when the axes are parallel (0°, 180°) and zero when they are perpendicular (90°, 270°).
parts.working: B1: two maxima and two minima (zero) per rotation. B1: maxima at axes parallel, zero at axes perpendicular.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the intensity of the light emerging from A when the angle between the transmission axes of P and A is 150°.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the intensity of the unpolarised beam before it reaches P.
parts.working: A polariser transmits half the intensity of unpolarised light: 2 × 24 = 48 W m⁻² (B1).

practice.stem: A beam of plane-polarised laser light passes through a polarising filter that can be rotated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State Malus's law.
parts.answer: The transmitted intensity I = I₀ cos²θ, where θ is the angle between the plane of polarisation of the light and the transmission axis of the filter.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the smallest angle through which the filter must be rotated from the position of maximum transmission so that the transmitted intensity is 20 % of the maximum.

practice.stem: A microwave transmitter emits plane-polarised microwaves towards a receiver connected to a meter. With the receiver aligned with the transmitter, the reading is 0.80 mA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assume the meter reading is proportional to the intensity received. Calculate the reading when the receiver is rotated through 60° about the beam axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the reading is zero when the receiver has been rotated through 90°.
parts.answer: The microwaves are plane-polarised; at 90° the receiver's axis is perpendicular to the plane of oscillation, so no component of the electric field oscillation is detected.
parts.working: B1 transmitter emits plane-polarised waves; B1 cos 90° = 0 / no component along receiver axis

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plane-polarised light passes through a polarising filter. The amplitude of the transmitted light is half the amplitude of the incident light. What is the angle between the plane of polarisation of the incident light and the transmission axis of the filter?
A 30°
B 45°
C 60°
D 75°
parts.working: Transmitted amplitude = A₀ cos θ, so cos θ = 0.5 and θ = 60°. B (45°) is the angle at which the intensity, not the amplitude, is halved.

practice.stem: A television transmitter near Murree broadcasts radio waves that are plane-polarised horizontally. A receiving aerial consists of metal rods that receive best when they are parallel to the plane of polarisation. Assume the power received is proportional to the intensity component along the rods, as in Malus's law.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by saying that the waves are polarised horizontally.
parts.answer: The oscillations of the electric field are all in one (horizontal) plane, containing the direction of travel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rods are mounted at 35° to the horizontal. Calculate the fraction of the maximum power that is received.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the angle between the rods and the horizontal for which the power received is one quarter of its maximum value.
parts.working: cos² θ = 0.25 (C1) so cos θ = 0.50 and θ = 60° (A1).

practice.stem:
A student shines light from a lamp through a polarising filter and then through a second filter (the analyser). A light meter measures the intensity I behind the analyser for different angles θ between the transmission axes.
θ / °: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80
I / lux: 480, 424, 282, 120, 14.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate cos² θ for each value of θ, giving your values to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: cos² θ = 1.000, 0.883, 0.587, 0.250, 0.030; B2 all correct, B1 for four correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a graph of I against cos² θ can be used to test whether the results obey Malus's law.
parts.answer: If I = I₀ cos² θ the graph is a straight line through the origin; the gradient equals I₀.
parts.working: B1: straight line through origin. B1: gradient = I₀ (the intensity at θ = 0).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the readings at θ = 0 and θ = 60° to determine the gradient of the graph.

parts.label: d
parts.text: At θ = 90° the meter reads 9 lux instead of zero. Suggest a cause and an improvement.
parts.answer: Light from the room (background light) reaches the meter; do the experiment in a darkened room, or shield the meter / subtract the background reading.
parts.working: B1: background (stray) light. B1: darken room / tube over meter / subtract background reading.

practice.stem: Unpolarised light of intensity 40 W m⁻² passes through polariser 1 and then polariser 3, whose transmission axis is at 90° to that of polariser 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that no light emerges from the arrangement when only polarisers 1 and 3 are present.
parts.answer: Their axes are at 90°, so I = I₁ cos² 90° = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Polariser 2 is now placed between them with its axis at 45° to both. Calculate the intensity of the light that emerges from polariser 3.
parts.working: after 1: 40/2 = 20 W m⁻² (C1); after 2: 20 cos² 45° = 10 W m⁻² (C1); after 3: 10 cos² 45° = 5.0 W m⁻² (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why inserting a filter, which absorbs light, increases the amount of light emerging.
parts.answer: Polariser 2 transmits a component of the light polarised at 45°; this light now has a component along the axis of polariser 3.
parts.working: B1 light leaving 2 polarised at 45°; B1 has non-zero component along axis of 3

practice.stem: Plane-polarised light of intensity 12.0 W m⁻² falls on a polarising filter. The angle between the plane of polarisation and the transmission axis of the filter is θ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by plane-polarised light.
parts.answer: Light in which the oscillations (of the electric field) occur in one plane only, which contains the direction of travel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the transmitted intensity when θ is (i) 20° and (ii) 70°.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why polarisation provides evidence that light is a transverse wave.
parts.answer: Only transverse waves have oscillations perpendicular to the direction of travel that can be restricted to one plane.

practice.stem: Vertically plane-polarised light of intensity 80 W m⁻² is to have its plane of polarisation turned to horizontal by passing it through a series of polarising filters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a single filter with a horizontal transmission axis cannot do this.
parts.answer: The angle would be 90°, so I = I₀ cos² 90° = 0: no light is transmitted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Three filters are used, with transmission axes at 30°, 60° and 90° to the vertical, in that order. Calculate the intensity of the light that emerges.
parts.working: Each filter is at 30° to the previous plane (M1); I = 80 × (cos² 30°)³ (M1) = 80 × 0.75³ = 33.8 W m⁻² (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Six filters are used instead, each turned 15° further than the one before, the last being horizontal. Calculate the emerging intensity.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State and explain what happens to the emerging intensity as the number of filters is increased further.
parts.answer: It increases towards 80 W m⁻²: each step angle gets smaller so cos² of the step gets closer to 1 and the product approaches 1.
parts.working: B1: tends towards (but never reaches) 80 W m⁻², with reason.

practice.stem: A beam of light is a mixture of unpolarised light of intensity I_u and plane-polarised light of intensity I_p. It passes through a polarising filter that is slowly rotated. The transmitted intensity varies between a maximum of 70 W m⁻² and a minimum of 20 W m⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the transmitted intensity never falls to zero.
parts.answer: The filter always transmits half of the unpolarised component, whatever its orientation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine I_u and I_p.
parts.answer: I_u = 40 W m⁻², I_p = 50 W m⁻²
parts.working: Minimum: I_u/2 = 20, so I_u = 40 W m⁻² (M1 A1). Maximum: I_u/2 + I_p = 70, so I_p = 50 W m⁻² (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the beam's intensity that is polarised.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the transmitted intensity when the filter is at 45° to the position that gives the maximum.

practice.stem: Unpolarised light passes through two polarising filters. The second filter can be rotated about the direction of the beam.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The transmitted intensity is 15% of the intensity of the unpolarised light. Calculate the angle between the transmission axes of the filters.
parts.working: After first filter: 0.50 I₀ (B1). 0.50 cos² θ = 0.15 so cos² θ = 0.30 (M1); θ = 56.8° (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the largest possible fraction of the unpolarised intensity that the pair of filters can transmit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The second filter is now made to rotate steadily at 2.0 revolutions per second. Calculate the number of times per second the transmitted intensity falls to zero, and the time between successive zeros.
parts.working: Two zeros per revolution × 2.0 rev s⁻¹ = 4 s⁻¹ (B1); interval = 1/4 = 0.25 s (B1).

practice.stem: An ambulance travels at 25 m s⁻¹ along a straight road in Rawalpindi. Its siren emits sound of frequency 950 Hz. A man stands at the roadside. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency heard by the man as the ambulance approaches.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency he hears after it has passed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of wavefronts, why a stationary observer hears a higher frequency when a sound source moves towards him.
parts.answer: The source moves towards the observer between emitting successive wavefronts, so the wavefronts in front are closer together; the wavelength is shorter and, with the same wave speed, more wavefronts arrive per second.
parts.working: B1 wavefronts bunched/shorter wavelength; B1 same speed so higher frequency received

parts.label: b
parts.text: A police car with a 700 Hz siren approaches at 30 m s⁻¹. The speed of sound is 330 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency heard.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A car sounds its horn, of frequency 400 Hz, while travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ directly towards a stationary observer. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency does the observer hear?
A 376 Hz
B 400 Hz
C 424 Hz
D 425 Hz
parts.working: f₀ = f_s v/(v − v_s) = 400 × 340/320 = 425 Hz. A uses f_s(v − v_s)/v, which inverts the ratio; C uses f_s(v + v_s)/v, which is not the moving-source formula.

practice.stem: A delivery drone carries a buzzer that emits sound of frequency 2000 Hz. The drone flies at a constant 16 m s⁻¹ directly towards a girl standing in a park, passes over her and flies directly away. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency heard by the girl as the drone approaches.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the sound in the air in front of the drone.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the frequency heard by the girl as the drone moves away from her.

practice.stem: A motorcyclist rides at a constant 30 m s⁻¹ along a straight road past a stationary listener. The engine emits a note of constant frequency. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the pitch heard by the listener changes as the motorcycle approaches, passes and moves away.
parts.answer: Constant higher pitch while approaching; falls quickly as it passes; constant lower pitch while moving away.
parts.working: B1: higher (constant) on approach, lower (constant) when receding. B1: sudden drop as it passes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The listener hears a frequency of 250 Hz as the motorcycle approaches. Calculate the frequency emitted by the engine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the frequency heard as the motorcycle moves away.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A source emitting sound of frequency 500 Hz moves directly away from a stationary observer, who hears a frequency of 480 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the speed of the source?
A 13.6 m s⁻¹
B 14.2 m s⁻¹
C 20.0 m s⁻¹
D 34.0 m s⁻¹
parts.working: 480 = 500 × 340/(340 + v_s) → 340 + v_s = 354.2 → v_s = 14.2 m s⁻¹. 13.6 m s⁻¹ uses 340 × (20/500), the formula for a moving observer.

practice.stem: A girl on a station platform hears the horn of a train passing at constant speed without stopping. The frequency she hears is 560 Hz as the train approaches and 480 Hz as it moves away. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the speed of the train is about 26 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency emitted by the horn.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A source of sound moves at constant speed directly towards a stationary observer. Compared with when the source is at rest, what happens to the wavelength of the sound reaching the observer and to the speed of that sound in the air?
A wavelength decreases, speed unchanged
B wavelength decreases, speed increases
C wavelength unchanged, speed increases
D wavelength increases, speed unchanged
parts.working: The source moves after each wavefront, so the wavefronts ahead are closer together (shorter λ). The speed depends only on the air, not on the source, so B is wrong.

practice.stem: A train on a straight track near Jhelum sounds its horn, which emits a frequency of 800 Hz. A microphone beside the track records a frequency of 880 Hz while the train approaches at constant speed. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the train.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency recorded after the train has passed the microphone.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the change in frequency on approach (80 Hz) is greater than the change after passing.
parts.answer: On approach the denominator (v − v_s) is smaller than (v + v_s) on receding, so the fractional change is larger on approach.

practice.stem: On a hot afternoon in Jacobabad, students measure the speed of sound using the Doppler effect. A buzzer of frequency 500.0 Hz is fixed to a car that drives directly towards a microphone at 25.0 m s⁻¹. The microphone records a frequency of 538.0 Hz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the speed of sound v is given by v = v_s f₀/(f₀ − f_s), where v_s is the speed of the source, f₀ the observed frequency and f_s the emitted frequency.
parts.answer: f₀(v − v_s) = f_s v so v(f₀ − f_s) = f₀ v_s, giving v = v_s f₀/(f₀ − f_s).
parts.working: M1: start from f₀ = f_s v/(v − v_s). A1: rearrangement shown.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of sound.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The observed frequency has an uncertainty of ±0.5 Hz. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in (f₀ − f_s), and explain why this method gives an imprecise value of v.
parts.answer: 1.3%; the difference (f₀ − f_s) is small, so a small uncertainty in f₀ gives a large percentage uncertainty in v.
parts.working: 0.5/38.0 × 100 = 1.3% (A1). B1: small difference of two similar values.

practice.stem: A fire engine starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2.0 m s⁻² along a straight road directly towards a stationary observer. Its siren emits sound of frequency 1200 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency heard by the observer for the sound emitted when the fire engine has been moving for 5.0 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency heard for the sound emitted when it has been moving for 10.0 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the frequency heard by the observer changes while the fire engine is accelerating towards him.
parts.answer: It rises continuously (the pitch keeps increasing) because the source speed keeps increasing.

practice.stem: A small loudspeaker emitting a 1200 Hz note is attached to the end of a rod and moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.80 m at 2.5 revolutions per second. A student stands far away in the plane of the circle. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the loudspeaker.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum and minimum frequencies heard by the student.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the position of the loudspeaker when the student hears the frequency 1200 Hz. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: When it is moving perpendicular to the line to the student (nearest and furthest points of the circle), there is no velocity component towards or away from her.

practice.stem: A source emitting sound of frequency 600 Hz moves at constant speed v_s directly towards a stationary observer. The speed of sound in still air is 340 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed v_s for which the observer hears a frequency of 1200 Hz.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The source passes the observer and moves away at the same speed. Calculate the frequency now heard.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what happens to the spacing of the wavefronts in front of the source as v_s approaches 340 m s⁻¹, and state what the Doppler equation predicts.
parts.answer: The wavefronts in front crowd together, their spacing (wavelength) tending to zero; the equation predicts the observed frequency tends to infinity (a shock wave forms).
parts.working: B1: spacing → 0 / wavefronts pile up. B1: f₀ → ∞ (formula breaks down).

practice.stem: A stationary listener hears the horn of a passing car. The frequency heard while the car approaches is 1.25 times the frequency heard while it moves away. The car travels at constant speed and the speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the speed of the car is v/9, where v is the speed of sound.
parts.working: M1: ratio f_app/f_rec = (v + v_s)/(v − v_s). M1: rearrangement. A1: v_s = v/9.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the car.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The frequency heard while the car approaches is 450 Hz. Calculate the frequency emitted by the horn.

practice.stem: A small buzzer emitting sound of frequency 3000 Hz is released from rest at the edge of a high cliff and falls vertically. A microphone at the top of the cliff, next to the release point, records the sound. Air resistance is negligible, g = 9.81 m s⁻² and the speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency recorded for sound emitted 2.0 s after release.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time after release at which this sound reaches the microphone.
parts.working: Distance fallen = ½gt² = 19.6 m (C1); travel time 19.6/340 = 0.058 s, so arrives at 2.06 s (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the frequency recorded decreases continuously as the buzzer falls.
parts.answer: The buzzer's speed away from the microphone keeps increasing, so v + v_s increases and f₀ decreases.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which list places the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing wavelength?
A γ-rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio waves
B radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, γ-rays
C γ-rays, ultraviolet, X-rays, visible, microwaves, infrared, radio waves
D X-rays, γ-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, radio waves, microwaves
parts.answer: A γ-rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio waves
parts.working: γ-rays have the shortest wavelength and radio waves the longest. B is the same list in order of decreasing wavelength.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the approximate range of wavelengths of visible light in a vacuum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of orange light of wavelength 600 nm in a vacuum.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the region of the spectrum for a wavelength of (i) 3 cm, (ii) 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Electromagnetic radiation has a wavelength in a vacuum of 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. In which region of the electromagnetic spectrum is it?
A microwaves
B infrared
C ultraviolet
D X-rays
parts.working: Visible light is about 400–700 nm; 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m = 1000 nm is just longer than red, so infrared. Ultraviolet is shorter than 400 nm.

practice.stem: A microwave oven uses electromagnetic waves of frequency 2.45 GHz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of these waves in a vacuum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the speed of all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one use of (i) X-rays, (ii) ultraviolet radiation.
parts.answer: (i) imaging bones / medical diagnosis or airport baggage scanning; (ii) sterilising water or equipment / detecting forged banknotes.

practice.stem:
Three electromagnetic waves in a vacuum have frequencies of
P: 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz
Q: 3.0 × 10¹⁸ Hz
R: 1.0 × 10⁸ Hz

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of each wave.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum for each wave.
parts.answer: P visible (orange-red) light; Q X-rays; R radio waves

practice.stem: The radar at an airport near Islamabad sends out a short pulse of electromagnetic waves of wavelength 10 cm. The pulse is reflected by an aircraft and the echo is received 0.24 ms after the pulse was sent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the radar waves and name the region of the spectrum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the distance from the radar to the aircraft.
parts.working: Pulse travels there and back: d = ct/2 (M1) = 3.00 × 10⁸ × 0.24 × 10⁻³/2 = 3.6 × 10⁴ m (36 km) (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two properties shared by all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum.
parts.answer: Any two: same speed 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; transverse; can be polarised; travel through a vacuum; consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time for a radio signal to travel from the Earth to the Moon, a distance of 3.84 × 10⁸ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An electromagnetic wave has a frequency of 1.0 × 10¹⁰ Hz. In which region of the spectrum is it?
A radio waves
B microwaves
C infrared
D ultraviolet
parts.working: λ = 3.0 × 10⁸/1.0 × 10¹⁰ = 0.030 m = 3 cm, which is in the microwave region. Radio waves have wavelengths longer than about 0.1–1 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the ratio (frequency of ultraviolet radiation of wavelength 200 nm)/(frequency of infrared radiation of wavelength 10 µm)?
A 0.020
B 5.0
C 50
D 500
parts.working: f ∝ 1/λ, so ratio = (10 × 10⁻⁶)/(200 × 10⁻⁹) = 50. A is the inverse; D comes from treating µm as 10⁻⁵ m.

practice.stem: A telephone call between Karachi and London is relayed by a communications satellite that is 3.58 × 10⁷ m above the Earth's surface. Assume the satellite is at this distance from both the speaker and the listener.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time for the signal to travel from the speaker to the listener.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The listener replies immediately. Calculate the shortest time between the speaker finishing a question and hearing the start of the reply.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the signal is sent using microwaves or radio waves rather than visible light.
parts.answer: They pass through the atmosphere and clouds with little absorption/scattering (visible light is blocked by cloud).

practice.stem: Red light from a laser has a wavelength of 650 nm in a vacuum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the light.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of complete wavelengths of this light in a distance of 1.0 mm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the three regions of the electromagnetic spectrum whose radiation is most dangerous to living cells, and state a reason.
parts.answer: Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays; they have high frequency (high photon energy) and can ionise atoms / damage DNA.
parts.working: B1: all three regions. B1: ionising / high-energy reason.

practice.stem: A home router in Karachi transmits Wi-Fi signals at 2.4 GHz, and a local FM radio station broadcasts at 101 MHz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of (i) the Wi-Fi signal, (ii) the FM radio signal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A navigation satellite is 2.02 × 10⁷ m above a receiver. Calculate the time for its signal to reach the receiver.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A timing error of 1.0 µs is made in measuring this travel time. Calculate the resulting error in the calculated distance.

practice.stem: Orange light of wavelength 600 nm in a vacuum enters a glass block, in which the speed of light is 2.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the light.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the frequency changes when the light enters the glass, and calculate the wavelength in the glass.
parts.working: Frequency set by source, unchanged (B1); λ = v/f = 2.0 × 10⁸/5.0 × 10¹⁴ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ m (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how much longer the light takes to travel through 5.0 mm of the glass than through 5.0 mm of vacuum.
parts.working: t_glass = 2.5 × 10⁻¹¹ s, t_vac = 1.67 × 10⁻¹¹ s (C1); difference = 8.33 × 10⁻¹² s (A1).

practice.stem: A solar flare on the Sun emits X-rays, visible light and a stream of charged particles at the same instant. The Sun is 1.50 × 10¹¹ m from the Earth. The particles travel at an average speed of 4.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the X-rays and the visible light from the flare reach the Earth at the same time.
parts.answer: Both are electromagnetic waves and all EM waves travel at the same speed (c) in a vacuum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the light to reach the Earth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how long after the light the particles arrive. Give your answer in hours.

practice.stem: A laser rangefinder used by surveyors on the Karakoram Highway emits short pulses of radiation of wavelength 1064 nm. It measures distance by timing how long a pulse takes to return after reflection from a target.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum of this radiation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The distance to a target is to be measured to within ±1.0 cm. Calculate the uncertainty in the time measurement that this requires.
parts.working: Light travels the extra 1.0 cm twice: Δt = 2 × 0.010/3.00 × 10⁸ (M1) = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ s (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each pulse lasts 5.0 ns. Calculate the length of a pulse in the air and the number of wavelengths it contains. (Assume the speed in air is 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave.
parts.answer: Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer. Longitudinal: oscillations parallel to the direction of energy transfer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of each type of wave.
parts.answer: Transverse: light / any EM wave / waves on a string. Longitudinal: sound / ultrasound / P-waves.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which wave do the particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction in which the wave transfers energy?
A light from a lamp
B a ripple on water
C sound in air
D a wave on a guitar string
parts.working: Sound in air is longitudinal. A guitar-string wave is transverse: the string moves perpendicular to the wave direction.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is a longitudinal wave?
A microwaves in a microwave oven
B ultrasound travelling through body tissue
C a wave on a stretched guitar string
D light from a laser
parts.answer: B ultrasound travelling through body tissue
parts.working: Ultrasound is a sound wave: the tissue particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Microwaves, light and string waves are transverse.

practice.stem: A student shakes one end of a long rope up and down to send a transverse wave along it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the motion of a small piece of the rope as the wave passes.
parts.answer: It oscillates up and down about its rest position, perpendicular to the direction the wave travels; it does not move along the rope.
parts.working: B1: oscillates about fixed position. B1: perpendicular to direction of travel / energy transfer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For a longitudinal wave, state what is meant by its wavelength in terms of compressions.
parts.answer: The distance between the centres of two adjacent compressions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student makes 3.0 oscillations per second and there are exactly 6 complete waves along 4.2 m of the rope. Calculate the speed of the wave.

practice.stem: A longitudinal wave is sent along a stretched slinky spring by a vibrator of frequency 4.0 Hz. At one instant the centres of four successive compressions are at distances of 0.10 m, 0.55 m, 1.00 m and 1.45 m from the vibrator.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the wavelength.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the wave.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time for a compression to travel from 0.10 m to 1.45 m.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the direction of oscillation of the coils of the spring relative to the direction of travel of the wave.
parts.answer: Parallel (backwards and forwards along the spring).

practice.stem: In a railway yard in Lahore, a worker strikes one end of a straight steel rail 600 m long with a hammer. A second worker at the other end hears two sounds: one through the rail and one through the air. The speed of sound is 5100 m s⁻¹ in steel and 340 m s⁻¹ in air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time interval between the two sounds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether sound in air is a transverse or a longitudinal wave, and explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
parts.answer: Longitudinal; sound needs particles (a medium) to vibrate and pass on the energy, and a vacuum has none.
parts.working: B1: longitudinal. B1: needs a medium / particles.

practice.stem: One end of a long stretched slinky spring is pushed and pulled along its length at 2.5 Hz. The distance between the centres of two adjacent compressions is 0.72 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a compression and a rarefaction.
parts.answer: Compression: region where the coils (particles) are closer together than normal; rarefaction: region where they are further apart than normal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the wave.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the distance between a compression and the nearest rarefaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz travels through air. At time t = 0 the centre of a compression is at point P. What is at point P at time t = 1.0 ms?
A the centre of a compression
B the centre of a rarefaction
C a point of normal pressure, with the pressure falling
D the same compression, which has stopped moving
parts.answer: B the centre of a rarefaction
parts.working: T = 1/500 = 2.0 ms, so 1.0 ms is half a period; the pressure at P has gone through half a cycle, from maximum to minimum: a rarefaction. A would need a whole period.

practice.stem: A fishing boat off the coast of Karachi uses an echo sounder. A pulse of sound is sent vertically down and the echo from the sea bed returns after 0.084 s. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depth of the sea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of wave used and the direction of oscillation of the water particles.
parts.answer: Longitudinal; particles oscillate parallel to the direction of travel (vertical here).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why light from the Sun can reach the Earth through space but sound from the Sun cannot.
parts.answer: Light is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium; sound is a mechanical wave that needs particles, and space is (almost) a vacuum.
parts.working: B1: EM waves travel through vacuum. B1: sound needs a medium.

practice.stem: A transverse wave of frequency 5.0 Hz travels to the right along a long rope. At one instant point P on the rope is at a crest. Point Q is a quarter of a wavelength to the right of P, and point R is half a wavelength to the right of P.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the displacement of Q and of R at this instant (zero, maximum positive or maximum negative).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction in which Q is moving at this instant. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Upwards: the crest at P is travelling to the right towards Q, so Q is about to rise to a crest.
parts.working: B1: upwards. B1: next displacement at Q is that now at P (crest approaching).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the phase difference between the oscillations of P and R.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the time after this instant at which Q first reaches a crest.

practice.stem: Plane water waves are produced in a ripple tank. In the deep part of the tank their speed is 0.30 m s⁻¹ and their wavelength is 1.5 cm. The waves then pass into a shallow region, where the wavelength is 1.0 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the waves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the frequency is the same in both regions.
parts.answer: The frequency is set by the source (vibrator); the number of waves arriving at the boundary each second equals the number leaving.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the waves in the shallow region.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the time for a wavefront to cross 12 cm of the shallow region.

practice.stem: An earthquake produces longitudinal P-waves travelling at 6.0 km s⁻¹ and transverse S-waves travelling at 3.5 km s⁻¹ through rock. A seismic station in Quetta records the S-waves arriving 24 s after the P-waves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance from the earthquake to the station.

parts.label: b
parts.text: S-waves do not pass through the Earth's liquid outer core. Suggest why.
parts.answer: S-waves are transverse; a liquid cannot support the sideways (shear) forces needed for transverse waves.

practice.stem:
A longitudinal wave of frequency 850 Hz travels to the right through air. At one instant the displacements of air particles from their rest positions are as follows (positive = displaced to the right).
rest position x / cm: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40
displacement / mm: 0, +2.1, +3.0, +2.1, 0, −2.1, −3.0, −2.1, 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the amplitude and the wavelength of the wave.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the rest position of the centre of a compression between x = 0 and x = 40 cm. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: x = 20 cm: particles just to its left are displaced to the right and particles just to its right are displaced to the left, so they crowd together there.
parts.working: B1: 20 cm. B1: neighbours displaced towards this point.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the positions of the centres of rarefactions in the same range.
parts.working: B1: particles displaced away from these points.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the wave.

practice.stem: A sound wave of frequency 680 Hz travels through air at 340 m s⁻¹. The amplitude of oscillation of the air particles is 0.10 mm. Two particles X and Y are 0.25 m apart along the direction of travel when no sound is present.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength and hence the phase difference between the oscillations of X and Y.
parts.working: λ = 340/680 = 0.50 m (A1); 0.25 m = λ/2 so phase difference 180° (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the minimum and the maximum separation of X and Y while the sound passes.
parts.working: In antiphase they move in opposite directions: separation varies by 2 × 0.10 mm either way (M1): 250.0 ± 0.2 mm (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the separation of two particles that are 0.50 m apart at rest, and explain why it does not change.
parts.answer: Always 0.50 m: they are one wavelength apart, in phase, so they have the same displacement at every instant.

practice.stem: A loudspeaker sends a continuous sound wave along a tube. A pressure sensor moved along the tube finds the centres of compressions (maximum pressure) at 0.20 m and 1.00 m from the loudspeaker, with the pressure in between never as high again.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the wavelength and state the position of the centre of the rarefaction between the two compressions.
parts.working: λ = 1.00 − 0.20 = 0.80 m (B1); rarefaction halfway, at 0.60 m (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: At the centre of a compression the air particles have zero displacement. State two positions between 0.20 m and 1.00 m where the particle displacement is a maximum, and the pressure there at that instant.
parts.answer: 0.40 m and 0.80 m (midway between compression and rarefaction); the pressure there is normal (atmospheric).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence state the phase difference between the variation of particle displacement and the variation of pressure along the wave.
parts.answer: 90° (a quarter of a cycle, π/2 rad)

practice.stem: Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define electric potential at a point.
parts.answer: The work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small test charge from infinity to the point.
parts.working: B1 work done per unit positive charge; B1 from infinity

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electric potential 0.30 m from a point charge of +5.0 nC.

practice.stem: Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an equipotential surface.
parts.answer: A surface on which every point has the same electric potential.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the angle between field lines and equipotential surfaces, and explain why no work is done moving a charge along an equipotential.
parts.answer: 90°; there is no potential difference between points on it, so W = qΔV = 0.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference between two points at 0.10 m and 0.20 m from a point charge of +4.0 nC.

practice.stem: Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the electric potential near an isolated negative charge is negative.
parts.answer: Potential is zero at infinity; a positive test charge is attracted, so work is done by the field (negative work done on it) as it is brought in from infinity.
parts.working: B1 zero at infinity; B1 attraction → work done on charge is negative

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electric potential energy of an electron and a proton separated by 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the electric potential at a point.
parts.answer: The electric potential at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small test charge from infinity to that point.
parts.working: 1 mark for work done; 1 mark for per unit positive charge from infinity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A point charge of +6.0 nC is in a vacuum. Calculate the electric potential at a point 0.15 m from the charge. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the potential at 0.30 m from the charge and explain why it is not double the value in (b).
parts.answer: 180 V; the potential is inversely proportional to r, so doubling r halves V (it does not double).
parts.working: V = 360/2 = 180 V. 1 mark for the value; 1 mark for V ∝ 1/r, so doubling the distance halves the potential.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron is at rest at a point where the electric potential is −50 V. It is moved to a point where the potential is +120 V. Explain, in terms of the electric potential energy, why the electron gains kinetic energy.
parts.answer: The potential energy of a negative charge is U = qV, so it is higher at lower potential. Moving to higher potential lowers its electric potential energy, and that energy is converted into kinetic energy (energy is conserved).
parts.working: 1 mark for U = qV with q negative; 1 mark for energy conservation with KE increasing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in electric potential energy of the electron.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the electron at the point where the potential is +120 V, using the energy change in (b).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two protons are held 0.50 nm apart. Explain why work must be done to bring them closer together, and state the sign of their electric potential energy.
parts.answer: Like charges repel, so work must be done against the repulsive force to bring them closer; the electric potential energy is positive (energy must be supplied to the system).
parts.working: 1 mark for repulsion requiring work; 1 mark for positive potential energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electric potential energy of the pair of protons. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Express the answer in electron-volts.

practice.stem: An isolated metal sphere of radius 0.10 m carries a charge of +8.0 nC. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the potential at the surface of the sphere.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the potential at a point 0.40 m from the centre of the sphere.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the work done in moving a charge of +2.0 nC from the point 0.40 m from the centre to the surface of the sphere.

practice.stem: An alpha particle with kinetic energy 5.0 MeV travels directly towards a gold nucleus. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the alpha particle slows down as it approaches the nucleus.
parts.answer: It is repelled by the positive nucleus; its kinetic energy is converted to electric potential energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the distance of closest approach. The charge of the gold nucleus is +79e and of the alpha particle +2e. Treat the nucleus as fixed.

practice.stem: The electric potential is 900 V at a distance of 0.20 m from a point charge and 600 V at 0.30 m from it. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the data are consistent with a point charge, and calculate the charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the relationship between field strength and potential gradient to calculate the field strength at 0.20 m from the charge.

practice.stem: An electron starts from rest at a point where the electric potential is −200 V and moves, under electric forces only, to a point where the potential is +300 V. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the gain in kinetic energy of the electron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate its final speed.

practice.stem: Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one similarity and one difference between gravitational potential near a mass and electric potential near a positive point charge.
parts.answer: Similarity: both ∝ 1/r and both zero at infinity. Difference: gravitational potential is always negative; potential near a positive charge is positive.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the work done in bringing a charge of +1.5 µC from infinity to a point 0.25 m from a fixed point charge of +40 nC.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A point charge of +2.0 nC is fixed at the origin and a point charge of −3.0 nC is fixed at x = 0.40 m on the same line. Calculate the electric potential at the midpoint between the charges.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electric potential at the point P, which is on the same line at x = 0.30 m.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that there is a point between the charges where the potential is zero, and find its distance from the +2.0 nC charge.
parts.working: 1 mark for setting the two potentials equal in magnitude; 1 mark for x = 0.16 m (the positive charge is nearer to the zero point).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A particle of mass 3.0 mg and charge +2.0 μC is released from rest at a point where the electric potential is +400 V. Calculate the kinetic energy it gains when it reaches a point where the potential is +100 V.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the particle at this point.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the result depends on the path taken between the two points.
parts.answer: No. Electric force is conservative, so the work done (and the kinetic energy gained) depends only on the potential difference.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A singly-charged positive ion of mass 2.99 × 10⁻²⁶ kg is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 1.5 kV in a vacuum. Explain why its kinetic energy after acceleration equals qV.
parts.answer: The work done by the electric field on the ion equals the change in electric potential energy, qV. With no other forces doing work, all of this becomes kinetic energy: ΔKE = qV.
parts.working: 1 mark for work done by the field equals qΔV; 1 mark for energy conservation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the ion after acceleration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the acceleration must take place in a vacuum.
parts.answer: Gas molecules would collide with the ion and reduce its speed, so the ion would not gain the full kinetic energy qV.

practice.stem: Two small spheres, each of mass 2.0 g and charge +3.0 µC, are held 0.10 m apart. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric potential energy of the system at the start.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The spheres are released from rest and move apart along a frictionless horizontal track. Calculate the speed of each sphere when they are very far apart.
parts.working: by symmetry each gets half the energy: 0.405 J (C1); ½ × 0.0020 × v² = 0.405 (C1); v = 20 m s⁻¹ (A1)

practice.stem: A point charge of +4.0 nC is fixed at A and a point charge of −1.0 nC is fixed at B, 0.30 m from A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance from A of the point between A and B where the electric potential is zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the electric field strength at this point is not zero.
parts.answer: E is the (negative) potential gradient, not the potential; between opposite charges the fields of both point in the same direction (from A towards B), so they add.
parts.working: B1 E = −dV/dx / V = 0 does not mean gradient zero; B1 fields in same direction

practice.stem: An isolated conducting sphere of radius 0.050 m carries a charge of +6.0 nC in a vacuum. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric potential at the surface of the sphere.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A proton is released from rest at the surface. Calculate its speed when it is very far from the sphere.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the proton's acceleration decreases as it moves away.
parts.answer: The field strength (force) decreases with distance as 1/r².
