practice.stem: A hollow metal sphere of radius 0.12 m is charged so that the potential at its surface is 6000 V. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge on the sphere.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength just outside the surface.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the electric potential and the field strength at the centre of the sphere.
parts.working: B1 V same as surface (6000 V); B1 E = 0 inside a conductor

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the potential at 0.30 m from the centre.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Four point charges are fixed at the corners of a square ABCD of side 0.20 m. Charges of +5.0 nC are at A, B and C, and a charge of −3.0 nC is at D. Show that the electric potential at the centre of the square is about 760 V.
parts.answer: Distance from centre to each corner = 0.20/√2 = 0.1414 m. V = K Σq/d = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (15 − 3) × 10⁻⁹/0.1414 = 763 V ≈ 760 V.
parts.working: 1 mark for the distance to each corner; 1 mark for the sum of charges (+12 nC); 1 mark for V ≈ 760 V.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the work done in bringing a charge of +2.0 nC from infinity to the centre of the square.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the sign of the potential at the centre of the square and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Positive: the net charge of the four point charges is +12 nC, so the sum of the kQ/r terms is positive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An isolated metal sphere of radius 0.050 m has a potential of 600 V at its surface. Calculate the charge on the sphere.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the potential at a distance 0.10 m from the centre of the sphere.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength at 0.10 m from the centre.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the potential inside the sphere is the same everywhere and equal to 600 V.
parts.answer: The electric field inside a charged conductor is zero, so no work is done in moving a test charge within the interior; the potential is therefore constant and equal to the surface value.
parts.working: 1 mark for zero field inside a conductor; 1 mark for no work done so potential is constant.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: Two small charged spheres, of charges +3.0 nC and −5.0 nC, are held with their centres 4.0 cm apart in air. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State Coulomb's law.
parts.answer: The force between two point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.
parts.working: B1 ∝ product of charges; B1 ∝ 1/separation² (point charges)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the force between the charges and state whether it is attractive or repulsive.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: An isolated point charge of +12 nC is in a vacuum. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define electric field strength.
parts.answer: Force per unit positive charge (acting on a small stationary charge).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength at a point 0.25 m from the charge.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the force on an electron at this point and state its direction.
parts.working: F = eE = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1.73 × 10³ = 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ N (B1); towards the positive charge (B1)

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pattern of electric field lines around an isolated positive point charge.
parts.answer: Straight radial lines, pointing outwards from the charge, getting further apart with distance.
parts.working: B1 radial/straight lines outwards; B1 spacing increases with distance

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the field lines show where the field is strongest.
parts.answer: The field is strongest where the lines are closest together (near the charge).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The field strength at a distance r from the charge is E. Calculate the field strength at distance 3r, in terms of E.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: A thundercloud model treats a region of charge as a point charge of −6.0 µC. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength 2.0 m from the charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction of the field at this point.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two point charges of +8.0 μC and +2.0 μC are in a vacuum 0.60 m apart. Calculate the magnitude of the electric force between them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction of the force on the +2.0 μC charge.
parts.answer: Away from the +8.0 μC charge (repulsion, since the charges have the same sign).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the magnitude and direction of the force on the +8.0 μC charge and name the law that relates them.
parts.answer: 0.40 N, directed towards the +2.0 μC charge (equal and opposite)
parts.working: Newton's third law: the forces on the two charges are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define electric field strength.
parts.answer: The electric field strength at a point is the force per unit positive charge placed at that point.
parts.working: 1 mark for force; 1 mark for per unit positive charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A point charge of +4.0 μC is in a vacuum. Calculate the distance from the charge at which the electric field strength is 500 N C⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the direction of the field at this point.
parts.answer: Radially outwards, away from the positive charge.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: The spherical metal dome of a Van de Graaff generator in a school science club has radius 0.15 m. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the charge on the sphere may be treated as a point charge at its centre for points outside the sphere.
parts.answer: The charge is distributed uniformly over the surface (by symmetry), so outside the sphere the field is the same as for a point charge at the centre.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Air breaks down when the field strength exceeds 3.0 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹. Calculate the maximum charge the dome can hold.

parts.label: c
parts.text: With this maximum charge, calculate the field strength at a distance of 0.45 m from the centre of the dome.
parts.working: r is 3 times larger, E ∝ 1/r² (C1); E = 3.0 × 10⁶/9 = 3.3 × 10⁵ V m⁻¹ (A1)

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: A point charge of +4.0 µC is fixed at point A and a point charge of +1.0 µC is fixed at point B, 0.30 m from A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why there is a point between the charges where the electric field strength is zero.
parts.answer: Both charges are positive, so their fields point in opposite directions between them and can cancel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the distance of this point from A.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the ratio (electric force)/(gravitational force) between two protons is independent of their separation.
parts.answer: Both forces are proportional to 1/r², so r cancels in the ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate this ratio. The gravitational constant G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why gravitational forces, not electric forces, dominate the motion of planets.
parts.answer: Planets are electrically neutral overall, so the net electric force is negligible, but mass is always positive so gravity always attracts.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: Two identical small conducting spheres, each of mass 0.20 g, hang from the same point on insulating threads. They are given equal charges and come to rest with each thread at 10° to the vertical. The distance between the centres of the spheres is then 5.0 cm. g = 9.81 m s⁻². Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the electric force between the spheres is about 3.5 × 10⁻⁴ N.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge on each sphere.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three point charges lie on the x-axis in a vacuum: +2.0 nC at x = 0, +3.0 nC at x = 0.20 m and −4.0 nC at x = 0.50 m. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the electric force from the +2.0 nC charge on the +3.0 nC charge.
parts.answer: 1.35 × 10⁻⁶ N (≈ 1.35 × 10⁻⁶ N), in the +x direction (away from the +2.0 nC charge)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the electric force from the −4.0 nC charge on the +3.0 nC charge.
parts.working: F = K(3.0 × 10⁻⁹)(4.0 × 10⁻⁹)/0.30² = 1.20 × 10⁻⁶ N, attractive (towards the −4.0 nC charge at +x).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the resultant force on the +3.0 nC charge.
parts.working: Both forces point in +x, so F = 1.35 × 10⁻⁶ + 1.20 × 10⁻⁶ = 2.55 × 10⁻⁶ N.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small charged bead of mass 2.0 g hangs in equilibrium 0.40 m directly below a fixed point charge of +5.0 μC. State the sign of the charge on the bead and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Negative. The bead is held up by an attractive electric force directed upwards towards the positive charge; the bead must be attracted to the +5.0 μC charge, so its charge is negative.
parts.working: 1 mark for negative; 1 mark for attraction balancing the weight.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the charge on the bead. Take g = 9.81 N kg⁻¹.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two point charges of +3.0 nC are fixed at points (−0.20 m, 0) and (+0.20 m, 0) in a vacuum. Point P is at (0, 0.30 m). Calculate the electric field strength at P due to one of the charges.
parts.working: Distance from each charge to P = √(0.20² + 0.30²) = 0.3606 m. E = K Q/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 3.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.1300 = 207.5 N C⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resultant electric field strength at P.
parts.working: Horizontal components cancel; each vertical component is E × (0.30/0.3606) = 172.7 N C⁻¹. Resultant = 2 × 172.7 = 345 N C⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the direction of the resultant field at P.
parts.answer: Directly away from the midpoint of the two charges, i.e. in the +y direction (along the perpendicular bisector).

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two identical small conducting spheres A and B carry charges +6.0 nC and −2.0 nC. Their centres are 0.20 m apart in a vacuum. Calculate the electric force between them and state whether it is attractive or repulsive.
parts.working: F = K(6.0 × 10⁻⁹)(2.0 × 10⁻⁹)/0.20² = 2.70 × 10⁻⁶ N; the charges have opposite signs, so the force is attractive.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The spheres are brought into contact and then separated. Calculate the charge on each sphere after separation.
parts.working: Total charge +4.0 nC shared equally between identical spheres: +2.0 nC each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the new electric force between the spheres and state whether it is attractive or repulsive.
parts.working: F = K(2.0 × 10⁻⁹)²/0.20² = 8.99 × 10⁻⁷ N; both charges are positive, so the force is repulsive.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the electric field strength is zero at some point along the line through two charges of opposite sign only outside the line segment joining them, not between them.
parts.answer: Between the charges the fields from both charges point in the same direction (towards the negative charge), so they cannot cancel. Outside the segment, the fields point in opposite directions, so a point of zero field is possible, nearer the smaller charge.
parts.working: 1 mark for fields in same direction between the charges; 1 mark for opposite directions outside, where cancellation can occur.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A charge of +6.0 μC is at x = 0 and a charge of −2.0 μC is at x = 0.40 m. Calculate the distance from the +6.0 μC charge to the point on the x-axis, beyond the −2.0 μC charge, where the field strength is zero.
parts.working: Zero field where 6.0/(0.40 + d)² = 2.0/d², so √3·d = 0.40 + d, d = 0.546 m beyond the −2.0 μC charge. Distance from +6.0 μC = 0.40 + 0.546 = 0.946 m.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: Point charges of +2.0 nC and −2.0 nC are fixed at points A and B respectively, 0.10 m apart in a vacuum. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength at the midpoint M of AB and state its direction.
parts.working: each field = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.050² = 7.19 × 10³ N C⁻¹ (C1); both point from A towards B, so they add (C1); 1.44 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ towards B (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Point P lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, 0.12 m from M. Determine the electric field strength at P.
parts.answer: 8.2 × 10² N C⁻¹, parallel to AB, towards B
parts.working: AP = BP = 0.13 m; each field = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.13² = 1.06 × 10³ N C⁻¹ (C1); perpendicular components cancel, parallel components add: 2 × 1.06 × 10³ × (0.050/0.13) (C1) = 8.2 × 10² N C⁻¹ parallel to AB towards B (A1)

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem: In a simple model of the hydrogen atom, an electron moves in a circular orbit of radius 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m around a proton. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric force on the electron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: This force provides the centripetal force. Calculate the speed of the electron.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge
practice.stem:
A probe measures the electric field strength E at distances r from the centre of a charged metal sphere.
r / m: 0.20, 0.30, 0.40
E / 10⁴ V m⁻¹: 4.50, 2.00, 1.125
Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the data are consistent with the field of a point charge at the centre of the sphere.
parts.answer: Er² = 1800 V m in each case, so E ∝ 1/r².
parts.working: M1 calculates Er² (or ratio) for all three; A1 constant 1.80 × 10³ V m so inverse-square

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the charge on the sphere.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the distance from the centre at which the field strength would be 5.0 × 10³ V m⁻¹.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge

parts.label: a
parts.text: The electric force between two point charges in air is 0.45 N when their separation is 0.30 m. The relative permittivity of water is 80. Explain how the force changes when the same charges are placed in water at the same separation.
parts.answer: In a medium the force is F = Qq/(4πε₀ε_r r²), so the force is divided by the relative permittivity: the force decreases by a factor of 80.
parts.working: 1 mark for the expression with ε_r; 1 mark for the force being reduced by a factor of 80.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electric force between the charges when they are in water at a separation of 0.30 m.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the separation in water at which the force between the same charges equals 0.45 N.
parts.working: F ∝ 1/(ε_r r²). For the force to be 0.45 N again, ε_r r² must equal 0.30² = 0.09, so r² = 0.09/80 = 1.125 × 10⁻³ m² and r = 0.0335 m. The distance must fall, not rise, because the force is weaker at a given separation in water.

practice.subtopic: Coulomb's law & field of a point charge

parts.label: a
parts.text: A charged metal sphere has charge Q. A test charge of +2.0 nC is placed at several distances r from the centre of the sphere, and the force F is measured. Results: r/m: 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25. F/N: 2.70 × 10⁻⁵, 1.20 × 10⁻⁵, 6.74 × 10⁻⁶, 4.31 × 10⁻⁶. Calculate the values of 1/r² (in m⁻²) for the four distances.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plot a graph of F against 1/r². State the shape expected from Coulomb's law and calculate the gradient.
parts.answer: straight line through the origin; gradient ≈ 2.70 × 10⁻⁷ N m²
parts.working: F = kQq(1/r²) so the graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient kQq. Gradient = (2.70 × 10⁻⁵ − 4.31 × 10⁻⁶)/(100 − 16.0) = 2.70 × 10⁻⁷ N m².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the gradient to determine the charge Q on the sphere.

practice.stem: Two parallel horizontal metal plates are 4.0 cm apart. The potential difference between them is 600 V. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength between the plates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the force on an oil drop carrying a charge of +3e between the plates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the electric field between two parallel charged plates, away from the edges.
parts.answer: Uniform: field lines parallel, equally spaced, perpendicular to the plates, from positive to negative plate.
parts.working: B1 parallel/equally spaced (uniform); B1 perpendicular to plates, + to −

parts.label: b
parts.text: The plates are 2.5 mm apart in an air-filled capacitor with a p.d. of 9.0 V. Calculate the field strength.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the force on a charged particle varies as it moves from one plate to the other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two parallel metal plates are 5.0 cm apart with a potential difference of 1.5 kV between them. Calculate the electric field strength between the plates, away from the edges.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electric force on a proton placed between the plates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the proton. The mass of a proton is 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the electric field between two large parallel charged plates is uniform, away from the edges.
parts.answer: The plates produce equally spaced, parallel field lines, so the field has the same magnitude and direction everywhere between them (away from the edges, where the field lines bulge out).
parts.working: 1 mark for parallel and equally spaced field lines; 1 mark for uniform field away from edges.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The upper plate is positive and the lower plate is negative. State the direction of the electric force on an electron between the plates.
parts.answer: Upwards, towards the positive upper plate (the electron is negative and the field points downwards).

parts.label: c
parts.text: An electron enters the field horizontally. Explain why its path is a parabola.
parts.answer: The electric force is constant and perpendicular to the initial horizontal velocity, so the horizontal velocity is constant and the vertical acceleration is constant; this gives a parabolic path.
parts.working: 1 mark for constant horizontal velocity; 1 mark for constant vertical acceleration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two vertical parallel plates are 12 mm apart and the potential difference between them is 480 V. Calculate the electric field strength between the plates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the force on a point charge of +3.0 μC placed between the plates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the direction of this force if the left-hand plate is positive.
parts.answer: To the right, from the positive plate towards the negative plate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A charge of +2.0 μC is moved 0.15 m in the direction of a uniform electric field of strength 4.0 × 10³ V m⁻¹. Calculate the work done by the field on the charge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the field does positive or negative work if the charge is moved against the field.
parts.answer: Negative work: the field does work on the charge only when the charge moves in the direction of the force; moving against the field, work is done on the field by the charge (the work done by the field is negative).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference between the two points.

practice.stem: An oil drop of mass 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held stationary between two horizontal plates 6.0 mm apart when the potential difference between them is 294 V. g = 9.81 m s⁻². Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the direction of the electric force on the drop and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Upwards, to balance its weight (resultant force zero).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge on the drop.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Deduce the number of excess electrons or missing electrons on the drop, and state which it is if the upper plate is positive.
parts.working: 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹/1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3 (B1); force upward towards positive plate, so negative: 3 excess electrons (B1)

practice.stem: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 250 V in an electron gun. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy gained by the electron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the final speed of the electron.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect on the final speed of doubling the accelerating potential difference.
parts.answer: Speed increases by a factor of √2.

practice.stem: In an electrostatic dust collector in a cement factory chimney, two vertical parallel plates 0.20 m apart have a potential difference of 40 kV between them. A dust particle of mass 1.0 × 10⁻¹² kg carries a charge of 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength between the plates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the dust particle, ignoring gravity and air resistance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The particle starts from rest midway between the plates. Calculate the time it takes to reach a plate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron enters the uniform field between two horizontal parallel plates with velocity 5.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, parallel to the plates. The plates are 20 mm apart and the potential difference is 16 V. Calculate the electric field strength between the plates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the electron perpendicular to the plates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The plates are 0.050 m long. Calculate the vertical deflection of the electron as it leaves the plates, and state whether it hits a plate.
parts.answer: 7.0 mm; it does not hit a plate
parts.working: Time in plates t = 0.050/5.0 × 10⁶ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ s. y = ½at² = ½ × 1.41 × 10¹⁴ × (1.0 × 10⁻⁸)² = 7.0 mm, which is less than half the separation (10 mm), so the electron leaves the plates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A charged oil drop of mass 1.96 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held stationary between two horizontal parallel plates 5.0 mm apart when the potential difference across them is 200 V. State the condition for the drop to remain at rest.
parts.answer: The electric force on the drop must be equal and opposite to its weight, so qE = mg (the electric force acts upwards).
parts.working: 1 mark for electric force = weight; 1 mark for upward electric force.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge on the drop.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence determine the number of excess electrons on the drop. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
parts.working: n = q/e = 4.81 × 10⁻¹⁹/1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.00, so the drop carries 3 excess electrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small sphere of mass 0.50 g is held stationary in a uniform electric field of strength 2.0 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ directed vertically downwards. State the sign of the charge on the sphere and explain.
parts.answer: Negative. The electric force must act upwards to balance the weight; a negative charge experiences a force opposite to the field direction, i.e. upwards.
parts.working: 1 mark for negative charge; 1 mark for force opposite to the field, balancing weight.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the charge on the sphere.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A proton is released from rest in a uniform electric field of strength 500 V m⁻¹ and moves 0.80 m in the direction of the field. Calculate the work done by the field on the proton.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the proton after it has moved this distance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the acceleration of the proton is constant while it is in the field.
parts.answer: The field is uniform, so the electric force (qE) is constant; by Newton's second law the acceleration is constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron and a proton are placed at rest at the same point in a uniform electric field. Compare the magnitudes of the electric forces they experience.
parts.answer: The forces are equal in magnitude (F = qE with |q| the same for both), but opposite in direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mass of a proton is 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and the mass of an electron is 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. Calculate the ratio of the acceleration of the electron to the acceleration of the proton.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain which particle has the greater acceleration.
parts.answer: The electron, because it has the much smaller mass for the same force.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two large parallel metal plates each carry charge of magnitude 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ C, of opposite sign. Each plate has area 0.040 m². Explain why the field between the plates depends only on the charge per unit area.
parts.answer: The field between large parallel plates is E = σ/ε₀, where σ = Q/A is the charge per unit area; the field does not depend on the separation of the plates.
parts.working: 1 mark for E = σ/ε₀; 1 mark for independence from separation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the electric field strength between the plates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The plates are 2.0 mm apart. Calculate the potential difference between the plates.

practice.stem: An electron moving horizontally at 2.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ enters the uniform field between two horizontal parallel plates midway between them. The plates are 5.0 cm long and 2.0 cm apart, with a potential difference of 150 V between them. Ignore gravity. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, mₚ = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg where needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the electron between the plates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time the electron spends between the plates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the vertical deflection of the electron as it leaves the plates, and state whether it hits a plate.
parts.answer: 4.1 mm; it does not hit a plate (it is 10 mm from each plate)
parts.working: y = ½at² = ½ × 1.32 × 10¹⁵ × (2.5 × 10⁻⁹)² = 4.1 × 10⁻³ m (C1); 4.1 mm < 10 mm so it emerges (A1)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the shape of the path of the electron between the plates.
parts.answer: A parabola (constant horizontal velocity, constant vertical acceleration).

practice.stem: A proton and an alpha particle, both initially at rest, are accelerated through the same potential difference V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the speed of a charged particle accelerated from rest through a p.d. V is v = √(2qV/m).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio (speed of proton)/(speed of alpha particle). Take the alpha particle mass as 4mₚ and charge 2e.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the ratio (kinetic energy of proton)/(kinetic energy of alpha particle).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An alpha particle (mass 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, charge +2e) enters a uniform electric field of strength 2.0 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ at right angles to the field, with speed 1.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. Calculate its acceleration in the field.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The field region is 0.040 m long. Calculate the time the alpha particle spends in the field.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the angle through which the alpha particle is deflected, measured from its original direction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron enters a uniform electric field of strength E with velocity v, perpendicular to the field, and travels a horizontal distance L within the field. Show that its vertical deflection on leaving the field is y = eEL²/(2mv²).
parts.answer: Time in field t = L/v. Vertical acceleration a = eE/m. Deflection y = ½at² = ½(eE/m)(L/v)² = eEL²/(2mv²).
parts.working: 1 mark for t = L/v; 1 mark for a = eE/m; 1 mark for y = ½at² leading to the result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For E = 3.0 × 10³ N C⁻¹, L = 0.060 m and v = 4.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, calculate the deflection y. Take m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 100 V and then enters a region of uniform field strength 2.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ at right angles to the field. Calculate the speed of the electron as it enters the field region.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The field region is 0.020 m long in the direction of the electron's motion. Calculate the time the electron spends in the field.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the deflection of the electron in the field direction at the end of the field region. State whether the electron would leave the region if the plates were 50 mm apart.
parts.answer: 20.0 mm; it leaves, since the deflection is less than 25 mm
parts.working: a = eE/m = 3.51 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻²; y = ½at² = 20.0 mm. This is less than half the separation (25 mm), so the electron emerges from the region.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define simple harmonic motion.
parts.answer: Motion in which the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from a fixed point and is always directed towards that point (opposite to the displacement).
parts.working: B1 a ∝ x; B1 directed towards the fixed point / opposite to x

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the defining equation of simple harmonic motion and state the meaning of each symbol.
parts.answer: a = −ω²x; a acceleration, ω angular frequency, x displacement from equilibrium.

practice.stem: A mass hanging from a spring oscillates vertically. A student measures the time for 20 complete oscillations as 13.6 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the period of the oscillations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the angular frequency.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the student times 20 oscillations rather than one.
parts.answer: To reduce the percentage uncertainty in the period (reaction time is a smaller fraction of the total time).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define (i) the period and (ii) the angular frequency of an oscillation.
parts.answer: (i) the time for one complete oscillation; (ii) 2π × frequency (rate of change of phase angle), ω = 2π/T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The mains supply in Pakistan has a frequency of 50 Hz. Calculate its period and its angular frequency.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each motion, state whether it is simple harmonic and give a reason.
(i) a ball bouncing vertically on a hard floor
(ii) a mass oscillating on a vertical spring
(iii) a child on a swing with small amplitude
parts.answer: (i) not SHM – acceleration is constant (g) during flight, not proportional to displacement; (ii) SHM – restoring force ∝ displacement; (iii) approximately SHM for small angles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the condition needed for a simple pendulum to move with approximately simple harmonic motion.

practice.stem: A particle moves with simple harmonic motion of angular frequency 15 rad s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the particle when its displacement is +2.0 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the oscillation.

practice.stem: In a simple model of a solid, each atom vibrates with simple harmonic motion about a fixed point. For one atom the frequency is 5.0 × 10¹² Hz and the amplitude is 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular frequency of the vibration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the atom.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum acceleration of the atom and state where in the oscillation it occurs.
parts.answer: 9.9 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻², at maximum displacement (either extreme)
parts.working: A1 a₀ = ω²x₀ = 9.9 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻²; B1 at the extremes

practice.stem: An object moves with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 6.0 cm and period 0.80 s. At time t = 0 it passes through its equilibrium position.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the object when its displacement is 3.0 cm.
parts.working: C1 ω = 7.85 rad s⁻¹; A1 v = ω√(x₀² − x²) = 0.408 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of its acceleration at this displacement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using x = x₀ sin ωt, calculate the time taken to move from the equilibrium position to a displacement of 3.0 cm.

practice.stem: The needle of a sewing machine moves up and down with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 3.0 cm and frequency 2.0 Hz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the needle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum acceleration of the needle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where in its motion the needle has its maximum acceleration.
parts.answer: At the extremes of its motion (maximum displacement).

practice.stem: A trolley held between two springs oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 5.0 cm and angular frequency 8.0 rad s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the trolley.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the trolley when its displacement is 3.0 cm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of its acceleration at this displacement.

practice.stem: A block of mass 0.40 kg oscillates with simple harmonic motion of angular frequency 6.0 rad s⁻¹ and amplitude 5.0 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy of the oscillations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy and the potential energy when the displacement is 3.0 cm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the kinetic energy varies with displacement x, and state the shape of the graph of kinetic energy against x.
parts.answer: KE is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±x₀; the graph is an inverted parabola.
parts.working: B1 max at centre, zero at ends; B1 inverted parabola

practice.stem:
A data-logger records the acceleration a of a pendulum bob at different displacements x.
x / cm: −4.0, −2.0, 0, 2.0, 4.0
a / m s⁻²: 1.58, 0.79, 0, −0.79, −1.58

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the data show that the motion is simple harmonic.
parts.answer: a is proportional to x (a/x constant = −39.5 s⁻²) and opposite in sign to x.
parts.working: B1 proportional; B1 opposite sign/directed to equilibrium

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the angular frequency and the period of the oscillation.

practice.stem: Two identical pendulums A and B each have period 2.0 s. B reaches its maximum displacement to the right 0.25 s after A does.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the phase difference between the two pendulums in degrees and in radians.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which pendulum leads.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Pendulum B is adjusted so that it reaches maximum displacement on one side at the same instant as A reaches maximum displacement on the other side. State the new phase difference.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the graph of acceleration a against displacement x for an object moving with simple harmonic motion.
parts.answer: A straight line through the origin with negative gradient, extending from −x₀ to +x₀.
parts.working: B1 straight line through origin; B1 negative gradient, between ±x₀

parts.label: b
parts.text: For one oscillator the gradient of this graph is −25 s⁻². Calculate the period.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the shape of the graph of velocity against displacement.
parts.answer: An ellipse (a circle if axes are suitably scaled), centred on the origin.

practice.stem: An oscillator moving with simple harmonic motion has total energy 2.4 mJ and amplitude 2.0 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the potential energy of the oscillator when its displacement is 1.0 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy at this displacement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the displacement at which the kinetic energy equals the potential energy.

practice.stem: Water in a U-tube is displaced and then oscillates. The acceleration a of the water surface is related to its displacement x from equilibrium by a = −(2g/L)x, where L = 0.40 m is the total length of the water column and g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the motion of the liquid is simple harmonic.
parts.answer: The acceleration is proportional to the displacement and in the opposite direction (a = −(2g/L)x has the form a = −ω²x).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the period of oscillation of the liquid.

practice.stem: A data-logger shows that the velocity of a swinging lantern varies sinusoidally with time, with maximum value 0.60 m s⁻¹ and period 1.5 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amplitude of the oscillation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum acceleration.

practice.stem: A buoy in the sea at Gwadar bobs up and down with simple harmonic motion. It makes 12 complete oscillations in 30 s and the vertical distance between its highest and lowest positions is 0.50 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the period and the maximum speed of the buoy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the displacement of the buoy 0.40 s after it passes upwards through its equilibrium position.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the phase difference between (i) the velocity and the displacement, (ii) the acceleration and the displacement.
parts.answer: (i) π/2 rad (velocity leads by 90°) (ii) π rad (antiphase)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The maximum speed of an oscillator is 0.80 m s⁻¹. Calculate its speed when the displacement is half the amplitude.

practice.stem: A block of mass 0.50 kg on a smooth horizontal surface is attached to a spring of spring constant 200 N m⁻¹. It is pulled 4.0 cm from equilibrium and released, and moves with simple harmonic motion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the angular frequency is 20 rad s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total energy of the oscillation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the displacement at which the kinetic energy equals the potential energy.
parts.working: M1 ½kx² = ½E → x = x₀/√2; A1 2.83 cm

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the block at this displacement.
parts.working: A1 v = ω√(x₀² − x²) = 0.566 m s⁻¹

practice.stem:
A student hangs different masses m from a spring and times 10 oscillations for each. Theory suggests T = 2π√(m/k), where k is the spring constant.
m / kg: 0.100, 0.200, 0.300, 0.400, 0.500
time for 10 oscillations / s: 3.97, 5.62, 6.88, 7.95, 8.89

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student timed 10 oscillations rather than one.
parts.answer: To reduce the percentage uncertainty in the period (reaction-time error is shared over 10 periods).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the graph that should be plotted to test the relationship, and the expected gradient.
parts.answer: T² against m; a straight line through the origin with gradient 4π²/k.
parts.working: B1 T² v m; B1 gradient 4π²/k

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the first and last results to determine the gradient, and hence k.
parts.answer: gradient ≈ 1.58 s² kg⁻¹; k ≈ 25 N m⁻¹
parts.working: C1 T² = 0.158 and 0.790 s²; M1 gradient = 0.632/0.400 = 1.58 s² kg⁻¹; A1 k = 4π²/gradient = 25 N m⁻¹

practice.stem: The displacement x of an oscillating object is given by x = 0.12 sin(5.0t), where x is in metres and t is in seconds (angles in radians).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the amplitude and the period of the oscillation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the displacement and the velocity of the object at t = 0.40 s.
parts.working: x = 0.12 sin(2.0 rad) = 0.109 m (B1); v = 0.12 × 5.0 cos(2.0 rad) (C1) = −0.25 m s⁻¹, i.e. moving back towards equilibrium (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the first time after t = 0 at which the displacement is 0.060 m.

practice.stem: The piston of a car engine moves with approximately simple harmonic motion. The total distance moved between its highest and lowest positions (the stroke) is 9.0 cm. The engine turns at 3000 revolutions per minute, with one oscillation of the piston per revolution. The mass of the piston is 0.35 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular frequency of the piston's motion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum acceleration of the piston.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum resultant force on the piston.

practice.stem: At a harbour near Karachi the height of the sea above its mean level varies approximately with simple harmonic motion, with amplitude 1.8 m and period 12.4 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation for the height h of the water above mean level at time t, taking h = +1.8 m (high tide) at t = 0.
parts.working: B1 cos form with amplitude 1.8; B1 ω = 2π/12.4 = 0.507 rad h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: A ship can only pass the harbour entrance when the water is at least 1.0 m above mean level. Calculate the length of time in each tidal cycle during which the ship can pass.
parts.working: 1.8 cos ωt = 1.0 → ωt = 0.982 rad (C1); time from 0.982/0.507 = 1.94 h before to 1.94 h after high tide (C1); window = 3.9 h (A1)

practice.stem: A trolley of mass 0.25 kg on a horizontal frictionless track is attached to a spring system that provides a restoring force F = −kx, where k = 40 N m⁻¹ and x is the displacement. The trolley is pulled 4.0 cm from equilibrium and released.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By considering the resultant force, show that the trolley moves with simple harmonic motion and that ω = √(k/m).
parts.answer: F = −kx so a = −(k/m)x, which has the form a = −ω²x with ω² = k/m.
parts.working: M1 F = −kx and a = F/m; A1 compare with a = −ω²x

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the period of the oscillations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed and the maximum kinetic energy of the trolley.

practice.stem: An object moves with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 2.5 cm. At t = 0 it passes through its equilibrium position moving in the positive direction. It first reaches its maximum positive displacement at t = 0.15 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the period and the angular frequency.
parts.working: max displacement reached at a quarter period, so T = 4 × 0.15 = 0.60 s (B1); ω = 2π/0.60 = 10.5 rad s⁻¹ (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the velocity of the object at t = 0.10 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the object at t = 0.10 s.
parts.working: a = −ω²x₀ sin ωt = −10.5² × 0.025 × sin(1.05 rad) (C1) = −2.4 m s⁻² (A1)

practice.stem: A coin rests on a horizontal platform that oscillates vertically with simple harmonic motion of frequency 4.0 Hz. The amplitude is slowly increased. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the coin may lose contact with the platform, and state at which point in the oscillation this first happens.
parts.answer: At the top of the motion the platform's downward acceleration is greatest; if this exceeds g, the coin (whose maximum downward acceleration is g) cannot follow and leaves the surface.
parts.working: B1 needed downward acceleration > g; B1 at the highest point

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum amplitude at which the coin loses contact.

practice.stem: The tip of each prong of a tuning fork vibrates with simple harmonic motion of frequency 440 Hz and amplitude 0.50 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the tip of the prong.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum acceleration of the tip and express it as a multiple of g (9.81 m s⁻²).

practice.stem: When four passengers of total mass 300 kg get into a car, the car body moves down by 4.9 cm. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the effective spring constant of the suspension.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The loaded car (total mass 1500 kg) bounces vertically after going over a bump. Assuming the motion is simple harmonic with ω = √(k/m), calculate the period.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain the effect on the period of the passengers leaving the car.
parts.answer: The period decreases because the mass decreases (T ∝ √m).

practice.stem: A test tube of total mass 0.040 kg (including lead shot) floats upright in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. Its uniform external cross-sectional area is 2.0 cm². It is pushed down a small distance and released. Ignore damping; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: When the tube is displaced downwards by x from its equilibrium position, show that the resultant force on it is −ρgAx.
parts.answer: Extra volume submerged = Ax, so extra upthrust = ρgAx upwards; at equilibrium weight = upthrust, so the resultant force is ρgAx towards equilibrium: F = −ρgAx.
parts.working: B1 extra upthrust ρAxg; B1 opposite to displacement (weight balanced at equilibrium)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the motion is simple harmonic.
parts.answer: Acceleration = −(ρgA/m)x: proportional to displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the period of the oscillations.
parts.working: C1 ω² = ρgA/m; C1 ω = 7.0 rad s⁻¹; A1 T = 2π/ω = 0.897 s

practice.stem: An oscillator moves with simple harmonic motion. When its displacement is 2.0 cm its speed is 0.30 m s⁻¹, and when its displacement is 4.0 cm its speed is 0.20 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use v = ω√(x₀² − x²) to calculate the angular frequency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amplitude.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum acceleration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by damping.
parts.answer: The loss of energy (and so a decrease in amplitude) of an oscillating system caused by resistive forces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the motion of a system that is (i) lightly damped, (ii) critically damped, (iii) heavily damped, after being displaced and released.
parts.answer: (i) oscillates with amplitude decreasing gradually (period nearly unchanged); (ii) returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating; (iii) returns to equilibrium slowly without oscillating.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which type of damping is used in the suspension of a car and explain why.
parts.answer: Critical damping, so the car returns to its rest position quickly without bouncing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two examples where resonance is useful.
parts.answer: Any two of: tuning a radio receiver to one station; a quartz crystal in a clock or watch; magnetic resonance imaging (MRI); the body of a musical instrument amplifying sound.
parts.working: B1 each for two valid examples

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples where resonance causes problems, and state one way of reducing each problem.
parts.answer: e.g. bridges or tall buildings swaying in wind or under footsteps – add dampers; machinery or car panels rattling at certain engine speeds – stiffen or add rubber mountings.
parts.working: B1 two valid examples; B1 matching method of reducing (damping / changing natural frequency)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the natural frequency of an oscillating system.
parts.answer: The frequency at which it oscillates freely, with no driving force, after being displaced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a forced oscillation.
parts.answer: An oscillation caused by a periodic external driving force; the system oscillates at the driving frequency.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the condition for resonance and describe what is observed.
parts.answer: The driving frequency equals the natural frequency; the amplitude of the oscillations becomes a maximum.
parts.working: B1 driving frequency = natural frequency; B1 maximum amplitude

practice.stem: A child on a swing is released and not pushed again. After a few swings the amplitude of the swing has fallen from 1.2 m to 0.90 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the relationship between the energy of an oscillator and its amplitude.
parts.answer: Energy is proportional to the square of the amplitude.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the original energy that has been lost.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what has happened to the lost energy.
parts.answer: It has been transferred to thermal energy (internal energy) of the surroundings, mainly by air resistance and friction at the pivot.

practice.stem: A swing in a park has a natural period of 2.8 s. A father pushes his daughter on it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the natural frequency of the swing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the father times his pushes to match the natural frequency of the swing.
parts.answer: Each push is then in phase with the motion (in the direction of the velocity), so energy is transferred to the swing every cycle and the amplitude builds up – resonance.
parts.working: B1 driving frequency = natural frequency (resonance); B1 maximum energy transfer each cycle → large amplitude

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why pushing once every 5.6 s also increases the amplitude.
parts.answer: The push still happens at the same point in every second cycle, so it is always in phase with the motion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by critical damping.
parts.answer: The amount of damping that makes the system return to its equilibrium position in the shortest possible time without oscillating.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A spring-loaded door closer returns an open door to the closed position. Explain why the closer is designed to be close to critically damped.
parts.answer: With light damping the door would swing past and oscillate/slam; with heavy damping it would close very slowly. Critical damping closes it quickly without overshooting.
parts.working: B1 light damping → overshoot/oscillation; B1 heavy damping → too slow

practice.stem: The quartz crystal in a watch is made to vibrate by an electric circuit. It has a sharp resonance at 32 768 Hz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the period of the vibration, in microseconds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a crystal with very little damping is chosen.
parts.answer: With very light damping the resonance peak is very sharp, so the crystal oscillates only at a precise, stable frequency, keeping accurate time.
parts.working: B1 light damping → sharp/narrow resonance peak; B1 frequency precisely defined / stable

parts.label: c
parts.text: The watch counts vibrations to measure time. State how many vibrations it counts for each second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a radio receiver uses resonance to select one station from many.
parts.answer: The tuning circuit has a natural frequency that is adjusted to equal the frequency of the wanted station; it resonates with that signal, giving a large response, while other frequencies give only small responses.
parts.working: B1 natural frequency of circuit adjusted to station's frequency; B1 resonance gives large amplitude for that frequency only

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the tuning circuit should have only light damping.
parts.answer: A lightly damped system has a sharp, narrow resonance peak, so nearby stations are not received at the same time.

practice.stem:
Three oscillating systems are each displaced and released.
System X: a needle on an analogue meter swings past the final reading, back, and then settles after about two oscillations.
System Y: a mass on a spring in thick oil creeps back to equilibrium very slowly without overshooting.
System Z: a car body pressed down at one corner returns to its rest position quickly without overshooting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of damping in each system.
parts.answer: X: light (under-) damping; Y: heavy (over-) damping; Z: critical damping

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the displacement–time graph of system X.
parts.answer: An oscillation about the equilibrium position whose amplitude decreases gradually with time (about the same period throughout).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by resonance.
parts.answer: When the driving frequency of a forced oscillation equals the natural frequency of the system, the amplitude is a maximum (maximum energy transfer).
parts.working: B1 driving frequency = natural frequency; B1 maximum amplitude

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of increasing the damping on the graph of amplitude against driving frequency.
parts.answer: The peak amplitude is lower at all frequencies, the peak becomes broader (flatter), and the resonant frequency shifts slightly lower.
parts.working: B1 lower amplitude; B1 broader peak; B1 peak moves to lower frequency

practice.stem: A lightly damped pendulum is released with amplitude 10.0 cm. After 5 complete oscillations its amplitude is 8.0 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the original energy that remains after 5 oscillations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume the amplitude decreases by the same fraction in every 5 oscillations. Calculate the amplitude after 10 oscillations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one cause of the damping.
parts.answer: Air resistance (or friction at the pivot).

practice.stem:
A mass on a spring is driven by a vibration generator. The amplitude A of the forced oscillations is measured at different driving frequencies f.
f / Hz: 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0
A / cm: 0.8, 1.6, 4.9, 1.9, 0.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the natural frequency of the system and explain how you identified it.
parts.answer: About 2.0 Hz, where the amplitude is a maximum (resonance).
parts.working: B1 2.0 Hz; B1 maximum amplitude at resonance

parts.label: b
parts.text: The oscillating mass is 0.30 kg. Using ω² = k/m, estimate the spring constant of the spring.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The mass is replaced by one of 1.20 kg. State the new natural frequency.

practice.stem:
A pendulum is released and its amplitude is measured at the end of each complete oscillation.
number of oscillations: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
amplitude / cm: 20.0, 16.0, 12.8, 10.2, 8.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the amplitude decreases by the same fraction each oscillation.
parts.working: M1 calculate at least three ratios; A1 all ≈ 0.80

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the amplitude after 8 oscillations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the original energy that remains after 4 oscillations.

practice.stem: In a 'Barton's pendulums' demonstration, a heavy driver pendulum hangs from a horizontal string together with several light paper-cone pendulums of different lengths. One light pendulum P has the same length as the driver. The driver is set swinging.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State and explain which light pendulum swings with the largest amplitude.
parts.answer: P, because its natural frequency equals the driving frequency (same length), so it resonates.
parts.working: B1 P; B1 natural frequency = driving frequency

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the frequency at which all the light pendulums oscillate once steady.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The paper cones are removed from the light pendulums, so that they are less damped. State two changes in what is observed.
parts.answer: P swings with a larger amplitude; the response is more selective (sharper resonance): pendulums of other lengths swing with much smaller amplitudes than P.
parts.working: B1 amplitude of P (at resonance) increases; B1 resonance sharper – pendulums whose lengths differ from the driver's respond much less than P

practice.stem: A washing machine is switched on to spin. The speed of its drum rises steadily from 0 to 1200 revolutions per minute. As the drum passes 600 revolutions per minute, the whole machine vibrates violently for a few seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the machine vibrates violently at this speed only.
parts.answer: The unbalanced drum provides a periodic driving force at the rotation frequency; at 600 rev min⁻¹ (10 Hz) this equals the natural frequency of the machine on its mountings, so resonance occurs.
parts.working: B1 rotating drum = periodic driving force; B1 driving frequency = natural frequency → resonance (maximum amplitude)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the natural frequency of the machine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two changes to the design that would reduce the vibration.
parts.answer: Increase the damping (e.g. add shock absorbers/rubber feet); change the natural frequency so it is well outside the operating range (e.g. stiffer mountings or extra mass); pass through the resonant speed quickly.
parts.working: B1 each for two valid suggestions

practice.stem: A thin wine glass has a natural frequency of 880 Hz. A loudspeaker emitting a loud note of this frequency is placed close to the glass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the period of the natural oscillations of the glass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the glass may shatter.
parts.answer: The sound wave is a periodic driving force at the natural frequency, so the glass resonates; energy builds up each cycle until the amplitude of vibration (strain in the glass) is large enough to break it.
parts.working: B1 resonance – driving frequency = natural frequency; B1 amplitude grows large enough to fracture

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a thick glass with a heavy base is much less likely to shatter.
parts.answer: It is more heavily damped (and stiffer), so the amplitude at resonance is much smaller.

practice.stem:
A forced oscillator is tested twice, with different amounts of damping. The amplitude A is measured at different driving frequencies f.
f / Hz: 1.6, 1.8, 2.0, 2.2, 2.4
Test 1, A / cm: 1.2, 2.5, 9.0, 2.6, 1.2
Test 2, A / cm: 0.9, 1.3, 1.8, 1.3, 0.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: State, with a reason, which test had the greater damping.
parts.answer: Test 2 – its maximum amplitude is much smaller.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the natural frequency of the oscillator.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe two ways in which increasing the damping changes the shape of the graph of A against f.
parts.answer: The peak amplitude is lower; the peak is broader (flatter); and the peak occurs at a slightly lower frequency. Amplitude is reduced at all frequencies.

practice.stem: A very tall office tower sways in strong winds with a natural period of 6.5 s. To reduce the swaying, engineers hang a large mass near the top of the building, connected to the structure through powerful dampers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the natural frequency of the tower.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the swaying can become large if gusts of wind arrive with a period close to 6.5 s.
parts.answer: Gusts act as a periodic driving force; when its frequency matches the natural frequency, resonance occurs and the amplitude becomes very large.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the hanging mass and its dampers reduce the amplitude of the swaying.
parts.answer: The mass moves relative to the building and the dampers transfer the energy of oscillation to thermal energy, i.e. they increase the damping of the building.

practice.stem: A car's rear-view mirror vibrates strongly, blurring the image, only when the engine turns at a certain rate. The mirror on its mounting has a natural frequency of 24 Hz. Assume the engine produces one vibration per revolution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the engine speed, in revolutions per minute, at which the mirror vibrates most strongly.
parts.working: C1 resonance at 24 revolutions per second; A1 1.44 × 10³ rev min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one change to the mirror mounting that would reduce the problem, and explain it.
parts.answer: e.g. a rubber mounting (increases damping, so smaller amplitude at resonance) or a stiffer/lighter mounting (raises the natural frequency above the engine's range).

practice.stem: The propeller shaft of a ship turns at 120 revolutions per minute. The propeller has three blades, and each blade passing close to the hull gives the hull a small push. A steel deck panel has a natural frequency of 6.0 Hz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the pushes on the hull.
parts.working: C1 shaft frequency = 2.0 Hz; A1 3 pushes per revolution → 6.0 Hz

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the deck panel vibrates noisily at this shaft speed.
parts.answer: The pushes form a periodic driving force at 6.0 Hz, equal to the natural frequency of the panel, so it resonates and its amplitude is large.
parts.working: B1 driving frequency = natural frequency; B1 resonance → large amplitude

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the shaft speed, in revolutions per minute, of a propeller with four blades that would cause the same problem.

practice.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg has a suspension of effective spring constant 6.0 × 10⁴ N m⁻¹. It drives over a series of speed bumps spaced 9.0 m apart along a road in Islamabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the natural frequency of vertical oscillation of the car on its suspension, using f = (1/2π)√(k/m).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed at which the car would bounce with the largest amplitude, and explain your answer.
parts.working: bumps act as a periodic driving force (B1); resonance when bump frequency v/9.0 = 1.13 Hz (C1); v = 10 m s⁻¹ (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the shock absorbers are designed to give a large amount of damping (close to critical damping).
parts.answer: The damping reduces the amplitude at resonance and makes the car return to its rest position quickly, without continuing to bounce.
parts.working: B1 smaller amplitude at resonance / oscillations die away quickly

practice.stem: A footbridge across a canal has a natural frequency of vertical oscillation of 2.0 Hz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A group of joggers, each with a stride of 1.5 m, crosses the bridge in step. Calculate the jogging speed at which the bridge would oscillate with the largest amplitude.
parts.working: resonance when step frequency = 2.0 Hz (C1); v = 2.0 × 1.5 = 3.0 m s⁻¹ (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why soldiers are often told to break step when marching across a bridge.
parts.answer: Marching in step gives a periodic driving force; if its frequency matches the natural frequency of the bridge, resonance causes large, possibly damaging, oscillations.
parts.working: B1 periodic force at one frequency; B1 resonance → large amplitude

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way engineers can reduce the risk without changing the bridge's natural frequency.
parts.answer: Fit dampers (e.g. tuned mass dampers or viscous dampers) to increase damping.

practice.stem: A mass of 0.20 kg oscillates on a spring of spring constant 80 N m⁻¹ in air. Its amplitude falls from 5.0 cm to 3.0 cm in 10 complete oscillations. Assume the period is not affected by the damping.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy lost by the oscillator in these 10 oscillations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the period of the oscillations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of loss of energy over the 10 oscillations.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the rate of loss of energy decreases as the amplitude decreases.
parts.answer: The speed of the mass is smaller, so the resistive force (and energy lost per cycle) is smaller.

practice.stem: A lightly damped pendulum of period 1.6 s loses 4.0% of its amplitude in each complete oscillation (each amplitude is 0.96 of the one before).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of complete oscillations after which the amplitude has first fallen below 25% of its initial value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for these oscillations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the initial energy remaining at this time.

practice.stem: A mass of 0.50 kg on a spring is driven at its natural angular frequency of 10 rad s⁻¹. The amplitude grows and then stays constant at 3.0 cm. At this amplitude the system loses 5.0% of its stored energy in each cycle through damping.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the amplitude stops increasing.
parts.answer: Energy lost per cycle through damping increases with amplitude; the amplitude becomes steady when the energy supplied by the driver each cycle equals the energy lost each cycle.
parts.working: B1 losses increase with amplitude; B1 steady when input energy per cycle = energy lost per cycle

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total energy of the oscillation at this amplitude.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean power that the driver must supply.
parts.working: C1 energy per cycle = 1.125 × 10⁻³ J and T = 0.628 s; A1 P = 1.79 × 10⁻³ W

practice.stem: Engineers use a rough rule that the natural frequency of sideways sway of a building is f ≈ 10/N hertz, where N is the number of storeys. During an earthquake the ground shakes with a frequency of about 2.0 Hz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the rule to identify the height of building, in storeys, most at risk, and explain why.
parts.answer: 5 storeys; its natural frequency (10/5 = 2.0 Hz) equals the driving frequency, so it resonates with large amplitude.
parts.working: A1 N = 5; B1 resonance – natural frequency = frequency of ground shaking

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a 30-storey building nearby may suffer less shaking from the same earthquake.
parts.answer: Its natural frequency (about 0.33 Hz) is far from 2.0 Hz, so its amplitude of forced oscillation is small.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some buildings are mounted on flexible rubber 'base isolators' that lower the natural frequency of the whole building and increase damping. Explain how each change helps.
parts.answer: Lowering the natural frequency moves it away from the frequency of ground shaking (no resonance); extra damping reduces the amplitude of any oscillation and removes energy quickly.
parts.working: B1 natural frequency moved away from driving frequency; B1 damping reduces amplitude

practice.stem: A trolley of mass 0.40 kg is held between springs with a combined spring constant of 60 N m⁻¹. A vibration generator drives the system. For a mass on a spring, ω² = k/m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the driving frequency at which resonance occurs.
parts.working: C1 ω = √(k/m) = 12.2 rad s⁻¹; A1 f = ω/2π = 1.95 Hz

parts.label: b
parts.text: A 0.40 kg load is added to the trolley. Calculate the new resonant frequency.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Instead of adding the load, the springs are replaced by stiffer springs with a combined spring constant of 120 N m⁻¹. Calculate the resonant frequency.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the amplitude at resonance does not become infinite.
parts.answer: There is always some damping, which removes energy each cycle.

practice.stem:
A student displaces a pendulum and records its amplitude A at different times t. It is suggested that A = A₀e^(−kt), where A₀ and k are constants.
t / s: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
A / cm: 12.0, 9.0, 6.8, 5.1, 3.8, 2.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a graph of ln (A / cm) against t can be used to test the suggestion.
parts.answer: ln A = ln A₀ − kt, which has the form y = c + mx, so the graph should be a straight line with gradient −k and intercept ln A₀.
parts.working: B1 ln A = ln A₀ − kt; B1 straight line, gradient −k

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ln (A / cm) for t = 0 and t = 50 s and use them to estimate k.
parts.working: A1 both ln values; A1 k = 0.028 s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time for the amplitude to halve.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one practical technique to measure the amplitude more accurately.
parts.answer: Use a video camera with a scale behind the pendulum and step through frames; or use a motion sensor / data-logger; view at eye level to avoid parallax.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A mass on a spring oscillates vertically. A student suggests that the time taken for the amplitude to halve depends on the area of a horizontal card attached to the mass.
Design a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between the time for the amplitude to halve and the area of the card. You should draw attention to:
• the procedure to be followed
• the measurements to be taken
• the control of variables
• the analysis of the data
• any safety precautions.
parts.answer: A full plan covering: independent variable card area; dependent variable time to halve; controls; method of measuring amplitude and time; analysis by plotting graph; safety.
parts.working:
Defining the problem (3): B1 independent variable = area of card; B1 dependent variable = time for amplitude to halve; B1 keep total oscillating mass (card mass + slotted mass) and spring constant constant.
Methods (6): B1 labelled set-up: spring from clamp, mass with card attached, metre rule fixed vertically beside it; B1 measure card area with ruler (A = length × width); B1 displace by fixed initial amplitude and release; B1 measure amplitude using pointer against rule / video camera with scale / motion sensor; B1 stopwatch (or video frame timing) for time until amplitude is half the initial value; B1 repeat for each area and average; B1 use same shape of card (e.g. squares) so only area changes; B1 adjust slotted masses so total mass constant for each card; B1 ensure card is horizontal and air is still (no draughts).
Analysis (2): B1 plot graph of t½ against A (or log t½ against log A); B1 relationship valid if straight line / state how proportionality or power law is tested (e.g. gradient of log–log gives power).
Safety (1): B1 clamp stand secured / weighted to prevent toppling; or goggles in case spring snaps.
Additional detail (up to 3): B1 any further relevant detail, e.g. use of a fiducial marker; check the period is not changed significantly; card cut from same material/thickness; preliminary experiment to choose suitable range of areas; use video to reduce reaction-time error.

practice.stem: The pendulum of a clock has period 2.0 s and swings with simple harmonic motion with a constant amplitude of 5.0 cm (measured as a horizontal displacement of the bob). The bob has mass 0.50 kg. Damping removes 1.0% of the energy of the oscillation in each cycle, and the clock's mechanism replaces it with a small push each cycle. The mechanism is driven by a 2.0 kg mass that falls slowly through 1.2 m. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the pendulum needs a push every cycle to keep its amplitude constant.
parts.answer: Damping (air resistance, friction at the pivot) continually transfers energy away from the pendulum, so energy must be supplied to keep the amplitude constant.
parts.working: B1 damping removes energy each cycle, which must be replaced

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total energy of the oscillation.
parts.working: C1 ω = 2π/T = π rad s⁻¹; A1 E = ½mω²x₀² = ½ × 0.50 × π² × 0.050² = 6.17 × 10⁻³ J

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean power that the mechanism must supply to the pendulum.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Assuming all the energy from the falling mass is passed to the pendulum, calculate how many days the clock runs before the mass must be raised again.

practice.stem: Mass of proton = 1.007276 u; mass of neutron = 1.008665 u; mass of ⁴₂He nucleus = 4.001506 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define mass defect of a nucleus.
parts.answer: The difference between the total mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass defect of a helium-4 nucleus in u.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the binding energy per nucleon of helium-4 in MeV.

practice.stem: Speed of light c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the equation that relates energy to mass, explaining each symbol.
parts.answer: E = mc², where E is energy, m is mass and c is the speed of light in a vacuum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy equivalent of 1.0 g of mass.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Sun radiates energy at a rate of 3.85 × 10²⁶ W. Calculate the mass the Sun loses each second because of this.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the general shape of a graph of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number A.
parts.answer: Rises steeply from very low values for the lightest nuclei (with ⁴He a local peak); reaches a broad maximum of about 8.8 MeV near A ≈ 56–62 (iron/nickel); then decreases slowly to about 7.6 MeV for the heaviest nuclei.
parts.working: B1 steep rise for small A; B1 maximum ≈ 8.8 MeV around A ≈ 56 (Fe); B1 gradual decrease for large A.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the shape of the graph to explain why both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei release energy.
parts.answer: In both cases the products have a higher binding energy per nucleon than the original nuclei (they move towards the peak), so the total binding energy increases and the mass decreases; the mass difference is released as energy.
parts.working: B1 products have greater BE per nucleon (closer to peak); B1 increase in total BE / decrease in mass released as energy.

practice.stem: A deuteron (²₁H nucleus) has a mass of 2.013553 u. Mass of proton = 1.007276 u; mass of neutron = 1.008665 u.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that 1 u is equivalent to about 934 MeV using u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the binding energy of the deuteron in joules, using u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Express this binding energy in MeV.

practice.stem: A possible fission reaction is ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + x ¹₀n. The total mass of the products is 0.186 u less than the total mass of the reactants. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the value of x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in one fission, in MeV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the neutrons produced can lead to a chain reaction, and why a moderator is needed in a reactor.
parts.answer: Each fission releases more than one neutron, and each can cause a further fission; a moderator slows the fast neutrons down so they are more likely to be absorbed by U-235 and cause fission.
parts.working: B1 neutrons released go on to cause further fissions; B1 moderator slows neutrons (thermal neutrons more likely to cause fission).

practice.stem: Mass of proton = 1.007276 u; mass of neutron = 1.008665 u; mass of an ¹⁶₈O nucleus = 15.990523 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the binding energy of a nucleus.
parts.answer: The minimum energy needed to separate a nucleus completely into its individual (free) protons and neutrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass defect of the ¹⁶₈O nucleus.
parts.working: C1 8 protons + 8 neutrons = 16.127564 u; A1 Δm = 0.1370 u

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the binding energy per nucleon of ¹⁶₈O, in MeV.
parts.working: C1 BE = 127.6 MeV; A1 7.98 MeV per nucleon

practice.stem: A nuclear power station produces 1.2 GW of electrical power. The overall efficiency of converting nuclear energy to electrical energy is 33%. Speed of light c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the nuclear energy released in the reactor in one day.
parts.working: C1 input power = 3.64 × 10⁹ W; A1 E = 3.14 × 10¹⁴ J

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the decrease in mass of the fuel, in grams, that corresponds to this energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A coal-fired power station with the same electrical output has an efficiency of 38%. Burning 1.0 kg of coal releases 3.0 × 10⁷ J. Calculate the mass of coal burned in one day.

practice.stem: One possible fission of uranium-235 is: ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴⁰₅₄Xe + ⁹⁴₃₈Sr + x ¹₀n

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that proton number is conserved in this reaction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why energy is released, with reference to binding energy per nucleon and mass.
parts.answer: The fragments have a greater binding energy per nucleon than uranium-235, so the total mass of the products is less than the mass of the reactants; the mass difference is released as energy (E = mc²), mainly as kinetic energy of the products.
parts.working: B1 products have higher binding energy per nucleon; B1 total mass decreases, Δm c² released

practice.stem: Mass of proton = 1.007276 u; mass of neutron = 1.008665 u; mass of a ³₂He nucleus = 3.014931 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the binding energy of the ³₂He nucleus in MeV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the binding energy per nucleon.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The binding energy per nucleon of ⁴₂He is 7.07 MeV. State which of the two nuclei is more stable and explain why.
parts.answer: ⁴₂He – more energy per nucleon is needed to pull it apart.

practice.stem: Neutrons were first identified using the reaction ⁹₄Be + ⁴₂He → ¹²₆C + ¹₀n. Atomic masses: ⁹Be 9.012183 u; ⁴He 4.002603 u; ¹²C 12.000000 u. Mass of neutron = 1.008665 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in mass in this reaction.
parts.working: C1 reactants 13.014786 u, products 13.008665 u; A1 0.00612 u decrease

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released, in MeV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why atomic masses may be used here instead of nuclear masses.
parts.answer: The numbers of electrons on each side are equal (4 + 2 = 6), so the electron masses cancel.

practice.stem: The nucleus ⁵⁶₂₆Fe has a mass of 55.920662 u. Mass of proton = 1.007276 u; mass of neutron = 1.008665 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the binding energy of an iron-56 nucleus in MeV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the binding energy per nucleon.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why iron-56 cannot release energy by either fission or fusion.
parts.answer: It is at (or very near) the peak of the binding energy per nucleon curve; any products of fission or fusion would have lower binding energy per nucleon, so energy would have to be supplied.
parts.working: B1 near maximum BE per nucleon; B1 products would have lower BE/nucleon, so energy absorbed not released.
