practice.stem: In a fusion reactor, deuterium and tritium fuse: ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n. Masses: ²₁H 2.014102 u; ³₁H 3.016049 u; ⁴₂He 4.002603 u; ¹₀n 1.008665 u. (These are atomic masses; the electron masses cancel.) 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in one reaction, in MeV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why fusion requires a very high temperature.
parts.answer: The nuclei are both positively charged and repel; they need very high kinetic energies (high temperature) to overcome the electrostatic repulsion and get close enough for the strong force to act.
parts.working: B1 electrostatic repulsion between positive nuclei; B1 high KE to approach closely (within range of strong force).

practice.stem: Each fission of a uranium-235 nucleus releases about 200 MeV. Molar mass of U-235 = 0.235 kg mol⁻¹; Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J; 1 day = 86 400 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the energy released by the complete fission of 1.0 kg of uranium-235 is about 8 × 10¹³ J.
parts.working: Number of nuclei = (1.0 ÷ 0.235) × 6.02 × 10²³ = 2.56 × 10²⁴ (M1); energy per fission = 200 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J (M1); total = 8.20 × 10¹³ J (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A power station produces 600 MW of electrical power with an overall efficiency of 33%. Calculate the mass of uranium-235 used each day.
parts.working: Input power = 600 ÷ 0.33 = 1820 MW (C1); energy per day = 1.57 × 10¹⁴ J (M1); mass = 1.92 kg (A1).

practice.stem: Radium-226 decays by α-emission to radon-222. Atomic masses: Ra-226 226.025410 u; Rn-222 222.017578 u; He-4 4.002603 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the nuclear equation for this decay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in the decay, in MeV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the alpha particle carries away most of this energy as kinetic energy.
parts.answer: Momentum is conserved and the radium was at rest, so the α-particle and radon nucleus have equal and opposite momenta; KE = p²/2m, so the much lighter α-particle has much more KE.
parts.working: B1 equal and opposite momenta; B1 KE = p²/2m so lighter particle has greater KE.

practice.stem: Binding energies per nucleon: ²³⁵₉₂U 7.591 MeV; ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba 8.326 MeV; ⁹²₃₆Kr 8.513 MeV. Consider the fission ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3 ¹₀n.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the binding energy of the free neutrons does not appear in the calculation.
parts.answer: A free neutron is not bound in a nucleus, so its binding energy is zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total binding energy of each of the three nuclei.
parts.working: BE = A × (BE per nucleon) (M1); three correct values (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the energy released in the fission.

practice.stem: A radon-222 nucleus at rest decays by α-emission to polonium-218. The α-particle is emitted with a kinetic energy of 5.49 MeV. Atomic masses: ²¹⁸Po 218.008973 u; ⁴He 4.002603 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV. Use nucleon numbers for the ratio of the masses of the α-particle and the polonium nucleus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the α-particle and the polonium nucleus move off in opposite directions with momenta of equal magnitude.
parts.answer: The radon nucleus has zero momentum before the decay, and momentum is conserved, so the total momentum afterwards is zero.
parts.working: B1 initial momentum zero + conservation of momentum

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the recoiling polonium nucleus.
parts.working: M1 KE = p²/2m with equal p, so KE_Po/KE_α = 4/218; A1 KE_Po = 5.49 × 4/218 = 0.101 MeV

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total energy released in the decay.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the atomic mass of radon-222, in u, to 7 significant figures.

practice.stem: In boron neutron capture therapy for some tumours, boron-10 absorbs a slow neutron: ¹⁰₅B + ¹₀n → ⁷₃Li + ⁴₂He. Atomic masses: ¹⁰B 10.012937 u; ⁷Li 7.016003 u; ⁴He 4.002603 u. Mass of neutron = 1.008665 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV; 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in one reaction, in MeV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of reactions needed to deliver 1.0 J of energy to the tumour.
parts.working: C1 energy per reaction = 4.47 × 10⁻¹³ J; A1 2.2 × 10¹²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the energy is deposited only very close to the boron atoms.
parts.answer: The products are heavy, charged particles (α and Li ions), which are very strongly ionising and stop within a very short distance.

practice.stem: Carbon-14 decays by β⁻ emission to nitrogen-14. Atomic masses: ¹⁴C 14.003242 u; ¹⁴N 14.003074 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the nuclear equation for the decay.
parts.working: B1 correct nuclides and β⁻; B1 antineutrino

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the energy released can be found from the difference in atomic masses without adding the mass of an electron.
parts.answer: The nitrogen atom has one more electron than the carbon atom; that extra electron's mass is the emitted β⁻ particle, so it is already included.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy released, in keV.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Measured β-particles from this decay have a range of kinetic energies up to about this value. Explain why.
parts.answer: The energy is shared between the β-particle and the antineutrino (and a tiny recoil of the nucleus) in varying proportions.

practice.stem: Two deuterium nuclei can fuse: ²₁H + ²₁H → ³₂He + ¹₀n. Atomic masses: ²H 2.014102 u; ³He 3.016029 u. Mass of neutron = 1.008665 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV; 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in one reaction, in MeV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released if 1.0 kg of deuterium were completely used in this reaction.
parts.working: C1 number of deuterium atoms = 1.0/(2.014102 × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷) = 2.99 × 10²⁶; M1 number of reactions = half of this; A1 7.8 × 10¹³ J

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why such fusion is hard to achieve on Earth.
parts.answer: The nuclei repel each other electrically, so extremely high temperatures (and densities/confinement) are needed for them to get close enough to fuse.

practice.stem: Binding energies per nucleon: ²₁H 1.11 MeV; ⁴₂He 7.07 MeV; ¹²₆C 7.68 MeV; ⁵⁶₂₆Fe 8.79 MeV; ¹²⁰₅₀Sn 8.50 MeV; ²³⁸₉₂U 7.57 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which of these nuclei is the most stable, and give a reason.
parts.answer: ⁵⁶₂₆Fe – it has the greatest binding energy per nucleon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total binding energy of the ²³⁸₉₂U nucleus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy released when two ²₁H nuclei fuse to form one ⁴₂He nucleus.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State which of these nuclides would release the most energy if it split into two nuclei of about half its nucleon number, and explain why.
parts.answer: ²³⁸₉₂U – fragments with A ≈ 119 have binding energy per nucleon about 8.5 MeV, much greater than 7.57 MeV.

practice.stem: In the fusion reaction ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n, the energy released is 17.6 MeV, shared as kinetic energy between the helium nucleus and the neutron.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assuming the initial momentum is negligible, show that the neutron receives about 4/5 of the energy released.
parts.answer: Equal and opposite momenta p; KE = p²/2m, so KEₙ/KE_α = m_α/mₙ ≈ 4; neutron gets 4/(4 + 1) = 4/5.
parts.working: M1 equal momenta and KE = p²/2m; A1 ratio 4:1 hence 4/5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the neutron in MeV, using the mass ratio m_α/mₙ = 4.002603/1.008665.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the neutron, treating it non-relativistically. (mass of neutron = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the energy of fusion reactors is captured using a blanket of material surrounding the plasma.
parts.answer: The neutrons are uncharged so magnetic fields cannot contain them; they escape the plasma and deposit their kinetic energy (as heat) in the blanket.

practice.stem: In the core of the Sun the net effect of a chain of fusion reactions is 4 ¹₁p → ⁴₂He + 2 ⁰₊₁e + 2ν. Mass of proton = 1.007276 u; mass of ⁴₂He nucleus = 4.001506 u; mass of positron = 0.000549 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in this reaction, in MeV, ignoring the neutrinos' mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: When the annihilation of the two positrons is included, the total energy released per helium nucleus formed is 26.7 MeV. The Sun's power output is 3.85 × 10²⁶ W. Calculate the number of helium nuclei formed in the Sun each second.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the mass of hydrogen (protons) converted each second. (mass of proton = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)

practice.stem: A D–T fusion reaction (²₁H + ³₁H) releases 17.6 MeV. A fission of U-235 (²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n) releases 200 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per nucleon of reactants for each reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence calculate the ratio (energy released per kilogram of fusion fuel) ÷ (energy released per kilogram of fission fuel).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the fission reaction still releases much more energy per reaction than the fusion reaction.
parts.answer: Energy released = change in total binding energy; uranium has 236 nucleons, each gaining about 0.85 MeV of binding energy, so the total is large even though the gain per nucleon is small.
parts.working: B1 many more nucleons involved; B1 total = number of nucleons × increase in BE per nucleon.

practice.stem: Binding energies per nucleon: ⁶₃Li 5.33 MeV; ⁴₂He 7.07 MeV; ³₁H 2.83 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in the reaction ⁶₃Li + ¹₀n → ⁴₂He + ³₁H.
parts.working: Total BE: He-4 = 4 × 7.07 = 28.28 MeV; H-3 = 3 × 2.83 = 8.49 MeV; Li-6 = 6 × 5.33 = 31.98 MeV (M1); energy released = BE(products) − BE(reactants) (M1) = 28.28 + 8.49 − 31.98 = 4.79 MeV (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the free neutron contributes nothing to the reactants' binding energy.
parts.answer: It is not part of a nucleus, so it has no binding energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: This reaction is used to make tritium for fusion reactors. Explain why it releases energy even though neither reaction type is 'fission of heavy' or 'fusion of light' nuclei in the usual sense.
parts.answer: Energy is released whenever the products have a greater total binding energy than the reactants; ⁴He has an unusually high binding energy per nucleon, so the total binding energy increases.
parts.working: B1 total BE increases; B1 helium-4 especially tightly bound.

practice.stem: Plutonium-239 decays by α-emission: ²³⁹₉₄Pu → ²³⁵₉₂U + ⁴₂He. Atomic masses: Pu-239 239.052163 u; U-235 235.043930 u; He-4 4.002603 u. Use nucleon numbers for the ratio of masses. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in the decay in MeV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the α-particle carries a fraction 235/239 of this energy, and calculate its kinetic energy.
parts.working: Equal and opposite momenta (M1); KE_α/KE_U = m_U/m_α = 235/4, so KE_α = E × 235/239 (M1); = 5.16 MeV (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the recoiling uranium nucleus.

practice.stem: One of the final steps of fusion in the Sun is ³₂He + ³₂He → ⁴₂He + 2¹₁H. Atomic masses: ³He 3.016029 u; ⁴He 4.002603 u; ¹H 1.007825 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV; 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released in one reaction, in MeV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the rest mass of the reactants that is converted into other forms of energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy released per kilogram of helium-3 used.
parts.working: C1 energy per reaction 2.06 × 10⁻¹² J, mass of reactants 1.00 × 10⁻²⁶ kg; A1 2.1 × 10¹⁴ J kg⁻¹

practice.stem: Binding energies per nucleon: ⁵⁶₂₆Fe 8.79 MeV; ²⁸₁₄Si 8.45 MeV. For a nucleus with A = 240, about 7.6 MeV; for a nucleus with A = 120, about 8.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the energy released when a nucleus with A = 240 splits into two nuclei each with A = 120 (ignore any neutrons released).
parts.working: M1 total BE after − before = 240 × 8.5 − 240 × 7.6; A1 ≈ 220 MeV (216 MeV)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy change if a ⁵⁶₂₆Fe nucleus were split into two ²⁸₁₄Si nuclei, and state whether energy is released or must be supplied.
parts.working: M1 56 × 8.45 − 56 × 8.79 = −19 MeV; A1 energy must be supplied (19 MeV)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why iron-56 is found at the peak of the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve and why neither fission nor fusion of iron releases energy.
parts.answer: Iron has the highest binding energy per nucleon; any change (splitting or joining) would produce nuclei with lower binding energy per nucleon, so energy would have to be supplied.
parts.working: B1 Fe has maximum BE per nucleon; B1 products of fission or fusion of Fe would have lower BE per nucleon → energy absorbed

practice.stem: The binding energy per nucleon of ²⁰⁸₈₂Pb is 7.867 MeV. Mass of proton = 1.007276 u; mass of neutron = 1.008665 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total binding energy of the nucleus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass defect in u.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of the ²⁰⁸₈₂Pb nucleus in u, giving your answer to 6 significant figures.

practice.stem: When 1.0 kg of natural gas burns completely, about 5.5 × 10⁷ J of energy is released. When a uranium-235 nucleus undergoes fission (with a neutron), about 200 MeV is released. c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹; 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the decrease in mass when 1.0 kg of natural gas (plus its oxygen) burns.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the rest mass of the reactants (²³⁵U + n, total about 236 u) that is converted in one fission.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why chemists can treat mass as conserved in reactions, even though E = mc² applies to all energy changes.
parts.answer: Chemical energy changes are so small that the mass change (about 10⁻¹⁰ of the mass) is far too small to measure, whereas nuclear changes are about a million times larger per unit mass.
parts.working: B1 mass change in chemical reaction is negligible / unmeasurable; B1 comparison with nuclear fraction

practice.stem: A deuteron can be split into a proton and a neutron by a γ-ray photon (photodisintegration). Atomic masses: ²H 2.014102 u; ¹H 1.007825 u. Mass of neutron = 1.008665 u. 1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV; 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J; h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the binding energy of the deuteron in MeV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum wavelength of a photon that can split a deuteron, assuming all the photon energy is used to separate the particles.
parts.working: C1 E = hc/λ with E = 3.56 × 10⁻¹³ J; A1 λ = 5.59 × 10⁻¹³ m

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why, in practice, the photon needs slightly more energy than this.
parts.answer: Momentum must be conserved: the photon's momentum is passed to the proton and neutron, which therefore must have some kinetic energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the decay constant of a radioactive nuclide.
parts.answer: The probability per unit time that a nucleus will decay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the relationship between the decay constant λ and the half-life t½.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Iodine-131, used to treat thyroid conditions, has a half-life of 8.02 days. Calculate its decay constant in s⁻¹.

practice.stem: Cobalt-60 has a half-life of 5.27 years. 1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the activity of a radioactive sample.
parts.answer: The number of nuclei decaying per unit time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the decay constant of cobalt-60 in s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the activity of a sample containing 2.0 × 10¹² cobalt-60 nuclei.

practice.stem: A hospital in Islamabad prepares a technetium-99m sample for a medical scan. Its initial activity is 800 MBq and its half-life is 6.0 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activity of the sample 24 hours after it is prepared.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activity 9.0 hours after it is prepared.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a short half-life is useful for a tracer injected into a patient.
parts.answer: The activity in the body falls quickly, so the patient receives a smaller total dose of radiation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by radioactive decay being (i) spontaneous and (ii) random.
parts.answer: (i) It is not affected by external conditions such as temperature or pressure; (ii) it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay (each nucleus has a constant probability of decay per unit time).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the evidence for the random nature of decay that can be seen when using a Geiger–Müller counter.
parts.answer: The count rate fluctuates (repeated counts over equal time intervals vary).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A counter records 350 counts in 5.0 minutes near a source. The background count rate is 25 counts per minute. Calculate the corrected count rate due to the source.
parts.working: 350 ÷ 5.0 = 70 counts per minute (M1); 70 − 25 = 45 counts per minute (A1).

practice.stem: Wood from an ancient boat found near the Indus has a carbon-14 activity of 0.115 Bq per gram of carbon. Living wood has an activity of 0.250 Bq per gram of carbon. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5730 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that A = A₀e^(−λt) can be rearranged to give t = (t½/ln 2) × ln(A₀/A).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the age of the wood.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption made in this calculation.
parts.answer: The activity per gram of living wood was the same when the tree died as it is today (atmospheric C-14 level constant) / the sample has not been contaminated.

practice.stem: The activity of a sample of a radioactive nuclide falls from 640 Bq to 80 Bq in 24 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the half-life of the nuclide.
parts.working: C1 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 is 3 half-lives; A1 t½ = 8.0 h

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the decay constant in s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the activity after a further 12 hours.

practice.stem: A radioactive nuclide has a half-life of 3.0 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the original nuclei that remain undecayed after 15 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fraction that has decayed after 15 minutes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use N = N₀e^(−λt) to calculate the fraction remaining after 10 minutes.

practice.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube records 54 counts in 2.0 minutes with no source present. With a source placed in front of it, the count rate is 1240 min⁻¹. 30 minutes later the count rate with the source is 330 min⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the background count rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected count rate from the source at the start and after 30 minutes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence determine the half-life of the source.
parts.working: M1 1213/303 ≈ 4.0 → 2 half-lives (or use ln); A1 15 min

practice.stem: A student records the number of counts from a weak radioactive source in six successive 10 s intervals: 23, 31, 27, 19, 25, 29. The background count is negligible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the readings are not all the same.
parts.answer: Radioactive decay is random: it is not possible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay, so the number of decays in equal intervals fluctuates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean count rate in counts per second.
parts.working: C1 total 154 counts in 60 s; A1 2.57 s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could obtain a more reliable value for the count rate.
parts.answer: Count for a much longer time (or repeat many more times) and average.

practice.stem: A sample contains 1.0 µg of strontium-90 (half-life 28.8 years). Unified atomic mass unit u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. 1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of strontium-90 nuclei in the sample.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activity of the sample.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the activity after 50 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Starting from dN/dt = −λN, state the expression for the number N of undecayed nuclei after time t, and explain why the activity follows the same law.
parts.answer: N = N₀e^(−λt); A = λN, and λ is constant, so A = A₀e^(−λt).
parts.working: B1 N = N₀e^(−λt); B1 A ∝ N.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time for the activity of a sodium-24 sample (half-life 15.0 hours) to fall to 10% of its initial value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the time to fall from 100% to 50% is the same as the time to fall from 20% to 10%.
parts.answer: Decay is exponential: the half-life is constant, independent of the amount present.

practice.stem: Fluorine-18, used in PET scanning, has a half-life of 110 minutes. A patient must receive an activity of 400 MBq at the time of injection, 2.5 hours after the dose is prepared in a cyclotron unit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activity that must be prepared.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activity remaining in the patient 12 hours after injection, ignoring any loss from the body.

practice.stem:
A student records the count rate C (corrected for background) from a short-lived source.
t / min: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25
C / min⁻¹: 1200, 778, 505, 327, 212, 138
ln (C / min⁻¹): 7.09, 6.66, 6.22, 5.79, 5.36, 4.93

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a graph of ln C against t should be a straight line, and state what its gradient represents.
parts.answer: C = C₀e^(−λt) gives ln C = ln C₀ − λt (form y = c + mx); gradient = −λ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the first and last values of ln C to find the gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence determine the half-life of the source.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why it is better to plot ln C against t than to read the half-life directly from a graph of C against t.
parts.answer: A straight-line graph tests the exponential relationship and uses all the data (best-fit line), reducing the effect of random fluctuations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two sources P and Q have the same initial activity. The half-life of P is 2.0 hours and that of Q is 6.0 hours. Calculate the ratio (activity of P) ÷ (activity of Q) after 12 hours.
parts.working: P: 12/2 = 6 half-lives, A = A₀/64 (M1); Q: 2 half-lives, A = A₀/4 (M1); ratio = 4/64 = 1/16 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the ratio (number of undecayed nuclei of P) ÷ (number of undecayed nuclei of Q) at the start.
parts.working: A = λN so N ∝ A/λ ∝ A × t½ (M1); equal A, so N_P/N_Q = 2.0/6.0 = 1/3 (A1).

practice.stem: A household smoke detector contains americium-241, half-life 432 years, with an activity of 37 kBq. 1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s; 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the decay constant of americium-241 in s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of americium-241 nuclei in the detector.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of americium-241 in the detector.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the detector does not need a new source during its working life of 10 years.
parts.answer: 10 years is tiny compared with 432 years, so the activity hardly changes (falls by about 1.6 %).

practice.stem: Phosphorus-32 (half-life 14.3 days) is used in the treatment of some blood disorders. A patient is given a dose with an activity of 400 MBq.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activity of the dose after 14 days.
parts.working: C1 A = A₀e^(−λt) with λ = 0.0485 day⁻¹; A1 203 MBq

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time after which the activity has fallen to 30 MBq.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the activity in the patient's body may fall faster than your calculation suggests.
parts.answer: Some phosphorus is excreted from the body (biological removal), as well as decaying.

practice.stem: A radioactive source has an activity of 2400 Bq. Exactly 3.0 hours later its activity is 1750 Bq.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the decay constant, in h⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the half-life.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the activity 24 hours after the first measurement.

practice.stem: Engineers find a leak in an underground water pipe by adding a solution containing sodium-24 (half-life 15.0 hours) to the water. The detection equipment needs the solution to have an activity of at least 50 MBq 48 hours after it is prepared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum activity of the solution when it is prepared.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why a nuclide with a half-life of about 15 hours is suitable for this use.
parts.answer: Long enough for the solution to be prepared, transported and the leak traced; short enough that the activity left in the ground/water soon becomes negligible.
parts.working: B1 long enough to complete the test; B1 short enough to avoid long-term contamination

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sodium-24 emits β⁻ particles and γ-rays. State which radiation is detected at the surface and why.
parts.answer: γ-rays – they can pass through the soil, whereas β⁻ particles are absorbed.

practice.stem: A sample contains 2.0 mg of sodium-24 (half-life 15.0 hours), which decays to stable magnesium-24.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sodium-24 remaining after 24 hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of magnesium-24 formed in this time. Assume the masses of the parent and daughter atoms are equal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of magnesium-24 atoms to sodium-24 atoms after 24 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Starting from N = N₀e^(−λt), show that the half-life is given by t½ = ln 2/λ.
parts.answer: At t = t½, N = N₀/2: ½ = e^(−λt½) → ln 2 = λt½.
parts.working: M1 N = N₀/2 substituted; A1 rearrangement

parts.label: b
parts.text: A nuclide has decay constant 0.0125 s⁻¹. Calculate its half-life.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many half-lives must pass for the activity to fall to 10% of its initial value.

practice.stem: Uranium-238 decays through a chain of short-lived nuclides to stable lead-206; the overall half-life is 4.47 × 10⁹ years. A rock sample contains 0.30 lead-206 nuclei for every uranium-238 nucleus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the number of uranium-238 nuclei remaining is 1/1.30 of the original number.
parts.working: Each decayed U nucleus gives one Pb nucleus, so N₀ = N_U + N_Pb = N_U(1 + 0.30) (M1, A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the age of the rock.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two assumptions made.
parts.answer: No lead-206 was present when the rock formed; no uranium or lead has entered or left the rock (and the intermediate nuclides in the chain are negligible).

practice.stem: A cobalt-60 source (half-life 5.27 years) for a cancer treatment machine must have an initial activity of 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq. u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. 1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of cobalt-60 nuclei needed for an activity of 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of cobalt-60 needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The source is replaced when its activity falls below 2.0 × 10¹⁰ Bq. Calculate how long after manufacture this happens.

practice.stem: Air in a basement contains radon-222 (half-life 3.82 days) with an activity of 200 Bq per cubic metre. u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; 1 day = 86 400 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of radon-222 atoms in each cubic metre of air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of radon in each cubic metre of air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The supply of radon from the ground is stopped by sealing the floor. Calculate how many days it takes for the activity to fall to 20 Bq m⁻³, assuming no ventilation.

practice.stem: Polonium-210 (half-life 138 days) emits α-particles of energy 5.30 MeV and has been used as a compact heat source in spacecraft. u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J; 1 day = 86 400 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the initial activity of 1.0 g of polonium-210.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the initial thermal power produced, assuming all the α-particle energy is absorbed in the capsule.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time, in days, for the power to fall to 25 W.
parts.working: P ∝ A, so t = (t½/ln 2) ln(P₀/25) (M1) = 345 days (A1).

practice.stem: A detector placed near a small caesium-137 source (half-life 30.2 years) records a count rate of 480 per minute after correction for background. The detector records only 2.0% of the emissions from the source. u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. 1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activity of the source.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of caesium-137 nuclei in the source.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of caesium-137 in the source.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the detector records only a small fraction of the emissions.
parts.answer: Emissions go in all directions and only a small fraction enter the detector window (and not all that enter are detected).

practice.stem: A source contains two radioactive nuclides, X (half-life 2.0 minutes) and Y (half-life 60 minutes). At t = 0 each contributes an activity of 800 Bq. The daughter nuclides are stable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total activity of the source at t = 10 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A graph of ln(total activity) against time is plotted for 0 to 120 minutes. Describe its shape and explain how the half-life of Y could be found from it.
parts.answer: Steep curve at first, then (after about 15 minutes, when X has effectively decayed) a straight line; the gradient of the straight part is −λ_Y, and t½ = ln 2/λ_Y.
parts.working: B1 initially steeper / curved; B1 straight line once X negligible; B1 gradient = −λ_Y → t½ = ln 2/λ

practice.stem: The curie was once defined as the activity of 1.0 g of radium-226 (half-life 1600 years). 1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s; 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of nuclei in 1.0 g of radium-226.
parts.working: C1 mass of one atom = 226 × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; A1 2.67 × 10²¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activity of 1.0 g of radium-226.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the activity after 100 years as a percentage of the initial activity, and explain why the curie could be defined in this way.
parts.answer: 95.8%; the activity changes very little over a human lifetime
parts.working: A1 95.8 %; B1 long half-life → activity effectively constant

practice.stem: Caesium-137, half-life 30.2 years, is a long-lived fission product in nuclear waste.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the time for the activity to fall to a fraction F of its initial value is t = t½ × ln(1/F)/ln 2.
parts.answer: A = A₀e^(−λt) → F = e^(−λt) → λt = ln(1/F), and λ = ln 2/t½.
parts.working: M1 F = e^(−λt); A1 substitute λ = ln 2/t½

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time for the activity of the caesium-137 to fall to 1.0% of its initial value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that after 10 half-lives the activity is less than 0.1% of its initial value.

practice.stem: Samarium-147 is an α-emitter with a half-life so long that its activity does not change measurably during an experiment. A 1.00 g sample of pure samarium-147 has a measured activity of 848 Bq. 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; 1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the half-life of samarium-147 cannot be found by measuring how its activity changes with time.
parts.answer: The activity falls by an immeasurably small fraction over any practical time, so the decrease would be hidden by the random fluctuations in the count.
parts.working: B1 change in activity far too small to detect (compared with random variation)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of samarium-147 nuclei in the sample.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the decay constant and hence the half-life of samarium-147 in years.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the samarium-147 present when the Earth formed, 4.5 × 10⁹ years ago, that has since decayed.

practice.stem:
A student uses a protactinium generator to study the decay of protactinium-234m. The count rate C, corrected for background, is recorded every 20 s.
t / s: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100
C / counts per 10 s: 412, 337, 276, 226, 185, 152

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate ln (C) for t = 0 and t = 100 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a graph of ln C against t should be a straight line, and state what its gradient represents.
parts.answer: C = C₀e^(−λt) so ln C = ln C₀ − λt: a straight line with gradient −λ.
parts.working: B1 ln C = ln C₀ − λt; B1 gradient = −λ

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the two values from (a) to estimate λ and the half-life.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The background count was measured once, for 10 s. Explain why this could cause the later points to deviate from the line, and suggest an improvement.
parts.answer: The background is random and was measured for only a short time, so its value is uncertain; this error is a larger fraction of the small later counts. Measure background over a long time (e.g. 5 minutes) and average.
parts.working: B1 uncertainty in background affects low count rates most; B1 measure background for longer / repeat

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a photon.
parts.answer: A discrete quantum (packet) of electromagnetic energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A green laser pointer emits light of wavelength 532 nm. Calculate the energy of one photon in joules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Express this energy in electronvolts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define work function.
parts.answer: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of the metal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define threshold frequency.
parts.answer: The minimum frequency of electromagnetic radiation that causes electrons to be emitted from the surface.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The work function of zinc is 4.30 eV. Calculate its threshold frequency.
parts.working: C1 φ = hf₀ with φ = 4.30 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; A1 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the momentum of a photon of red light of wavelength 650 nm.
parts.working: C1 p = h/λ; A1 1.02 × 10⁻²⁷ N s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the energy E of a photon is related to its momentum p by E = pc, and use this to find the photon energy.
parts.answer: E = hf = hc/λ = (h/λ)c = pc; E = 3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three observations from photoelectric emission experiments that cannot be explained by a wave theory of light.
parts.answer: Any three: no emission below a threshold frequency however intense the light; emission is instantaneous even at low intensity; the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons depends on frequency, not intensity; increasing intensity increases the rate of emission only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the photon model accounts for the existence of a threshold frequency.
parts.answer: Each electron absorbs the energy of one photon, E = hf; if hf is less than the work function no electron can escape, however many photons arrive.
parts.working: B1 one photon to one electron; B1 hf < φ means no emission

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the electronvolt.
parts.answer: The energy gained (transferred) when an electron moves through a potential difference of one volt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert 3.5 eV into joules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of a photon of energy 3.5 eV and state the region of the electromagnetic spectrum.
parts.working: B1 λ = hc/E value; B1 ultraviolet

parts.label: a
parts.text: An FM radio station in Islamabad broadcasts at 98.6 MHz. Calculate the energy of one of its photons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why radio waves cannot cause photoelectric emission from a metal, however intense they are.
parts.answer: Each photon's energy is far below any metal's work function (a few eV ≈ 10⁻¹⁹ J), and an electron absorbs only one photon, so no electron gains enough energy.
parts.working: B1 photon energy much less than work function; B1 one photon per electron / intensity only increases number of photons

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the relation between the energy of a photon and the frequency of the radiation, and name the constant it contains.
parts.answer: E = hf, where h is the Planck constant (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).
parts.working: 1 mark for E = hf and the constant named.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy of a photon of frequency 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz, in joules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Express this energy in electronvolts.
parts.working: E = 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹/(1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 2.49 eV. M1 divide by e; A1 answer.

practice.stem: Ultraviolet radiation of wavelength 250 nm falls on a clean potassium surface. The work function of potassium is 2.30 eV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy of each photon in eV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons in eV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the emitted electrons.
parts.working: C1 ½mv² = 4.28 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; A1 v = 9.69 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why most emitted electrons have less than this kinetic energy.
parts.answer: Electrons below the surface lose energy (in collisions) before escaping, or need more than the work function to escape.

practice.stem:
In a photoelectric experiment, light of different frequencies f falls on a metal surface, and the maximum kinetic energy KE_max of the emitted electrons is measured in electronvolts.
f / 10¹⁴ Hz | KE_max / eV
6.0 | 0.25
7.0 | 0.64
8.0 | 1.06
9.0 | 1.50
10.0 | 1.88

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that a graph of KE_max (in eV) against f should be a straight line, and state expressions for its gradient and its intercept on the KE_max axis.
parts.answer: hf = φ + KE_max, so KE_max = (h/e)f − φ/e with KE in eV; gradient = h/e, intercept = −φ (in eV).
parts.working: B1 rearranged equation; B1 gradient h/e and intercept −φ/e

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the first and last rows (or a best-fit line), determine a value for the Planck constant.
parts.working: M1 gradient (in V s) × e; A1 h in range with unit

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the work function of the metal in eV.
parts.working: M1 φ = hf/e − KE_max for a point on the line (or −intercept); A1 φ

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the threshold frequency.
parts.working: f₀ = φ/h, or the intercept on the f axis: 6.0 × 10¹⁴ − 0.25/(gradient 4.075 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s) (A1, consistent with (b) and (c))

practice.stem: A red laser pointer emits light of wavelength 650 nm with an output power of 5.0 mW.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of photons emitted per second.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A second laser of the same power emits blue light of wavelength 450 nm. State and explain whether it emits more or fewer photons per second.
parts.answer: Fewer: each blue photon has more energy (E = hc/λ, smaller λ), so fewer photons are needed for the same power.

practice.stem: A metal with work function 2.20 eV is illuminated with light containing only two wavelengths, 420 nm and 610 nm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the threshold wavelength for this metal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of the two wavelengths causes photoelectric emission.
parts.answer: 420 nm only (it is shorter than the threshold wavelength; 610 nm is longer).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the emitted electrons.
parts.working: C1 KE_max = hc/λ − φ = 1.22 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; A1 5.17 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Electrons in a dental X-ray tube are accelerated through a p.d. of 25 kV. State the maximum energy of an X-ray photon produced, in keV.
parts.working: An electron can lose all its kinetic energy (25 keV) to one photon (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum wavelength of the X-rays.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the X-rays produced have a continuous range of wavelengths above this minimum.
parts.answer: Electrons lose different amounts of energy in each deceleration (some in several steps), so photons of all energies up to the maximum are produced.

practice.stem: Graphs of the maximum kinetic energy KE_max of photoelectrons against frequency f are plotted for two metals, P and Q. Both are straight lines. The line for P meets the frequency axis at 5.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz and the line for Q meets it at 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the two lines are parallel.
parts.answer: The gradient of each line equals the Planck constant h (or h/e if KE_max is in eV), which is the same for all metals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the work function of each metal in eV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the intercept that each line would make if extended to the KE_max axis.
parts.answer: −2.28 eV for P and −3.32 eV for Q (minus the work function)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A red LED emits photons of wavelength 630 nm. Each photon is produced when one electron loses energy crossing the junction. Estimate the minimum p.d. needed across the LED.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a blue LED needs a larger p.d. than a red LED.
parts.answer: Blue photons have shorter wavelength and so more energy, so each electron must be given more energy (eV).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A zinc surface has a threshold wavelength of 310 nm. Calculate the work function of zinc, in eV.
parts.working: φ = hc/λ₀ = 1240 eV nm/310 nm = 4.00 eV (using hc = 1.240 × 10⁻⁶ eV m; with 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ the value is 4.01 eV, which rounds to the same 2 s.f.).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 240 nm falls on the zinc. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, in eV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the stopping potential that would stop these electrons.
parts.working: eV_s = E_k(max), so V_s = 1.17 V (numerically equal to the kinetic energy in eV).

practice.stem: Light of wavelength 400 nm and power 2.0 µW falls on the cathode of a photocell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of photons arriving at the cathode per second.
parts.working: C1 E = hc/λ; A1 N = P/E = 4.02 × 10¹² s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: On average, one photon in 500 releases an electron, and all released electrons reach the anode. Calculate the photoelectric current.
parts.working: M1 electrons per second = 8.04 × 10⁹; A1 I = Ne = 1.29 × 10⁻⁹ A

parts.label: c
parts.text: The intensity of the light is doubled at the same wavelength. State the effect on (i) the current and (ii) the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons, and explain.
parts.answer: (i) current doubles, since twice as many photons arrive per second; (ii) maximum KE unchanged, since each photon's energy hf is unchanged.

practice.stem: Photons carry momentum as well as energy. Solar sails use this to propel spacecraft.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the force exerted on a surface that absorbs all the light falling on it is P/c, where P is the power of the light.
parts.answer: Each photon has momentum E/c; the photons arriving per second carry momentum P/c per second; when absorbed, rate of change of momentum = force = P/c.
parts.working: B1 p = E/c per photon; B1 rate of change of momentum = P/c

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the force on a 1.0 m² black panel facing the Sun just outside the Earth's atmosphere, where the intensity is 1.36 kW m⁻².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the force if the panel is replaced by a perfect mirror, and explain the difference.
parts.answer: 9.07 × 10⁻⁶ N; each photon's momentum is reversed, so its change of momentum (and the force) is doubled.

practice.stem: Monochromatic radiation of wavelength 300 nm falls on a metal surface and the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons is 1.85 eV. When radiation of wavelength 450 nm is used, the maximum kinetic energy is 0.47 eV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use these results to determine a value for the Planck constant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the work function of the metal, in eV.
parts.working: C1 φ = hc/λ₁ − KE₁; A1 2.29 eV

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the longest wavelength that will cause emission from this metal.

practice.stem: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 330 nm falls on a metal plate of work function 2.10 eV in a vacuum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons, in eV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the electrons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The fastest electrons enter a uniform magnetic field of flux density 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ T at right angles to the field. Calculate the radius of their circular path.
parts.working: C1 Bev = mv²/r, so r = mv/(Be); A1 0.0363 m

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe how the paths of slower electrons from the same surface differ.
parts.answer: They move in circles of smaller radius (r ∝ v), in the same sense of rotation.

practice.stem: On a dark night in the Thar desert, a dark-adapted human eye can just detect green light of wavelength 510 nm when 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ W enters the pupil. The pupil diameter is 7.0 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of photons per second entering the eye at this threshold.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the intensity at the eye at this threshold.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A lamp radiates 5.0 W of visible light of wavelength 510 nm uniformly in all directions. Estimate the greatest distance at which it could just be seen, ignoring absorption in the air.
parts.working: M1 I = P/(4πd²) set equal to 5.20 × 10⁻¹³ W m⁻²; A1 d = 8.75 × 10⁵ m

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the de Broglie relation, explaining the symbols.
parts.answer: λ = h/p, where λ is the de Broglie wavelength, h the Planck constant and p the momentum of the particle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at 2.5 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one phenomenon that provides evidence for the wave nature of electrons and one that provides evidence for the particle nature of electromagnetic radiation.
parts.answer: Electron diffraction (by a thin graphite/crystal film); the photoelectric effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In an electron diffraction tube, the electrons form rings on a fluorescent screen. Explain why this shows wave behaviour.
parts.answer: Rings are a diffraction/interference pattern: maxima and minima form where waves from the atomic layers reinforce or cancel, which particles alone would not produce.
parts.working: B1 diffraction/interference; B1 by the regular atomic spacing comparable with λ

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the wave–particle duality of matter.
parts.answer: Particles such as electrons and neutrons show wave-like behaviour (diffraction and interference) as well as particle behaviour (momentum and collisions); a particle of momentum p has de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p, which links the two.
parts.working: 1 mark for wave-like behaviour shown by diffraction or interference; 1 mark for linking the particle momentum p to a wavelength λ = h/p.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A neutron moves with speed 1.2 × 10³ m s⁻¹. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength. The mass of a neutron is 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference V. Show that its de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/√(2meV).
parts.working: eV = ½mv², so mv = √(2meV) and λ = h/p = h/√(2meV). M1 eV = ½mv²; A1 rearrangement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of electrons accelerated through 100 V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength for electrons accelerated through 400 V and state the effect of increasing V on the wavelength.
parts.working: λ ∝ 1/√V, so quadrupling V halves the wavelength: 6.14 × 10⁻¹¹ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Electron diffraction and the photoelectric effect provide evidence for the wave and particle natures of matter and radiation. State one observation that shows the wave nature of electrons, and one observation that shows the particle nature of electromagnetic radiation.
parts.answer: Wave nature of electrons: diffraction rings/patterns when electrons pass through a thin crystal or graphite film. Particle nature of light: photoelectric emission is instantaneous and occurs only above a threshold frequency.
parts.working: 1 mark for electron diffraction (or interference); 1 mark for photoelectric effect (threshold frequency or instant emission).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron moves with de Broglie wavelength 0.15 nm. Calculate its momentum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the electron.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through a p.d. V is λ = h/√(2meV).
parts.answer: eV = ½mv² = p²/2m, so p = √(2meV); λ = h/p = h/√(2meV).
parts.working: B1 KE = eV = p²/2m; B1 substitution

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength for V = 150 V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The atomic spacing in a crystal is about 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Explain why electrons of this energy are diffracted significantly by the crystal.
parts.answer: Their wavelength is similar to (the same order as) the atomic spacing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg bowled at 40 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the ball shows no observable diffraction when it passes between the stumps.
parts.answer: The wavelength is far smaller than the gap or any obstacle (by more than 30 orders of magnitude), so diffraction is negligible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The accelerating p.d. in an electron diffraction tube is increased from 3.0 kV to 5.0 kV. Calculate the ratio new wavelength ÷ old wavelength.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the effect on the diameter of the rings on the screen.
parts.answer: The rings become smaller: the shorter wavelength is diffracted through smaller angles.
parts.working: B1 smaller; B1 shorter wavelength, less diffraction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Electrons in an electron microscope are accelerated through 12 kV. Calculate their de Broglie wavelength.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Visible light has wavelength 500 nm. Explain why an electron microscope can resolve much finer detail than an optical microscope.
parts.answer: The electron wavelength (about 10⁻¹¹ m) is much smaller than that of visible light (5 × 10⁻⁷ m), so diffraction limits the resolution far less.
parts.working: 1 mark for a much shorter electron wavelength; 1 mark for resolution being limited by wavelength (diffraction).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron has kinetic energy 2.0 eV. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength. Use λ = h/√(2mE_k).
parts.working: E_k = 2.0 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/√(2 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 3.20 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 8.68 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. M1 kinetic energy in J; M1 substitution; A1 answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare this wavelength with the spacing of atoms in a solid (about 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) and comment on the diffraction you would expect.
parts.answer: The wavelength (about 0.9 nm) is larger than the atomic spacing, so diffraction by the atoms would be weak or not observed for a low-energy electron of this kind.
parts.working: 1 mark for a comparison of wavelength with spacing; 1 mark for a sensible comment on diffraction (not strong, because λ is larger than the spacing).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A proton and an electron both have de Broglie wavelength 0.20 nm. Show that the speed of a particle of mass m with this wavelength is v = h/(mλ).
parts.working: λ = h/p = h/(mv), so v = h/(mλ).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the proton and the speed of the electron.
parts.answer: proton: 1990 m s⁻¹; electron: 3.64 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the ratio (speed of the electron)/(speed of the proton) and state what it equals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A table tennis ball of mass 0.0027 kg moves at 15 m s⁻¹ and a dust particle of mass 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ kg drifts at 0.50 m s⁻¹. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of each, and show that both are very small compared with the size of a nucleus (about 1 × 10⁻¹⁵ m).
parts.answer: ball: 1.64 × 10⁻³² m; dust particle: 1.33 × 10⁻²⁴ m; both are far smaller than a nucleus
parts.working: λ = h/(mv): ball 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(0.0027 × 15) = 1.6 × 10⁻³² m; dust particle 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(1.0 × 10⁻⁹ × 0.50) = 1.3 × 10⁻²⁴ m. Both are much smaller than a nucleus, so the wave nature cannot be detected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the wave nature of these everyday objects is not observed, even though the de Broglie relation applies to them.
parts.answer: The wavelengths are far too small for any aperture or spacing that can be used, so no diffraction is observable.
parts.working: 1 mark: the wavelength is negligible compared with the size of any obstacle or aperture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Electrons of kinetic energy 120 eV are directed at a crystal whose atomic spacing is 0.22 nm. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on whether these electrons would be expected to show strong diffraction by the crystal.
parts.answer: The wavelength (0.112 nm) is about half the atomic spacing (0.22 nm), so the wavelength is comparable with the spacing and strong diffraction is expected.
parts.working: 1 mark for comparing λ with the spacing; 1 mark for a conclusion that diffraction is significant (λ comparable with d).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy. Show that the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths, λ_electron/λ_proton, equals √(m_p/m_e), and calculate its value.
parts.working: M1 p = √(2mE_k); M1 λ = h/√(2mE_k), so ratio = √(m_p/m_e); A1 42.8

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a proton accelerated from rest through 2.0 kV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a neutron of speed 2200 m s⁻¹ (mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate its kinetic energy in eV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why slow neutrons like these are useful for studying the arrangement of atoms in solids.
parts.answer: Their wavelength is about the same as the atomic spacing, so they are diffracted by the crystal lattice (and being uncharged they penetrate the material).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy of a photon of wavelength 0.20 nm, in eV.
parts.working: C1 E = hc/λ = 9.94 × 10⁻¹⁶ J; A1 value in eV

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of an electron with de Broglie wavelength 0.20 nm, in eV.
parts.working: M1 p = h/λ = 3.31 × 10⁻²⁴ N s; M1 E = p²/2m = 6.03 × 10⁻¹⁸ J; A1 value in eV

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why electrons, rather than X-rays, are used to study the structure of thin surface layers.
parts.answer: Electrons of the same wavelength have much less energy, so they penetrate only a short distance and interact strongly with surface atoms (and cause less damage).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An alpha particle (mass 6.64 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) and an electron (mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) each have kinetic energy 5.0 keV. Show that the de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/√(2mE_k).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of the electron.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the ratio λ(alpha)/λ(electron) and explain which particle has the more diffracted wavelength at this energy.
parts.working: λ ∝ 1/√m at equal KE, so λ(α)/λ(e) = √(m_e/m_α) = 0.0117. The electron has the much longer wavelength, so it is the one more readily diffracted by atomic-scale slits or crystals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that an electron accelerated through a potential difference V has de Broglie wavelength λ = 1.23 nm/√V when V is in volts, and rearrange to show that the accelerating potential needed for a wavelength λ is V = h²/(2meλ²).
parts.answer: λ = h/√(2meV) = (1.23 × 10⁻⁹ m V½)/√V = 1.23 nm/√V; squaring and rearranging gives V = h²/(2meλ²).
parts.working: h/√(2me) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/√(2 × 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 1.23 × 10⁻⁹ m V½. From λ = h/√(2meV): λ² = h²/(2meV), so V = h²/(2meλ²). M1 evaluate h/√(2me); M1 squaring and rearranging; A1 final form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the accelerating potential needed for electrons to have a wavelength of 0.050 nm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether relativistic effects need to be considered for these electrons.
parts.answer: No: the speed v = √(2eV/m) ≈ 1.5 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹, only about 5% of the speed of light, so classical expressions are accurate enough.
parts.working: 1 mark: speed small compared with c (about 5%), so non-relativistic formulae are adequate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student accelerates electrons through several potential differences V and measures their de Broglie wavelengths λ:
V / V: 100, 400, 900, 1600
λ / nm: 0.1226, 0.0613, 0.0409, 0.0307
Show that a graph of λ against 1/√V should be a straight line through the origin, and state what its gradient represents.
parts.answer: λ = h/√(2me) × 1/√V, a straight line through the origin with gradient h/√(2me).
parts.working: 1 mark for λ ∝ 1/√V giving a line through the origin; 1 mark for the gradient h/√(2me).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gradient using the first and last points (in m V½), and hence determine a value for the Planck constant.
parts.answer: gradient ≈ 1.23 × 10⁻⁹ m V½; h ≈ 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ J s
parts.working: 1/√V = 0.100 V⁻½ and 0.025 V⁻½; gradient = (1.226 × 10⁻¹⁰ − 3.07 × 10⁻¹¹)/(0.100 − 0.025) = 1.23 × 10⁻⁹ m V½; h = gradient × √(2me) = 1.23 × 10⁻⁹ × 5.40 × 10⁻²⁵ = 6.62 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. M1 gradient; M1 relation to h; A1 value.

practice.stem: An electron in a hydrogen atom falls from the energy level at −1.51 eV to the level at −3.40 eV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy of the photon emitted, in eV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the emitted light and state its colour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A simplified atom has energy levels at −9.0 eV (ground state), −5.4 eV and −2.1 eV. Label them level 1 (−9.0 eV), level 2 (−5.4 eV) and level 3 (−2.1 eV). An electron falls from level 3 to level 1, and then from level 2 to level 1, in separate transitions. Calculate the wavelength of the photon emitted in each transition.
parts.working: ΔE = 6.9 eV for 3→1: λ = hc/ΔE = 1240 eV nm/6.9 eV = 180 nm. ΔE = 3.6 eV for 2→1: λ = 344 nm. 1 mark for each energy difference; 1 mark for each wavelength (in nm or m, correct to 3 s.f.).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which transition emits the photon of shorter wavelength, and explain.
parts.answer: 3→1, because it has the larger energy difference (6.9 eV compared with 3.6 eV) and λ is inversely proportional to energy.
parts.working: 1 mark for the transition with the larger energy change, with a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the ionisation energy of an atom.
parts.answer: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron completely from the atom in its ground state (to infinity, with zero kinetic energy).
parts.working: 1 mark for ground state and removal to infinity with zero KE.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An atom has ground-state energy −9.0 eV. Calculate its ionisation energy, in eV.
parts.working: The electron must be raised from −9.0 eV to 0 eV, a change of 9.0 eV.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the longest wavelength of light that can ionise this atom from its ground state.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the wavelength of a spectral line depends on the energy difference between two atomic levels, and why transitions with larger energy differences give lines at shorter wavelengths.
parts.answer: Electrons in atoms can only occupy discrete energy levels, so photons are emitted only with energies equal to the differences between the levels. Each element has its own set of energy levels, so its pattern of lines is characteristic.
parts.working: 1 mark: discrete (quantised) energy levels; 1 mark: photon energy equals the difference between two levels; 1 mark: each element has a unique set of levels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Light of energy 2.10 eV is emitted by an atom. Calculate its frequency in hertz.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of this light and state its colour.
parts.working: λ = c/f = 3.00 × 10⁸/5.07 × 10¹⁴ = 5.92 × 10⁻⁷ m = 592 nm; the light is yellow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A photon of wavelength 500 nm is emitted by a transition in an atom. Calculate its energy in eV.
parts.working: E = hc/λ = 1240 eV nm/500 nm = 2.48 eV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define an excited state of an atom.
parts.answer: A state in which the atom has more energy than its ground state (an electron occupies a higher energy level than in the lowest state).
parts.working: 1 mark for more energy than the ground state.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a hot, low-pressure gas produces an emission line spectrum.
parts.answer: Electrons in the atoms are excited to higher energy levels; they fall to lower levels, emitting photons; each photon's energy equals the difference between two discrete levels, hf = E₁ − E₂, so only certain frequencies appear.
parts.working: B1 excitation; B1 de-excitation emits photon; B1 discrete levels give discrete frequencies/hf = ΔE

parts.label: b
parts.text: White light passes through a cool gas. Explain why the spectrum of the transmitted light contains dark lines.
parts.answer: Atoms absorb photons whose energies exactly equal differences between their energy levels; these are re-emitted in all directions, so those wavelengths are missing (much weaker) in the forward beam.
parts.working: B1 absorb photons of energy = ΔE only; B1 re-emitted in all directions

practice.stem: Four energy levels of the hydrogen atom are −13.6 eV (ground state), −3.40 eV, −1.51 eV and −0.85 eV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of different photon energies that can be emitted as atoms in the −0.85 eV level return to the ground state by any route.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the shortest wavelength emitted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the energy levels are given negative values.
parts.answer: Zero energy is defined for an electron that is free of the atom (at infinity); a bound electron has less energy than this.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sodium vapour lamps emit two strong yellow lines at 589.0 nm and 589.6 nm. Calculate the energy of a photon at each wavelength, in eV.
parts.working: E = hc/λ = 1240 eV nm/589.0 nm = 2.11 eV and 1240/589.6 = 2.10 eV. 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the 589.0 nm line. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electron in a hydrogen-like atom drops from a level at −1.5 eV to a level at −3.4 eV, emitting a photon of wavelength 640 nm. Calculate the energy of the photon, in eV.
parts.working: E = hc/λ = 1240 eV nm/640 nm = 1.94 eV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another atom emits a photon of the same wavelength when an electron falls from a level at −1.5 eV to a lower level. Calculate the energy of this lower level.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a hot solid gives a continuous spectrum, while a low-pressure gas gives a line spectrum.
parts.answer: In a hot solid the atoms are closely packed and interact, so their energy levels merge into bands and photons of a continuous range of energies are emitted. In a low-pressure gas the atoms are far apart, so each has discrete energy levels and emits only specific photon energies.
parts.working: 1 mark: solids have closely spaced / merged levels (continuous range); 1 mark: gas atoms are isolated with discrete levels; 1 mark: photons only at specific energies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hydrogen atom in its ground state (−13.6 eV) absorbs a photon of energy 10.2 eV. Show that the atom is excited to the n = 2 level.
parts.answer: E = −13.6 + 10.2 = −3.4 eV, which equals E₂ = −13.6/2² = −3.40 eV, so the atom is excited to n = 2.
parts.working: 1 mark for the energy after absorption; 1 mark for matching it to the n = 2 level.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a photon of energy 11.0 eV is not absorbed by a hydrogen atom in its ground state.
parts.answer: 11.0 eV does not equal any difference between the energy levels (−13.6 + 11.0 = −2.6 eV is not a permitted level), so the photon is not absorbed.
parts.working: Photons are absorbed only when their energy exactly matches the difference between two levels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the ionisation energy of hydrogen in the n = 2 level, and calculate it in eV.
parts.answer: The energy needed to raise an electron from the n = 2 level (−3.40 eV) to the continuum (0 eV): 3.40 eV.
parts.working: 1 mark for the definition from the n = 2 level to zero energy; 1 mark for 3.40 eV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the photon of this energy, in nm.
parts.working: λ = hc/E = 1240 eV nm/3.40 eV = 365 nm (ultraviolet).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas atom has four energy levels E₁ = −10.0 eV, E₂ = −4.0 eV, E₃ = −2.0 eV and E₄ = −1.0 eV. Atoms in level 4 de-excite by any route to the ground state. State the number of different photon energies that can be emitted from the atom in this process, and calculate the shortest wavelength emitted.
parts.answer: 6 different photon energies (E₄→E₁, E₄→E₂, E₄→E₃ and the routes E₃→E₂, E₃→E₁, E₂→E₁ are all different). Shortest wavelength from 4→1, ΔE = 9.0 eV, λ = 1240/9.0 = 138 nm.
parts.working: 1 mark for 6 distinct energies (all transitions having different ΔE); 1 mark for choosing 4→1 as the largest energy change; 1 mark for λ = 138 nm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the longest wavelength emitted from the same atom, in nm.
parts.working: The smallest energy change is 4→3, ΔE = 1.0 eV, so λ = 1240/1.0 = 1240 nm (infrared).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ruby laser emits light of wavelength 694 nm. Calculate the energy of one photon, in eV.
parts.working: E = hc/λ = 1240 eV nm/694 nm = 1.79 eV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the laser needs a population inversion, with more electrons in the upper laser level than the lower level.
parts.answer: Stimulated emission is greater than absorption only when there are more atoms in the upper level than in the lower level; otherwise the photons are absorbed rather than amplified.
parts.working: 1 mark for stimulated emission being needed; 1 mark for more atoms in the upper level so that emission dominates absorption.

practice.stem: An electron with kinetic energy 12.2 eV collides with a hydrogen atom in its ground state. Energy levels of hydrogen: −13.6 eV, −3.40 eV, −1.51 eV, −0.85 eV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which energy levels the hydrogen atom can be excited to by the collision. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: To −3.40 eV (needs 10.2 eV) or −1.51 eV (needs 12.09 eV), not −0.85 eV (needs 12.75 eV, more than 12.2 eV). Unlike photons, an electron can give up only part of its energy.
parts.working: B1 levels −3.40 and −1.51 eV; B1 12.75 eV > 12.2 eV / electron can transfer part of its energy

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the electron after it excites an atom to the highest possible level.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the wavelengths of all the photons that could then be emitted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrogen energy levels are given by E_n = −13.6/n² eV. Show that the energy of the photon emitted when an electron falls from n = 5 to n = 3 is 0.97 eV, and calculate its wavelength.
parts.working: ΔE = 13.6(1/3² − 1/5²) = 13.6 × 0.0711 = 0.97 eV. λ = hc/ΔE = 1240 eV nm/0.97 eV = 1.28 × 10³ nm (infrared). M1 energy levels; M1 ΔE; A1 wavelength.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the photon emitted when an electron falls from n = 4 to n = 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the energy of a photon absorbed by a hydrogen atom in the ground state when it is raised to level n is E = 13.6(1 − 1/n²) eV. Hence calculate the photon energy and wavelength that take the atom from n = 1 to n = 3.
parts.working: E_n = −13.6/n², so E = E_n − E₁ = −13.6/n² + 13.6 = 13.6(1 − 1/n²). For n = 3: E = 12.1 eV. λ = 1240/12.09 = 103 nm (ultraviolet). M1 derivation; M1 E for n = 3; A1 energy; A1 wavelength.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas emits photons of wavelengths 410 nm, 434 nm, 486 nm and 656 nm. Convert each wavelength into a photon energy in eV, using hc = 1240 eV nm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: These lines belong to the Balmer series of hydrogen, with E_n = −13.6/n² eV. Identify the upper level n for each line, by using the transitions to n = 2.
parts.working: M1 ΔE = 13.6(1/4 − 1/n²); M1 matching at least two lines; A1 all four lines correctly identified.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the Balmer series is.
parts.answer: The set of spectral lines produced by transitions of electrons from higher levels to the n = 2 level of hydrogen.
parts.working: 1 mark for transitions ending at n = 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Lyman series of hydrogen consists of transitions that end on the n = 1 level. Calculate the wavelength of the photon emitted in the transition from n = ∞ to n = 1, which gives the shortest wavelength of the series. Use E_n = −13.6/n² eV.
parts.working: ΔE = 13.6 eV, so λ = 1240 eV nm/13.6 eV = 91.2 nm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the region of the electromagnetic spectrum to which this radiation belongs.
parts.working: 91 nm is shorter than visible light (about 400–700 nm) and lies in the ultraviolet region.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A car accelerates uniformly from 4.0 m s⁻¹ to 22 m s⁻¹ in a time of 6.0 s. What is the distance travelled in this time?
A 54 m
B 78 m
C 108 m
D 132 m
parts.working: s = ½(u + v)t = ½(4.0 + 22) × 6.0 = 78 m. 132 m wrongly uses the final speed for the whole time; 54 m uses only ½Δv × t and ignores the initial speed.

practice.stem: A motorcycle starts from rest at a traffic signal in Lahore and accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m s⁻² along a straight road for 8.0 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by acceleration.
parts.working: B1: change of velocity ÷ time taken (rate of change of velocity). 'Speed' instead of velocity scores 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the motorcycle at the end of the 8.0 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the distance travelled by the motorcycle in the 8.0 s.

practice.stem: A local train travels in a straight line between two stations. Its velocity–time graph is made of straight lines joining these points (time in s, velocity in m s⁻¹): (0, 0), (40, 16), (160, 16), (200, 0).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the train during the first 40 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the total distance travelled between the two stations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the average speed of the train for the whole journey.

practice.stem: A lift in an office tower starts from rest and accelerates upwards uniformly at 1.2 m s⁻² for 2.5 s. It then moves at constant speed for 9.0 s and finally decelerates uniformly to rest in 2.0 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum speed of the lift.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the deceleration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total height risen by the lift.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A stone is dropped from rest from a high bridge and falls freely for 3.0 s. Air resistance is negligible and g = 9.81 m s⁻². How far does it fall?
A 14.7 m
B 29.4 m
C 44.1 m
D 88.3 m
parts.working: s = ½gt² = ½ × 9.81 × 9.0 = 44.1 m. 29.4 m is gt (the final speed in m s⁻¹), not a distance; 88.3 m omits the ½.

practice.stem: A cyclist rides 4.2 km due north along a straight road in 10 min, then turns and rides 3.0 km due south in 5 min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between speed and velocity.
parts.answer: Speed is a scalar (distance per unit time); velocity is a vector (displacement per unit time, with direction).
parts.working: B1: velocity has direction / is a vector (rate of change of displacement); speed is scalar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average speed of the cyclist for the whole 15 min.
parts.working: Total distance 7200 m, total time 900 s (M1); 7200/900 = 8.0 m s⁻¹ (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the average velocity of the cyclist for the whole 15 min.
parts.working: Displacement = 4.2 − 3.0 = 1.2 km north (M1); 1200/900 = 1.33 m s⁻¹ north (A1; direction needed).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An object moving in a straight line with uniform acceleration has a velocity of 5.0 m s⁻¹. After travelling a further 24 m its velocity is 11 m s⁻¹. What is its acceleration?
A 0.25 m s⁻²
B 2.0 m s⁻²
C 2.5 m s⁻²
D 4.0 m s⁻²
parts.working: v² = u² + 2as → a = (121 − 25)/(2 × 24) = 2.0 m s⁻². 4.0 m s⁻² forgets the factor 2; 0.25 m s⁻² divides the change in speed by the distance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A train's speed falls uniformly from 15 m s⁻¹ to 5.0 m s⁻¹ in 8.0 s as it brakes. What is its displacement in this time?
A 40 m
B 80 m
C 120 m
D 160 m
parts.working: s = ½(u + v)t = ½(15 + 5.0) × 8.0 = 80 m. 120 m uses the initial speed for the whole 8.0 s; 160 m leaves out the ½; 40 m uses the change in speed (10 m s⁻¹) instead of the average speed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A trolley passes light gate 1 at 0.80 m s⁻¹ and light gate 2 at 1.60 m s⁻¹. The gates are 1.20 m apart on a straight, level track, and the trolley accelerates uniformly between them. Calculate the acceleration of the trolley.
parts.working: v² − u² = 2as: a = (1.60² − 0.80²)/(2 × 1.20) = 0.800 m s⁻². M1 correct equation; A1 answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the trolley to travel between the gates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption you made in (a).
parts.answer: The acceleration is uniform (constant) between the gates.
parts.working: Any reasonable assumption such as uniform acceleration, a straight track, or negligible friction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student measures her reaction time by catching a ruler. A partner releases the ruler from rest without warning, and the student catches it after it has fallen 0.245 m. Calculate the time the ruler takes to fall this distance. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻².
parts.working: s = ut + ½at² with u = 0: t = √(2s/g) = √(2 × 0.245/9.81) = 0.223 s. M1 correct equation; A1 answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the ruler just before it is caught.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption made in (a) and say whether it makes the calculated reaction time too large or too small.
parts.answer: Air resistance is negligible. With air resistance the ruler falls more slowly, so the true fall time is longer and the calculated reaction time is too small.
parts.working: 1 mark for the assumption (no air resistance / ruler dropped from rest). 1 mark for 'too small' with the reason that real fall time is longer.

practice.stem: A marble rolls from rest down a straight ramp of length 2.0 m. It reaches the bottom 1.6 s after release. Assume uniform acceleration on the ramp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define acceleration.
parts.answer: Rate of change of velocity (change in velocity per unit time).
parts.working: a = Δv/Δt; accept 'change of velocity divided by time taken'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the acceleration of the marble as it rolls down the ramp.
parts.working: s = ½at² with u = 0, so a = 2s/t² = 2 × 2.0/1.6² = 1.56 m s⁻².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the marble at the bottom of the ramp.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The marble then rolls along a flat floor and comes to rest after 4.0 s with uniform deceleration. Calculate the distance it travels on the floor.
parts.working: Average speed = (2.50 + 0)/2 = 1.25 m s⁻¹; distance = 1.25 × 4.0 = 5.0 m. Alternatively, ½ × 2.50 × 4.0 = 5.0 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A ball is thrown vertically upwards and is caught again at the same height. Air resistance is negligible. Upwards is taken as positive. Which statement describes the acceleration–time graph of the ball while it is in the air?
A a horizontal line at a negative value
B a sloping straight line from a positive value to a negative value
C a horizontal line at zero, because the ball returns to its starting point
D a horizontal line at a positive value until the top, then at a negative value
parts.answer: A a horizontal line at a negative value
parts.working: The only force is weight, so acceleration is g downwards (−9.81 m s⁻²) throughout, including at the top. The sloping line describes the velocity–time graph, not acceleration.

practice.stem: A driver on the M-2 motorway is travelling at 25 m s⁻¹ when he sees an obstruction. His reaction time is 0.65 s. The brakes then give a uniform deceleration of 6.5 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the thinking distance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the braking distance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the total stopping distance.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the stopping distance more than doubles when the initial speed is doubled.
parts.answer: Thinking distance doubles (∝ u) but braking distance quadruples (∝ u²).
parts.working: B1: thinking distance ∝ u so doubles; B1: braking distance ∝ u² so becomes four times as large, so total more than doubles.

practice.stem:
A trolley is released from rest on a slope. Its displacement s along the slope is recorded at time t:
t / s: 0, 0.50, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00
s / m: 0, 0.10, 0.40, 0.90, 1.60

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the data are consistent with uniform acceleration from rest.
parts.answer: s/t² is constant (0.40 m s⁻²) for every reading, so s ∝ t².
parts.working: M1: calculate s/t² for at least three readings (0.40, 0.40, 0.40, 0.40); A1: constant, so s = ½at² with constant a (starting from rest, s = 0 at t = 0).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the acceleration of the trolley.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the velocity of the trolley at t = 2.0 s.

practice.stem: A tennis ball is dropped from rest from a height of 1.8 m onto a hard floor. It leaves the floor with 70% of the speed it had just before impact. Air resistance is negligible; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the ball just before it hits the floor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the height reached by the ball after the bounce.
parts.working: Rebound speed 0.70 × 5.94 = 4.16 m s⁻¹ (M1); h = v²/2g = 0.882 m (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Taking downwards as positive, describe the velocity–time graph of the ball from release until it reaches the top of its first bounce.
parts.answer: Straight line from 0 rising to +5.94 m s⁻¹; near-vertical drop to −4.16 m s⁻¹ at the bounce; straight line from −4.16 m s⁻¹ back to 0, parallel to the first line.
