parts.working: 1 mark for 2.47 % of 340 m s⁻¹; 1 mark for the final value with its uncertainty (8 m s⁻¹ to 1 s.f.).

parts.label: d
parts.text: A student says that the frequency should be measured again to reduce the uncertainty in v the most. State which measurement should be improved first and give a reason.
parts.answer: The wavelength: its percentage uncertainty (1.5 %) is larger than that of the frequency (1.0 %), so it contributes more to the uncertainty in v.
parts.working: 1 mark for wavelength; 1 mark for comparing percentage uncertainties (1.47 % vs 1.0 %).

practice.stem: A steel ball bearing from a bicycle workshop has mass m = 28.4 ± 0.1 g. Its diameter d is measured with vernier calipers as 1.90 ± 0.02 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the density of the ball is about 7.9 × 10³ kg m⁻³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the absolute uncertainty in the density.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest, with a reason, which measurement should be made more precisely to reduce the uncertainty in the density most effectively.
parts.answer: The diameter, e.g. using a micrometer or digital calipers.
parts.working: B1 diameter; B1 its percentage uncertainty is multiplied by 3 / it dominates the total

practice.stem: A spring has length 24.3 ± 0.1 cm when unloaded. When a weight of 4.00 ± 0.02 N hangs from it, its length is 31.8 ± 0.1 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the extension of the spring and its absolute uncertainty.
parts.working: x = 31.8 − 24.3 = 7.5 cm (B1); uncertainties add when subtracting: 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2 cm (B1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the spring constant k and its absolute uncertainty.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the percentage uncertainty in the extension is much larger than that in either length reading.
parts.answer: The extension is a small difference of two similar lengths, but the absolute uncertainties add.

practice.stem: A trolley of mass 0.250 ± 0.002 kg travels at constant speed. It covers 1.500 ± 0.005 m in a time measured with a stopwatch as 0.62 ± 0.02 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed v of the trolley.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the trolley.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the absolute uncertainty in the kinetic energy.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one change to the experiment that would reduce the uncertainty in E most effectively.
parts.answer: Measure the time with light gates and an electronic timer (or use a longer distance).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student times 20 oscillations of a pendulum. The total time is 31.4 s and the uncertainty in this total time is ±0.2 s. Which gives the period T with its uncertainty?
A T = 1.57 s ± 0.20 s
B T = 1.57 s ± 0.01 s
C T = 31.4 s ± 0.2 s
D T = 1.57 s ± 0.04 s
parts.working: T = 31.4/20 = 1.57 s. The uncertainty in T is 0.2/20 = 0.01 s, because the uncertainty in the total time is shared across 20 oscillations. A uses the uncertainty of the total time without dividing; C gives the total time, not the period; D divides by 5 instead of 20.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of the following is an SI base unit?
A newton
B coulomb
C kelvin
D volt
parts.working: The kelvin is one of the base units (with kg, m, s, A, mol). The coulomb is a derived unit (A s), a common distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a base quantity and a derived quantity.
parts.answer: A base quantity is one of the chosen fundamental quantities (e.g. mass, length, time); a derived quantity is defined in terms of base quantities.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the unit of pressure, the pascal, is kg m⁻¹ s⁻² in SI base units.
parts.working: p = F/A; N = kg m s⁻² (C1); kg m s⁻² ÷ m² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻² (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Express the joule in SI base units.
parts.working: J = N m = kg m s⁻² × m (B1)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of quantities have the same SI base units?
A work and power
B momentum and impulse
C force and pressure
D charge and current
parts.working: Momentum kg m s⁻¹; impulse N s = kg m s⁻² × s = kg m s⁻¹. Charge (A s) and current (A) differ by a factor of s.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which quantity has SI base units kg m⁻¹ s⁻²?
A spring constant
B pressure
C density
D work
parts.working: Pressure = force/area = (kg m s⁻²)/m² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻². A: spring constant is kg s⁻². C: density is kg m⁻³. D: work is kg m² s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an equation being homogeneous.
parts.answer: Each term in the equation has the same base units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the equation v² = u² + 2as is homogeneous.
parts.answer: All terms have units m² s⁻².
parts.working: v², u²: (m s⁻¹)² = m² s⁻² (M1); 2as: m s⁻² × m = m² s⁻² (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The pressure p at depth h in a liquid of density ρ is p = ρgh. Show that this equation is homogeneous.
parts.working: ρgh: kg m⁻³ × m s⁻² × m (M1) = kg m⁻¹ s⁻² = unit of p (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the volt.
parts.answer: One joule of energy transferred per coulomb of charge (1 V = 1 J C⁻¹).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the volt is kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹ in SI base units.
parts.working: V = J/C = kg m² s⁻² ÷ (A s) (C1) = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹ (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence determine the SI base units of resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A small sphere of radius r moving at speed v through a thick oil experiences a drag force F given by F = Crv, where C is a constant. What are the SI base units of C?
A kg s⁻¹
B kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹
C kg m s⁻¹
D kg m⁻² s⁻¹
parts.working: C = F/(rv) = kg m s⁻² ÷ (m × m s⁻¹) = kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹. A forgets to divide by r.

practice.stem: Water flows steadily through a narrow pipe in a hospital drip. The volume flow rate Q is given by Q = πr⁴Δp/(8ηL), where r is the radius of the pipe, L its length, Δp the pressure difference between its ends and η a property of the liquid called viscosity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the SI base units of volume flow rate Q and of pressure difference Δp.
parts.answer: Q: m³ s⁻¹; Δp: kg m⁻¹ s⁻²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the SI base units of η.
parts.working: η = πr⁴Δp/(8QL) (C1); m⁴ × kg m⁻¹ s⁻² ÷ (m³ s⁻¹ × m) = kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A quantity Y is given by Y = mv²/r, where m is a mass, v is a speed and r is a radius. What are the SI base units of Y?
A kg m s⁻²
B kg m² s⁻²
C kg m⁻¹ s⁻²
D kg s⁻²
parts.working: mv²/r has units kg × (m s⁻¹)² / m = kg × m² s⁻² / m = kg m s⁻², which is the newton. B is energy; C is pressure; D is the spring constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The drag force on a small sphere moving slowly through a fluid is F = 6πηrv, where r is the radius of the sphere, v is its speed and η is the coefficient of viscosity. State the SI base units of F.
parts.working: 1 mark: F is a force, so kg m s⁻² (the newton).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the SI base units of η.
parts.answer: η = F/(rv), so the units are (kg m s⁻²)/(m × m s⁻¹) = kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ (equivalently Pa s)
parts.working: 1 mark for rearranging to η = F/(rv); 1 mark for kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹. The 6π is a pure number and has no units.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The energy Q needed to change the temperature of a mass m of a substance by Δθ is given by Q = mcΔθ, where c is the specific heat capacity. Determine the SI base units of c.
parts.answer: c = Q/(mΔθ). Q has units kg m² s⁻², so c has units (kg m² s⁻²)/(kg K) = m² s⁻² K⁻¹
parts.working: 1 mark for the base units of energy (kg m² s⁻²); 1 mark for rearranging to c = Q/(mΔθ); 1 mark for m² s⁻² K⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student measures Δθ in degrees Celsius instead of kelvin. Explain whether this changes the SI base units of k.
parts.answer: No. A temperature interval of 1 °C is equal to an interval of 1 K, so the numerical value of Δθ and the units of k are unchanged; the result is still expressed in SI units if the kelvin is used.
parts.working: 1 mark: the size of a 1 °C interval equals a 1 K interval; 1 mark: the units of k are unchanged.

practice.stem: The speed v of a transverse wave on a stretched sitar string depends on the tension T in the string and its mass per unit length μ. A student suggests v = k T^x μ^y, where k is a dimensionless constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the SI base units of T and of μ.
parts.answer: T: kg m s⁻²; μ: kg m⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use base units to find the values of x and y.
parts.working: kg: x + y = 0; m: x − y = 1; s: −2x = −1 (M1 for setting up, M1 solving); x = ½, y = −½ (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this method cannot give the value of k.
parts.answer: k is a pure number with no units, so it does not appear in the unit equation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student writes s = ut + at² for uniformly accelerated motion. Show that this equation is homogeneous.
parts.working: ut: m s⁻¹ × s = m (M1); at²: m s⁻² × s² = m (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the equation can be homogeneous but still incorrect.
parts.answer: Homogeneity cannot check dimensionless constants; the correct equation has ½at².

parts.label: c
parts.text: The gravitational force between two masses is F = Gm₁m₂/r². Determine the SI base units of G.
parts.working: G = Fr²/(m₁m₂) (C1) = kg m s⁻² × m² ÷ kg² = m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻² (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The frequency of a stretched string is f = (1/2L)√(T/μ), where T is the tension in newtons, μ is the mass per unit length in kg m⁻¹ and L is the length in metres. What are the SI base units of T/μ?
A kg m s⁻²
B m² s⁻²
C m s⁻¹
D kg⁻¹ m² s⁻²
parts.working: T is in kg m s⁻² and μ in kg m⁻¹, so T/μ = (kg m s⁻²)/(kg m⁻¹) = m² s⁻². Taking the square root gives m s⁻¹, and dividing by L gives s⁻¹, the unit of frequency, which confirms the equation. A is the newton; D is the inverse of μ/T.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A satellite of orbital radius r and period T around a planet of mass M obeys T² = 4π²r³/(GM), where G is the gravitational constant. Determine the SI base units of GM.
parts.answer: Rearranging, GM = 4π²r³/T², so GM has units m³ s⁻²
parts.working: 1 mark for rearranging to GM = 4π²r³/T²; 1 mark for m³ s⁻².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the equation T² = 4π²r³/(GM) is homogeneous.
parts.answer: T² has units s². r³/(GM) has units m³/(m³ s⁻²) = s². Both sides have units s², so the equation is homogeneous.
parts.working: 1 mark for the units of each side; 1 mark for the conclusion that the two sides match.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the SI base units of G.
parts.working: 1 mark: divide the units of GM (m³ s⁻²) by the unit of M (kg).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a scalar quantity and a vector quantity.
parts.answer: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
From the list below, state all the vector quantities.
kinetic energy, momentum, temperature, weight, speed, acceleration, power
parts.working: B2 all three and no scalars; B1 two correct

practice.stem: A traveller at Karachi airport pulls a wheeled suitcase with a force of 50.0 N along the handle. The handle makes an angle of 35° with the horizontal floor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the horizontal component of the force.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the vertical component of the force.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The suitcase moves at constant velocity. State the size of the frictional force on it.
parts.working: Equal and opposite to the horizontal component (B1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two forces act at the same point: 6.0 N due east and 8.0 N due north. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the direction of the resultant force, as an angle measured north of east.
parts.answer: tan θ = 8.0/6.0, θ = 53.1° north of east (equivalently 36.9° east of north)
parts.working: 1 mark for using tan θ = opposite/adjacent with the correct components; 1 mark for 53.1° north of east.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether each of the following is a scalar or a vector quantity: temperature, acceleration, pressure, momentum, electric potential, torque.
parts.answer: Temperature: scalar; acceleration: vector; pressure: scalar; momentum: vector; electric potential: scalar; torque: vector
parts.working: 1 mark for every two correct classifications (six items, three marks). Pressure and electric potential have magnitude only; torque and momentum need a direction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says that a velocity of 10 m s⁻¹ and a speed of 10 m s⁻¹ are the same thing. Explain why this is incorrect.
parts.answer: Velocity is a vector and has a direction; speed is a scalar with the same magnitude but no direction. A velocity of 10 m s⁻¹ east is different from 10 m s⁻¹ west.
parts.working: 1 mark for velocity having a direction; 1 mark for speed having magnitude only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A boat crosses a river 120 m wide. In still water its speed is 2.5 m s⁻¹, and it is steered directly across the river. Calculate the time taken to cross.
parts.working: 1 mark for using the cross-river component only; 1 mark for 48 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The river flows at 1.2 m s⁻¹. Calculate how far downstream the boat is carried during the crossing.
parts.working: 1 mark for using the river speed with the time from part (a); 1 mark for 58 m.

practice.stem: Two horizontal forces act on a crate on a smooth floor: 12.0 N towards the east and 5.0 N towards the north.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force on the crate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the angle between the resultant force and the east direction.

practice.stem: A light aircraft leaves Islamabad heading due north with a speed of 240 km h⁻¹ relative to the air. A steady wind blows from west to east at 60 km h⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the velocity of the aircraft relative to the ground.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the direction of this velocity as an angle from north.
parts.working: tan θ = 60/240 (C1); θ = 14.0° east of north (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A swimmer heads due north at 1.5 m s⁻¹ relative to still water. The river flows due east at 0.80 m s⁻¹. Calculate the magnitude of the swimmer's velocity relative to the ground.
parts.working: 1 mark for adding perpendicular components by Pythagoras; 1 mark for 1.70 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the angle between the swimmer's velocity relative to the ground and due north.
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct ratio tan θ = 0.80/1.5; 1 mark for 28.1°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A walker moves 4.0 m in a direction 30° north of east, then 3.0 m due south. Calculate the magnitude of the walker's resultant displacement from the start.
parts.answer: x = 4.0 cos 30° = 3.46 m (east); y = 4.0 sin 30° − 3.0 = −1.0 m (north); displacement = √(3.46² + 1.0²) = 3.61 m
parts.working: 1 mark for resolving the first displacement into components; 1 mark for the second displacement in the y-direction (negative); 1 mark for 3.61 m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the direction of the resultant displacement, measured as an angle from due east.
parts.answer: tan θ = 1.0/3.46, θ = 16.1° south of east
parts.working: 1 mark for 16.1° south of east (the resultant points south of east because the y-component is negative).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A block of weight 80 N rests on a slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal. A force of 25 N acts up the slope, parallel to it. Calculate the component of the weight acting down the slope.
parts.working: 1 mark for 40 N (weight component down the slope = W sin θ).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The block is at rest. Calculate the magnitude of the friction force acting on the block, and state its direction.
parts.answer: Net force along the slope is zero: friction = 40 − 25 = 15 N, acting up the slope
parts.working: 1 mark for 15 N; 1 mark for stating the friction acts up the slope.

practice.stem: A ferry crosses a river 180 m wide. The water flows parallel to the banks at 1.5 m s⁻¹. The speed of the ferry relative to the water is 3.0 m s⁻¹. The ferry must travel straight across, perpendicular to the banks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle between the direction in which the ferry must be steered and the straight-across direction (perpendicular to the banks) so that the ferry moves straight across. State whether the ferry is steered upstream or downstream.
parts.answer: 30° upstream of the straight-across direction (60° to the bank)
parts.working: The upstream component of the ferry's velocity must cancel the current: sin θ = 1.5/3.0 (C1); θ = 30°, steered upstream (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken to cross the river.

practice.stem: A street lamp of weight 30.0 N hangs at rest from two cables tied at the same point. One cable makes an angle of 40° with the horizontal and the other makes an angle of 60° with the horizontal, on the opposite side.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the condition for the point where the cables meet to be in equilibrium.
parts.answer: The resultant force on it is zero (the horizontal components balance and the vertical components balance).
parts.working: B1 resultant (vector sum of) force zero

parts.label: b
parts.text: By resolving forces horizontally and vertically, determine the tension in each cable.
parts.answer: Cable at 40°: 15.2 N; cable at 60°: 23.3 N
parts.working: Horizontal: T₁ cos 40° = T₂ cos 60° (C1); vertical: T₁ sin 40° + T₂ sin 60° = 30.0 (C1); solving T₂ = 23.3 N (A1); T₁ = 15.2 N (A1)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three coplanar forces act at a point and are in equilibrium. Two of the forces are 30 N due east and 40 N due north. Calculate the magnitude of the third force.
parts.answer: The resultant of the first two forces is √(30² + 40²) = 50 N, so the third force is 50 N
parts.working: 1 mark for the resultant of the two forces; 1 mark for the third force being equal and opposite.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction of the third force as an angle measured anticlockwise from the 30 N force.
parts.answer: The first two forces give a resultant at 53.1° anticlockwise from east; the third force points opposite to it, at 233° anticlockwise from east
parts.working: 1 mark for 53.1° as the direction of the resultant; 1 mark for adding 180° to give 233°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ball of mass 0.20 kg moves east at 8.0 m s⁻¹ and hits a wall. It leaves the wall moving north at 6.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the magnitude of the change in momentum of the ball.
parts.answer: Taking the initial momentum as (−) east and the final as north: Δp = m(v − u) = 0.20 × (6.0 north − 8.0 east), so |Δp| = 0.20 × √(8.0² + 6.0²) = 2.0 kg m s⁻¹
parts.working: 1 mark for the change in momentum as a vector subtraction; 1 mark for each component (−1.6 and 1.2 kg m s⁻¹); 1 mark for 2.0 kg m s⁻¹. Adding or subtracting the speeds (2.8 or 0.4) earns no credit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the direction of the change in momentum, measured as an angle north of west.
parts.answer: tan θ = 1.2/1.6, θ = 36.9° north of west
parts.working: 1 mark for the correct ratio of components; 1 mark for 36.9° north of west.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ship sails 12 km on a bearing of 060° and then 5.0 km on a bearing of 150°. Calculate the magnitude of the ship's displacement from its start point.
parts.working: 1 mark for each pair of components (east and north); 1 mark for 13.0 km.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the bearing of the ship from its start point.
parts.working: 1 mark for using the east and north components with tan θ; 1 mark for a bearing of 083° (measured clockwise from north).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the best estimate of the kinetic energy of a family car travelling on a motorway?
A 10³ J
B 10⁴ J
C 10⁶ J
D 10⁸ J
parts.working: m ≈ 1500 kg, v ≈ 30 m s⁻¹: E = ½ × 1500 × 30² ≈ 7 × 10⁵ J ≈ 10⁶ J. 10⁴ J would correspond to a speed of only about 4 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write each quantity in SI units using powers of ten:
(i) 450 nm (ii) 2.5 GHz (iii) 3.3 kΩ (iv) 470 µF
parts.working: B2 all four; B1 two or three

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write 0.000 038 A and 72 000 000 W using a suitable prefix.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Estimate the number of heartbeats in one day for an adult whose heart beats 70 times per minute.
A 1 × 10³
B 1 × 10⁴
C 1 × 10⁵
D 1 × 10⁷
parts.working: 70 × 60 × 24 = 100 800 ≈ 1 × 10⁵. A, B and D differ from this by a factor of 10 or more.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the best estimate of the time taken by a sprinter to run 100 m?
A 0.1 s
B 1 s
C 10 s
D 1000 s
parts.working: A world-class sprinter takes about 10 s. A and B are far too short for 100 m, and D is about 17 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A swimming pool is 25 m long, 10 m wide and 2.0 m deep, and it is full of water. Estimate the volume of water in the pool in litres, giving your answer in standard form.
parts.working: 1 mark for the volume in m³; 1 mark for converting with 1 m³ = 1000 L and giving standard form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why your answer is only an estimate.
parts.answer: The pool may not be a uniform rectangular box (for example a sloping floor), and the water level may not be exactly at the top.
parts.working: 1 mark for any sensible reason that the shape or depth is not exactly uniform.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the number of seconds in 100 years, giving your answer in standard form.
parts.working: 1 mark for the number of seconds in one year (about 3 × 10⁷ s); 1 mark for multiplying by 100 and giving the answer in standard form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sheet of A4 paper has a thickness of 0.10 mm. Estimate the height of a stack of 500 sheets, in cm.
parts.working: 1 mark for the total height in mm; 1 mark for converting to 5.0 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the gain in gravitational potential energy of a student who runs up one flight of stairs between two floors of a school building. State the values you assume.
parts.working: B1 sensible values (mass 50–80 kg, height 3–4 m); B1 mgh in range 1.5–3 × 10³ J

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student takes about 4 s. Estimate the useful power output.
parts.working: B1 P = E/t, consistent with (a), in range 300–800 W

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electric kettle has a power of 2.2 kW and an efficiency of 80 %. It heats 1.5 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. Calculate the energy transferred to the water.
parts.working: 1 mark for using Q = mcΔθ with c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; 1 mark for 5.04 × 10⁵ J.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken to heat the water, using the 80 % efficiency.
parts.answer: Energy supplied = 5.04 × 10⁵/0.80 = 6.30 × 10⁵ J; t = 6.30 × 10⁵/2200 ≈ 286 s (about 5 minutes)
parts.working: 1 mark for dividing by the efficiency (or using useful power = 0.80 × 2200 W); 1 mark for 286 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write 36 km h⁻¹ in m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write 1.8 g cm⁻³ in kg m⁻³.
parts.working: 1 mark: 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³, so 1.8 g cm⁻³ = 1800 kg m⁻³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write 250 mL in m³.
parts.working: 1 mark: 1 mL = 10⁻⁶ m³, so 250 mL = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The heart of an adult pumps about 70 cm³ of blood per beat, at a rate of 70 beats per minute. Estimate the volume of blood pumped in one day, in m³.
parts.working: 1 mark for using 1440 minutes per day with the rate; 1 mark for 7.1 m³ (1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one assumption that you made to obtain this estimate.
parts.answer: The stroke volume and heart rate are assumed constant throughout the day.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid assumption, such as the heart rate and stroke volume being constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the volume of air in a typical classroom of floor area 8 m × 6 m and height 3 m, and hence its mass. The density of air is 1.2 kg m⁻³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the weight of this air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Most students are surprised by this answer. Suggest why we do not feel the weight of the air in a room.
parts.answer: Air pressure acts in all directions, so the forces on our body from the air balance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copper has density 8960 kg m⁻³ and molar mass 63.5 g mol⁻¹. Show that the amount of copper in a cube of side 1.0 mm is about 1.4 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
parts.working: 1 mark for the mass of the cube; 1 mark for dividing by the molar mass (in consistent units).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Avogadro constant is 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Estimate the number of copper atoms in the cube.
parts.working: 1 mark for multiplying by the Avogadro constant; 1 mark for 8.5 × 10¹⁹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A glass holds 250 cm³ of water. The density of water is 1000 kg m⁻³ and its molar mass is 18 g mol⁻¹. Estimate the number of water molecules in the glass. The Avogadro constant is 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
parts.working: 1 mark for the mass of water; 1 mark for the number of moles; 1 mark for 8.4 × 10²⁴.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A nuclear power station produces electrical output at a steady power of 1.0 GW for one year. Calculate the energy output in joules, using 1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s. Give your answer in standard form.
parts.working: 1 mark for using E = Pt with the prefix G = 10⁹; 1 mark for 3.16 × 10¹⁶ J.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express this energy in terajoules (1 TJ = 10¹² J).
parts.working: 1 mark: divide by 10¹² to convert J to TJ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by rectification.
parts.answer: The conversion of an alternating current (or voltage) into a direct current (one-directional).
parts.working: B1: a.c. → d.c. (current in one direction only).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A single diode is connected in series with a resistor across a sinusoidal a.c. supply. Describe the variation with time of the pd across the resistor.
parts.answer: Positive half-cycles of the sine wave appear; during the negative half-cycles the pd is zero.
parts.working: B1: half-cycles of one polarity only (same shape as input); B1: zero for alternate half-cycles (diode reverse-biased).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name given to this type of rectification and one disadvantage of it.
parts.answer: Half-wave rectification; output is zero for half the time (large ripple, less power).
parts.working: B1: half-wave; B1: no output for half of each cycle / mean power only half / needs large smoothing capacitor.

practice.stem: Four ideal diodes D1–D4 form a bridge rectifier. The a.c. supply is connected between points P and Q. A load resistor R is connected between points X and Y. The diodes are connected as follows: D1 from P to X, D2 from Q to X, D3 from Y to Q, D4 from Y to P (each diode conducts in the direction stated, e.g. D1 allows current from P to X only).

parts.label: a
parts.text: During the half-cycle when P is positive with respect to Q, state which two diodes conduct, and the direction of the current in R (from X to Y or from Y to X).
parts.answer: D1 and D3; from X to Y
parts.working: B1: D1 (P→X) and D3 (Y→Q); B1: current X to Y.

parts.label: b
parts.text: During the next half-cycle, when Q is positive with respect to P, state which two diodes conduct and the direction of the current in R.
parts.answer: D2 and D4; still from X to Y
parts.working: B1: D2 (Q→X) and D4 (Y→P); B1: current still X to Y.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name of this type of rectification and describe the waveform of the pd across R.
parts.answer: Full-wave rectification; a series of positive humps with no gaps — every half-cycle appears with the same polarity.
parts.working: B1: full-wave; B1: both halves of each cycle give output of the same polarity (|sin| shape).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the condition relating the time constant RC of the smoothing circuit to the period T of the a.c. supply for good smoothing.
parts.answer: RC must be much greater than T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this condition is needed.
parts.answer: So that only a small fraction of the charge leaks away between peaks, keeping the fall in pd (ripple) small.
parts.working: B1: capacitor discharges very little in one period; B1: pd remains close to peak value — small ripple.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For a 50 Hz half-wave supply and a load of 2.0 kΩ, suggest a suitable minimum capacitance, explaining your choice.
parts.answer: About 100 µF or more (RC = 0.2 s, ten times the 20 ms period).
parts.working: B1: period 20 ms; B1: choose C so RC ≥ about 10T, e.g. C ≥ 100 µF (accept other justified values).

parts.label: a
parts.text: One diode in a bridge rectifier breaks and becomes an open circuit. Describe and explain the effect on the output waveform.
parts.answer: The output becomes half-wave: one set of half-cycles is lost because the current path for those half-cycles goes through the broken diode.
parts.working: B1: half-wave output (every other hump missing); B1: in that half-cycle the conducting pair includes the faulty diode, so no complete circuit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect of this fault on the ripple of the smoothed output, giving a reason.
parts.answer: Ripple increases (about doubles) because the capacitor discharges for twice as long between peaks.

practice.stem: An ideal diode is connected in series with a 1.5 kΩ resistor to a sinusoidal supply of peak voltage 6.0 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the peak current in the resistor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the fraction of each cycle for which there is a current in the resistor, and explain why.
parts.answer: One half; the diode conducts only when forward biased, i.e. during one half-cycle.
parts.working: B1: half; B1: diode has (near) infinite resistance when reverse biased.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The diode is reversed. State the effect on the output.
parts.answer: The other half-cycles are passed: the pd across the resistor is now negative (opposite polarity) during the other half-cycles.
parts.working: B1: output of opposite polarity in the alternate half-cycles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a mobile phone charger must rectify the mains supply before it can charge the battery.
parts.answer: The battery needs current in one direction to store energy chemically; alternating current would charge and discharge it in turn, giving no net charging.
parts.working: B1: charging requires one-way (d.c.) current; B1: a.c. reverses direction every half-cycle so average charge flow is zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why a smoothing capacitor is also included.
parts.answer: To reduce the variation (ripple) of the output so that electronic circuits receive a nearly steady pd.

practice.stem: A single ideal diode is connected in series with a resistor across a sinusoidal supply of peak voltage 10 V and frequency 50 Hz. The output pd across the resistor is measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the frequency of the output pd across the resistor.
parts.working: Half-wave rectification keeps one pulse per cycle, so the output repeats at the supply frequency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean output pd across the resistor over a whole cycle.
parts.working: Mean over the full cycle = (1/2π) × ∫₀^π 10 sinθ dθ = 20/(2π) = 10/π = 3.18 V. 1 mark for the method (mean over one cycle with the negative half zero), 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A battery charger for a 12 V car battery uses a full-wave rectifier, with ideal diodes, fed from a supply whose peak voltage is 15 V. The output is not smoothed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the mean output of a full-wave rectifier is greater than that of a half-wave rectifier from the same supply.
parts.answer: Both halves of each cycle are used, so the output is positive for the whole cycle, not just for half of it.
parts.working: 1 mark: the full-wave output is positive for the whole cycle, so both halves are used; 1 mark: the mean is 2V₀/π, twice the half-wave mean V₀/π.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean output pd.
parts.working: Mean = 2V₀/π = 2 × 15 / π = 9.55 V. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether this unsmoothed output alone can charge the 12 V battery, and give a reason.
parts.answer: No: the mean output (9.55 V) is less than the 12 V battery pd, so no charging current flows.
parts.working: B1: compare the 9.55 V mean with the 12 V battery pd; no charging current flows while the output is below the battery pd.

practice.stem: A 2200 µF smoothing capacitor is connected across the output of a power supply. The peak output pd is 16 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge stored on the capacitor at the peak output.
parts.working: Q = CV = 2200 × 10⁻⁶ × 16 = 0.0352 C. 1 mark for Q = CV, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored on the capacitor at the peak output.
parts.working: W = ½CV² = ½ × 2200 × 10⁻⁶ × 16² = 0.282 J. 1 mark for the formula, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A student connects a 4700 µF capacitor directly across a 12 V r.m.s. a.c. supply and says the capacitor will give a smooth d.c. output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: The capacitor charges and discharges as the a.c. changes direction, so its pd still alternates and its average value is zero: the output is still a.c.
parts.working: 1 mark: the pd reverses with the supply, so the capacitor charges and discharges in both directions; 1 mark: the average pd is zero and the output is not d.c.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the component that must be added to make the output unidirectional, and its role.
parts.answer: A diode (rectifier) in series, so that current flows in one direction only and the capacitor can then be charged to the peak value.
parts.working: B1: a diode in series, so the current flows one way only and the capacitor charges to the peak.

practice.stem: A capacitor is connected in parallel with the load resistor of a rectifier circuit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the capacitor smooths the output pd.
parts.answer: As the rectified pd rises, the capacitor charges to the peak value; when the rectified pd falls below the capacitor pd, the diode stops conducting and the capacitor discharges through the load, keeping the pd high until the next peak recharges it.
parts.working: B1: capacitor charges as rectified pd rises (to peak); B1: when input falls, capacitor discharges through the load resistor (diode reverse biased so it cannot discharge back through the supply); B1: discharge is slow (time constant ≫ period), so pd falls only a little before the next peak.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain the effect on the ripple of (i) increasing the capacitance, (ii) increasing the load resistance.
parts.answer: (i) ripple decreases; (ii) ripple decreases — both increase the time constant RC so the capacitor discharges more slowly.
parts.working: B1: both reduce ripple; B1: larger RC → slower discharge.

practice.stem: A half-wave rectifier fed from a 50 Hz supply gives a peak output of 12.0 V. It is smoothed by a 2200 µF capacitor and the load resistance is 1.0 kΩ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time constant of the smoothing circuit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume the capacitor discharges for a full period of the supply between peaks. Calculate the minimum pd across the load.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence state the peak-to-peak ripple voltage.

practice.stem: A bridge rectifier is connected to an a.c. supply of r.m.s. voltage 9.0 V. Each conducting diode has a constant pd of 0.70 V across it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the peak value of the a.c. input.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the peak output is less than the peak input, and calculate the peak output.
parts.working: B1: two diodes conduct in series in each half-cycle, each dropping 0.70 V; A1: 12.7 − 1.40 = 11.3 V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A capacitor is added across the load so that the output is well smoothed. State the approximate output pd and the frequency of the ripple when the supply frequency is 50 Hz.
parts.working: B1: approximately the peak output; B1: full-wave → ripple frequency 2 × 50 = 100 Hz.

practice.stem: A rectified and smoothed output from a 50 Hz supply is displayed on an oscilloscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the frequency of the ripple for (i) half-wave and (ii) full-wave rectification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The time-base of the oscilloscope is set at 5.0 ms per division. Calculate the number of divisions between successive peaks of the full-wave output.
parts.working: Period of ripple = 10 ms (M1 implied); 10/5.0 = 2.0 div (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Y-gain is 2.0 V per division. The smoothed full-wave trace varies between 4.3 and 4.0 divisions above the zero line. Calculate the peak-to-peak ripple voltage and the mean output voltage (assume the ripple is a symmetrical sawtooth).

practice.stem: The output of a smoothed rectifier varies between a maximum of 8.6 V and a minimum of 7.9 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of the smoothed output waveform over one ripple cycle.
parts.answer: A short steep rise as the capacitor recharges near each peak, followed by a longer, gradual (exponential) fall as it discharges through the load.
parts.working: B1: brief charging near peak; B1: longer slow exponential decay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the peak-to-peak ripple and express it as a percentage of the maximum output.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the charge on the capacitor at the peak that flows away through the load before the next recharge.

practice.stem: A rectified output is smoothed by a capacitor connected across a load resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of the following changes, state whether the ripple increases, decreases or stays the same, giving a reason: (i) replacing a half-wave rectifier by a full-wave rectifier; (ii) connecting a second identical load resistor in parallel with the first; (iii) increasing the supply frequency from 50 Hz to 400 Hz.
parts.working: (i) B1 decreases, B1 capacitor discharges for half as long between peaks; (ii) B1 increases, B1 load resistance halves, so RC halves and discharge is faster; (iii) B1 decreases, B1 shorter time between peaks so less discharge.

practice.stem: A 50 Hz supply is rectified to give a peak of 9.0 V across a 1.0 kΩ load smoothed by a 1000 µF capacitor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ripple voltage for half-wave rectification, assuming the capacitor discharges for one whole period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ripple voltage for full-wave rectification.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the ratio of your answers.
parts.answer: About 2 : 1 — full-wave halves the ripple, because the discharge time is halved (and RC ≫ T so the fall is nearly linear).

practice.stem: A half-wave rectifier with an ideal diode is fed from a 12.0 V peak, 50 Hz supply. The output is smoothed by a capacitor connected across a 4.7 kΩ load resistor. The ripple pd must not exceed 0.50 V, so the capacitor is assumed to discharge for one full period T = 0.020 s between charging peaks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum capacitance needed.
parts.working: Ripple ΔV = V₀T/(RC), so C = V₀T/(RΔV) = 12.0 × 0.020 / (4700 × 0.50) = 1.02 × 10⁻⁴ F. 1 mark for the ripple formula; 1 mark for rearranging; 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the effect on the ripple of using a capacitor with a larger capacitance.
parts.answer: The ripple decreases, because the capacitor loses less charge (and pd) during each discharge.
parts.working: B1: ΔV = V₀T/(RC), so a larger C gives a smaller ripple (ripple ∝ 1/C).

practice.stem: A full-wave rectifier fed from a 50 Hz supply gives a smoothed output for a school public-address amplifier. The mean load current is 0.40 A and the smoothing capacitor is 3300 µF.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the frequency of the ripple.
parts.working: Full-wave rectification gives two output pulses per supply cycle, so the ripple frequency is 2 × 50 = 100 Hz.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the peak-to-peak ripple pd.
parts.working: The capacitor supplies the load current for one ripple period T = 1/100 s, so ΔV = IT/C = 0.40 / (100 × 3.3 × 10⁻³) = 1.21 V. 1 mark for ΔV = IT/C, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the ripple would be larger if a half-wave rectifier were used instead.
parts.answer: Half-wave gives one pulse per cycle, so the ripple frequency is halved and the capacitor discharges for twice as long, giving twice the ripple.
parts.working: B1: half-wave ripple frequency is 50 Hz, so the discharge lasts twice as long and the ripple doubles.

practice.stem: A smoothed full-wave output supplies a load. At a load current of 0.25 A the peak-to-peak ripple is 0.80 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that, for the capacitor discharging linearly between pulses, the ripple is proportional to the load current.
parts.answer: For a fixed capacitor and frequency, ΔV = IT/C. With C, T fixed, ΔV ∝ I.
parts.working: 1 mark for ΔV = IT/C (charge removed = IT); 1 mark for stating that C and T are constant, so ΔV ∝ I.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ripple when the load current falls to 0.10 A.
parts.working: ΔV ∝ I, so ΔV = 0.80 × (0.10 / 0.25) = 0.32 V. 1 mark for the ratio, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A half-wave rectifier with a silicon diode is fed from a transformer whose secondary has an r.m.s. voltage of 12 V. The diode has a forward pd of 0.70 V and is treated as having a constant 0.70 V across it when conducting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the peak input pd from the transformer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the peak output pd across the load.
parts.working: Peak output = 16.97 − 0.70 = 16.27 V. 1 mark for subtracting the diode pd, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the peak output is less than the peak input.
parts.answer: The diode needs a forward pd of about 0.70 V before it conducts, so this pd is lost across the diode.
parts.working: B1: the diode needs about 0.70 V forward pd before it conducts, and this is lost across the diode.

practice.stem: A 4700 µF smoothing capacitor is used in a full-wave supply with a ripple frequency of 100 Hz. The pd across the capacitor falls by 1.2 V during each ripple cycle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge removed from the capacitor during each ripple cycle.
parts.working: Q = CΔV = 4700 × 10⁻⁶ × 1.2 = 5.64 × 10⁻³ C. 1 mark for Q = CΔV, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence calculate the mean load current.
parts.working: The charge is supplied by the capacitor in one period T = 1/100 s, so I = Q/T = 5.64 × 10⁻³ × 100 = 0.564 A. 1 mark for I = Q/T, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A full-wave rectifier connected to a 50 Hz supply gives a peak output of 15 V across a 470 Ω load. A smoothing capacitor is to be connected across the load.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the time between successive peaks of the rectified output.
parts.working: B1: full-wave → two peaks per cycle → 1/100 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming the capacitor discharges for this whole time, calculate the minimum capacitance that keeps the ripple to no more than 5% of the peak pd.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the actual ripple will be slightly smaller than this calculation suggests.
parts.answer: The capacitor starts recharging before the next peak, so it discharges for slightly less than 0.010 s.
parts.working: B1: discharge time is less than the full interval between peaks.

practice.stem: A sinusoidal supply of peak voltage 20 V is rectified and connected to a 100 Ω resistor. The diodes are ideal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean power in the resistor with full-wave rectification (no smoothing).
parts.working: Full-wave output has the same r.m.s. value as the sine wave: V_rms = 20/√2 = 14.1 V (M1); P = V²/R = 2.0 W (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mean power with half-wave rectification is half of this, and calculate it.
parts.working: B1: output is zero for half of each cycle and identical otherwise, so the energy per cycle is halved; A1: 1.0 W.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the r.m.s. voltage of the half-wave rectified output.

practice.stem: An oscilloscope shows the output of a full-wave rectifier (50 Hz supply) smoothed by a capacitor, across a 2.0 kΩ load. During each discharge the pd falls from 10.0 V to 9.2 V in 8.5 ms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time constant of the smoothing circuit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the capacitance of the smoothing capacitor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the discharge lasts 8.5 ms rather than the full 10 ms between peaks.
parts.answer: The rectified input rises above the capacitor pd before the peak, so recharging starts early.
parts.working: B1: capacitor begins to recharge before the next peak.

practice.stem: A full-wave rectifier (50 Hz supply) with peak output 15 V feeds a 500 Ω load smoothed by a 1000 µF capacitor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time constant and the fall in pd during one discharge, assuming the discharge lasts the full time between peaks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge that flows from the capacitor through the load during one discharge, and hence the mean load current.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how much charge the rectifier must supply to the capacitor during each brief recharge.
parts.working: B1: the same charge as is lost in each discharge (steady state).

practice.stem: A sinusoidal supply of peak voltage V₀ is used with (a) half-wave and (b) full-wave rectification, with ideal diodes and no smoothing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the mean value over a whole cycle of the half-wave output is V₀/π.
parts.answer: The output is V₀ sinθ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π and zero for π ≤ θ ≤ 2π. Mean = (1/2π) × ∫₀^π V₀ sinθ dθ = (1/2π) × 2V₀ = V₀/π. 1 mark for the zero half-cycle; 1 mark for the integral of sinθ over 0 to π as 2; 1 mark for the result V₀/π.
parts.working: 1 mark: zero output for π ≤ θ ≤ 2π; 1 mark: ∫₀^π V₀ sinθ dθ = 2V₀; 1 mark: mean = (1/2π)(2V₀) = V₀/π.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean outputs for both forms of rectification when V₀ = 16 V.
parts.working: Half-wave: 16/π = 5.09 V. Full-wave has twice the mean: 2 × 16/π = 10.2 V. 1 mark for each correct value (accept either to 2 s.f. consistent with the working).

practice.stem: A full-wave smoothed supply has a peak output of 18.0 V. During each discharge the pd falls to 16.5 V after 0.0100 s, when the next peak arrives. The capacitor is 4700 µF and the pd falls exponentially (V = V₀e^(−t/RC)) during the discharge.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the equation for the pd V during the discharge in terms of V₀, t, R and C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the value of the product RC.
parts.working: e^(−t/RC) = 16.5/18.0, so t/RC = ln(18.0/16.5) = 0.0870, and RC = 0.0100/0.0870 = 0.115 s. 1 mark for the logarithm, 1 mark for RC.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the load resistance R.
parts.working: R = (RC)/C = 0.115 / (4700 × 10⁻⁶) = 24.5 Ω. 1 mark for R = (RC)/C, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A mains supply of 230 V r.m.s. at 50 Hz is stepped down by an ideal transformer to 23 V r.m.s. The secondary is connected to a full-wave bridge rectifier. Each conducting diode has a constant forward pd of 0.70 V. The output is smoothed by a 2200 µF capacitor across a 100 Ω load.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the peak output pd of the rectifier before smoothing.
parts.working: Peak input = 23 × √2 = 32.5 V. Two diodes conduct at any time, so the output peak = 32.5 − 2 × 0.70 = 31.1 V. 1 mark for the peak input and the two diode drops; 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the peak-to-peak ripple pd, assuming the capacitor discharges exponentially for the full 0.0100 s between peaks.

practice.stem: A capacitor of 200 µF is used with a 1.0 kΩ load in two supplies that give the same peak output of 15 V, but one is half-wave (ripple frequency 50 Hz) and one is full-wave (ripple frequency 100 Hz). The discharge is exponential, V = V₀e^(−t/RC).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the ripple (ΔV = V₀ − V) for a discharge lasting time t is ΔV = V₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)).
parts.answer: Pd at the end of the discharge is V = V₀e^(−t/RC), so the ripple is ΔV = V₀ − V = V₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)).
parts.working: 1 mark for V = V₀e^(−t/RC); 1 mark for subtracting from V₀ to get V₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ripple for each supply, taking the discharge time as one ripple period.
parts.answer: Half-wave (t = 0.020 s): 1.43 V. Full-wave (t = 0.010 s): 0.73 V.
parts.working: RC = 0.200 s. Half-wave: 15(1 − e^(−0.1)) = 1.43 V. Full-wave: 15(1 − e^(−0.05)) = 0.73 V. 1 mark for each correct value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the half-wave ripple to the full-wave ripple, and comment on how close it is to 2.
parts.answer: Ratio = 1.95, close to 2 because t/RC is small, so e^(−t/RC) ≈ 1 − t/RC and the ripple is approximately proportional to t.
parts.working: B1: ratio = 1.43/0.73 = 1.95; the ratio is near 2 because t/RC is small.

practice.stem: The mains electricity supply in Pakistan has an r.m.s. voltage of 230 V and a frequency of 50 Hz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the peak voltage of the mains supply.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the period of the supply.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how many times each second the current is momentarily zero.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) value of an alternating current.
parts.answer: The value of the steady (direct) current that would produce the same mean power (heating effect) in a resistor.
parts.working: B1: steady/direct current; B1: same (mean) power dissipation in the same resistance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the relationship between the r.m.s. current and the peak current for a sinusoidal alternating current.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A sinusoidal current has a peak value of 3.0 A. Calculate its r.m.s. value.

practice.stem: A sinusoidal alternating current of peak value 5.0 A passes through a resistor of resistance 48 Ω.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the r.m.s. current.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean power dissipated in the resistor.
parts.working: P = I_rms²R (M1) = (5.0²/2) × 48 = 600 W (A1). Using I₀²R (1200 W) scores 0.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the value of the steady direct current that would give the same mean power in the resistor.
parts.working: B1: equal to the r.m.s. current, 3.54 A (by definition of r.m.s.).

practice.stem: Some countries use a mains supply of 120 V r.m.s. at 60 Hz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the peak voltage of a 120 V r.m.s. supply.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the period of a 60 Hz supply.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A hair dryer designed for 230 V r.m.s. is used on a 120 V r.m.s. supply. Assuming its resistance is constant, calculate the fraction of its normal power it produces.

practice.stem: The time-base of an oscilloscope is set to 5.0 ms per division. The trace of a sinusoidal alternating voltage shows exactly 2.0 complete cycles across 10 divisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the period of the voltage.
parts.working: 10 divisions × 5.0 ms = 50 ms for 2 cycles, so T = 25 ms. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency.

practice.stem: A battery eliminator transformer supplies a sinusoidal output of 9.0 V r.m.s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the peak voltage of the output.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A voltmeter on the a.c. range is connected to the output. State the reading and explain why.
parts.answer: 9.0 V: the voltmeter reads the r.m.s. value, which is the d.c. voltage that would give the same heating effect.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reading 9.0 V; 1 mark for the r.m.s. definition (equal heating effect to a d.c. supply).

practice.stem: A 60 W filament lamp is designed to work at 230 V r.m.s. on a 50 Hz mains supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the lamp when it operates normally.
parts.working: R = V²/P = 230² / 60 = 882 Ω. 1 mark for R = V²/P, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the r.m.s. current through the lamp.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the peak current.

practice.stem: A sinusoidal alternating current flows through a resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the mean value of the current over one complete cycle is zero, but the mean power dissipated in the resistor is not zero.
parts.answer: The current is positive for half the cycle and negative for the other half, so its average is zero. Power is proportional to I², which is always positive, so the power is never zero and its mean is not zero.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive and negative halves cancel; 1 mark: P = I²R is always positive, so energy is dissipated on both halves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the time between successive zero crossings of the current for a 50 Hz supply.
parts.working: The period is 20 ms; the current crosses zero twice per period, so zero crossings are 10 ms apart.

practice.stem: A sinusoidal voltage has a period of 8.0 ms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the angular frequency ω.
parts.working: ω = 2πf = 2π × 125 = 785 rad s⁻¹. 1 mark for ω = 2πf, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A sinusoidal alternating voltage has a peak value of 17 V and a period of 20 ms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the r.m.s. voltage.
parts.working: V_rms = V₀/√2 = 17/1.414 = 12.0 V. 1 mark for the formula, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the voltage to fall from its peak value to zero for the first time.
parts.working: A quarter of a period: T/4 = 20/4 = 5.0 ms. 1 mark for the quarter-period idea, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: An electric kettle is rated at 2.0 kW for use on a 230 V r.m.s. supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the r.m.s. current and the peak current.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the heating element.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the maximum instantaneous power and state its relationship to the mean power.

practice.stem: An alternating voltage V (in volts) varies with time t (in seconds) according to V = 311 sin(100πt), with the angle in radians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the peak voltage and the frequency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the r.m.s. voltage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the voltage at t = 2.5 ms.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the earliest time after t = 0 at which the voltage is 155.5 V.

practice.stem: A sinusoidal signal is displayed on an oscilloscope. The Y-gain is 2.0 V per division and the time-base is 0.50 ms per division. The trace has a peak-to-peak height of 6.4 divisions and one complete cycle occupies 4.0 divisions horizontally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the peak voltage of the signal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the r.m.s. voltage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the signal.

practice.stem: A filament lamp is rated 12 V, 36 W for use on a d.c. supply. It is to be run on a 50 Hz sinusoidal a.c. supply instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the peak value of the alternating voltage needed for the lamp to have its normal brightness.
parts.working: Normal brightness needs V_rms = 12 V (M1); V₀ = 12√2 = 17.0 V (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the peak current in the lamp.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the lamp does not appear to flicker even though the power falls to zero twice every cycle.
parts.answer: The filament stays hot between peaks (it cannot cool quickly), and the eye cannot follow changes at 100 times per second.
parts.working: B1: thermal inertia of filament / persistence of vision at 100 Hz.

practice.stem: In a country whose mains frequency is 60 Hz, the current I (in amperes) in a 40 Ω resistor is I = 2.5 sin(120πt).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the frequency of the current.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the r.m.s. current.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean power dissipated in the resistor.

practice.stem: An electric iron of resistance 40 Ω is used on the 230 V r.m.s. mains supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean power of the iron.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy transferred in 15 minutes, in joules and in kilowatt-hours.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the peak current.

practice.stem: A 1.8 kW electric water heater is connected to the 230 V r.m.s. mains supply. A fuse must be chosen for its circuit. Standard fuse ratings are 3 A, 5 A, 10 A and 13 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the r.m.s. current in the heater.
parts.working: I_rms = P/V = 1800/230 = 7.83 A. 1 mark for I = P/V, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the peak current.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Choose the fuse rating and justify your choice.
parts.answer: 10 A: it is above the r.m.s. current (7.8 A), so it does not blow in normal use, and the 5 A fuse would blow.
parts.working: 1 mark for 10 A; 1 mark for the reason that fuses are rated on r.m.s. current and 5 A is too small.

practice.stem: A 75 W filament lamp is switched on for 6.0 hours on a 230 V r.m.s. supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy transferred, in kilowatt-hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert this energy to joules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the maximum instantaneous power dissipated in the lamp and explain its relationship to the mean power.
parts.answer: 150 W. The maximum power is twice the mean power (75 W), because the power varies as sin² and has mean value half its maximum.
parts.working: 1 mark for 150 W; 1 mark for the factor of 2 with the reason (mean of sin² is ½).

practice.stem: A sinusoidal voltage V = V₀ sin(ωt) has peak value V₀ = 12 V and frequency 50 Hz. Take t = 0 when V = 0 and increasing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the earliest time after t = 0 at which V = 6.0 V.
parts.working: sin(ωt) = 0.5 gives ωt = π/6, so t = (π/6)/(2π × 50) = 1/600 s = 1.67 ms. 1 mark for ωt = π/6, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the earliest time after the first peak at which V = 6.0 V on the way down.
parts.working: sin(ωt) = 0.5 with ωt = 5π/6, so t = (5π/6)/(100π) = 5/600 s = 8.33 ms. 1 mark for ωt = 5π/6, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: The instantaneous current in a 25 Ω resistor is I = 3.0 sin(314t), where I is in amperes and t is in seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the current.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the power dissipated in the resistor at t = 2.0 ms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean power dissipated in the resistor.
parts.working: I_rms = 3.0/√2, so P_mean = I_rms² R = (9.0/2) × 25 = 112.5 W. 1 mark for I_rms, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A 3.0 V d.c. supply is compared with a sinusoidal a.c. supply of peak voltage 4.5 V. Each supply is connected in turn across the same lamp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the d.c. voltage that would give the same heating effect as the a.c. supply.
parts.working: The equivalent d.c. voltage is the r.m.s. value: 4.5 / √2 = 3.18 V. 1 mark for the r.m.s. formula, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which supply gives the greater power to the lamp, and by what percentage.
parts.answer: The a.c. supply. Power is proportional to V², so (3.18/3.0)² = 1.125; the a.c. gives about 12.5% more power.
parts.working: 1 mark for the a.c. supply; 1 mark for the ratio of powers (1.125, so 12.5% more).

practice.stem: A sinusoidal current of r.m.s. value 2.0 A flows through a 40 Ω resistor for 5.0 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean power dissipated in the resistor.
parts.working: P = I_rms² R = 2.0² × 40 = 160 W. 1 mark for the formula, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy transferred in the resistor, in kilojoules.
parts.working: E = Pt = 160 × 300 = 4.8 × 10⁴ J = 48 kJ. 1 mark for the time in seconds, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A square-wave voltage alternates between +5.0 V and −5.0 V, spending equal times at each. State its r.m.s. value, explaining your reasoning.
parts.working: B1: V² = 25 V² at all times; B1: mean of V² = 25, so r.m.s. = 5.0 V.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the mean power produced in a resistor by this square wave to that produced by a sinusoidal voltage of the same peak value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A different voltage is +6.0 V for one third of each period and zero for the rest. Calculate its r.m.s. value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The current in a resistor of resistance R is I = I₀ sin ωt. Write down an expression for the instantaneous power and state the mean value of sin² ωt over one cycle.
parts.answer: P = I₀²R sin² ωt; mean of sin² ωt = ½
parts.working: B1: P = I²R = I₀²R sin² ωt; B1: ½ (graph of sin² is symmetrical about ½).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence show that I_rms = I₀/√2.
parts.answer: Mean power = ½I₀²R = I_rms²R, so I_rms = I₀/√2.
parts.working: M1: mean power = ½I₀²R; A1: equate to I_rms²R.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For I₀ = 4.0 A and R = 25 Ω, calculate the mean power.

practice.stem: A signal generator produces a voltage V = 4.0 + 3.0 sin ωt (in volts): a steady 4.0 V with a sinusoidal variation of amplitude 3.0 V added to it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the r.m.s. value of this voltage is not simply 4.0 + 3.0/√2.
parts.answer: The r.m.s. value depends on the mean of V², and (a + b)² ≠ a² + b² in general; the r.m.s. values do not add.
parts.working: B1: r.m.s. found from mean of square; values do not simply add.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that the mean value of sin ωt over a cycle is zero and the mean value of sin² ωt is ½, calculate the r.m.s. value of the voltage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean power this voltage would produce in a 10 Ω resistor.

practice.stem: A sinusoidal voltage of peak value V₀ is passed through a half-wave rectifier, so the output is V₀ sin(ωt) for the positive half-cycle and zero for the negative half-cycle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the r.m.s. value of the output over a complete cycle is V₀/2.
parts.answer: V_rms² = (1/T) ∫ v² dt. Over the positive half-cycle v² = V₀² sin²θ with mean value V₀²/2 (over π), and the negative half contributes zero. So the mean of v² over the full cycle = ½ × V₀²/2 = V₀²/4 and V_rms = V₀/2.
parts.working: 1 mark for setting V_rms² as the mean of v²; 1 mark for the mean of sin² being ½ on the positive half and zero on the negative half; 1 mark for V_rms = V₀/2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For V₀ = 16 V, calculate the mean power dissipated in a 10 Ω resistor, and compare it with the full-wave rectified output of the same peak.
parts.answer: Half-wave: V_rms = 8.0 V, P = 64/10 = 6.4 W. Full-wave: V_rms = 16/√2 = 11.3 V, P = 12.8 W, so the half-wave power is half the full-wave power.
parts.working: 1 mark for 6.4 W; 1 mark for 12.8 W for full-wave and the comparison (half).

practice.stem: A triangular alternating voltage rises linearly from zero to its peak V₀ in a quarter of a period, falls linearly back through zero to −V₀ in the next half-period, and returns to zero in the final quarter period. Its pattern repeats every period T.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the mean value of v² over one period is V₀²/3, and hence that the r.m.s. value is V₀/√3.
parts.answer: In the first quarter-period v = (4V₀/T)t, so the mean of v² over that quarter is (1/(T/4)) ∫₀^(T/4) (4V₀t/T)² dt = V₀²/3. Every quarter-period has the same mean of v², so the mean over T is V₀²/3 and V_rms = V₀/√3.
parts.working: 1 mark for v = (4V₀/T)t in one quarter; 1 mark for integrating to get V₀²/3; 1 mark for V_rms = V₀/√3 with all quarters equal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the r.m.s. value for a peak of 6.0 V.
parts.working: V_rms = 6.0 / √3 = 3.46 V. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem:
A sinusoidal voltage of peak 10 V and frequency 50 Hz is sampled at intervals. The values of the voltage at times t after the start of a positive half-cycle are given below.
t / ms: 0, 2.5, 5.0, 7.5, 10.0
V / V: 0.00, 7.07, 10.00, 7.07, 0.00

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the table of V² for these times.
parts.working: B1: each V² is the square of the value in the table: 0, 50.0, 100, 50.0, 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the trapezium rule over the half-cycle (0 to 10.0 ms) to estimate the mean value of V².
parts.working: 1 mark for the trapezium sum with spacing 2.5 ms; 1 mark for dividing by 10.0 ms to give 50.0 V².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence estimate the r.m.s. voltage, and explain why this equals the r.m.s. over a full cycle.
parts.answer: V_rms = √50.0 = 7.1 V. The waveform is symmetrical about zero, so the positive and negative half-cycles have the same mean of V².
parts.working: 1 mark for the square root (7.1 V); 1 mark for the symmetry argument.

practice.stem: The current in a resistor alternates such that, over one period T, it is I = I₀ sin(ωt) for the positive half-cycle and I = (I₀/2) sin(ωt) for the negative half-cycle (sin ωt is negative there), so the negative half-cycle has half the peak size. The resistor is 8.0 Ω and I₀ = 6.0 A.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the r.m.s. current is I₀√5/4, and calculate its value for I₀ = 6.0 A.
parts.answer: I_rms² = (1/T)∫i² dt = ½[I₀² × ½ + (I₀²/4) × ½] = ½ × (5I₀²/8) = 5I₀²/16. I_rms = I₀√5/4 = 6.0 × 2.236/4 = 3.35 A. 1 mark for the mean of i² on each half-cycle; 1 mark for 5I₀²/16; 1 mark for the value 3.35 A.
parts.working: 1 mark: mean of i² on each half cycle is I₀²/2 (positive) and I₀²/8 (negative, amplitude I₀/2); 1 mark: I_rms² = 5I₀²/16; 1 mark: I_rms = 3.35 A.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean power dissipated in the 8.0 Ω resistor.
parts.working: P_mean = I_rms² R = (3.354)² × 8.0 = 90 W. 1 mark for P = I_rms²R, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A sinusoidal voltage of peak value 325 V is passed through a full-wave rectifier with ideal diodes and no smoothing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the r.m.s. value of the rectified output is the same as the r.m.s. value of the original sine wave.
parts.answer: The output is |V₀ sinθ|, so its square is V₀² sin²θ, the same as for the original sine. Its mean of v² is therefore V₀²/2 and V_rms = V₀/√2 for both waveforms.
parts.working: 1 mark for the output squared being V₀² sin²θ; 1 mark for mean of sin² being ½; 1 mark for V_rms = V₀/√2 in both cases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean value of the full-wave rectified output.
parts.working: Mean = 2V₀/π = 2 × 325 / π = 206.9 V. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases.
parts.answer: Any four of: molecules are in continuous random motion; collisions (with each other and the walls) are perfectly elastic; the volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas; there are no intermolecular forces (except during collisions); the time of a collision is negligible compared with the time between collisions; there is a very large number of molecules.
parts.working: B1 each for any four of the listed assumptions

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of molecules, how a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container.
parts.answer: Molecules collide with the wall and rebound, so their momentum changes; the wall exerts a force on each molecule and so (Newton's third law) the molecules exert a force on the wall; many collisions per second give a steady average force, and pressure = force/area.
parts.working: B1 change of momentum on collision with wall; B1 force = rate of change of momentum (and Newton's third law); B1 pressure = total force/area of wall

practice.stem: Air in a room is at 27 °C (300 K). Nitrogen molecules have a mass of 28 u. Take the Boltzmann constant k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean translational kinetic energy of a nitrogen molecule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the root-mean-square speed of the nitrogen molecules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the mean kinetic energy of an oxygen molecule in the same air compares with that of a nitrogen molecule.
parts.answer: It is the same, because the mean kinetic energy depends only on the temperature.

practice.stem: A sealed flask contains an ideal gas. Take the Boltzmann constant k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean translational kinetic energy of the molecules at 100 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says that heating the gas from 0 °C to 100 °C makes the mean kinetic energy of the molecules 'infinitely larger'. Calculate the actual ratio (mean KE at 100 °C)/(mean KE at 0 °C) and explain the student's error.
parts.answer: ratio = 373/273 = 1.37; the mean KE is proportional to the thermodynamic (kelvin) temperature, not to the Celsius temperature.
parts.working: B1 1.37; B1 must use kelvin: ⟨Eₖ⟩ ∝ T in K, and 0 °C is not zero energy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the equation pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ can be written as p = ⅓ρ⟨c²⟩, where ρ is the density of the gas.
parts.answer: Nm is the total mass of the gas and Nm/V = ρ, so p = ⅓(Nm/V)⟨c²⟩ = ⅓ρ⟨c²⟩.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Air at sea level in Gwadar has a pressure of 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and a density of 1.20 kg m⁻³. Calculate the root-mean-square speed of the air molecules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why individual air molecules travel much less than 500 m in one second along a straight line.
parts.answer: They collide very frequently with other molecules, changing direction (random path).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the motion of molecules, why the pressure of a fixed mass of gas increases when it is heated at constant volume.
parts.answer: Higher temperature → greater mean kinetic energy, so molecules move faster; each collision with the walls gives a larger change in momentum and collisions happen more often; so a larger force per unit area (pressure).
parts.working: B1 mean KE/speed of molecules increases; B1 larger momentum change per collision; B1 more frequent collisions → greater rate of change of momentum → greater pressure

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sealed can of air at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 20 °C is left on a car dashboard in Hyderabad in summer, where it reaches 60 °C. Calculate the new pressure. Assume the volume of the can is constant.
parts.working: p/T constant, T in kelvin: 293 K → 333 K (C1); p = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 333/293 = 1.14 × 10⁵ Pa (A1)

practice.stem: A container of volume 0.040 m³ holds 2.4 × 10²⁴ molecules of nitrogen, each of mass 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg. The pressure of the gas is 2.5 × 10⁵ Pa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the root-mean-square speed of the molecules of a gas.
parts.answer: The square root of the mean of the squares of the speeds of all the molecules.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean-square speed ⟨c²⟩ of the molecules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the r.m.s. speed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the relationship between the mean translational kinetic energy of a molecule of an ideal gas and its thermodynamic temperature, and give the equation.
parts.answer: Mean translational KE is directly proportional to the thermodynamic (kelvin) temperature: E_k = (3/2)kT.
parts.working: 1 mark for direct proportionality to T (in kelvin); 1 mark for E = (3/2)kT.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean translational kinetic energy of a helium atom at 320 K. Take k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Smoke particles viewed under a microscope are seen to move randomly, an effect called Brownian motion. Describe how this observation provides evidence for the kinetic theory of gases.
parts.answer: The particles are continually bombarded by fast-moving gas molecules from random directions; unequal impacts produce the random motion, showing that molecules are in constant random motion.
parts.working: 1 mark for molecules colliding with the particles from random directions; 1 mark for the molecules being in constant, random motion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A helium atom has mass 6.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. At a certain temperature the root-mean-square speed of helium atoms is 1300 m s⁻¹. Calculate this temperature, using ⟨c²⟩ = 3kT/m. Take k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
parts.working: T = m⟨c²⟩/(3k) = 6.6 × 10⁻²⁷ × (1300)²/(3 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³) = 269 K. M1 correct expression; M1 substitution; A1 answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of molecular motion, why the pressure of a fixed mass of gas increases when its volume is reduced at constant temperature.
parts.answer: At constant temperature the mean kinetic energy and speed of the molecules are unchanged. With a smaller volume, molecules hit the walls more often per second, so the rate of change of momentum (force) on the walls increases and so does the pressure.
parts.working: 1 mark: molecules hit the walls more frequently; 1 mark: each collision/average speed unchanged at constant T; 1 mark: greater rate of momentum change gives greater force per area, so higher pressure.

practice.stem: Take the Boltzmann constant k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the equations pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ and pV = NkT to show that the mean translational kinetic energy of a molecule is (3/2)kT.
parts.answer: ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ = NkT, so m⟨c²⟩ = 3kT and ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT.
parts.working: M1 equate the two expressions; M1 m⟨c²⟩ = 3kT; A1 multiply by ½ to obtain ⟨Eₖ⟩ = ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the temperature at which the mean translational kinetic energy of a helium atom is 1.0 × 10⁻²⁰ J.

practice.stem: In a computer model of a gas, five molecules have speeds of 300 m s⁻¹, 400 m s⁻¹, 500 m s⁻¹, 600 m s⁻¹ and 700 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean speed of the five molecules.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the root-mean-square speed of the five molecules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the r.m.s. speed is always greater than the mean speed unless all the speeds are equal.
parts.answer: Squaring gives extra weight to the larger speeds, so the square root of the mean of the squares exceeds the mean.

practice.stem: Take the Boltzmann constant k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of a graph of c_rms (y-axis) against thermodynamic temperature T (x-axis) for an ideal gas.
parts.answer: A curve through the origin with decreasing gradient: c_rms ∝ √T.
parts.working: B1 passes through the origin; B1 curve with gradient decreasing (c_rms ∝ √T)

parts.label: b
parts.text: The r.m.s. speed of the molecules of a gas at 300 K is v. State the temperature at which the r.m.s. speed is 2v.
parts.working: B1 c_rms ∝ √T so T increases by a factor of 4

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the temperature at which the r.m.s. speed of carbon dioxide molecules (mass 44 u) is 400 m s⁻¹.

practice.stem: Argon is a monatomic gas. Take R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ and k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why, for an ideal monatomic gas, the internal energy is equal to the total translational kinetic energy of its atoms.
parts.answer: There are no intermolecular forces in an ideal gas, so the potential energy of the atoms is zero; a monatomic gas has only translational kinetic energy.
parts.working: B1 no intermolecular forces so no potential energy; B1 internal energy = sum of KE (and PE) of the particles

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the internal energy U of n moles of an ideal monatomic gas at thermodynamic temperature T is (3/2)nRT.
parts.answer: U = N × (3/2)kT, and Nk = nN_A × (R/N_A) = nR, so U = (3/2)nRT.
parts.working: M1 U = N(3/2)kT; A1 Nk = nR

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the increase in internal energy when 2.0 mol of argon is heated from 300 K to 400 K.

practice.stem:
A computer simulation gives the mean-square speed ⟨c²⟩ of the atoms of a monatomic gas at different thermodynamic temperatures T.

T/K: 250, 300, 350, 400, 450
⟨c²⟩/10⁵ m² s⁻²: 1.56, 1.87, 2.18, 2.49, 2.81

It is suggested that ⟨c²⟩ = 3kT/m, where m is the mass of one atom. k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a graph of ⟨c²⟩ against T should be a straight line through the origin, and state an expression for its gradient.
parts.answer: ⟨c²⟩ = (3k/m)T, which has the form y = mx with no intercept; gradient = 3k/m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the gradient of the graph.
parts.working: M1 large triangle, e.g. (450, 2.81 × 10⁵) and (250, 1.56 × 10⁵); A1 gradient = 1.25 × 10⁵/200 = 625 m² s⁻² K⁻¹ (allow 620–630)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your gradient to determine the mass of one gas atom, in kg and in u.
parts.working: C1 m = 3k/gradient = 3 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³/625; A1 6.62 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, which is 40 u

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict the value of c_rms at 600 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature at which the mean translational kinetic energy of the particles of a gas is 1.0 eV. (1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹)

parts.label: b
parts.text: At 5800 K, the temperature of the Sun's surface, many atoms have kinetic energies greater than 1.0 eV. Explain why this is possible even though your answer to (a) is higher than 5800 K.
parts.answer: (3/2)kT is only the mean; the particles have a range of energies and some have much more than the mean.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the temperature at which the mean kinetic energy would be 0.50 eV.
parts.working: B1 ⟨Eₖ⟩ ∝ T, so half the temperature

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a computer model, 200 molecules of a gas are sorted by speed. Their speeds are grouped as follows, using the midpoint speed of each group:
midpoint speed / m s⁻¹: 100, 300, 500, 700, 900
number of molecules: 8, 45, 70, 55, 22
Calculate the mean speed of the molecules.
parts.working: Mean speed = Σ(n × v)/N = 107 600/200 = 538 m s⁻¹. M1 weighted sum; A1 answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the root-mean-square speed of these molecules.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the values in (a) and (b) are only estimates of the true mean and r.m.s. speeds.
parts.answer: Each group is represented by its midpoint speed, so the actual speeds of the molecules within each group are not known; the values are therefore approximate.
parts.working: 1 mark for the midpoint approximation (individual speeds within each group are lost); 1 mark for concluding that the mean and r.m.s. values are approximate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitrogen molecules (mass 28 u) at 300 K have a root-mean-square speed of 517 m s⁻¹. Show that the root-mean-square speed doubles when the temperature is raised to 1200 K, and state the factor by which the temperature is changed.
parts.answer: T increases by a factor of 4; since c_rms ∝ √T, the r.m.s. speed doubles.
parts.working: 1 mark for T ratio 4 (1200/300); 1 mark for c_rms ∝ √T so the factor is 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the temperature at which the r.m.s. speed of nitrogen molecules is 1034 m s⁻¹, using the molecular mass 28 u = 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg and k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
