parts.working: T = m⟨c²⟩/(3k) = 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ × 1034²/(3 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³) = 1200 K. The answer is the same as the factor of 4 above.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Neon atoms (mass 20 u) and krypton atoms (mass 84 u) are in a mixture at the same thermodynamic temperature. Using ⟨c²⟩ = 3kT/m, show that the ratio of their r.m.s. speeds is c_rms(Ne)/c_rms(Kr) = √(84/20).
parts.working: c_rms = √(3kT/m) with equal T, so c_rms ∝ 1/√m; c_rms(Ne)/c_rms(Kr) = √(m_Kr/m_Ne) = √(84/20). 1 mark for c_rms ∝ 1/√m at constant T; 1 mark for the ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the numerical value of this ratio.
parts.working: Ratio = √4.2 = 2.05, so neon atoms move about twice as fast as krypton atoms on average (in r.m.s. terms).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 0.020 m³ container holds 1.0 × 10²⁴ helium atoms, each of mass 6.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, at a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Using the kinetic theory equation pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩, calculate the r.m.s. speed of the atoms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence calculate the temperature of the helium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A molecule of mass m moves with velocity component cₓ perpendicular to one face of a cube of side L. It collides elastically with this face. State the change in momentum of the molecule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the average force exerted on this face by the molecule is mcₓ²/L.
parts.answer: Time between collisions with the same face = 2L/cₓ; F = Δp/Δt = 2mcₓ/(2L/cₓ) = mcₓ²/L.
parts.working: M1 time between collisions 2L/cₓ; A1 force = rate of change of momentum = mcₓ²/L

parts.label: c
parts.text: The cube contains N identical molecules moving at random. Use your answer to (b) to derive the equation pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩.
parts.answer: Total force = Nm⟨cₓ²⟩/L, so p = F/L² = Nm⟨cₓ²⟩/L³ = Nm⟨cₓ²⟩/V. For random motion ⟨c²⟩ = ⟨cₓ²⟩ + ⟨c_y²⟩ + ⟨c_z²⟩ = 3⟨cₓ²⟩, so pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩.
parts.working: M1 total force = Nm⟨cₓ²⟩/L and p = F/L²; M1 V = L³; A1 ⟨cₓ²⟩ = ⅓⟨c²⟩ because motion is random (no preferred direction), giving pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one point in the derivation where an assumption of the kinetic theory is used, and name the assumption.
parts.answer: e.g. the momentum change 2mcₓ uses perfectly elastic collisions; or ignoring collisions between molecules on the way across uses negligible molecular volume / no intermolecular forces.

practice.stem: Take the Boltzmann constant k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrogen molecules have a mass of 2.0 u and oxygen molecules a mass of 32 u. Show that, at the same temperature, the r.m.s. speed of hydrogen molecules is four times that of oxygen molecules.
parts.answer: ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT is the same for both, so c_rms ∝ 1/√m; ratio = √(32/2.0) = 4.
parts.working: M1 same mean KE at same T so c_rms ∝ m^(−1/2); A1 √16 = 4

parts.label: b
parts.text: In the upper atmosphere the temperature can reach 1000 K. Calculate the r.m.s. speed of hydrogen molecules at this temperature.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The escape speed from the Earth is 11.2 km s⁻¹. Your answer to (b) is only about one third of this. Suggest why hydrogen has nevertheless escaped from the Earth's atmosphere over its history, but oxygen has not.
parts.answer: The r.m.s. is an average: some molecules move much faster than c_rms, and over millions of years enough reach escape speed and leave; oxygen molecules are four times slower, so the fraction reaching 11.2 km s⁻¹ is negligible.
parts.working: B1 molecules have a range (distribution) of speeds, some ≫ c_rms; B1 oxygen's c_rms is 4 times smaller so (almost) none reach escape speed

practice.stem: An oxygen molecule of mass 5.3 × 10⁻²⁶ kg moves backwards and forwards at 450 m s⁻¹ between two opposite walls of a cubical box of side 0.20 m, hitting each wall at right angles. Collisions are elastic and the molecule hits nothing else.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in momentum of the molecule in one collision with the wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time between successive collisions of the molecule with this wall.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the average force exerted on the wall by this molecule, and the resulting pressure on the wall.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The box actually contains 2.0 × 10²³ such molecules at the same r.m.s. speed of 450 m s⁻¹, moving randomly. Determine the pressure in the box.
parts.working: M1 only one-third of the motion is perpendicular to each wall on average: p = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩/V; A1 ⅓ × 2.0 × 10²³ × 5.3 × 10⁻²⁶ × 450²/0.0080 = 89400 Pa

practice.stem: A tube contains a mixture of helium and argon at a temperature of 290 K. Take the Boltzmann constant k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the r.m.s. speed of (i) the helium atoms (4.0 u), (ii) the argon atoms (40 u).
parts.working: C1 c_rms = √(3kT/m); A1 helium 1340 m s⁻¹; A1 argon 425 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: State and explain how the mean kinetic energies of the two kinds of atom compare.
parts.answer: They are equal, because the gases are in thermal equilibrium at the same temperature and ⟨Eₖ⟩ = (3/2)kT depends only on T.
parts.working: B1 equal; B1 same T and ⟨Eₖ⟩ depends only on T

parts.label: c
parts.text: The mixture is heated until the r.m.s. speed of the argon atoms equals the r.m.s. speed the helium atoms had at 290 K. Determine the new temperature.
parts.working: M1 c_rms² ∝ T/m, need c² × 10 for argon so T × 10; A1 2900 K

practice.stem: Nitrogen gas is stored in a cylinder. k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of molecules per cubic metre of the gas at 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and 273 K.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Treating each molecule as a sphere of diameter 3.7 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, estimate the fraction of the volume of the gas occupied by the molecules themselves.
parts.working: volume of one molecule = 4/3 π (1.85 × 10⁻¹⁰)³ = 2.65 × 10⁻²⁹ m³ (C1); fraction = 2.68 × 10²⁵ × 2.65 × 10⁻²⁹ = 7.1 × 10⁻⁴ (A1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The gas is compressed to 300 times this pressure at the same temperature. Assuming it still behaves ideally, estimate the new fraction, and explain why the gas would no longer behave as an ideal gas.
parts.answer: about 0.21; the volume of the molecules is no longer negligible, and molecules are close enough for intermolecular forces to matter.
parts.working: B1 0.21 (300 × answer to (b)); B1 assumption of negligible molecular volume fails; B1 intermolecular forces no longer negligible

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the kinetic theory equations to show that equal volumes of any two ideal gases at the same pressure and temperature contain the same number of molecules.
parts.answer: pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ = ⅔N × ½m⟨c²⟩ = ⅔N(3/2 kT) = NkT; so N = pV/kT, which depends only on p, V and T, not on the type of molecule.
parts.working: M1 write pV = ⅔N⟨Eₖ⟩; M1 ⟨Eₖ⟩ = (3/2)kT is the same for any gas at the same T; A1 N = pV/kT, same for both

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two flasks, each of volume 0.0250 m³, contain hydrogen and carbon dioxide respectively at 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa and 310 K. Calculate the number of molecules in each flask. (k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which flask contains the greater mass of gas and explain why the pressures are equal although the molecules have very different masses.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide (heavier molecules). Its molecules move more slowly (lower c_rms), so each has the same mean KE; the product m⟨c²⟩ is the same, so the pressure is the same.
parts.working: B1 carbon dioxide flask; B1 lighter molecules move faster, m⟨c²⟩ (mean KE) equal so p equal

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the internal energy U of an ideal gas containing N molecules, each with mean translational kinetic energy ½m⟨c²⟩, is given by U = (3/2)pV. Use pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ and the fact that the internal energy is the total translational kinetic energy of the molecules.
parts.working: U = N × ½m⟨c²⟩ = ½Nm⟨c²⟩; from pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩, Nm⟨c²⟩ = 3pV, so U = ½ × 3pV = (3/2)pV. M1 U as total KE; M1 use of pV equation; A1 result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the internal energy of 0.50 m³ of an ideal monatomic gas at a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A molecule of mass m = 4.8 × 10⁻²⁶ kg moves with speed c perpendicular to one face of a cube of side L = 0.25 m and bounces elastically off it. Its speed is c = 450 m s⁻¹. The molecule bounces back and forth between two opposite faces. Show that the time between successive collisions with the same face is t = 2L/c, and that the average force on that face due to the molecule is F = mc²/L.
parts.working: Time between collisions with the same face t = 2L/c; each collision changes momentum by 2mc, so F = 2mc/t = 2mc × c/(2L) = mc²/L. M1 time between collisions; M1 change in momentum 2mc; A1 F = mc²/L.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate this average force.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A model treats conduction electrons in a metal as a gas of particles of mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. Calculate the temperature at which the r.m.s. speed of such particles would be 1.0 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why this simple gas model is not a good description of conduction electrons in a metal.
parts.answer: Electrons interact strongly with each other and with the lattice, and they are governed by quantum rules, so they are not independent classical molecules.
parts.working: Any valid reason: interactions, quantum behaviour, electrons are not classical molecules; the model assumes no forces between particles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sample of argon (atomic mass 40 u = 6.64 × 10⁻²⁶ kg) has a mean-square speed ⟨c²⟩ = 2.4 × 10⁵ m² s⁻². Calculate the thermodynamic temperature of the sample. Take k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The sample is then heated until the mean translational kinetic energy of each atom doubles. Calculate the new temperature.
parts.working: E_k ∝ T, so doubling E_k doubles T: T = 2 × 385 K = 770 K.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)
practice.stem: N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an ideal gas.
parts.answer: A gas that obeys pV ∝ T (pV = nRT) at all pressures, volumes and temperatures.
parts.working: B1 pV ∝ T (T thermodynamic temperature) for all p, V, T

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the Avogadro constant.
parts.answer: The number of particles (atoms or molecules) in one mole of a substance, 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
parts.working: B1 number of particles in one mole (the mole is defined by this fixed number)

parts.label: c
parts.text: A sample of oxygen gas has a mass of 64 g. The molar mass of oxygen (O₂) is 32 g mol⁻¹. Calculate (i) the amount of gas in moles, (ii) the number of oxygen molecules.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)
practice.stem: An oxygen cylinder at a hospital in Lahore has an internal volume of 0.010 m³. The oxygen is at a pressure of 1.37 × 10⁷ Pa and a temperature of 20 °C (293 K). Take R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ and k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of oxygen, in mol, in the cylinder.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen in the cylinder. The molar mass of oxygen is 0.032 kg mol⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use pV = NkT to calculate the number of molecules in the cylinder.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)
practice.stem: Before a journey from Lahore to Islamabad, the air in a car tyre is at a pressure of 2.2 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 15 °C. After the journey the temperature of the air in the tyre is 45 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the pressure of the air in the tyre after the journey. Assume the volume of the tyre does not change.
parts.working: p₁/T₁ = p₂/T₂ with T in K: 288 K and 318 K (C1); p₂ = 2.2 × 10⁵ × 318/288 = 2.43 × 10⁵ Pa (A1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the temperatures must be converted to kelvin before using the gas equation.
parts.answer: p is proportional to the thermodynamic (absolute) temperature, which is zero when p would be zero; the Celsius scale has an arbitrary zero.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption, apart from constant volume, made in your calculation.
parts.answer: No air leaks out (amount of gas constant) / air behaves as an ideal gas.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)
practice.stem: R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that k = R/N_A and calculate its value.
parts.working: M1 pV = nRT = NkT with N = nN_A, so k = R/N_A; A1 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of gas molecules in 1.0 cm³ of air at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 300 K.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the ideal gas equation, and state the unit of each quantity it contains.
parts.answer: pV = nRT; p in pascals (Pa), V in cubic metres (m³), n in moles (mol), R in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, T in kelvin (K).
parts.working: 1 mark for the equation; 1 mark for the units (SI).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample of 0.25 mol of an ideal gas is at 300 K in a container of volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Calculate the pressure of the gas. R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas cylinder contains 2.5 L of an ideal gas at 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 35 °C. Convert the temperature to kelvin and the volume to m³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount of gas in the cylinder.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carbon dioxide occupies 500 cm³ at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 298 K. Calculate the number of moles of carbon dioxide in the container. R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of CO₂ molecules in the container. N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rigid tank of volume 5.0 m³ contains nitrogen (M = 28 g mol⁻¹) at a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 290 K. Calculate the mass of nitrogen in the tank.
parts.working: n = pV/(RT) = (2.0 × 10⁵ × 5.0)/(8.31 × 290) = 415 mol; m = nM = 415 × 0.028 = 11.6 kg. M1 moles; M1 conversion of molar mass; A1 answer.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the molar volume of a gas.
parts.answer: The volume occupied by one mole of the gas at a stated temperature and pressure.
parts.working: Accept the volume of 1 mol of gas at a given p and T.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the molar volume of an ideal gas at 273 K and 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa, giving your answer in dm³.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the ideal gas equation to explain why a sealed balloon containing gas at constant pressure expands when it is heated.
parts.answer: pV = nRT with p and n constant gives V ∝ T, so the volume increases as the temperature (in kelvin) increases.
parts.working: 1 mark for V ∝ T at constant p and n; 1 mark for the conclusion that the volume increases.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)
practice.stem: A weather balloon is filled with helium at ground level, where the pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and the temperature is 290 K. Its volume is 4.0 m³. It rises to a height where the pressure is 3.0 × 10⁴ Pa and the temperature is 240 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of the balloon at the high altitude. Assume no gas escapes and the pressure inside equals the pressure outside.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the amount of helium in the balloon, in mol. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)
practice.stem: A room in Quetta measures 5.0 m × 4.0 m × 3.0 m. Because the city is at high altitude, the air pressure is 8.0 × 10⁴ Pa. The air temperature is 283 K. Take R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ and k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of air molecules in the room.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of air in the room. The mean molar mass of air is 0.029 kg mol⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The heater raises the air temperature to 293 K while the pressure stays constant. Explain what happens to the number of molecules in the room.
parts.answer: It decreases (to 1.19 × 10²⁷): N = pV/kT, so with p and V fixed N ∝ 1/T; some air leaves the room through gaps.
parts.working: B1 N decreases; B1 N ∝ 1/T at constant p and V, air escapes through gaps/windows

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)
practice.stem: Container A, of volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³, contains an ideal gas at 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Container B, of volume 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, contains the same gas at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. They are joined by a narrow tube with a closed tap. Both containers are at the same constant temperature. The tap is opened.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the total value of pV for the two containers is the same before and after the tap is opened.
parts.answer: pV = nRT; the total amount n and the temperature are unchanged, so Σ pV is unchanged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the final pressure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the fraction of the total gas that was originally in container A.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)
practice.stem:
A student compresses air in a sealed syringe connected to a pressure gauge, keeping the temperature at 295 K. She records the volume V and pressure p.

V/cm³: 20, 25, 30, 40, 50
p/kPa: 200.5, 160.2, 133.6, 100.3, 80.1

R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a graph of p against 1/V should be a straight line through the origin, and give an expression for its gradient.
parts.answer: pV = nRT so p = nRT × (1/V): linear with zero intercept for constant n and T; gradient = nRT.
parts.working: B1 p ∝ 1/V at constant T and n; B1 gradient = nRT

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate 1/V for each result, in units of 10⁴ m⁻³.
parts.working: B1 all values (V in m³: 20 cm³ = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ m³ → 5.00 × 10⁴ m⁻³)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the gradient of the graph, using the first and last points, and hence the amount of gas in mol.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why the syringe is pushed in slowly.
parts.answer: So that the temperature of the gas stays constant (work done on the gas heats it if compressed quickly).

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)
practice.stem: R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the density ρ of an ideal gas of molar mass M is given by ρ = pM/(RT).
parts.answer: n = m/M, so pV = (m/M)RT and ρ = m/V = pM/(RT).
parts.working: M1 n = mass/M; A1 rearrangement to ρ = pM/RT

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the density of carbon dioxide (M = 0.044 kg mol⁻¹) and of air (M = 0.029 kg mol⁻¹) at 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and 298 K.
parts.answer: CO₂: 1.79 kg m⁻³; air: 1.18 kg m⁻³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why carbon dioxide leaking from a fire extinguisher collects at floor level.
parts.answer: At the same p and T, CO₂ is about 1.5 times denser than air, so it sinks below the air.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas cylinder contains a fixed mass of gas at a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁶ Pa and a temperature of 288 K. The cylinder is left in the sun and its temperature rises to 318 K. Assume the volume of the cylinder is constant and no gas escapes. Calculate the new pressure.
parts.working: p₂/T₂ = p₁/T₁ (V and n constant), so p₂ = 2.0 × 10⁶ × 318/288 = 2.21 × 10⁶ Pa.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the motion of the molecules, why the pressure increases.
parts.answer: The molecules move faster on average, so they strike the walls with greater momentum change and more often; this increases the force per unit area.
parts.working: 1 mark for faster molecules (greater mean KE); 1 mark for more frequent and harder collisions with the walls.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas is at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and occupies 0.060 m³ at a temperature of 300 K. It is compressed slowly at constant temperature until its volume is 0.015 m³. Calculate the new pressure.
parts.working: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ at constant T: p₂ = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 0.060/0.015 = 4.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gas is then heated at constant volume to 400 K. Calculate the pressure after heating.
parts.working: p₃/T₃ = p₂/T₂ at constant V: p₃ = 4.0 × 10⁵ × 400/300 = 5.3 × 10⁵ Pa.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)
practice.stem: A sealed storage tank of volume 50 m³ contains methane at a pressure of 1.1 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 285 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of methane in the tank, in mol.
parts.working: n = pV/(RT) = (1.1 × 10⁵ × 50)/(8.31 × 285) = 2.32 × 10³ mol. 1 mark for rearranging pV = nRT; 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of methane molecules in the tank. N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
parts.working: N = nN_A = 2322 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.40 × 10²⁷ molecules. 1 mark for N = nN_A; 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption made in your calculations.
parts.answer: The methane behaves as an ideal gas (and its temperature is uniform throughout the tank).
parts.working: Any valid assumption: ideal gas behaviour; uniform temperature and pressure in the tank.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The volume of a human lung is about 3.0 dm³ when it is full. Take the air in the lung to be at 37 °C (310 K) and 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate the amount of air in the lung, in mol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of air molecules in the lung.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas cylinder of volume 40 L contains argon (M = 40 g mol⁻¹) at a pressure of 1.5 × 10⁷ Pa and a temperature of 288 K. Calculate the amount of argon in the cylinder.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of argon in the cylinder.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Air in the troposphere at ground level in Lahore has pressure 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and temperature 288 K. Calculate the number of molecules per cubic metre, n = N/V. Take k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At 10 km altitude the pressure is 2.65 × 10⁴ Pa and the temperature is 223 K. Calculate the ratio of the number density at 10 km to the number density at ground level.
parts.working: Ratio = (p₂/T₂)/(p₁/T₁) = (2.65 × 10⁴/223)/(1.01 × 10⁵/288) = 0.339, i.e. about 34% of the ground-level value.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas has density 1.42 kg m⁻³ at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 300 K. Show that the molar mass M of the gas is given by M = ρRT/p.
parts.working: ρ = m/V = nM/V; from pV = nRT, n/V = p/(RT), so ρ = pM/(RT) and M = ρRT/p. M1 ρ = nM/V; M1 use of pV = nRT.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the molar mass of the gas, in g mol⁻¹.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas syringe contains 0.0020 mol of an ideal gas in a volume of 50 cm³ at a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate the temperature of the gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The plunger is pushed in until the volume is 25 cm³ at the same temperature. Calculate the new pressure.
parts.working: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ at constant T: p₂ = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 50/25 = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: The density of air at 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and 293 K is 1.20 kg m⁻³. Using ρ = pM/(RT), show that at the same pressure the density is inversely proportional to the thermodynamic temperature.
parts.working: At constant p, M and R: ρ = pM/(RT), so ρ ∝ 1/T. M1 identifying constant quantities; A1 proportionality.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the density of this air when it is heated to 373 K at the same pressure.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)
practice.stem: Two glass bulbs X and Y, each of volume 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³, are joined by a thin tube of negligible volume. Initially bulb X is at 300 K and bulb Y at 400 K, and the gas pressure throughout is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total amount of gas in the two bulbs, in mol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Bulb Y is now heated to 500 K, while bulb X is kept at 300 K. Gas flows through the tube until the pressures are equal. Calculate the new pressure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the direction in which gas flows while bulb Y is being heated, and explain why.
parts.answer: From Y to X: heating Y raises its pressure above that in X, so gas moves to X until pressures are equal.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)
practice.stem:
A student investigates how the volume V of a fixed mass of air, trapped in a narrow glass tube by a thread of oil, varies with temperature θ at constant pressure. The tube is placed in a water bath, which is stirred and heated.

θ/°C: 10, 30, 50, 70, 90
V/cm³: 28.3, 30.4, 32.3, 34.3, 36.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a graph of V against θ is expected to be a straight line, and what the intercept on the θ-axis represents.
parts.answer: At constant p, V = (nR/p)T = (nR/p)(θ + 273), which is linear in θ; V = 0 where θ = −273 °C, so the θ-intercept represents absolute zero.
parts.working: B1 V ∝ T at constant p, linear in θ; B1 intercept (V = 0) gives absolute zero

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the gradient of the line, using the first and last results as points on the best-fit line.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your gradient to determine the value of absolute zero in °C.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The pressure of the trapped air is 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa. Use the result at 10 °C to calculate the amount of air trapped, in mol. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
parts.working: n = pV/RT with V = 28.3 × 10⁻⁶ m³ and T = 283 K (C1); n = 1.22 × 10⁻³ mol (A1)

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the extrapolation to V = 0 may not give an accurate value for absolute zero.
parts.answer: Long extrapolation magnifies small errors in the gradient; the thread/trapped air may not be at the bath temperature (insufficient time); water vapour in the trapped air; real gas liquefies before reaching absolute zero.
parts.working: B1 each for any two sensible reasons

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)
practice.stem: A steel cylinder of fixed volume contains 2.4 kg of compressed gas at 6.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 300 K. Over a cold night the valve leaks. In the morning the pressure is 4.2 × 10⁵ Pa and the temperature is 290 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the fraction of the original gas that remains in the cylinder.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of gas that has escaped.
parts.working: B1 remaining mass = 2.4 × 0.724 = 1.74 kg, so 0.662 kg escaped

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student calculates the fraction remaining as 4.2/6.0 = 0.70. Explain why this is incorrect.
parts.answer: The temperature has also fallen; at the lower temperature the same amount of gas would have a lower pressure, so p alone does not measure the amount.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A closed glass tube of length 0.60 m is lowered vertically, open end first, into a lake until the open end is at depth h. Air is trapped inside at atmospheric pressure p₀ = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and the air temperature is constant. Show that the pressure of the trapped air is p = p₀ + ρgh, where ρ is the density of water, and hence calculate the length of the air column when h = 2.0 m. Take ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³ and g = 9.81 m s⁻².
parts.working: p = p₀ + ρgh (hydrostatic pressure at depth h). Boyle's law: p₀ × 0.60 = (p₀ + ρgh) × L; L = 0.60 p₀/(p₀ + ρgh) = 0.60 × 1.0 × 10⁵/(1.0 × 10⁵ + 1.96 × 10⁴) = 0.502 m. M1 p = p₀ + ρgh; M1 Boyle's law; M1 substitution; A1 answer.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The pressure of a fixed amount of gas in a sealed container of volume 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m³ is measured at several temperatures. The data (for 0.010 mol of gas) are:
T / K: 280, 300, 320, 340
p / 10⁵ Pa: 0.931, 0.997, 1.06, 1.13
Explain why a graph of p against T should be a straight line through the origin in kelvin, and state what its gradient represents.
parts.answer: At constant V and n, p ∝ T so the graph is a straight line through the origin; the gradient is nR/V.
parts.working: 1 mark for p ∝ T (pV = nRT, constant V and n); 1 mark for gradient nR/V.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the gradient of the line between the first and last points, in Pa K⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence determine the amount of gas, using your gradient.

practice.subtopic: Equation of state (pV = nRT = NkT, mole)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small bubble of air of volume 2.0 cm³ is released at the bottom of a lake 40 m deep. The water temperature is constant throughout. Atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, the density of water is 1000 kg m⁻³ and g = 9.81 m s⁻². Show that the pressure at the bottom of the lake is about 4.9 × 10⁵ Pa.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming the air in the bubble behaves as an ideal gas at constant temperature, calculate the volume of the bubble when it reaches the surface.
parts.working: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂: V_surface = 2.0 cm³ × (4.92 × 10⁵)/(1.0 × 10⁵) = 9.85 cm³. M1 Boyle's law applied; M1 pressures; A1 answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how X-rays are produced in an X-ray tube.
parts.answer: Electrons from a heated cathode are accelerated through a large p.d. to the anode; they strike a metal target and decelerate rapidly, emitting X-ray photons (braking radiation); characteristic lines come from inner-shell electron transitions in the target atoms.
parts.working: B1: electrons emitted by thermionic emission and accelerated through a high p.d. B1: electrons hit a (high-melting-point, e.g. tungsten) metal target. B1: rapid deceleration produces X-ray photons (continuous spectrum) / electron transitions in target atoms give characteristic lines.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The accelerating potential difference is 80 kV. Calculate the minimum wavelength of the X-rays produced.
parts.working: C1: eV = hc/λ_min (all KE of one electron → one photon). A1: λ_min = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 80 × 10³) = 1.55 × 10⁻¹¹ m.

practice.stem: A parallel beam of X-rays passes through 4.0 cm of muscle. The linear attenuation coefficient of muscle for these X-rays is 0.20 cm⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the linear attenuation coefficient µ.
parts.answer: The fraction (proportion) of the intensity of the beam absorbed/removed per unit thickness of the material (µ in I = I₀e^(−µx)).
parts.working: B1: fractional decrease in intensity per unit distance travelled (or the constant µ in I = I₀e^(−µx)).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the incident intensity that emerges from the muscle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why a parallel beam is assumed in this calculation.
parts.answer: So that any decrease in intensity is due only to attenuation, not to the beam spreading out.
parts.working: B1: no reduction in intensity due to divergence of the beam.

practice.stem: A metal filter used in an X-ray machine has a linear attenuation coefficient of 0.46 mm⁻¹ for X-rays of a particular energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the half-value thickness x½ is related to µ by x½ = ln 2 / µ.
parts.working: M1: I = I₀/2 when x = x½: ½ = e^(−µx½). A1: ln 2 = µx½.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the half-value thickness of the filter material.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the thickness that reduces the intensity to 1/32 of its incident value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the sharpness of an X-ray image, and suggest one way it is improved.
parts.answer: Sharpness is how clearly the edges/boundaries of structures are defined; improved by a smaller area of the target hit by electrons (smaller focal spot), or a lead grid / aperture to produce a narrower, more parallel beam.
parts.working: B1: edges well defined / how clearly boundaries are seen. B1: small anode area (focal spot) / collimate beam / lead grid in front of detector.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by the contrast of an X-ray image.
parts.answer: The difference in degree of blackening (brightness) between different areas/tissues of the image.
parts.working: B1: difference in blackening between structures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a thin aluminium filter is placed in the X-ray beam before it reaches the patient.
parts.answer: It absorbs the low-energy (long-wavelength) X-rays, which would be absorbed in the skin and tissue near the surface without reaching the detector, so they would increase the patient's dose without improving the image.
parts.working: B1: removes low-energy X-ray photons. B1: these would only be absorbed by the patient (skin) — dose without contributing to the image.

practice.stem: A dental X-ray tube operates with an accelerating potential difference of 30 kV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum energy, in joules, of an X-ray photon produced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The tube current is 25 mA and 1.0% of the electron beam's energy is converted to X-rays. Calculate the rate at which thermal energy is produced in the anode.
parts.working: C1: power of beam = IV = 25 × 10⁻³ × 30 × 10³ = 750 W. A1: thermal power = 0.99 × 750 = 742.5 W ≈ 743 W (accept 742 W).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the anode in many X-ray tubes is made to rotate.
parts.answer: So that the heating is spread over a larger area of the target, preventing it from overheating/melting.
parts.working: B1: spreads the heat over a larger area / reduces local temperature.

practice.stem: The shortest wavelength in the X-ray spectrum from a hospital X-ray tube is 2.5 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why there is a minimum wavelength in the X-ray spectrum.
parts.answer: An electron can give at most all its kinetic energy (eV) to a single photon; the largest photon energy corresponds to the shortest wavelength (E = hc/λ).
parts.working: B1: maximum photon energy = electron's kinetic energy eV. B1: E = hc/λ so λ has a minimum.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the accelerating potential difference of the tube.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The tube current is 4.0 mA. Calculate the number of electrons striking the anode each second.

practice.stem: A parallel beam of X-rays passes through 2.5 cm of bone. The linear attenuation coefficient of bone for these X-rays is 0.60 cm⁻¹ and that of soft tissue is 0.20 cm⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the incident intensity transmitted by the bone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the thickness of soft tissue that would transmit the same percentage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why bone shows up clearly on an X-ray image of a limb.
parts.answer: Bone absorbs much more strongly than soft tissue, so far fewer X-rays reach the detector behind bone; the two regions have very different exposure (good contrast).

practice.stem: A parallel X-ray beam passes through a patient's arm along two paths of the same total length, 6.0 cm. Path 1 is through soft tissue only. Path 2 is through 2.5 cm of bone and 3.5 cm of soft tissue. Linear attenuation coefficients: soft tissue 0.24 cm⁻¹, bone 0.62 cm⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate, for each path, the fraction of the incident intensity that emerges.
parts.working: C1: I/I₀ = e^(−µx), adding the exponents for successive layers. A1: tissue only: e^(−1.44) = 0.237. A1: bone path: e^(−(1.55 + 0.84)) = 0.0916.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of these intensities and state whether the bone will be clearly visible on the image.
parts.working: A1: 0.237/0.0916 = 2.59. B1: large ratio → clear difference in blackening, good contrast.

practice.stem: A block of tissue-equivalent plastic 3.5 cm thick transmits 18% of the intensity of a parallel X-ray beam.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the linear attenuation coefficient of the material.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the half-value thickness of the material.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain how µ would change if X-rays of higher photon energy were used.
parts.answer: µ would decrease: higher-energy photons are more penetrating, so a smaller fraction is absorbed per unit thickness.
parts.working: B1: decreases. B1: more penetrating / less absorption per unit thickness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a CT scan produces a three-dimensional image of a section of the body.
parts.answer: Images of many thin slices are taken; for each slice, an X-ray tube rotates around the patient and detectors on the opposite side record the intensity from many directions; a computer calculates the attenuation for each voxel and builds an image of each slice; images of successive slices are combined to give a 3D image that can be viewed from any angle.
parts.working: B1: image of a thin slice (section) taken. B1: X-ray tube (and detectors) rotate around the patient, many directions in the plane of the slice. B1: computer deduces value for each voxel/pixel of the slice. B1: many slices combined into 3D image that can be rotated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of a CT scan compared with a single X-ray image.
parts.answer: Advantage: 3D image / soft tissues and structures at different depths can be distinguished (no overlapping shadows). Disadvantage: much larger radiation dose (and higher cost, longer time).
parts.working: B1: advantage, e.g. 3D, can be viewed from any angle, better contrast for soft tissue, no overlap. B1: disadvantage, e.g. higher dose.

practice.stem:
A simple model of a CT slice has four voxels arranged in a square: P (top left), Q (top right), R (bottom left) and S (bottom right). Each detector reading equals the sum of the voxel values along the beam.
Beam along top row (P, Q): 10
Beam along bottom row (R, S): 14
Beam down left column (P, R): 8
Beam along the diagonal (P, S): 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why at least four readings are needed to find the four voxel values.
parts.answer: There are four unknowns, so four independent equations (readings) are needed.
parts.working: B1: four unknowns need four independent equations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the values of P, Q, R and S.

practice.stem: A lead apron used by a radiographer has a linear attenuation coefficient of 0.62 mm⁻¹ for the scattered X-rays in the room.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the thickness of lead needed to reduce the intensity of the beam to 5.0% of its incident value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many half-value thicknesses this represents.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the intensity of the beam never becomes exactly zero, however thick the lead.
parts.answer: Attenuation is exponential: each extra thickness removes the same fraction, so the intensity approaches but never reaches zero.
parts.working: B1: exponential decrease — constant fraction removed per unit thickness.

practice.stem: Electrons in a dental X-ray tube are accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 25 kV. Mass of electron = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the electrons as they reach the anode, ignoring relativistic effects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum wavelength of the X-rays produced.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the anode becomes very hot and suggest how this problem is reduced.
parts.answer: Most electrons lose their energy in many small interactions with anode atoms, which becomes internal energy (about 99%); the anode is made of a high-melting-point metal such as tungsten, mounted on copper/oil-cooled or rotated.
parts.working: B1: most kinetic energy → thermal energy. B1: any valid method (rotating anode, cooling oil/fins, high melting point metal).

practice.stem: An aluminium filter of thickness 1.2 mm reduces the intensity of a parallel X-ray beam by 30%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the linear attenuation coefficient of aluminium for these X-rays.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the half-value thickness of aluminium.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the thickness of aluminium needed to reduce the intensity to 10% of its initial value.

practice.stem:
Linear attenuation coefficients for two X-ray photon energies are:
40 keV: bone 1.30 cm⁻¹, soft tissue 0.27 cm⁻¹
100 keV: bone 0.40 cm⁻¹, soft tissue 0.17 cm⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each photon energy, calculate the ratio (intensity through 3.0 cm of soft tissue)/(intensity through 3.0 cm of bone).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fraction transmitted through 3.0 cm of bone at each energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answers, discuss the choice of photon energy for imaging a bone fracture.
parts.answer: Lower energy gives much better contrast between bone and tissue, but far less is transmitted, so a larger dose is needed for enough intensity at the detector; a compromise energy is chosen.
parts.working: B1: low energy → better contrast. B1: but more absorbed by patient / higher dose / weak signal through thick parts — compromise.

practice.stem: A parallel X-ray beam passes through a patient's leg. In order, it crosses 0.80 cm of skin and fat (µ = 0.18 cm⁻¹), 2.0 cm of bone (µ = 0.55 cm⁻¹) and 3.0 cm of muscle (µ = 0.23 cm⁻¹).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the incident intensity that leaves the leg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the thickness of muscle alone that would produce the same attenuation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The beam is not parallel but spreads out from the tube. State the effect on the measured intensity at the detector and explain why this does not change the contrast between two neighbouring paths.
parts.answer: The measured intensity is lower (beam spreads over a larger area), but both neighbouring paths are reduced by the same factor, so their ratio (contrast) is unchanged.
parts.working: B1: lower intensity due to divergence. B1: same factor for both paths, so ratio unchanged.

practice.stem:
A hospital physicist measures the intensity I (arbitrary units) of a narrow parallel X-ray beam after it passes through thickness x of a test absorber. It is suggested that I = I₀e^(−µx).
x / mm: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
I: 1000, 793, 633, 500, 399, 317

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a graph of ln I against x should be a straight line, and state how µ is found from it.
parts.answer: ln I = ln I₀ − µx, which has the form y = c + mx; µ = −gradient.
parts.working: B1: ln I = −µx + ln I₀ (linear in x). B1: µ = −gradient (intercept = ln I₀).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ln I for x = 6 mm and x = 10 mm, giving your answers to 3 decimal places.
parts.working: A1: ln 500 = 6.215; ln 317 = 5.759 (3 d.p., matching the 3 s.f. data).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the first and last points (which lie on the best-fit line), determine µ.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the half-value thickness of the absorber.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Each reading of I has an uncertainty of ±10 (arbitrary units). Calculate the absolute uncertainty in ln I for the reading at x = 10 mm.

practice.stem: For the X-rays used, the linear attenuation coefficient of soft tissue is 0.25 cm⁻¹ and that of a barium-sulfate meal is 4.2 cm⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a plain X-ray image of the intestine shows poor contrast with the surrounding tissue.
parts.answer: Intestine walls and surrounding soft tissues have similar densities/atomic numbers and therefore similar attenuation coefficients, so they absorb X-rays to a similar extent.
parts.working: B1: similar attenuation coefficients (similar density / Z). B1: so similar transmitted intensities, little difference in blackening.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A patient swallows a barium meal. Calculate the fraction of incident intensity transmitted through 1.5 cm of barium meal and through 1.5 cm of soft tissue, and the ratio of the two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why barium is effective as a contrast medium.
parts.answer: It has a high atomic number (proton number), so it absorbs X-rays strongly.
parts.working: B1: high Z → large attenuation coefficient.

practice.stem: Two parallel X-ray beams pass through a patient's abdomen along neighbouring paths, each 8.0 cm long. Path 1 is through soft tissue only (µ = 0.18 cm⁻¹). Path 2 passes through a tumour of thickness d (µ = 0.30 cm⁻¹), the rest of the path being soft tissue. The intensity emerging from path 2 is 0.85 times that from path 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the incident intensity that emerges from path 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that I₂/I₁ = e^(−(0.30 − 0.18)d) and hence calculate d.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The image contrast between the tumour and the surrounding tissue is poor. Suggest one way in which it could be improved.
parts.answer: Use a contrast medium that collects in the tumour / use lower-energy X-ray photons (where the difference in µ is larger).

practice.stem:
A very simple model of a CT slice has four voxels in a square: P (top left), Q (top right), R (bottom left) and S (bottom right). Each detector reading equals the sum of the values of the voxels along the beam.
Top row (P, Q): 9
Bottom row (R, S): 13
Left column (P, R): 12
Right column (Q, S): 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that these four readings do not fix the voxel values uniquely, by giving two different sets of values that fit them.
parts.answer: For example P = 4, Q = 5, R = 8, S = 5 and P = 5, Q = 4, R = 7, S = 6 (both fit all four readings).
parts.working: B1: one correct set. B1: a second, different correct set.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A diagonal beam through P and S gives a reading of 9. Determine the value of each voxel.
parts.working: P + S = 9 and P + Q = 9 so Q = S (M1); Q + S = 10 so Q = S = 5 (M1); P = 4, R = 8 (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a CT scanner obtains enough information to build up a three-dimensional image.
parts.answer: The X-ray tube and detectors rotate around the patient, taking readings from many directions for each slice; many thin slices are imaged and a computer combines the slices into a 3-D image.
parts.working: B1: many directions / rotation for one slice. B1: many slices combined by computer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a piezoelectric transducer produces a pulse of ultrasound.
parts.answer: An alternating p.d. at ultrasonic frequency is applied across a piezoelectric crystal; the crystal changes shape (expands and contracts) with the p.d.; it vibrates (resonantly when the frequency matches its natural frequency), sending out ultrasound waves.
parts.working: B1: alternating p.d. applied across the crystal. B1: crystal changes shape/thickness with the p.d. B1: it vibrates at the frequency of the p.d. (ultrasonic, >20 kHz), producing ultrasound (large amplitude at resonance).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the same transducer detects the reflected pulse.
parts.answer: The returning ultrasound makes the crystal vibrate (change shape), which produces an alternating p.d. across it that is detected and processed.
parts.working: B1: reflected wave makes the crystal vibrate / deform. B1: this generates an alternating e.m.f. across the crystal.

practice.stem:
Data for two tissues:
muscle: density 1075 kg m⁻³, speed of ultrasound 1590 m s⁻¹
fat: density 925 kg m⁻³, speed of ultrasound 1450 m s⁻¹

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define specific acoustic impedance.
parts.answer: The product of the density of a medium and the speed of sound (ultrasound) in it: Z = ρc.
parts.working: B1: Z = density × speed of sound in the medium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the specific acoustic impedance of each tissue.
parts.answer: muscle 1.71 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹; fat 1.34 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient at a fat–muscle boundary.
parts.working: C1: α = (Z₂ − Z₁)²/(Z₂ + Z₁)². A1: α = 0.0146.

practice.stem: An ultrasound pulse is sent into a patient's abdomen. The echo from a boundary between two organs is received 65 µs after the pulse is emitted. The average speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depth of the boundary below the skin.
parts.working: C1: pulse travels to the boundary and back: 2d = ct. A1: d = 1540 × 65 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 0.0501 m = 5.01 cm (accept 5.0 cm).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the ultrasound is sent in short pulses rather than as a continuous wave.
parts.answer: So that the time between emission and the arrival of each echo can be measured (the transducer can act as a receiver between pulses).
parts.working: B1: to time the echo / allow the transducer to receive between pulses.

practice.stem: A medical ultrasound probe operates at a frequency of 5.0 MHz. The speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by ultrasound.
parts.answer: Longitudinal (sound) waves with frequency above the upper limit of human hearing (about 20 kHz).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the ultrasound in soft tissue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a higher frequency would show finer detail but could not be used to image deep organs.
parts.answer: Shorter wavelength resolves smaller structures; but attenuation increases with frequency, so the echoes from deep organs would be too weak.
parts.working: B1: shorter wavelength → better resolution. B1: greater attenuation at higher frequency.

practice.stem: The density of a sample of bone is 1900 kg m⁻³ and the speed of ultrasound in it is 4080 m s⁻¹. The specific acoustic impedance of soft tissue is 1.63 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the specific acoustic impedance of the bone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient for ultrasound at a boundary between soft tissue and this bone.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the fraction of the incident intensity that passes into the bone.

practice.stem: To find the specific acoustic impedance of a plastic used in an ultrasound training model, a technician places a transducer on one face of a block of the plastic 3.0 cm thick. The echo from the opposite face returns 22.2 µs after the pulse is emitted. The density of the plastic is 1190 kg m⁻³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of ultrasound in the plastic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the specific acoustic impedance of the plastic.
parts.working: Z = ρc = 1190 × 2702.7 = 3.22 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹ (use the unrounded speed; 1190 × 2700 would give 3.21 × 10⁶) (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a layer of gel is placed between the transducer and the block.
parts.answer: To exclude air: an air gap would reflect almost all the ultrasound because air's acoustic impedance is very different.

practice.stem: An ultrasound scan can be displayed as an A-scan or as a B-scan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how an A-scan displays the echoes.
parts.answer: As a graph (trace) of echo strength against time: each echo is a peak whose horizontal position gives the depth of the boundary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a B-scan builds up a two-dimensional image.
parts.answer: The probe is moved (or an array of transducers is used) to send pulses along many lines; each echo is shown as a dot whose position depends on the probe direction and echo time (depth) and whose brightness depends on the echo strength; the dots form a 2-D image.
parts.working: B1: many lines / probe moved or array. B1: position from direction and time delay. B1: brightness ∝ echo intensity.

practice.stem: Specific acoustic impedances: air 430 kg m⁻² s⁻¹, skin 1.6 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹, coupling gel 1.5 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient at an air–skin boundary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient when a gel is placed between the transducer and the skin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain the purpose of the gel.
parts.answer: Without gel, almost all the ultrasound is reflected at the skin surface and very little enters the body; the gel has an acoustic impedance close to that of skin, so almost all the ultrasound is transmitted.
parts.working: B1: air gap reflects nearly all (99.9%) of the ultrasound. B1: gel impedance-matches, so nearly all is transmitted into the body.

practice.stem: Ultrasound is attenuated exponentially in soft tissue with an attenuation coefficient of 48 m⁻¹. A boundary 4.0 cm below the skin has an intensity reflection coefficient of 0.0080. Ignore reflection at the skin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the total distance travelled through the tissue by the ultrasound that returns to the transducer from the boundary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio (intensity of the echo received at the transducer)/(intensity transmitted into the tissue).
parts.working: C1: attenuation factor e^(−48 × 0.080) = 0.0215. C1: multiply by α = 0.0080. A1: 1.72 × 10⁻⁴.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the received echoes from deeper boundaries are amplified more before display.
parts.answer: They have travelled further through tissue and been attenuated more, so amplification compensates for the extra attenuation.
parts.working: B1: greater attenuation over a longer path.

practice.stem: An A-scan of a patient's thigh shows the transmitted pulse at time zero, an echo from the fat–muscle boundary at 26 µs and an echo from the muscle–bone boundary at 92 µs. The transducer is in contact with the fat layer. Speeds of ultrasound: fat 1450 m s⁻¹, muscle 1590 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the thickness of the fat layer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the thickness of the muscle layer.
parts.working: C1: time in muscle = 92 − 26 = 66 µs (there and back). A1: d = 1590 × 66 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 5.25 cm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the echo from the muscle–bone boundary is much stronger than that from the fat–muscle boundary.
parts.answer: The difference in acoustic impedance between muscle and bone is much greater, so a much larger fraction is reflected.
parts.working: B1: larger difference in Z → larger reflection coefficient.

practice.stem: An ultrasound scanner sends a short pulse into the body and must receive all echoes from depths of up to 15 cm before it sends the next pulse. The average speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time for an echo to return from a depth of 15 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum number of pulses that can be sent each second.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what would go wrong if pulses were sent more often than this.
parts.answer: Echoes from deep boundaries would arrive after the next pulse was sent and be wrongly read as echoes from shallow depths.

practice.stem: In an experiment, the intensity of a parallel beam of ultrasound falls to 20% of its initial value after travelling 5.0 cm through a tissue sample.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the attenuation coefficient of the tissue, in m⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the initial intensity remaining after the beam has travelled 12 cm through the tissue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the thickness of tissue that halves the intensity.

practice.stem: During a pregnancy scan in a Peshawar hospital, the probe is held so that the beam passes straight through the baby's head. Echoes from the near and far surfaces of the skull are received 61.0 µs and 173 µs after the pulse is emitted. Take the speed of ultrasound in all tissues to be 1540 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depth of the near surface of the skull below the probe.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the diameter of the baby's head along the beam.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption made in these calculations, apart from the speed being the same in all tissues.
parts.answer: The beam travels in a straight line perpendicular to both surfaces (the echoes come from the ends of a diameter).

practice.stem: The specific acoustic impedance of air is 430 kg m⁻² s⁻¹ and that of soft tissue is 1.63 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient at a boundary between soft tissue and air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the intensity transmitted across the boundary.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why ultrasound cannot produce useful images of structures behind the air-filled lungs.
parts.answer: Almost all of the ultrasound is reflected at the tissue–air boundary, so (almost) none reaches structures beyond it.

practice.stem: Ultrasound in soft tissue travels at 1540 m s⁻¹. The attenuation coefficient is 40 m⁻¹ at 3.5 MHz and 115 m⁻¹ at 10 MHz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength in soft tissue at each frequency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate, for each frequency, the fraction of intensity remaining after the ultrasound travels to an organ 6.0 cm deep and back, considering attenuation only.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why 10 MHz is used for imaging an eye or a tendon close to the skin but 3.5 MHz is used for imaging an organ deep in the abdomen.
parts.answer: Higher frequency → shorter wavelength → finer detail (better resolution) but much greater attenuation, so only usable for shallow structures; deep organs need lower frequency to give a detectable echo, accepting poorer resolution.
parts.working: B1: shorter wavelength resolves smaller details. B1: high frequency attenuated much more (echo ~10⁻⁶, undetectable from deep). B1: so trade-off: high f for shallow, low f for deep.

practice.stem: Ultrasound enters a fat layer from a transducer, then passes into muscle and is partly reflected at bone. Specific acoustic impedances: fat 1.34 × 10⁶, muscle 1.71 × 10⁶, bone 7.80 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the intensity reflection coefficients at the fat–muscle and muscle–bone boundaries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ignoring absorption, calculate the fraction of the intensity entering the fat that returns to the transducer as the echo from the muscle–bone boundary.
parts.working: C1: transmitted into muscle: 1 − 0.0147. C1: reflected at bone then transmitted back through the fat–muscle boundary: × 0.410 × (1 − 0.0147). A1: 0.398.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why structures lying behind a bone are difficult to image with ultrasound.
parts.answer: A large fraction of the ultrasound is reflected at the bone surface (and bone absorbs strongly), so little passes beyond it.
parts.working: B1: large reflection at the bone boundary — little intensity transmitted.

practice.stem: A coupling gel has specific acoustic impedance 1.50 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹. At the boundary between the gel and a tissue of greater acoustic impedance, the intensity reflection coefficient is measured to be 0.0025.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that (Z_T − Z_G)/(Z_T + Z_G) = 0.050, where Z_T and Z_G are the specific acoustic impedances of the tissue and the gel.
parts.working: B1: α = ((Z_T − Z_G)/(Z_T + Z_G))², square root = 0.050.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Z_T.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The speed of ultrasound in the tissue is 1560 m s⁻¹. Calculate the density of the tissue.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the fraction of the incident intensity transmitted into the tissue.

practice.stem: Ultrasound passes through 6.0 cm of soft tissue, of specific acoustic impedance 1.63 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹, to reach the surface of a kidney, of specific acoustic impedance 1.65 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹. The attenuation coefficient of soft tissue at the frequency used is 60 m⁻¹. Ignore reflection at the skin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient at the tissue–kidney boundary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the incident intensity (at the skin) that returns to the probe as the echo from this boundary.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the scanner amplifies echoes that arrive later more than those that arrive earlier.
parts.answer: Later echoes come from deeper boundaries and have been attenuated more, so extra amplification makes similar boundaries appear equally bright.

practice.stem: In soft tissue, the attenuation coefficient µ of ultrasound is approximately proportional to frequency f: µ = kf, where k = 11.5 m⁻¹ per MHz. An organ is 12 cm below the skin. For a useful image, the intensity lost by attenuation alone on the way to the organ and back must not reduce the intensity below 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ of its initial value. The speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the highest frequency that can be used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength in tissue at this frequency.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A 10 MHz probe gives sharper images. Explain why it is used for structures close to the skin, such as the thyroid, but not for this organ.
parts.answer: At 10 MHz µ = 115 m⁻¹, so the round-trip factor at 12 cm is e^(−27.6), far below 10⁻⁴; near the surface the path is short so attenuation is acceptable and the short wavelength gives better resolution.
parts.working: B1: attenuation too great at depth. B1: short path near surface + better resolution.

practice.stem: A transducer emits pulses each containing 3 complete cycles of ultrasound of frequency 5.0 MHz. The speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the duration of each pulse and its length in the tissue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two boundaries lie one behind the other along the beam. Their echoes can be distinguished only if the second echo starts after the first has finished. Calculate the smallest separation of the boundaries that can be distinguished.
parts.working: Extra path = 2d ≥ pulse length (M1); d ≥ 9.24 × 10⁻⁴/2 = 4.62 × 10⁻⁴ m (0.46 mm) (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two changes to the pulses that would allow closer boundaries to be distinguished.
parts.answer: Use a higher frequency; use fewer cycles per pulse (shorter pulses, more heavily damped transducer).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a tracer.
parts.answer: A radioactive substance (radionuclide attached to a compound) introduced into the body that is absorbed by tissue and whose emissions show where it has gone.
parts.working: B1: substance containing a radioactive nuclide that is absorbed by the tissue being studied.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens when a positron emitted by the tracer meets an electron.
parts.answer: They annihilate: the total mass of the positron and electron is converted into energy in the form of two gamma photons.
parts.working: B1: annihilation of particle and antiparticle. B1: all mass converted to energy of two γ-ray photons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how detecting the gamma photons allows an image of tracer concentration to be produced.
parts.answer: The two photons travel in opposite directions and are detected at the same time by detectors in a ring around the patient; the event lies on the line joining the two detectors; the difference in arrival times locates the point, and many such events build up an image.
parts.working: B1: photons detected simultaneously by detectors on opposite sides of the ring → event lies on the line between them. B1: arrival-time difference / many lines intersecting give the location; number of events shows concentration.

practice.stem: In a PET scanner, a positron and an electron, both effectively at rest, annihilate to produce two gamma photons. Mass of electron and of positron = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy of each gamma photon, in J and in MeV.
parts.working: C1: total energy 2m_ec², shared between two photons, so each has m_ec². A1: 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J. A1: 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴/1.60 × 10⁻¹³ = 0.512 MeV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of each gamma photon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using a conservation law, why the two gamma photons travel in opposite directions.
parts.answer: The total momentum before annihilation is (approximately) zero; momentum is conserved, so the two photons must have equal and opposite momenta.
parts.working: B1: initial momentum zero (particles at rest). B1: conservation of momentum → equal and opposite momenta → opposite directions (and equal energies).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The tracer contains fluorine-18, of half-life 110 minutes. Calculate the fraction of the fluorine-18 nuclei remaining 3.0 hours after the tracer is made.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a short half-life is chosen for a PET tracer.
parts.answer: The tracer's activity falls quickly after the scan, so the patient's total radiation dose is small.
parts.working: B1: small dose to patient / tracer does not stay active in the body for long.

practice.stem: The tracer used in many PET scans contains fluorine-18 (¹⁸₉F), which decays by β⁺ emission to an isotope of oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a nuclear equation for the decay.
parts.working: B1: ¹⁸₈O with correct numbers. B1: positron and (electron) neutrino.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a positron.
parts.answer: The antiparticle of the electron: same mass, charge +e.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the positron in a patient travels only a very short distance before it is annihilated.
parts.answer: Body tissue contains a very large number of electrons; the positron quickly slows down and meets one.

practice.stem: In a PET scanner, a positron and an electron, both effectively at rest, annihilate. Each gamma photon produced has energy 0.511 MeV. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of each photon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total energy released, in joules, when 5.0 × 10⁹ such annihilations occur.
parts.working: Each annihilation gives two photons, so 1.0 × 10¹⁰ photons (M1); energy = 1.0 × 10¹⁰ × 8.18 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 8.18 × 10⁻⁴ J (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two photons have equal energies.
parts.answer: The total momentum is zero, so the photons have equal and opposite momenta and therefore equal energies (E = pc).

practice.stem: A common PET tracer is fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), a form of glucose labelled with fluorine-18, of half-life 110 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why a tracer based on glucose is useful for finding cancer.
parts.answer: Tumour cells are very active and absorb more glucose than normal tissue, so the tracer concentrates there.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the half-life of the tracer should be (i) not too long, (ii) not too short.
parts.answer: (i) so the patient does not stay radioactive for long (lower dose); (ii) so enough activity remains after production, transport and uptake to give an image.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the gamma photons, rather than the positrons, are detected outside the body.
parts.answer: The positrons are annihilated within about a millimetre of the source; the gamma photons are penetrating and escape the body.

practice.stem: PET scans and CT scans are often carried out together in one machine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the information given by a PET scan and by a CT scan.
parts.answer: PET shows where the tracer collects, i.e. the function/metabolic activity of tissue; CT shows the structure (anatomy) from differences in X-ray attenuation (density).
parts.working: B1: PET → function/activity. B1: CT → structure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of combining the two scans.
parts.answer: Regions of high activity can be located precisely on the anatomy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why a β⁺ emitter is used for PET rather than an α emitter.
parts.answer: It produces gamma photons (via annihilation) that leave the body and can be detected; α particles would be absorbed in the body, causing damage, and could not be detected outside.

practice.stem: In a PET scanner, two detectors A and B lie directly opposite each other on the ring, 0.80 m apart. Two gamma photons from one annihilation event are detected; the photon at A arrives 0.60 ns before the photon at B. Speed of gamma photons = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance of the annihilation point from the centre of the line joining the detectors, and state which detector it is nearer to.
parts.answer: 9.00 cm from the centre, nearer detector A
parts.working: C1: if the event is a distance x from the centre, one photon travels x further than the other: path difference = 2x. C1: 2x = cΔt = 3.00 × 10⁸ × 0.60 × 10⁻⁹. A1: x = 9.00 cm, nearer A (which receives first).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why detectors on opposite sides of the ring record an event only if the two photons arrive within a few nanoseconds of each other.
parts.answer: Photons from the same annihilation arrive almost simultaneously; requiring coincidence rejects unrelated photons (from different events or scattered photons), so only genuine pairs define a line.
parts.working: B1: photons from one annihilation reach the detectors at nearly the same time (maximum difference ~ ring diameter/c). B1: rejects photons from separate events / scatter.

practice.stem: A patient is injected with a fluorine-18 glucose tracer of activity 370 MBq. The half-life of fluorine-18 is 110 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activity of the tracer 75 minutes after injection, when the scan begins.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of fluorine-18 nuclei in the dose at the time of injection.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the patient is asked to rest quietly between injection and scan when imaging glucose uptake in the brain.
parts.answer: Muscle activity would take up the glucose-based tracer, reducing the amount reaching the brain and adding unwanted signal from muscles.
parts.working: B1: active muscles absorb the tracer / tracer goes where glucose is used.

practice.stem: A positron is emitted with kinetic energy 0.25 MeV. Usually it slows to rest before annihilating, but suppose instead that it annihilates with a stationary electron while still moving with this kinetic energy. The rest energy of an electron and of a positron is 0.511 MeV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy of the gamma radiation produced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why, in this case, the two photons are not emitted exactly in opposite directions.
parts.answer: The positron has momentum before the annihilation; momentum is conserved, so the photons' momenta must add up to this non-zero value and cannot be exactly equal and opposite.
parts.working: B1: initial momentum not zero. B1: conservation of momentum → resultant photon momentum not zero.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how this affects the image.
parts.answer: The line joining the detected photons may not pass exactly through the point of annihilation, so the image is slightly blurred.

practice.stem: In a time-of-flight PET scanner, the difference in arrival times of the two photons at opposite detectors is used to locate the annihilation along the line joining them. The speed of the photons is 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that a point a distance x from the midpoint of the line gives a time difference Δt = 2x/c.
parts.answer: One photon travels (L/2 − x), the other (L/2 + x); path difference = 2x, so Δt = 2x/c.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the timing precision needed to locate the point to within 5.0 mm along the line.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A scanner has a timing precision of 400 ps. Calculate the uncertainty in position along the line and suggest how a sharp image is still produced.
parts.answer: 0.060 m; many lines of response through each point are combined (by computer) and the point is where they intersect.
parts.working: x = cΔt/2 = 0.060 m (A1). B1: many lines from different directions intersect.

practice.stem: A small tumour contains a fluorine-18 tracer with an activity of 2.0 MBq. Each decay produces a positron that annihilates to give two 0.511 MeV gamma photons. Take e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of gamma photons produced each second.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the power carried by the gamma radiation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Only 1.5% of the annihilations are recorded as a pair of photons. Calculate the number of pairs recorded per second.

practice.stem: Four positron emitters that can be used as PET tracers have these half-lives: carbon-11, 20.4 min; nitrogen-13, 10.0 min; oxygen-15, 2.04 min; fluorine-18, 110 min. A hospital without its own cyclotron receives tracers 60 minutes after they are made.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the original nuclei remaining after 60 minutes for carbon-11 and for fluorine-18.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fraction remaining for oxygen-15.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain which tracer is most practical for this hospital.
parts.answer: Fluorine-18: most of it remains after transport; oxygen-15 and nitrogen-13 decay almost completely, so they can only be used next to a cyclotron.

practice.stem: Detectors in a PET scanner measure the energy of each gamma photon and only accept photons with energies close to 0.511 MeV. A photon from an annihilation is scattered in the patient's body and reaches a detector with energy 0.340 MeV. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the scattered photon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why scattered photons are rejected by the detectors.
parts.answer: A scattered photon has changed direction, so the line joining the two detectors would not pass through the annihilation point; it is recognised by its energy being less than 0.511 MeV.
parts.working: B1: direction changed → wrong line of response. B1: identified by lower energy.

practice.stem: In a PET scan the positron and electron are at rest when they annihilate. Mass of electron = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; speed of light = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the momentum of each gamma photon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each decay produces one positron, which annihilates. Calculate the total power emitted as gamma radiation when the activity of the tracer in the body is 200 MBq.
parts.working: C1: energy per annihilation = 2m_ec² = 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J. C1: P = activity × energy per decay. A1: P = 200 × 10⁶ × 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ = 3.28 × 10⁻⁵ W.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is an advantage that gamma photons of this energy are produced, compared with lower-energy photons.
parts.answer: High-energy photons are very penetrating, so most leave the body without being absorbed; this gives a strong signal at the detectors and less energy deposited in the patient.
parts.working: B1: penetrating — most escape the body. B1: detectable signal / lower absorbed dose / less scattering.

practice.stem: A PET tracer uses fluorine-18, half-life 110 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The tracer is produced in a cyclotron and takes 2.5 hours to reach the hospital and be injected. Calculate the activity it must have when it leaves the cyclotron so that 370 MBq is available at injection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one problem with using a positron emitter with a half-life of only 2 minutes, and one problem with a half-life of 2 days.
parts.answer: 2 minutes: decays before it can be transported and absorbed by the tissue (needs a cyclotron on site); 2 days: remains active in the body long after the scan, giving the patient an unnecessary dose.
parts.working: B1: very short: too little activity left by the time of the scan / needs on-site production. B1: long: prolonged exposure / higher dose to patient (and others).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is meant by annihilation in terms of mass and energy.
parts.answer: A particle meets its antiparticle and their total mass (together with their kinetic energy) is converted into energy in the form of photons (two γ-ray photons).
parts.working: B1: particle and antiparticle; all mass converted to photon energy.

practice.stem: A patient is given a dose of fluorine-18 tracer with an activity of 400 MBq. The half-life of fluorine-18 is 110 minutes. Take 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and the mass of a fluorine-18 atom as 18 u.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the decay constant of fluorine-18 in s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of fluorine-18 nuclei in the dose and their mass.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of positrons emitted in the first hour after the dose is given.

practice.stem: The detectors of a PET scanner form a ring of diameter 0.85 m around the patient. Two photons are accepted as a pair from the same annihilation if they are detected within a short 'coincidence window' of each other. The speed of the photons is 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the greatest possible difference in arrival times for the two photons from one annihilation inside the ring.
parts.working: Largest path difference ≈ diameter = 0.85 m (M1); Δt = 0.85/3.00 × 10⁸ = 2.83 × 10⁻⁹ s (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the coincidence window should be a little longer than this, but not much longer.
parts.answer: Longer, so that no genuine pairs are missed (allowing for detector timing errors); not much longer, otherwise more photons from two different annihilations are wrongly paired (random coincidences).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a random coincidence produces an error in the image.
parts.answer: The line joining the two detectors does not pass through either annihilation point, so activity is recorded in the wrong place (background noise).

practice.stem: A PET detector ring has radius 0.40 m with its centre at the origin of x–y coordinates (in metres). Two annihilation events occur at the same point in the patient. The photons from the first event are detected by detectors at (−0.40, 0) and (0.40, 0); those from the second event are detected by detectors at (0, 0.40) and (0.20, −0.346).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the annihilation point lies on the straight line joining each pair of detectors.
parts.answer: The two photons travel in exactly opposite directions from the annihilation point, so the point lies on the line between the detectors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the coordinates of the point where the events occurred.
parts.working: First line: y = 0 (B1). Second line: x = 0.20t, y = 0.40 − 0.746t (M1); y = 0 at t = 0.536, x = 0.107 m (A1).
