parts.label: c
parts.text: For the first pair, calculate the difference in arrival times of the two photons.

practice.stem: A patient is injected with a fluorine-18 tracer of activity 350 MBq at 08:00. The scan runs from 09:00 to 09:20. The half-life of fluorine-18 is 110 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activity at 09:00.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of fluorine-18 nuclei that decay during the scan.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of gamma photons produced during the scan.

practice.stem: A 470 µF capacitor is connected to a 12.0 V d.c. supply until fully charged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define capacitance.
parts.answer: Charge stored per unit potential difference (C = Q/V).
parts.working: B1: ratio of charge (on one plate) to potential difference between the plates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge stored.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored.

practice.stem: Two capacitors have capacitances 2.0 µF and 6.0 µF.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the combined capacitance when the capacitors are connected in series.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the combined capacitance when they are connected in parallel.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When connected in series to a battery, state which capacitor has the larger potential difference across it, giving a reason.
parts.working: B1: capacitors in series carry the same charge; B1: V = Q/C so the smaller capacitance has the larger pd.

practice.stem: The flash unit in a camera uses a 150 µF capacitor charged to 330 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in the capacitor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The capacitor discharges through the flash tube in 1.0 ms. Calculate the average power delivered.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a capacitor, rather than the 1.5 V battery directly, is used to power the flash.
parts.answer: The capacitor can release its energy very quickly (very high power/current) at high pd; the battery cannot.
parts.working: B1: capacitor discharges rapidly, giving high power that a battery cannot deliver.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express the farad in terms of SI base units.
parts.working: M1: F = C V⁻¹ = A s/(J C⁻¹) = A² s²/J (or V = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹); A1: A² s⁴ kg⁻¹ m⁻².

parts.label: b
parts.text: A 2200 µF capacitor stores a charge of 0.0198 C. Calculate the potential difference across it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the combined capacitance C of capacitors C₁ and C₂ in series is given by 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂.
parts.answer: Same charge Q on each; V = V₁ + V₂; Q/C = Q/C₁ + Q/C₂; divide by Q.
parts.working: B1: charge on each capacitor is the same, Q; B1: total pd = sum of pds; B1: V = Q/C substitution and division by Q.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two practical uses of capacitors in electrical circuits.
parts.answer: e.g. smoothing a rectified supply; storing energy for a flash or back-up supply; timing circuits.
parts.working: B1 each for any two: smoothing; energy store (flash, back-up memory, defibrillator); timing (RC); blocking d.c.

practice.stem: A 33 µF capacitor in a motion-sensor circuit is charged by a 6.0 V supply until it is fully charged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge stored on the capacitor.
parts.working: Q = CV = 33 × 10⁻⁶ × 6.0 = 1.98 × 10⁻⁴ C. 1 mark for Q = CV, 1 mark for the value with unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in the capacitor.
parts.working: W = ½CV² = ½ × 33 × 10⁻⁶ × 6.0² = 5.94 × 10⁻⁴ J. 1 mark for the formula, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: Three identical 10 µF capacitors are available. They can be connected either all in parallel or all in series across a 6.0 V supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total capacitance when the three capacitors are in parallel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total capacitance when the three capacitors are in series.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored by each arrangement at 6.0 V, and state which arrangement stores more energy.
parts.answer: Parallel: 5.4 × 10⁻⁴ J; series: 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ J. The parallel arrangement stores more energy (nine times as much).
parts.working: Parallel: W = ½ × 30 × 10⁻⁶ × 6.0² = 5.4 × 10⁻⁴ J. Series: W = ½ × (10/3) × 10⁻⁶ × 6.0² = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ J. 1 mark each for the two energies; 1 mark for the parallel arrangement storing more (the larger total capacitance at the same pd).

practice.stem: A capacitor stores 2.4 mC of charge when the pd across its plates is 12 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define capacitance.
parts.answer: The charge stored per unit potential difference across the capacitor (C = Q/V).
parts.working: Capacitance is charge divided by pd; accept C = Q/V in words.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the capacitance.
parts.working: C = Q/V = 2.4 × 10⁻³ / 12 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ F. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored at this pd.
parts.working: W = ½QV = ½ × 2.4 × 10⁻³ × 12 = 0.0144 J. 1 mark for the formula, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A ceramic capacitor of capacitance 4700 pF is connected across a 12 V d.c. supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that 1 farad is equivalent to 1 A s V⁻¹.
parts.answer: C = Q/V and Q = It, so 1 F = 1 C / 1 V = 1 A s / 1 V = 1 A s V⁻¹.
parts.working: 1 mark for C = Q/V with Q = It; 1 mark for the substitution giving A s V⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge stored on the capacitor, in coulombs.
parts.working: Q = CV = 4700 × 10⁻¹² × 12 = 5.64 × 10⁻⁸ C. 1 mark for conversion of pF to F, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: Three capacitors of capacitance 100 µF, 220 µF and 470 µF are connected in parallel across a 9.0 V supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total capacitance of the combination.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total charge stored by the three capacitors.
parts.working: Q = CV = 790 × 10⁻⁶ × 9.0 = 7.11 × 10⁻³ C. 1 mark for using the total capacitance, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total energy stored by the combination.
parts.working: W = ½CV² = ½ × 790 × 10⁻⁶ × 9.0² = 0.0320 J. 1 mark for the formula, 1 mark for the value to 3 s.f.

practice.stem: A 3.0 µF capacitor is connected in series with a parallel combination of a 4.0 µF capacitor and a 2.0 µF capacitor. The network is connected to a 9.0 V battery and the capacitors are fully charged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total capacitance of the network.
parts.working: Parallel pair = 6.0 µF (M1); series with 3.0 µF: 1/C = 1/3 + 1/6 → 2.0 µF (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge on the 3.0 µF capacitor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the potential difference across the 4.0 µF capacitor and the charge on it.
parts.working: pd across 3.0 µF = 18/3.0 = 6.0 V (M1); pd across parallel pair = 9.0 − 6.0 = 3.0 V (A1); Q = 4.0 × 3.0 = 12 µC (A1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use a graph of potential difference V against charge Q for a capacitor to show that the energy stored is W = ½QV.
parts.answer: V ∝ Q gives a straight line through the origin; work done = area under the V–Q graph = ½QV.
parts.working: M1: work done adding small charge ΔQ at pd V is VΔQ, so energy = area under V–Q graph; A1: graph is a straight line through the origin, area of triangle = ½QV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A capacitor is charged to pd V by a battery of e.m.f. V through a resistor. Show that only half the energy supplied by the battery is stored in the capacitor, and state what happens to the rest.
parts.answer: Battery supplies QV (charge Q moved through e.m.f. V); capacitor stores ½QV; the other ½QV is dissipated as thermal energy in the resistance.
parts.working: B1: energy from battery = QV (constant e.m.f.); B1: stored = ½QV, so half; B1: rest dissipated as heat in the resistor/wires.

practice.stem: A solar garden light stores energy in a 50 F supercapacitor rated at 2.7 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored when the supercapacitor is fully charged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The lamp circuit works until the pd falls to 1.0 V. Calculate the energy available to the circuit.
parts.working: Energy at 1.0 V = ½ × 50 × 1.0² = 25 J (M1); available = 182 − 25 = 157 J (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The circuit takes a constant power of 0.50 W. Calculate how long it can run.

practice.stem:
As a capacitor is charged, the charge Q on it and the potential difference V across it are recorded:
Q / mC: 0, 1.5, 3.0, 4.5
V / V: 0, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the capacitance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the energy stored when the pd is 6.0 V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy transferred to the capacitor as its pd rises from 4.0 V to 6.0 V.

practice.stem: A capacitor stores 0.40 J of energy when the pd across it is 20 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capacitance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the pd needed for the capacitor to store 1.6 J.
parts.working: Energy ∝ V²: four times the energy needs twice the pd → 40 V (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the charge stored at this pd.

practice.stem: A 4.7 µF capacitor and a 10 µF capacitor are connected in series to a 15 V supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the combined capacitance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge on each capacitor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the pd across each capacitor.
parts.answer: 10.2 V across 4.7 µF; 4.80 V across 10 µF

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in the 4.7 µF capacitor.

practice.stem: Two identical 47 µF capacitors, X and Y, are used in a teaching experiment. X is charged to 6.0 V and Y is uncharged. The two capacitors are then connected in parallel, positive plate to positive plate and negative plate to negative plate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the final pd across the two capacitors.
parts.working: Charge is conserved: Q = 47 × 10⁻⁶ × 6.0 = 2.82 × 10⁻⁴ C shared between 94 µF, so V = 2.82 × 10⁻⁴ / 94 × 10⁻⁶ = 3.0 V. 1 mark for charge conservation, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in the two capacitors before and after they are connected together.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what fraction of the energy has been lost and suggest where it has gone.
parts.answer: One half (50%) is lost. It is transferred to thermal energy in the connecting wires (current through their resistance) and as a spark or sound when the connection is made.
parts.working: 1 mark for half (50%); 1 mark for thermal energy in the wires and/or a spark. Charge is conserved, so the loss is not a charge loss.

practice.stem: A 4.0 µF capacitor and an 8.0 µF capacitor are connected in series. This pair is connected in parallel with a 3.0 µF capacitor, and the whole combination is connected across a 10 V supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total capacitance of the combination.
parts.working: Series pair: 4.0 × 8.0 / (4.0 + 8.0) = 2.67 µF. Add the parallel 3.0 µF: 5.67 µF. 1 mark for the series pair, 1 mark for the total.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge drawn from the supply.
parts.working: Q = C_total × V = 5.67 × 10⁻⁶ × 10 = 5.67 × 10⁻⁵ C. 1 mark for Q = CV with the total capacitance, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in the 3.0 µF capacitor.
parts.working: The 3.0 µF capacitor is directly across the supply: W = ½ × 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 10² = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ J. 1 mark for the pd (10 V), 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A 2200 µF capacitor in a factory power-supply board is charged to 35 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in the capacitor when it is charged to 35 V.
parts.working: W = ½ × 2200 × 10⁻⁶ × 35² = 1.35 J (1.3475 J). 1 mark for the formula, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The capacitor then discharges until the pd falls to 12 V. Calculate the energy delivered during this discharge.
parts.working: Energy remaining at 12 V: ½ × 2200 × 10⁻⁶ × 12² = 0.158 J. Energy delivered = 1.3475 − 0.1584 = 1.19 J. 1 mark for the remaining energy, 1 mark for the difference.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Assume the energy delivered is used by a 0.25 W device at constant power. Calculate how long the device runs.
parts.working: t = E / P = 1.189 / 0.25 = 4.76 s. 1 mark for t = E/P, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A capacitor of capacitance 150 µF stores 0.36 J of energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the pd across the capacitor.
parts.working: W = ½CV², so V = √(2W/C) = √(2 × 0.36 / 150 × 10⁻⁶) = 69.3 V. 1 mark for rearranging, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge stored on the capacitor.
parts.working: Q = CV = 150 × 10⁻⁶ × 69.3 = 1.04 × 10⁻² C. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The pd across the capacitor is doubled. State the new energy stored.
parts.working: Energy is proportional to V², so doubling V multiplies the energy by 4: 4 × 0.36 = 1.44 J. 1 mark for the proportionality, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A 4.0 µF capacitor and a 12 µF capacitor are each charged separately to the same pd of 5.0 V. They are then disconnected from the supply and connected together in parallel, positive plate to positive plate and negative plate to negative plate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in each capacitor before they are connected together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total energy stored after the capacitors are connected in parallel.
parts.working: Total C = 16 µF at 5.0 V: W = ½ × 16 × 10⁻⁶ × 25 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ J. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the total energy is unchanged by the connection.
parts.answer: Both capacitors are already at the same pd, so no charge flows when they are connected; the energies simply add.
parts.working: 1 mark: no potential difference between the two, so no charge moves; 1 mark: the total energy is the sum of the separate energies.

practice.stem: A 20 µF capacitor is charged to 12 V and then disconnected from the supply. It is then connected across an uncharged 10 µF capacitor, positive plate to one plate and negative plate to the other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the final potential difference across the capacitors.
parts.working: Charge conserved: Q = 20 × 10⁻⁶ × 12 = 240 µC (M1); V = 240 µC/30 µF = 8.0 V (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total energy stored before and after the connection.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what has happened to the missing energy.
parts.answer: Dissipated as thermal energy in the connecting wires (and some as electromagnetic radiation) as charge flowed.
parts.working: B1: heating in resistance of wires (as current flows) / radiated.

practice.stem: A technician has a box of identical 100 µF capacitors, each with a maximum safe working voltage of 25 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe, without a diagram, an arrangement of the smallest number of these capacitors that has a total capacitance of 100 µF and can safely be used at 50 V. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: Four capacitors: two in series (50 µF, 50 V rating), and two such series pairs connected in parallel (100 µF).
parts.working: B1: two in series share 50 V, so 25 V each (safe); B1: series pair has capacitance 50 µF; B1: two pairs in parallel → 100 µF; B1: 4 is the minimum (one or two cannot give both 50 V rating and 100 µF; three in series give 33 µF). Also accept two parallel pairs (200 µF each) connected in series: 100 µF, 25 V across each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total energy stored by the arrangement at 50 V, and the energy stored in each capacitor.

practice.stem: A 1000 µF capacitor, initially uncharged, is charged by a constant current of 2.0 mA for 15 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the pd across the capacitor after 15 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored after 15 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate at which energy is being stored at t = 15 s, and explain why this rate is not constant.
parts.answer: 0.060 W; the pd rises steadily while the current is constant, so P = VI increases.
parts.working: P = VI = 30 × 2.0 × 10⁻³ = 0.060 W (A1); B1: V ∝ t so power ∝ t (energy ∝ t²).

practice.stem: A heart defibrillator uses a 32 µF capacitor charged to 5.0 kV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in the capacitor when fully charged.

parts.label: b
parts.text: During a pulse 300 J is delivered. Calculate the pd across the capacitor at the end of the pulse.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the fraction of the original charge still on the capacitor.

practice.stem: A 2.0 µF capacitor is connected in series with an unknown capacitor across a 24 V d.c. supply. The pd across the 2.0 µF capacitor is measured as 16 V. The capacitors were initially uncharged.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge stored on each capacitor.
parts.working: Series capacitors carry the same charge: Q = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 16 = 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ C. 1 mark for same charge in series, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the pd across the unknown capacitor and its capacitance.
parts.working: V_unknown = 24 − 16 = 8.0 V. C = Q/V = 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ / 8.0 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ F. 1 mark for the pd, 1 mark for the capacitance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in the unknown capacitor.
parts.working: W = ½ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 8.0² = 1.28 × 10⁻⁴ J. 1 mark for the formula with 8.0 V, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A capacitor of capacitance C₁ is charged to a pd V₀ and then disconnected from the supply. It is then connected in parallel with an uncharged capacitor of capacitance C₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the fraction of the initial energy lost is C₂ / (C₁ + C₂).
parts.answer: Initial energy = ½C₁V₀². Charge is conserved: C₁V₀ = (C₁ + C₂)V, so V = C₁V₀/(C₁ + C₂). Final energy = ½(C₁ + C₂)V² = ½C₁²V₀²/(C₁ + C₂). Fraction retained = C₁/(C₁ + C₂), so fraction lost = C₂/(C₁ + C₂).
parts.working: 1 mark for initial energy and charge conservation; 1 mark for the final pd and final energy; 1 mark for the fraction lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of energy lost when C₁ = 4.7 µF and C₂ = 10 µF.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain where the energy that is lost has gone.
parts.answer: Thermal energy in the connecting wires and any spark, as current flows through resistance during the sharing of charge.
parts.working: 1 mark for thermal energy (and/or sound/light from a spark).

practice.stem: A supercapacitor bank is made from four identical 2.5 F supercapacitors, each rated at 2.7 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total capacitance when the four capacitors are connected in series.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum pd across the series bank.
parts.working: Each capacitor may have 2.7 V, so the bank can have 4 × 2.7 = 10.8 V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored by the series bank at 10.8 V.
parts.working: W = ½ × 0.625 × 10.8² = 36.45 J. 1 mark for the formula, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Show that a parallel bank of the same four capacitors, charged to 2.7 V, stores the same energy.
parts.answer: Parallel: C = 4 × 2.5 = 10 F; W = ½ × 10 × 2.7² = 36.45 J. Generally: series gives ½(C/4)(4V)² = 2CV²; parallel gives ½(4C)V² = 2CV².
parts.working: 1 mark for C = 10 F and the energy; 1 mark for the general argument that both give 2CV².

practice.stem: A 10 µF capacitor is charged to a pd of 40 V. A 100 µF capacitor is then charged so that it stores the same energy as the 10 µF capacitor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in the 10 µF capacitor at 40 V.
parts.working: W = ½ × 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 40² = 8.0 × 10⁻³ J. 1 mark for the formula, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the pd across the 100 µF capacitor needed to store this same energy.
parts.working: V = √(2W/C) = √(2 × 8.0 × 10⁻³ / 100 × 10⁻⁶) = √160 = 12.6 V. 1 mark for rearranging, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the charge on each capacitor and state which capacitor has the larger charge.
parts.answer: 10 µF: 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ C; 100 µF: 1.26 × 10⁻³ C. The 100 µF capacitor has the larger charge.
parts.working: Q = CV: 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 40 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ C; 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 12.65 = 1.26 × 10⁻³ C. 1 mark for the charges, 1 mark for the comparison.

practice.stem: A student charges a capacitor from a 9.0 V d.c. supply through a switch. After charging is complete she measures the energy stored in the capacitor as 0.0195 J.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capacitance of the capacitor.
parts.working: W = ½CV², so C = 2W/V² = 2 × 0.0195 / 9.0² = 4.81 × 10⁻⁴ F. 1 mark for rearranging, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the energy supplied by the battery is equal to QV, and calculate its value.
parts.working: Energy supplied = QV. Since Q = CV, QV = CV² = 2 × (½CV²) = 2 × 0.0195 = 0.0390 J. 1 mark for the argument, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy dissipated during charging, and state where it is dissipated.
parts.answer: 0.0195 J, as thermal energy in the wires, switch and supply
parts.working: Energy dissipated = 0.0390 − 0.0195 = 0.0195 J, dissipated as thermal energy in the resistance of the circuit.

practice.stem: A 470 µF capacitor charged to 9.0 V is discharged through a 22 kΩ resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time constant of the circuit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the pd across the capacitor 5.0 s after the discharge starts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the time constant of a capacitor–resistor discharge circuit.
parts.answer: The time taken for the charge (or pd or current) to fall to 1/e (about 37%) of its initial value; equal to RC.
parts.working: B1: time for Q to fall to 1/e of initial value (accept τ = RC with symbols explained).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the product RC has the unit of seconds.
parts.answer: Ω × F = (V A⁻¹)(C V⁻¹) = C A⁻¹ = (A s) A⁻¹ = s.
parts.working: M1: Ω = V A⁻¹ and F = C V⁻¹; A1: C = A s so units reduce to s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the percentage of the initial charge remaining after a time equal to three time constants.

practice.stem: A charged capacitor is discharged through a resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the current in the resistor decreases with time.
parts.answer: As charge leaves the capacitor, the pd across it (V = Q/C) falls; the current I = V/R therefore falls.
parts.working: B1: charge decreases so pd decreases; B1: I = V/R decreases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the charge decreases exponentially rather than linearly.
parts.answer: The rate of loss of charge (current) is proportional to the charge remaining, so equal fractions are lost in equal times.
parts.working: B1: rate of discharge ∝ Q (since I = Q/RC); B1: constant fraction lost in equal time intervals → exponential.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the effect on the discharge time of increasing the resistance.
parts.working: B1: slower discharge, τ = RC larger.

practice.stem: A 1000 µF capacitor, charged to 6.0 V, is discharged through a 3.3 kΩ resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the initial current.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time constant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the current 6.6 s after the discharge begins.

practice.stem: A capacitor of capacitance 330 µF discharges through a 15 kΩ resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time constant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the initial charge remaining after 10 s.

practice.stem: A 680 µF capacitor charged to 9.0 V discharges through a 1.5 kΩ resistor. The discharge starts at t = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time constant of the circuit.
parts.working: τ = RC = 1500 × 680 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.02 s. 1 mark for τ = RC, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the initial current in the resistor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time after t = 0 at which the current has fallen to 1.0 mA.

practice.stem: A student is studying a capacitor–resistor discharge circuit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the product RC has the unit of seconds, using R = V/I and C = Q/V.
parts.answer: Resistance R = V/I has unit V A⁻¹. Capacitance C = Q/V has unit A s V⁻¹. RC has unit V A⁻¹ × A s V⁻¹ = s.
parts.working: 1 mark each for the units of R and C from the definitions; the product simplifies to s, so the unit of RC is seconds (1 mark for the combined step).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the fraction of the initial pd remaining after a time equal to 2 time constants, giving your answer as a percentage to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: e⁻² = 0.135, so 13.5% of the initial pd remains.
parts.working: V/V₀ = e^(−t/RC) = e^(−2) = 0.135 (1 mark for the equation, 1 mark for 13.5%).

practice.stem: The pd across a capacitor falls from 9.0 V to 4.5 V in 3.0 s as it discharges through a resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time constant of the circuit.
parts.working: Half the initial pd remains after t = τ ln 2, so τ = 3.0 / ln 2 = 4.33 s. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The capacitance is 2.0 mF. Calculate the resistance of the resistor.
parts.working: R = τ / C = 4.33 / (2.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.16 × 10³ Ω. 1 mark for R = τ/C, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A student wants to measure the time constant of a capacitor–resistor discharge circuit using a charged capacitor, a resistor, a voltmeter and a stopwatch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student can use these items to find the time constant.
parts.answer: Charge the capacitor to a known pd V₀ and start the stopwatch as the circuit is closed. Record the pd V at regular time intervals. Plot ln V against t; the graph is a straight line with gradient −1/RC, so τ = RC = −1/gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: charging to a known V₀ and starting the timer on closing the circuit; recording V at equal time intervals; plotting ln V against t (a straight line); gradient = −1/RC, so τ found from it; repeating readings to check.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the voltmeter must have a very high resistance.
parts.answer: A low-resistance voltmeter would take a significant current from the capacitor, so the capacitor would discharge through the meter and the readings would be wrong.
parts.working: 1 mark for the meter taking current from the capacitor; 1 mark for the effect on the readings (the discharge is changed, so τ is wrong).

practice.stem: A charged capacitor discharges through a resistor. At t = 0 the pd across it is V₀.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the time taken for the pd to fall to V₀/5 is t = RC ln 5.
parts.answer: V = V₀e^(−t/RC). Setting V = V₀/5 gives e^(−t/RC) = 1/5, so t = RC ln 5.
parts.working: 1 mark for V = V₀e^(−t/RC) with V = V₀/5; 1 mark for taking logarithms to get t = RC ln 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that the time constant RC is 0.80 s, calculate this time.

practice.stem: A 100 µF capacitor is charged to 12.0 V and then discharged through a 47 kΩ resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the initial discharge current.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge on the capacitor after 3.0 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the pd to halve.

practice.stem:
A capacitor discharges through a 50 kΩ resistor. The pd V across the capacitor is recorded at time t:
t = 0 s, V = 10.00 V
t = 10 s, V = 6.70 V
t = 20 s, V = 4.49 V
t = 30 s, V = 3.01 V
t = 40 s, V = 2.02 V

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that a graph of ln(V / V) against t should be a straight line, and state how the time constant can be found from it. (ln(V / V) means the natural log of the number of volts.)
parts.answer: ln V = ln V₀ − t/RC; gradient = −1/RC.
parts.working: M1: take logs of V = V₀e^(−t/RC); A1: straight line with gradient −1/RC (τ = −1/gradient).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate ln(V / V) for each reading.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the gradient of the line and hence the capacitance.

practice.stem: A 2200 µF capacitor is charged to 16 V and then discharged through a resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the initial energy stored.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that after one time constant the energy stored is e⁻² of its initial value.
parts.answer: V falls to V₀/e; W ∝ V², so W falls to W₀/e².
parts.working: M1: V = V₀e⁻¹ after t = RC; A1: W ∝ V² → factor e⁻².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored after one time constant.

practice.stem: A capacitor charged to 6.0 V discharges through a 1.2 kΩ resistor. The time constant of the circuit is 1.8 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the initial charge remaining after 2.5 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current at t = 2.5 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the capacitance.

practice.stem:
A student charges a capacitor to 8.0 V and lets it discharge through different resistors R. For each she times how long the pd takes to fall to 4.0 V (t½):
R = 10 kΩ, t½ = 7.0 s
R = 22 kΩ, t½ = 15.0 s
R = 33 kΩ, t½ = 23.1 s
R = 47 kΩ, t½ = 32.5 s
R = 68 kΩ, t½ = 47.3 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that t½ = (C ln 2) R.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A graph of t½ against R is a straight line through the origin with gradient 0.694 s kΩ⁻¹. Determine C.
parts.working: Gradient = C ln 2 (M1); C = 6.94 × 10⁻⁴ s Ω⁻¹/ln 2 = 0.00100 F (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The capacitor is labelled 1000 µF ± 20%. State whether the result is consistent with the label.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why timing with a stopwatch is less satisfactory for the smallest resistor, and an improvement.
parts.answer: The half-time is short (about 7 s), so reaction time is a large fraction of it; use a data logger with a voltage sensor, or use a larger capacitor/resistor.
parts.working: B1: short time → large % uncertainty from reaction time; B1: data logger / repeat and average / larger RC.

practice.stem: A capacitor of capacitance C discharges through a resistor of resistance R.

parts.label: a
parts.text: By applying Kirchhoff's second law to the circuit, show that dQ/dt = −Q/(RC), where Q is the charge on the capacitor.
parts.answer: Q/C = IR with I = −dQ/dt (charge decreasing), so dQ/dt = −Q/RC.
parts.working: M1: pd across C = pd across R: Q/C = IR; A1: I = −dQ/dt → result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the solution of this equation for a capacitor with initial charge Q₀.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For C = 680 µF and R = 4.7 kΩ, calculate the time for the charge to fall to 10% of Q₀.

practice.stem: A 4.7 mF capacitor is charged to 12 V and then discharges through a resistor R. The initial current in the resistor is 2.0 mA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance R.
parts.working: R = V₀/I₀ = 12 / (2.0 × 10⁻³) = 6000 Ω. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time constant of the circuit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the pd to fall to 3.0 V.
parts.working: V = V₀e^(−t/τ), so t = τ ln(V₀/V) = 28.2 × ln 4 = 39.1 s. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A capacitor with initial charge 1.5 mC discharges through a resistor. The time constant of the circuit is 4.0 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the charge that has flowed through the resistor in the first 2.0 s.
parts.working: Q(t) = Q₀e^(−t/τ) = 1.5 × 10⁻³ × e^(−0.5) = 9.10 × 10⁻⁴ C remains. Charge flowed = Q₀ − Q = 1.5 × 10⁻³ − 9.10 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.90 × 10⁻⁴ C. 1 mark for Q(t); 1 mark for the subtraction; 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the charge remaining on the capacitor after 2.0 s.

practice.stem: A capacitor of capacitance 470 µF is charged to 6.0 V and then discharges through a 2.2 kΩ resistor. Its pd V is given by V = V₀e^(−t/RC).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the gradient of the V–t graph at t = 0 is equal to −V₀/RC.
parts.answer: dV/dt = −(V₀/RC)e^(−t/RC). At t = 0 the exponential is 1, so dV/dt = −V₀/RC.
parts.working: 1 mark for differentiating to get −(V₀/RC)e^(−t/RC); 1 mark for setting t = 0 to get −V₀/RC.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate this gradient.
parts.working: RC = 2200 × 470 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.034 s; gradient = −6.0 / 1.034 = −5.80 V s⁻¹. 1 mark for RC, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A 150 µF capacitor charged to 14 V discharges through a 4.0 kΩ resistor. At t = 0 the energy stored in the capacitor is W₀.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the energy stored at time t is W = W₀e^(−2t/RC).
parts.answer: W = ½CV² with V = V₀e^(−t/RC), so W = ½CV₀²e^(−2t/RC) = W₀e^(−2t/RC).
parts.working: 1 mark for substituting V = V₀e^(−t/RC) into W = ½CV²; 1 mark for squaring the exponential to get W₀e^(−2t/RC).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in the capacitor at t = 0.30 s.
parts.working: W₀ = ½ × 150 × 10⁻⁶ × 14² = 0.0147 J; RC = 0.60 s, so 2t/RC = 1 and W = 0.0147 × e⁻¹ = 5.41 × 10⁻³ J. 1 mark for W₀ and the exponent; 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A 100 µF capacitor is charged and then discharges through a resistor. The charge on the capacitor falls to 1.0% of its initial value in 0.60 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time constant of the circuit.
parts.working: Q = Q₀e^(−t/τ), so 0.010 = e^(−0.60/τ), giving τ = 0.60 / ln 100 = 0.130 s. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the resistor.
parts.working: R = τ/C = 0.1303 / (100 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.30 × 10³ Ω. 1 mark for R = τ/C, 1 mark for the value.

practice.stem: A 1.5 mF capacitor charged to 9.0 V discharges through a 2.2 kΩ resistor, starting at t = 0.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time constant of the circuit.
parts.working: τ = RC = 2200 × 1.5 × 10⁻³ = 3.3 s. 1 mark for τ = RC, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the energy stored in the capacitor to fall to half of its value at t = 0.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this time is shorter than the time for the pd to fall to half of its initial value.
parts.answer: Energy is proportional to V², so it falls as e^(−2t/RC); the pd takes RC ln 2 = 2.29 s to halve, so the energy halves in half that time.
parts.working: B1: energy ∝ V², so the exponent is 2t/RC and the energy halves in half the pd half-life.

practice.stem: In a stairwell light timer, a 220 µF capacitor is charged to 6.0 V and then discharges through a resistor. The light switches off when the capacitor pd falls to 2.0 V. The delay required is 15 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the required resistance is given by R = t/(C ln(V₀/V)).
parts.answer: V = V₀e^(−t/RC) → ln(V₀/V) = t/RC → R = t/(C ln(V₀/V)).
parts.working: M1: take natural logs; A1: rearranged correctly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resistance needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Resistors are available in values of 47 kΩ, 56 kΩ, 68 kΩ and 82 kΩ. State which one gives a delay closest to 15 s and calculate that delay.
parts.working: Closest to 62.1 kΩ is 56 kΩ or 68 kΩ: delays 13.5 s and 16.4 s (M1); 68 kΩ gives the closer delay (A1).

practice.stem: A 0.47 F capacitor charged to 5.0 V keeps the clock memory of a digital radio working during a power cut. The memory circuit behaves like a 10 kΩ resistor and works until the pd falls to 2.0 V.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time constant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how long the memory is kept, in minutes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the stored energy that has been used when the memory fails.

practice.stem: To find an unknown capacitance, a student charges the capacitor and lets it discharge through a 100 kΩ resistor, timing how long the voltmeter reading across the capacitor takes to halve. The time is 6.9 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capacitance, assuming the voltmeter takes no current.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The voltmeter actually has a resistance of 10 MΩ and is connected across the capacitor. Calculate the corrected capacitance.
parts.working: Discharge resistance = 100 kΩ ∥ 10 MΩ = 99.0 kΩ (M1); C = 6.9/(99000 × ln 2) = 1.01 × 10⁻⁴ F (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on whether the voltmeter resistance matters in this experiment.
parts.answer: Only slightly: about a 1% difference, small compared with typical capacitor tolerances.
parts.working: B1: difference ≈ 1%, so negligible for most purposes (but would matter if R were comparable to the meter resistance).

practice.stem: A 470 µF capacitor charged to 12.0 V begins to discharge at t = 0 through a 10 kΩ resistor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the pd across the capacitor at t = 3.0 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At t = 3.0 s a switch opens so that a 20 kΩ resistor is added in series with the 10 kΩ resistor. Calculate the pd at t = 8.0 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the charge that has flowed through the 10 kΩ resistor between t = 0 and t = 8.0 s.

practice.stem: A 470 µF capacitor charged to 12 V discharges through a 6.0 kΩ resistor and a 3.0 kΩ resistor, which are connected in parallel with each other. This parallel pair is the only resistance in the circuit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the effective resistance of the parallel pair.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time constant of the circuit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for the pd to fall to 25% of its initial value.
parts.working: V = V₀/4 when e^(−t/τ) = 1/4, so t = τ ln 4 = 0.94 × 1.386 = 1.30 s. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the time is shorter than it would be with only the 6.0 kΩ resistor.
parts.answer: Adding the 3.0 kΩ resistor in parallel reduces the total resistance, so the time constant is smaller (with 6.0 kΩ alone, τ = 2.82 s and the time to reach 25% would be 3.91 s).
parts.working: 1 mark: lower total resistance gives a smaller τ, so the discharge is faster.

practice.stem: A 1000 µF capacitor is charged to 6.0 V. It is connected in parallel with a leakage resistor R, so that it slowly discharges even when no external load is connected. The pd falls to half its initial value in 10 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time constant of the circuit.
parts.working: V = V₀e^(−t/τ) with V = V₀/2 gives τ = t / ln 2 = 600 / 0.693 = 866 s. 1 mark for the method, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the leakage resistance R.
parts.working: R = τ/C = 866 / (1000 × 10⁻⁶) = 8.66 × 10⁵ Ω. 1 mark for R = τ/C, 1 mark for the value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a capacitor with a leakage resistance is unsuitable for storing energy over long periods.
parts.answer: It loses its charge (and stored energy) gradually even with no load connected, so it cannot hold its pd for a long time.
parts.working: 1 mark for stored charge leaking away continuously through the resistance.

practice.stem: A capacitor of capacitance C, charged to an initial pd V₀, discharges through a resistor of resistance R.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using energy conservation, why the total energy dissipated in the resistor during the discharge equals the energy stored in the capacitor at t = 0, and hence show that this energy is ½CV₀².
parts.answer: The capacitor ends with zero charge and zero pd, so all the energy stored at t = 0 must be transferred to the resistor. This energy is ½CV₀².
parts.working: 1 mark: all the stored energy is dissipated (the final state is uncharged, so energy is conserved); 1 mark: W = ½CV₀² from the energy stored at t = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy dissipated when C = 100 µF and V₀ = 20 V.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State at which instant the power dissipated in the resistor is greatest, and explain why.
parts.answer: At t = 0, because the pd is greatest then and P = V²/R.
parts.working: 1 mark: t = 0 with the reason that power is proportional to V² and V decreases.

practice.stem: A relay in a greenhouse humidity sensor is released when the pd across a 330 µF capacitor falls to 3.5 V. The capacitor is charged to 5.0 V at the start and discharges through a resistor R. The relay must release 12 s after the start.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that R = t / (C ln(V₀/V)), and calculate the value of R needed.
parts.working: 1 mark for taking logarithms to get t = RC ln(V₀/V); 1 mark for rearranging to R; 1 mark for the value (102 kΩ).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The available resistors are in the E12 series. Choose the nearest suitable value from 82 kΩ, 100 kΩ and 120 kΩ, and calculate the release time it gives.
parts.working: 100 kΩ is the closest to 102 kΩ. t = RC ln(V₀/V) = 33 × 0.357 = 11.8 s. 1 mark for the choice; 1 mark for the time.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: An electric kettle of power 2.2 kW contains 1.5 kg of water at 22 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define specific heat capacity.
parts.answer: The energy needed per unit mass to raise the temperature of a substance by one kelvin (1 °C).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to heat the water to 100 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the minimum time taken, assuming no energy is lost.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define specific latent heat of vaporisation.
parts.answer: The energy needed per unit mass to change a substance from liquid to vapour (gas) without any change of temperature.
parts.working: B1 energy per unit mass, liquid to gas; B1 at constant temperature

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to turn 0.25 kg of water at 100 °C into steam at 100 °C. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of molecules, why the temperature of a pure substance stays constant while it melts, even though energy is being supplied.
parts.answer: The energy supplied increases the potential energy of the molecules (breaking bonds / increasing separation), not their kinetic energy; temperature depends on the mean kinetic energy, so it stays constant.
parts.working: B1 energy increases potential energy of molecules; B1 mean kinetic energy (temperature) unchanged

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the specific latent heat of vaporisation of a substance is much greater than its specific latent heat of fusion.
parts.answer: On boiling the molecules are separated completely (to large distances), needing much more energy than the small increase in separation on melting; work is also done pushing back the atmosphere as the volume increases greatly.
parts.working: B1 much greater increase in separation / all bonds broken; B1 work done against atmosphere on expansion

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: Ice cubes of total mass 0.080 kg at 0 °C are taken from a freezer. The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to melt the ice and then warm the meltwater to 15 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why ice at 0 °C cools a drink more effectively than the same mass of water at 0 °C.
parts.answer: The ice must also absorb its latent heat of fusion while melting, taking much more energy from the drink.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to heat 80 kg of water in a geyser from 15 °C to 55 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time taken, in minutes, using a 2.0 kW electric element, assuming no energy loss.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define specific latent heat of fusion.
parts.answer: The energy needed per unit mass to change a substance from solid to liquid without a change of temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An ice-tray containing 0.50 kg of water at 0 °C is placed in a freezer. Calculate the energy that must be removed to freeze the water completely. The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The freezer removes energy from the water at a rate of 60 W. Calculate the time taken, in minutes.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to heat a 0.50 kg block of aluminium from 20 °C to 75 °C. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
parts.working: 1 mark for Q = mcΔθ with Δθ = 55 K; 1 mark for 2.5 × 10⁴ J (24 750 J).

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cup contains 0.30 kg of water that cools from 90 °C to 40 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate the energy given out by the water.
parts.working: 1 mark for mcΔθ with Δθ = 50 K; 1 mark for 6.3 × 10⁴ J.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why water, rather than oil, is used in the cooling system of a car engine. Use the specific heat capacities 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (water) and about 2000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (oil) in your answer.
parts.answer: Water has a higher specific heat capacity, so it absorbs more energy per kilogram for each kelvin rise in temperature, and so removes more heat from the engine for the same temperature rise.
parts.working: 1 mark for water having the higher specific heat capacity; 1 mark for more energy absorbed per kg per kelvin, so less mass or temperature rise is needed.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: A 1.00 kg aluminium block has an electric heater and a thermometer in holes drilled in it. The heater is connected to a 12.0 V supply and the current is 3.50 A. After 300 s the temperature has risen by 12.6 K.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy supplied by the heater.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium obtained from these results.
parts.working: C1 c = E/(mΔθ); A1 1000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: The accepted value is about 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Explain why the experimental value is larger, and suggest one improvement.
parts.answer: Some energy is lost to the surroundings, so less than the full energy raises the block's temperature; Δθ is too small and c too large. Improvement: insulate (lag) the block / start below room temperature and finish the same amount above.
parts.working: B1 heat loss gives smaller Δθ so larger c; B1 improvement

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: A 0.20 kg copper block at 95 °C is dropped into 0.30 kg of water at 20 °C in a polystyrene cup. The specific heat capacity of copper is 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the final temperature of the water, assuming no energy is lost to the surroundings or the cup.
parts.working: M1 energy lost by copper = energy gained by water; M1 0.20 × 385 × (95 − θ) = 0.30 × 4200 × (θ − 20); A1 θ = 24.3 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why, at the final temperature, there is no further net transfer of energy between the copper and the water.
parts.answer: They are at the same temperature, i.e. in thermal equilibrium.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: A rooftop solar water heater in Lahore has a collecting area of 2.4 m². At noon it receives 650 W of solar radiation per square metre, and 55 % of this is transferred to water flowing through the panel at a steady rate of 0.012 kg s⁻¹. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the useful power absorbed by the water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rise in temperature of the water as it passes through the panel.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain how the temperature rise would change if the flow rate were halved, with the same absorbed power.
parts.answer: It would double, because Δθ = P/((m/t)c) is inversely proportional to the mass flow rate.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: A 0.50 kg sample of a wax-like solid is heated by a 120 W heater; assume all the energy goes into the sample. Its temperature–time readings show: from t = 0 to t = 150 s the temperature rises steadily from 20 °C to 80 °C; from t = 150 s to t = 1050 s it stays at 80 °C; from t = 1050 s to t = 1150 s it rises steadily from 80 °C to 110 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the melting point of the substance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the specific heat capacity of the solid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the specific latent heat of fusion.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the specific heat capacity of the liquid.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy released when 5.0 g of steam at 100 °C condenses on the skin and the water then cools to 37 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy released by 5.0 g of boiling water cooling from 100 °C to 37 °C, and use your answers to explain why a steam scald is more serious.
parts.answer: 1320 J; steam releases about 9.5 times as much energy, mostly the latent heat of condensation.
parts.working: B1 value; B1 comparison referring to latent heat

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: A car engine's cooling system must remove waste energy at a rate of 25 kW. The coolant has a specific heat capacity of 3800 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and its temperature rises by 8.0 K as it passes through the engine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of coolant that must flow through the engine each second.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a liquid with a high specific heat capacity is chosen as the coolant.
parts.answer: It absorbs a large amount of energy for a small temperature rise (so a smaller flow rate is needed).

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: During one hour of a cricket match in hot weather in Multan, a fast bowler loses 0.80 kg of sweat, all of which evaporates from his skin. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water at skin temperature is 2.4 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy removed from the body by the evaporation of the sweat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of cooling.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of molecules, why evaporation cools the liquid that remains.
parts.answer: The molecules with the highest kinetic energies escape from the surface, so the mean kinetic energy of the remaining molecules falls, and temperature depends on mean kinetic energy.
parts.working: B1 most energetic molecules escape; B1 mean KE of the rest falls so temperature falls

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 0.20 kg block of ice is at −10 °C. The specific heat capacity of ice is 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and the specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. Calculate the energy needed to warm the ice to 0 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to melt the ice completely at 0 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence state the total energy needed to change the ice at −10 °C into water at 0 °C.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: Liquid nitrogen boils at a constant temperature. Its specific latent heat of vaporisation is 2.0 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. Calculate the mass of nitrogen that vaporises when it absorbs 4.8 × 10⁴ J of energy at its boiling point.
parts.working: 1 mark for m = Q/L; 1 mark for 0.24 kg.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: A heater of power 2.0 kW, with an efficiency of 90 %, is used to warm 1.2 kg of oil from 15 °C to 80 °C. The specific heat capacity of the oil is 2000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate the time taken.
parts.answer: Energy to warm the oil = 1.2 × 2000 × 65 = 1.56 × 10⁵ J; energy supplied = 1.56 × 10⁵/0.90 = 1.73 × 10⁵ J; t = 1.73 × 10⁵/2000 = 87 s
parts.working: 1 mark for Q = mcΔθ; 1 mark for dividing by the efficiency; 1 mark for using P = E/t; 1 mark for about 87 s (86.7 s).

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: A solid of mass 0.20 kg is at its melting point. A heater supplies energy at a constant rate of 50 W. The solid takes 120 s to melt completely, with no change in temperature. Calculate the specific latent heat of fusion of the solid.
parts.working: 1 mark for E = Pt; 1 mark for L = E/m; 1 mark for 3.0 × 10⁴ J kg⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After the solid has melted completely, the heater continues to supply energy at 50 W for a further 60 s and the liquid warms. Calculate the energy supplied in this 60 s.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: A liquid of mass 0.75 kg is heated electrically by a heater of power 12 W for 600 s. Its temperature rises from 20 °C to 28 °C. Assuming no energy is lost, calculate the specific heat capacity of the liquid.
parts.working: 1 mark for E = Pt; 1 mark for rearranging c = E/(mΔθ); 1 mark for 1200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the energy needed to vaporise 0.50 kg of water at 100 °C is about 1.1 MJ. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.
parts.working: 1 mark for Q = mL; 1 mark for 1.13 × 10⁶ J.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the energy needed to vaporise a given mass of water is much greater than the energy needed to warm the same mass by 1 °C.
parts.answer: Vaporisation requires energy to overcome the intermolecular forces completely, which is a large increase in potential energy; warming by 1 °C only raises the average kinetic energy slightly.
parts.working: 1 mark for overcoming intermolecular forces; 1 mark for the small kinetic energy change when warming.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: A liquid at its boiling point is evaporated by an immersed electric heater, in a flask that loses energy to the surroundings at a constant rate. With the heater at 50 W, 6.2 g of liquid evaporates in 300 s. With the heater at 80 W, 10.2 g evaporates in 300 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why two different heater powers are used.
parts.answer: The rate of energy loss is the same in both runs (same temperature), so subtracting the two results eliminates the energy lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the specific latent heat of vaporisation of the liquid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate of energy loss to the surroundings.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem:
In a continuous-flow experiment, a liquid flows steadily through a glass tube past an electric heating wire. The inlet temperature is 21.0 °C and the outlet temperature is 23.5 °C in both runs.
Run 1: p.d. 9.0 V, current 2.50 A, mass flow rate 2.0 × 10⁻³ kg s⁻¹.
Run 2: p.d. 12.0 V, current 3.18 A, mass flow rate 3.5 × 10⁻³ kg s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an equation relating the electrical power VI, the mass flow rate m/t, c, the temperature rise Δθ and the rate of energy loss h.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why keeping the inlet and outlet temperatures the same in both runs allows h to be eliminated.
parts.answer: The apparatus is at the same temperatures in both runs, so the rate of energy loss h is the same and cancels on subtraction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the specific heat capacity of the liquid.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate h.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: A can of cola, 0.33 kg, at 30 °C is to be cooled to 5 °C by adding ice cubes taken from a freezer at −10 °C. Treat the cola as water. Ignore energy exchange with the can and the surroundings. Specific heat capacity of ice = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy given out by the cola as it cools to 5 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy absorbed by 1.0 kg of ice warming from −10 °C to 0 °C, melting, and the meltwater warming to 5 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence calculate the mass of ice needed, in grams.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 25 m s⁻¹ on the M-2 motorway brakes to rest. Its steel brake discs have a total mass of 8.0 kg; the specific heat capacity of steel is 450 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rise in temperature of the discs, assuming all the kinetic energy of the car is transferred to them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the actual temperature rise is smaller.
parts.answer: Energy is transferred to the brake pads, tyres, road and air (and as sound); air resistance and rolling resistance also slow the car; the discs lose heat to the air while braking.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem:
A student investigates the melting of crushed ice at 0 °C by an immersed electric heater of power P. Meltwater drips from a funnel into a beaker; the mass m collected in t = 300 s is measured for each power. The ice also gains energy from the warm room at a constant rate.
P / W | m / g
20.0 | 21.7
30.0 | 30.4
40.0 | 39.7
50.0 | 48.4
60.0 | 57.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that P = L(m/t) − h, where h is the rate at which energy enters the ice from the surroundings. State the gradient and y-intercept of a graph of P against m/t.
parts.answer: Energy to melt per second = P + h = L(m/t), so P = L(m/t) − h; gradient = L, y-intercept = −h.
parts.working: B1 equation; B1 gradient L and intercept −h

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate m/t for each row, in mg s⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the first and last rows (or a best-fit line), determine L and h.
parts.answer: L ≈ 3.35 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹ (accept 3.1–3.6 × 10⁵); h ≈ 4.2 W (accept 2–6 W)
parts.working: M1 gradient using kg s⁻¹; A1 L; M1 intercept from y = mx + c; A1 h

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why it is better to obtain L from a graph of several readings than from a single reading with h ignored.
parts.answer: The graph separates the heat gained from the surroundings (intercept) from L (gradient), and averages out random errors.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat
practice.stem: A 2.0 kW kettle holds 1.2 kg of water at 20 °C. It takes 230 s for the water to reach 100 °C. The kettle is then left boiling for a further 3.0 minutes, during which the mass of water falls by 0.145 kg. Specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the energy supplied in the first 230 s that is used to heat the water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of energy loss from the kettle during the 3.0 min of boiling.
parts.working: M1 energy supplied = 2000 × 180 = 3.60 × 10⁵ J; M1 energy for vaporisation = 0.145 × 2.26 × 10⁶ = 3.28 × 10⁵ J; A1 loss rate = 179 W

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the percentage of energy wasted is greater during the first part of the heating than its rate of loss alone would suggest.
parts.answer: Energy is also needed to heat the kettle's own body and element, not just the water.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 0.15 kg metal block at 300 °C is dropped into 0.80 kg of water at 20 °C in an insulated container. The final common temperature is 24 °C. Assume no energy is lost to the container or the surroundings. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal.
parts.answer: Energy gained by water = 0.80 × 4200 × 4 = 13 440 J; energy lost by metal = 0.15 × c × (300 − 24) = 41.4c; so c = 13 440/41.4 = 325 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
parts.working: 1 mark for the energy gained by the water; 1 mark for the temperature drop of the metal (276 K); 1 mark for equating energies; 1 mark for 325 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

practice.subtopic: Specific heat capacity & specific latent heat

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electric heater of power 1.5 kW and efficiency 75 % heats 0.50 kg of water from 15 °C to 100 °C. The water then boils and 0.10 kg of it is evaporated at 100 °C. Calculate the total energy transferred to the water.
parts.working: 1 mark for the energy to warm the water; 1 mark for the energy to evaporate the water; 1 mark for the total 4.05 × 10⁵ J.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time for which the heater must operate to supply the energy in (a) (taking into account the efficiency).
parts.working: 1 mark for dividing by the efficiency; 1 mark for 360 s (about 6.0 min).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by two objects being in thermal equilibrium.
parts.answer: There is no net transfer of thermal energy between them when they are in thermal contact, because they are at the same temperature.
parts.working: B1 no net energy transfer; B1 same temperature

parts.label: b
parts.text: A metal spoon at 20 °C is placed in a cup of hot tea at 70 °C. State the direction of net thermal energy transfer and when it stops.
parts.answer: From the tea to the spoon; it stops when the spoon and tea reach the same temperature.
parts.working: B1 tea to spoon (hot to cold); B1 same temperature

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is meant by temperature, in terms of thermal energy transfer.
parts.answer: Temperature determines the direction of net thermal energy transfer: energy flows from a region of higher temperature to one of lower temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert a body temperature of 37.0 °C into kelvin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The temperature of a cup of tea falls by 25 °C. State the fall in temperature in kelvin, and explain.
parts.answer: 25 K; one kelvin is the same size interval as one degree Celsius.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K. Calculate this temperature in °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the thermodynamic (kelvin) scale is said not to depend on the property of any particular substance.
parts.answer: It is defined theoretically (from absolute zero and the triple point of water), whereas scales based on, for example, expansion of mercury or resistance of a wire depend on how that property varies, which differs between substances and need not be linear.
parts.working: B1 thermometric property scales depend on the substance / can disagree; B1 thermodynamic scale is absolute / theoretical

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by absolute zero.
parts.answer: The lowest possible temperature (0 K), at which a substance has minimum internal energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three physical properties that vary with temperature and can be used to measure temperature.
parts.answer: Any three: volume of a liquid (in a glass tube); resistance of a metal wire; resistance of a thermistor; e.m.f. of a thermocouple; pressure of a gas at constant volume.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features that make a physical property suitable for use in a thermometer.
parts.answer: Any two: it varies continuously (monotonically) with temperature; a measurable change for a small change in temperature (sensitive); it has a single value at each temperature; it varies over the required range; it is reproducible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert 25 °C into kelvin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert 40 °C below zero (−40 °C) into kelvin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Convert 300 K into degrees Celsius.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Object A is in thermal equilibrium with object C, and object B is also in thermal equilibrium with C. Explain what can be concluded about A and B if they are placed in thermal contact.
parts.answer: A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other: both are at the same temperature as C, so there is no net energy transfer between them.
parts.working: 1 mark for both at the same temperature as C; 1 mark for A and B therefore at the same temperature as each other; 1 mark for no net energy transfer when they are in contact.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student claims that the Celsius scale is absolute because its zero is at the freezing point of water. Explain why this claim is incorrect.
parts.answer: The zero of the Celsius scale is a chosen fixed point (the ice point of water), not the lowest possible temperature, so it is not absolute. The kelvin scale has its zero at absolute zero.
parts.working: 1 mark for the Celsius zero being an arbitrary fixed point rather than the lowest possible temperature; 1 mark for the kelvin zero being absolute zero.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the thermodynamic temperature of a gas at 100 °C to its thermodynamic temperature at 0 °C. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: 1 mark for converting both temperatures to kelvin; 1 mark for 1.37 (not 100/0, which is undefined).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the temperature of the ice point and of the steam point on the Celsius scale, and state the conditions for each.
parts.answer: Ice point: 0 °C, melting ice at standard atmospheric pressure. Steam point: 100 °C, boiling water at standard atmospheric pressure.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of the two fixed points with its value (0 °C and 100 °C) and the pressure condition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A furnace has a thermodynamic temperature of 1800 K. Calculate its temperature in degrees Celsius.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value of absolute zero in degrees Celsius.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why there is no temperature below 0 K on the thermodynamic scale.
parts.answer: 0 K (absolute zero) is the lowest temperature possible, at which the particles of a substance have their minimum possible energy; a lower temperature would require less than zero energy, which is not possible.
parts.working: 1 mark for 0 K being the lowest possible temperature (minimum energy); 1 mark for the impossibility of removing more energy than the minimum.

practice.stem: A platinum resistance thermometer has a resistance of 100.0 Ω at the ice point (0 °C) and 138.5 Ω at the steam point (100 °C). Placed in a warm oven, its resistance is 117.3 Ω.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature of the oven on the centigrade scale of this resistance thermometer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A mercury-in-glass thermometer placed beside it reads a slightly different value. Explain why, although both thermometers agree at 0 °C and 100 °C.
parts.answer: Each scale assumes its thermometric property varies linearly with temperature; resistance and mercury expansion do not vary in exactly the same (linear) way, so readings can differ between the fixed points.
parts.working: B1 scales assume linear variation; B1 properties vary differently / non-linearly

practice.stem: A thermocouple has its cold junction in melting ice at 0 °C. When its hot junction is at 100 °C the e.m.f. is 4.10 mV. The hot junction is then touched against the tip of a soldering iron in a repair shop, and the e.m.f. becomes 2.65 mV after the reading has settled (the tip has cooled while switched off).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assuming the e.m.f. varies linearly with temperature, calculate the temperature of the hot junction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages of a thermocouple over a liquid-in-glass thermometer for measuring the temperature of a small soldering-iron tip.
parts.answer: Any two: very small junction, so small heat capacity and does not cool the object; fast response; can measure the temperature at a point; wide range (high temperatures); electrical output can be recorded remotely.

practice.stem: In a constant-volume gas thermometer the pressure of the gas is proportional to its thermodynamic temperature. The pressure is 52.0 kPa at the triple point of water (273.16 K) and 71.5 kPa when the bulb is placed in a hot liquid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the thermodynamic temperature of the liquid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert this temperature to degrees Celsius.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says that heating air from 20 °C to 40 °C doubles its temperature. Explain why this is wrong.
parts.answer: Temperature ratios are only meaningful on the thermodynamic scale: 293 K to 313 K is an increase of only about 7 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the Celsius temperature at which the thermodynamic temperature of the air would be double its value at 20 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A platinum resistance thermometer has a resistance of 100.0 Ω at 0 °C and 138.5 Ω at 100 °C. Assume the resistance varies linearly with temperature. Calculate its resistance at 45 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark for the gradient 0.385 Ω °C⁻¹; 1 mark for 117.3 Ω.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The resistance of the thermometer in a furnace is 150 Ω. Calculate the temperature of the furnace.
parts.working: 1 mark for using θ = (R − R₀)/gradient; 1 mark for about 130 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A liquid-in-glass thermometer has a mercury column of length 2.0 cm at the ice point and 18.5 cm at the steam point. Calculate the temperature when the length of the column is 9.4 cm, stating any assumption made.
parts.answer: θ = (9.4 − 2.0)/(18.5 − 2.0) × 100 = 44.8 °C. Assumption: the length varies linearly with temperature and the bore is uniform.
parts.working: 1 mark for using the fixed points; 1 mark for the correct ratio × 100; 1 mark for 44.8 °C with the linearity assumption.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A thermocouple has its cold junction at 0 °C. Its e.m.f. is 0.30 mV when the hot junction is at 50 °C and 1.50 mV when the hot junction is at 250 °C. Assume the e.m.f. is proportional to the temperature. Calculate the sensitivity of the thermocouple in µV °C⁻¹.
parts.working: 1 mark for the gradient (1.50 − 0.30)/(250 − 50); 1 mark for 0.006 mV °C⁻¹ (6 µV °C⁻¹).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence calculate the temperature of the hot junction when the e.m.f. is 1.00 mV.
parts.working: 1 mark for using e.m.f. = sensitivity × θ; 1 mark for 167 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The resistance of a thermistor is 2.4 kΩ at 20 °C and 0.80 kΩ at 60 °C. A student estimates its resistance at 40 °C by assuming a linear relationship. State whether this estimate is likely to be accurate, giving a reason.
parts.answer: Linear estimate: 1.6 kΩ. It is unlikely to be accurate because the resistance of a thermistor varies non-linearly (exponentially) with temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark for the linear estimate 1.6 kΩ; 1 mark for the reason: thermistor resistance is non-linear with temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An oven operates at about 600 °C. Suggest which of a liquid-in-glass thermometer and a thermocouple is more suitable to measure its temperature, and explain your choice.
parts.answer: A thermocouple, because it can measure very high temperatures and responds quickly; mercury boils at about 357 °C, so a liquid-in-glass thermometer cannot be used at 600 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark for choosing the thermocouple; 1 mark for its much wider temperature range; 1 mark for the liquid boiling or the glass being damaged above the thermometer range (quicker response is also acceptable).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A thermometer is placed in a beaker of hot water and its reading rises slowly. Explain why the reading may be lower than the true temperature of the water until the thermometer and water reach thermal equilibrium.
parts.answer: Energy is needed to warm the thermometer and its liquid, so the thermometer lags behind the water; the reading only equals the water temperature when there is no net energy transfer between them.
parts.working: 1 mark for energy transferred to warm the thermometer first; 1 mark for the reading lagging behind; 1 mark for the reading equalling the water temperature only at thermal equilibrium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A platinum resistance thermometer is often more accurate and reproducible than a liquid-in-glass thermometer. Explain why.
parts.answer: The resistance of platinum changes smoothly and predictably with temperature, and the measurement is not affected by the non-uniform bore or the expansion of a liquid; it can be read with high precision by an electrical instrument.
parts.working: 1 mark for a predictable, smooth change of resistance with temperature; 1 mark for avoiding the liquid expansion and bore problems of a liquid-in-glass thermometer.

practice.stem: The resistance R of a platinum wire varies with Celsius temperature θ as R = R₀(1 + αθ + βθ²), where R₀ = 100.0 Ω, α = 3.9 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹ and β = −5.8 × 10⁻⁷ K⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the resistance of the wire at 100 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The resistance in a furnace is 150.0 Ω. Calculate the temperature given by a scale that assumes R varies linearly between 0 °C and 100 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the actual Celsius temperature of the furnace.
parts.working: M1 3.9 × 10⁻³θ − 5.8 × 10⁻⁷θ² = 0.500; M1 quadratic formula (smaller root); A1 130.7 °C

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the two values differ.
parts.answer: The resistance does not vary linearly with temperature (β ≠ 0), but the centigrade scale assumes it does.

practice.stem: A thermometer of heat capacity 12 J K⁻¹, initially at 22 °C, is placed in 25 g of water at 60 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature shown by the thermometer once thermal equilibrium is reached. Ignore energy exchange with the surroundings.
parts.working: M1 energy gained by thermometer = energy lost by water; M1 12(θ − 22) = 0.025 × 4200 × (60 − θ); A1 θ = 56.1 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the thermometer should be chosen to reduce this error.
parts.answer: Use a thermometer with a much smaller heat capacity (e.g. a thermocouple or small thermistor), or a much larger sample of water.

practice.stem:
A student calibrates an NTC thermistor for use as a thermometer. It is suggested that its resistance R is related to temperature by R = A e^(B/T), where A and B are constants. She records R at several Celsius temperatures θ using a water bath.
θ / °C | R / Ω
20.0 | 12340
35.0 | 6760
50.0 | 4030
65.0 | 2520
80.0 | 1590

parts.label: a
parts.text: A graph of ln R against 1/T is plotted, where T is the thermodynamic temperature. Express the gradient and y-intercept in terms of A and B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate 1/T (in 10⁻³ K⁻¹) and ln R for each row.
parts.working: B1 T = θ + 273.15 used; B1 ln R values to 2 or more d.p.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the first and last rows (or a best-fit line), determine B.
parts.working: M1 gradient using 1/T in K⁻¹; A1 B in range with unit K

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use your value of B and the reading at 50.0 °C to estimate the resistance at 0 °C.
parts.working: M1 R₀/R₅₀ = exp(B(1/273.15 − 1/323.15)); A1 answer consistent with B

parts.label: a
parts.text: A constant-volume gas thermometer has a pressure of 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa at the ice point (273.15 K). At an unknown temperature the pressure is 1.52 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate the thermodynamic temperature, assuming pressure is proportional to temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark for the proportional relation T ∝ p; 1 mark for 346.0 K.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence give the temperature in degrees Celsius.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wants to calibrate a thermistor so that its resistance can be used to find temperature. Describe an experiment to obtain a calibration graph of resistance against temperature. Include the apparatus, the measurements and how you would control the variables.
parts.answer: Place the thermistor in a water bath with a thermometer; heat or cool gradually and stir; at each temperature record the resistance (ohmmeter or voltmeter-ammeter) once the thermistor and water are in equilibrium; repeat over a suitable range and plot R against θ or T.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: a water bath with stirring; a thermometer next to the thermistor; measuring resistance with an ohmmeter or V and I; allowing thermal equilibrium before each reading; a range of temperatures; plotting R against T with a smooth curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mercury thermometer has a column length of 4.0 cm at 0 °C and 24.0 cm at 100 °C. When placed in a liquid, the column length is 14.5 cm. Calculate the temperature of the liquid, assuming a linear scale.
parts.working: 1 mark for using the two fixed points with the correct ratio; 1 mark for 52.5 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why the true temperature may differ from this value.
parts.answer: The thermometer may not have reached thermal equilibrium with the liquid, or the bore of the glass may not be uniform.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid reason (lag, non-uniform bore, a non-linear scale).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A thermocouple has a sensitivity of 40 µV °C⁻¹ and its cold junction is at 0 °C. Its e.m.f. is 3.2 mV when the hot junction is at 80 °C. Calculate the e.m.f. when the hot junction is at 200 °C and the cold junction is at 20 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark for using the sensitivity 40 µV °C⁻¹; 1 mark for ΔT = 180 °C (the difference between the junctions); 1 mark for 7.2 mV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two identical blocks of copper, each of mass 0.60 kg, are placed in thermal contact in an insulated container. One is at 80 °C and the other at 20 °C. Assuming no energy is lost, calculate the final common temperature.
parts.answer: The energy lost by the hot block equals the energy gained by the cold block: m c (80 − T) = m c (T − 20), so T = 50 °C
parts.working: 1 mark for equating the energy lost and gained; 1 mark for 50 °C (the masses and specific heat capacities cancel).
