practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the internal energy of a system.
parts.answer: The sum of a random distribution of kinetic and potential energies of the molecules in the system.
parts.working: B1 sum of kinetic and potential energies of molecules; B1 random distribution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the first law of thermodynamics, explaining the meaning of each symbol in ΔU = q + W.
parts.answer: The increase in internal energy ΔU of a system equals the thermal energy q supplied to the system plus the work W done on the system.
parts.working: B1 ΔU = increase in internal energy; B1 q = heating of system, W = work done on system.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the first law is related to the principle of conservation of energy.
parts.answer: It is a statement of conservation of energy: the energy of the system changes only by the energy transferred to it by heating and by work.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: A gas in a cylinder absorbs 500 J of thermal energy and, at the same time, does 200 J of work on its surroundings as it expands. Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the change in internal energy of the gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gas is ideal. State and explain what happens to its temperature.
parts.answer: It rises: for an ideal gas the internal energy is the total kinetic energy of the molecules, which is proportional to the thermodynamic temperature.
parts.working: B1 temperature increases; B1 internal energy of ideal gas is only random KE ∝ T.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: A gas is compressed at a constant pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa from a volume of 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³. Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the work done on the gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: During the compression 40 J of thermal energy is lost from the gas. Calculate the change in internal energy of the gas.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the internal energy of an ideal gas consists only of the kinetic energy of its molecules.
parts.answer: There are no intermolecular forces in an ideal gas (except during collisions), so the molecules have no potential energy; the internal energy is the random kinetic energy only.
parts.working: B1 no intermolecular forces; B1 so potential energy is zero.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a change in internal energy of an ideal gas is proportional to the change in its thermodynamic temperature.
parts.answer: Mean kinetic energy of a molecule = 3/2 kT, so the total kinetic energy of N molecules is 3/2 NkT; ΔU = 3/2 NkΔT ∝ ΔT.
parts.working: B1 mean KE ∝ T (= 3/2 kT); B1 U = N × mean KE so ΔU ∝ ΔT.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: A block of ice is melting in a glass of water at 0 °C on a summer afternoon in Lahore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what happens to the kinetic energy and to the potential energy of the molecules while the ice melts.
parts.answer: Kinetic energy stays the same (constant temperature); potential energy increases (bonds broken / molecules move further apart in the disordered liquid).
parts.working: B1 KE constant; B1 PE increases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in internal energy when 0.25 kg of ice melts at 0 °C. Assume the work done is negligible. (specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the internal energy increases even though the temperature does not.
parts.answer: Internal energy includes potential energy, and this increases during melting.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The air in a bicycle pump is compressed very quickly by pushing the handle in. Explain why q is approximately zero.
parts.answer: The compression happens so quickly that there is no time for significant thermal energy transfer to or from the surroundings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 18 J of work is done on the air during this compression. State the change in internal energy of the air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the pump feels warm afterwards.
parts.answer: The internal energy of the air increased, so its temperature rose; thermal energy then flows from the hot air to the pump barrel.
parts.working: B1 temperature of air rises; B1 heat transfer to the barrel.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.answer: (i) q +, W 0, ΔU +; (ii) q +, W −, ΔU 0; (iii) q 0, W +, ΔU +.
parts.working: 2 marks per process (all three signs correct 2 marks; two correct 1 mark): (i) volume constant so W = 0, ΔU = q > 0; (ii) T constant so ΔU = 0, gas does work so W < 0, hence q = −W > 0; (iii) q = 0, work done on gas W > 0, so ΔU > 0.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: A gas in a cylinder is heated with 150 J of thermal energy. It expands at a constant pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and its volume increases by 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the work done on the gas.
parts.working: Work done by gas = pΔV = 2.0 × 10⁵ × 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 60 J (M1); work done on gas W = −60 J (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in internal energy of the gas.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an isothermal change.
parts.answer: A change that takes place at constant temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An ideal gas is compressed isothermally and 250 J of work is done on it. Determine the thermal energy transferred, and state its direction.
parts.answer: 250 J transferred from the gas to the surroundings (q = −250 J)
parts.working: T constant, so ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas (M1); 0 = q + 250 (M1); q = −250 J, i.e. 250 J leaves the gas (A1).

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: 0.20 mol of an ideal monatomic gas is heated from 20 °C to 80 °C. The internal energy of n moles of an ideal monatomic gas is U = 3/2 nRT. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in internal energy of the gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gas is heated at constant volume. State the thermal energy supplied.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas in a cylinder absorbs 30 J of thermal energy from its surroundings while it expands and does 80 J of work on the surroundings. Convention: q is thermal energy supplied to the gas, W is work done on the gas, and ΔU = q + W. State the values of q and W for the gas, with signs.
parts.answer: q = +30 J; W = −80 J (work is done by the gas, so the work done on the gas is negative).
parts.working: 1 mark for q = +30 J; 1 mark for W = −80 J.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in internal energy of the gas and state what this tells you about its temperature (for an ideal gas).
parts.answer: ΔU = q + W = 30 − 80 = −50 J. The internal energy falls, so the temperature of the ideal gas decreases.
parts.working: 1 mark for ΔU = −50 J; 1 mark for temperature decreasing since internal energy of an ideal gas is proportional to T.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 0.40 kg block of ice at 0 °C freezes completely to form water at 0 °C with no change in volume of significance. The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. State the sign of q for the water and the sign of W, and justify each.
parts.answer: q is negative because thermal energy leaves the water during freezing; W is approximately zero because the volume change is negligible.
parts.working: 1 mark for q negative (energy released); 1 mark for W ≈ 0 (no significant volume change).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in internal energy of the water during freezing.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: Student A says: "When a gas is held at constant volume, no work is done, so its internal energy cannot change." Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: The statement is incorrect. At constant volume W = 0, so ΔU = q: supplying thermal energy (q > 0) still increases the internal energy.
parts.working: 1 mark for W = 0 at constant volume; 1 mark for ΔU = q so the internal energy does change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an ideal gas heated at constant volume gets hotter.
parts.answer: The increase in internal energy is the increase in the kinetic energy of the molecules, which for an ideal gas is proportional to T, so T increases.
parts.working: 1 mark for internal energy increase = kinetic energy increase; 1 mark for U ∝ T.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: For one mole of an ideal monatomic gas, U = (3/2)RT. Use this to show that the change in internal energy of n moles of an ideal monatomic gas is ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT.
parts.answer: U = (3/2)nRT for n moles, so ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in internal energy of 0.10 mol of an ideal monatomic gas when its temperature rises by 40 K. Take R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A paddle is turned by a falling mass of 5.0 kg that descends through a height of 2.0 m. The paddle stirs 0.50 kg of water in an insulated container; no thermal energy leaves the water. Explain why the work done on the water is equal to the increase in its internal energy.
parts.answer: No thermal energy enters or leaves, so q = 0 and ΔU = W. The work done on the water by the paddle equals the energy lost by the falling mass, mgh.
parts.working: 1 mark for q = 0 so ΔU = W; 1 mark for W = mgh.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in internal energy of the water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rise in temperature of the water. Take the specific heat capacity of water as 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fixed mass of ideal gas undergoes three processes. Using ΔU = q + W, complete the change in internal energy for each process. A: q = +120 J, W = −45 J. B: q = −60 J, W = +85 J. C: q = 0, W = −30 J.
parts.answer: A: ΔU = +75 J; B: ΔU = +25 J; C: ΔU = −30 J

parts.label: b
parts.text: State, for process C, whether the temperature of the ideal gas rises or falls, and explain why.
parts.answer: Falls: ΔU is negative, and for an ideal gas the internal energy is proportional to the temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark for falls; 1 mark for U ∝ T.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For process B, state whether the work is done on or by the gas and explain how the internal energy can still increase.
parts.answer: Work is done on the gas (W positive). The gas loses thermal energy, but the work done on it is greater, so the net change in internal energy is positive.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of atoms, why the internal energy of a solid increases when it is heated at constant volume.
parts.answer: The atoms vibrate about their fixed positions. Heating increases the average kinetic energy of the vibrations, and the mean separations and interatomic forces change so the average potential energy of the atoms also increases.
parts.working: 1 mark for increase in average kinetic energy of vibration; 1 mark for potential energy of atoms increasing; 1 mark for internal energy being the sum of both.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 0.30 kg mass of water cools from 60 °C to 40 °C. Calculate the change in internal energy of the water. Take c = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sign of the thermal energy transferred to the water during the cooling and explain why ΔU is negative.
parts.answer: Thermal energy is transferred from the water to its surroundings, so q is negative; with no work done, ΔU = q is negative.
parts.working: 1 mark for q negative; 1 mark for ΔU = q (no work done).

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A steel spoon of mass 50 g is heated from 20 °C to 150 °C. The specific heat capacity of steel is 490 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate the increase in internal energy of the spoon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the work done on the spoon during the heating and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Zero: the spoon is solid and its volume change is negligible, so W ≈ 0 and ΔU = q.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sample of 0.25 mol of an ideal monatomic gas is at 400 K. Calculate its internal energy. Take R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gas is heated to 500 K at constant volume. Calculate its internal energy at 500 K.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence state the thermal energy supplied to the gas in (b) and explain your answer.
parts.working: ΔU = 1558.1 − 1246.5 = 311.6 J ≈ 312 J; at constant volume no work is done, so q = ΔU ≈ 312 J.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: 1.0 kg of water at 100 °C is turned into steam at 100 °C at atmospheric pressure (1.01 × 10⁵ Pa). The volume changes from 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 1.67 m³. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the work done by the steam in pushing back the atmosphere.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in internal energy of the water as it becomes steam.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of molecules, why most of the latent heat increases the internal energy.
parts.answer: Most of the energy is used to separate the molecules (break intermolecular bonds), increasing their potential energy; only a small part does work against the atmosphere.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: 0.50 mol of an ideal monatomic gas is heated at a constant pressure of 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa from 300 K to 400 K. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; U = 3/2 nRT) Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the work done by the gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in internal energy of the gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the first law to calculate the thermal energy supplied.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: A fixed mass of gas is taken round a cycle A→B→C→D→A. A (1.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa); B (3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa); C (3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa); D (1.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa). Each stage is a straight line on a p–V graph. Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the work done on the gas in each of the four stages A→B, B→C, C→D and D→A.
parts.working: A→B expansion at 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa: W = −2.0 × 10⁵ × 2.0 × 10⁻³ = −400 J (B1); B→C and D→A constant volume, W = 0 (B1); C→D: +1.0 × 10⁵ × 2.0 × 10⁻³ = +200 J (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the total change in internal energy of the gas for one complete cycle.
parts.working: Returns to the same state, so ΔU = 0 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence determine the net thermal energy supplied to the gas in one cycle.
parts.working: 0 = q + (−400 + 200) (M1); q = +200 J (net heat in, equal to the area enclosed) (A1).

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: A gas expands from 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to 4.2 × 10⁻³ m³ against a constant atmospheric pressure of 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa while 520 J of thermal energy is supplied. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the work done on the gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in internal energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The gas is 0.15 mol of an ideal monatomic gas. Calculate its rise in temperature.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: 2.0 mol of an ideal monatomic gas is in a sealed rigid steel container. 1.5 kJ of thermal energy is supplied to it. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; U = 3/2 nRT) Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the work done on the gas and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Zero — the container is rigid, so the volume does not change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rise in temperature of the gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The initial temperature is 290 K. Calculate the ratio (final pressure ÷ initial pressure).
parts.working: p ∝ T at constant volume (M1); ratio = 350 ÷ 290 = 1.21 (A1).

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the kinetic model to explain why the temperature of a gas rises when a piston is pushed in quickly to compress it.
parts.answer: Molecules hitting the inward-moving piston rebound with a greater speed; so the mean kinetic energy of the molecules increases; mean KE ∝ T, so temperature rises.
parts.working: B1 molecules rebound faster from moving piston; B1 mean KE increases; B1 KE ∝ thermodynamic temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, using the first law, why the temperature rise is smaller if the piston is pushed in very slowly.
parts.answer: With a slow compression there is time for thermal energy to leave the gas (q negative), so ΔU = q + W is smaller than W.
parts.working: B1 heat lost to surroundings; B1 ΔU = W + q with q < 0, so smaller ΔU and ΔT.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: Gas is trapped in an insulated cylinder by a freely moving piston of area 4.0 × 10⁻³ m², so the gas pressure stays at 1.1 × 10⁵ Pa. A heater inside the cylinder carries a current of 2.0 A at 12 V for 30 s, and the piston moves out by 6.0 cm. Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the thermal energy supplied by the heater.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the work done on the gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the increase in internal energy of the gas.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one assumption made in (c).
parts.answer: No thermal energy is lost through the cylinder walls / all heater energy goes to the gas / friction at the piston negligible.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: A 0.50 kg copper block is heated from 25 °C to 65 °C. The specific heat capacity of copper is 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the thermal energy supplied.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the increase in internal energy of the block is almost exactly equal to this thermal energy.
parts.answer: A solid expands very little, so the work done against the atmosphere (pΔV) is negligible; W ≈ 0 so ΔU ≈ q.
parts.working: B1 very small volume change; B1 so W ≈ 0 and ΔU = q.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which form of molecular energy increases most significantly.
parts.answer: Kinetic energy of the vibrating atoms (and their potential energy also rises slightly).

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: An insulated container is divided into two halves by a thin partition. One half contains an ideal gas and the other half is a vacuum. The partition is suddenly removed and the gas fills the whole container. Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the values of q and W for this process, giving reasons.
parts.answer: q = 0 because the container is insulated; W = 0 because the gas expands into a vacuum and pushes against nothing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce what happens to the temperature of the gas.
parts.working: ΔU = q + W = 0 (M1); internal energy of ideal gas depends only on T, so T is unchanged (A1).

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: During an expansion, a gas does 350 J of work on its surroundings and its internal energy falls by 120 J. Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the values of ΔU and W for the gas, with correct signs.
parts.working: B1 ΔU negative (internal energy falls); B1 W = −350 J because the work is done by the gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate q and state whether thermal energy enters or leaves the gas.
parts.answer: 230 J — thermal energy enters the gas
parts.working: q = ΔU − W = −120 − (−350) (M1) = +230 J, so 230 J is supplied to the gas (A1).

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car of mass 900 kg travelling at 25 m s⁻¹ brakes to rest. Calculate its initial kinetic energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: About 60 % of this kinetic energy is transferred to the internal energy of a steel brake disc of mass 1.2 kg. Calculate the energy transferred to the disc.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rise in temperature of the disc. Take the specific heat capacity of steel as 490 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and assume no work is done on the disc.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fixed mass of 0.15 mol of an ideal monatomic gas expands at a constant pressure of 2.4 × 10⁵ Pa from a volume of 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³ to 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Calculate the work done on the gas. Include the sign.
parts.working: W = −pΔV = −2.4 × 10⁵ × (3.0 − 1.2) × 10⁻³ = -432 J. The gas does 432 J of work on the surroundings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in internal energy of the gas, using ΔU = (3/2)Δ(pV).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the thermal energy supplied to the gas during the expansion.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A heater of power 6.0 W is switched on for 2.0 minutes in a rigid sealed container holding 0.80 mol of ideal monatomic gas. State the work done on the gas and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Zero: the container is rigid, so the volume is constant and no work is done.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the thermal energy supplied by the heater.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rise in temperature of the gas.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 2.0 kg mass falls through 0.50 m and drives a piston that compresses a gas in an insulated cylinder. Assume no thermal energy is transferred to or from the gas. Calculate the work done on the gas.
parts.working: W = mgh = 2.0 × 9.81 × 0.50 = 9.81 J (positive, as work is done on the gas).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the value of q and hence the change in internal energy of the gas.
parts.working: No thermal energy transfer, so ΔU = q + W = W.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The gas is 0.50 mol of ideal monatomic gas. Calculate its rise in temperature.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: Water falls over a waterfall of height 35 m in a mountain valley. Assume that all the gravitational potential energy of the water is converted into internal energy of the water and that no thermal energy is lost. Calculate the gain in internal energy per kilogram of water.
parts.working: ΔU per kg = mgh/m = gh = 9.81 × 35 = 343 J kg⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rise in temperature of the water. Take c = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption made in part (b) and say whether it makes the answer an overestimate or an underestimate.
parts.answer: No thermal energy is transferred to the air or the rocks; this makes the calculated rise an overestimate.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electric heater of power 50 W is used to heat 0.40 kg of oil in an insulated container. The heater runs for 120 s and the temperature of the oil rises by 9.5 K. Calculate the thermal energy supplied.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence determine the specific heat capacity of the oil.
parts.answer: 1.58 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (≈ 1.6 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption made in part (b) and explain how it affects your value of c.
parts.answer: No thermal energy is lost to the surroundings (or the heater and container do not absorb energy). If energy is lost, the thermal energy reaching the oil is less than 6000 J, so c is overestimated.
parts.working: 1 mark for stating no heat loss; 1 mark for effect on c.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas undergoes two stages. Stage 1 is at constant pressure 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, expanding from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Stage 2 is at constant volume 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ in which the pressure falls to 5.0 × 10⁴ Pa. The gas is ideal and monatomic. Calculate the change in internal energy in stage 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the thermal energy supplied to the gas in stage 1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the overall change in internal energy and the overall thermal energy transferred for both stages together. Explain your result.
parts.answer: Overall ΔU = 0 J, because the initial and final states have the same pV (200 J), so the temperature is the same. Overall q = +500 − 300 = +200 J (stage 1: +500 J; stage 2: −300 J). The net work is −200 J, consistent with ΔU = q + W = 0.
parts.working: 1 mark for stage 2 ΔU = −300 J; 1 mark for overall ΔU = 0 (same T); 1 mark for overall q = +200 J.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two moles of an ideal monatomic gas are cooled at a constant pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa. The volume falls from 0.050 m³ to 0.030 m³. Calculate the work done on the gas, including its sign.
parts.working: W = −pΔV = −1.5 × 10⁵ × (0.030 − 0.050) = +3000 J (work is done on the gas).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in internal energy of the gas. (Hint: use the temperatures, from pV = nRT.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the thermal energy transferred to the gas and state whether it enters or leaves the gas.
parts.working: q = ΔU − W = −4500 − 3000 = -7500 J. The negative sign shows thermal energy leaves the gas.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 0.25 kg cup of coffee (assume the specific heat capacity of water) cools from 90 °C to 60 °C. Calculate the thermal energy lost by the coffee.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The coffee loses energy to its surroundings at an average rate of 5.0 W. Calculate the time taken for this cooling. Give your answer in minutes.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A lead bullet of mass 10 g travelling at 300 m s⁻¹ strikes a wooden block and comes to rest inside it. Calculate its kinetic energy just before impact.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume that half of this kinetic energy becomes internal energy of the bullet, and that the bullet does no work on itself. Calculate the energy transferred to the bullet.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rise in temperature of the bullet. Take c = 130 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ for lead.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: A gas is taken round a cycle. A→B: heated at constant volume, receiving 600 J of thermal energy. B→C: expands with no thermal energy transfer, doing 450 J of work on the surroundings. C→A: compressed at constant pressure back to A; 180 J of work is done on the gas. Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copy and complete a table giving q, W and ΔU (in J) for each stage A→B, B→C and C→A.
parts.working: B1 A→B row; B1 B→C row; B1 ΔU(C→A) = −150 J since total ΔU over cycle = 0; B1 q(C→A) = ΔU − W = −150 − 180 = −330 J.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net work done by the gas in one cycle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the efficiency of the cycle, defined as net work done by the gas ÷ thermal energy supplied.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: An ideal monatomic gas (U = 3/2 nRT = 3/2 pV) is at state A: pressure 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³, temperature 300 K. It is heated at constant volume to state B at 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa, then heated at constant pressure until its volume is 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ (state C). Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperatures at B and at C.
parts.working: A→B: constant V, T ∝ p, T_B = 3 × 300 = 900 K (B1); B→C: constant p, T ∝ V, T_C = 2 × 900 = 1800 K (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the increase in internal energy from A to B is 600 J.

parts.label: c
parts.text: For the change B→C, calculate the work done on the gas, the increase in internal energy and the thermal energy supplied.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: A 2.0 kW electric kettle is boiling water at 100 °C at atmospheric pressure (1.01 × 10⁵ Pa). Assume all the electrical energy is used to turn water into steam. Specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; density of steam at 100 °C = 0.598 kg m⁻³. Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water turned into steam each second.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of steam produced each second.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rate at which work is done by the steam against the atmosphere, ignoring the volume of the liquid water.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Hence calculate the rate of increase of internal energy of the water–steam system.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: 0.040 mol of an ideal monatomic gas is enclosed in a cylinder by a piston. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; U = 3/2 nRT) Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The gas is compressed quickly, with no thermal energy transfer, and 30 J of work is done on it. Calculate its rise in temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The piston is then held fixed and the gas cools back to its original temperature. State q, W and ΔU for this cooling.
parts.working: B1 W = 0 (no volume change) and ΔU = −30 J (back to original T); B1 q = −30 J.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Compare the final pressure with the initial pressure and explain.
parts.answer: Final pressure is higher: the temperature is the same but the volume is smaller, so p ∝ 1/V gives a larger pressure.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem:
An ideal gas is compressed slowly at constant temperature. Readings:
V / cm³: 100, 80, 60, 40
p / kPa: 100, 125, 166.7, 250
Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the trapezium rule to estimate the work done on the gas.
parts.working: Each strip ΔV = 20 × 10⁻⁶ m³ (C1); areas 2.250 J + 2.917 J + 4.167 J (M1); total = 9.33 J (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the change in internal energy of the gas and hence the thermal energy transferred.
parts.answer: ΔU = 0; q ≈ −9.33 J (thermal energy leaves the gas)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The exact work done is 9.16 J. Explain why the trapezium rule gives a larger value.
parts.answer: The p–V curve is concave upwards (curves below the straight chords), so the trapezia include area above the curve.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the internal energy of 1.0 mol of an ideal monatomic gas at 27 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean kinetic energy of one molecule of the gas at this temperature. (k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the Celsius temperature at which the internal energy of this gas would be doubled.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A real gas (e.g. steam) at the same temperature is allowed to expand at constant temperature. Explain why its internal energy increases although that of an ideal gas would not.
parts.answer: In a real gas there are attractive intermolecular forces, so molecules have (negative) potential energy; separating the molecules increases their potential energy, while the KE stays constant at constant T.
parts.working: B1 intermolecular forces / PE in real gas; B1 PE increases as separation increases, KE unchanged.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: 0.60 mol of an ideal monatomic gas is cooled at a constant pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa from 450 K to 300 K. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; U = 3/2 nRT) Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the work done on the gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in internal energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the thermal energy transferred and state its direction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the thermal energy removed is greater in magnitude than the decrease in internal energy.
parts.answer: Work is being done on the gas as it contracts, which adds energy; so more thermal energy must be removed than the fall in U.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem:
A student supplies energy Q from an electric heater to a gas held at constant pressure by a free piston, and measures the increase in volume ΔV.
Q / J: 30, 60, 90, 120, 150
ΔV / cm³: 98, 203, 297, 404, 499
Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the first law to show that, for an ideal monatomic gas heated at constant pressure p, Q = 5/2 pΔV.
parts.answer: ΔU = 3/2 nRΔT = 3/2 pΔV; W = −pΔV; Q = ΔU − W = 3/2 pΔV + pΔV = 5/2 pΔV.
parts.working: M1 ΔU = 3/2 pΔV and W = −pΔV; A1 combination.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the quantity that should be plotted against ΔV to give a straight line, and the expression for the gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the first and last readings to determine the gradient, in J m⁻³.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Hence determine the pressure of the gas.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the measured Q is likely to be larger than 5/2 pΔV in a real experiment.
parts.answer: Some of the heater energy is lost to the cylinder walls and surroundings (or heats the heater/cylinder) rather than the gas.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: A current of 0.20 A passes through a 47 Ω resistor. Electrical work done on the resistor counts as work done on the system. Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electrical work done on the resistor in 60 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Once the resistor has reached a steady temperature, state the change in its internal energy in 60 s and hence the thermal energy transferred.
parts.answer: ΔU = 0; q = −113 J (all transferred to the surroundings)
parts.working: Constant temperature so ΔU = 0 (B1); q = −W = −112.8 J ≈ −113 J (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: During the first 60 s after switching on, the resistor loses 30 J of thermal energy to the air. Calculate the increase in its internal energy.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics
practice.stem: Use the first law of thermodynamics in the form ΔU = q + W, where q is the thermal energy transferred to the system and W is the work done on the system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two identical samples of an ideal gas start in the same state. Sample X expands isothermally and sample Y expands with no thermal energy transfer (adiabatically), both to the same final volume. Use the first law to explain which sample ends at the lower temperature and which ends at the lower pressure.
parts.answer: Y ends at the lower temperature and the lower pressure. X: ΔU = 0, the work done by the gas is replaced by heat input, so T constant. Y: q = 0 and W is negative, so ΔU < 0 and T falls. At the same volume, p ∝ T, so Y has the lower pressure.
parts.working: B1 X: ΔU = 0 so q = −W (heat in balances work out); B1 Y: q = 0, W < 0 so ΔU < 0; B1 Y cooler; B1 same V so lower T means lower p (pV = nRT).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which sample does more work on its surroundings, and explain using a p–V graph described in words.
parts.answer: X: its pressure is higher at every volume during the expansion, so the area under its p–V curve is larger.
parts.working: B1 X; B1 its curve lies above Y's curve, so greater area = greater work.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas expands along a straight line on a p–V graph from (1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³) to (3.0 × 10⁵ Pa, 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³). Calculate the work done by the gas, using the area under the line.
parts.answer: 400 J done by the gas (W = -400 J on gas)
parts.working: Area under line = average pressure × ΔV = (2.0 × 10⁵)(2.0 × 10⁻³) = 400 J. This is work done by the gas, so W = −400 J.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in internal energy of the gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the thermal energy transferred to the gas during the expansion.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fixed mass of ideal monatomic gas is taken round the cycle A → B → C → A. State A: 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³. B: 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³. C: 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³. A → B and C → A: straight lines. Process A → B is at constant pressure; B → C is a straight line on the p–V graph; C → A is at constant volume. Calculate the work done on the gas in each stage.
parts.working: A→B: W = −pΔV = −1.0 × 10⁵ × 2.0 × 10⁻³ = −200 J. B→C: average p = 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa, ΔV = −2.0 × 10⁻³ m³, so W = +300 J. C→A: no change in volume, W = 0.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the net work done on the gas in one complete cycle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the change in internal energy of the gas over one complete cycle, and hence calculate the net thermal energy transferred to the gas.
parts.answer: ΔU = 0 because the gas returns to its initial state (same temperature). Net q = ΔU − W = 0 − 100 = −100 J; thermal energy of 100 J leaves the gas over the cycle.
parts.working: 1 mark for ΔU = 0 (state function); 1 mark for net q = ΔU − W; 1 mark for −100 J.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: An ideal monatomic gas (0.20 mol) is expanded adiabatically, so that there is no thermal energy transfer, and its temperature falls from 300 K to 250 K. State the value of q and explain what it means for the work done.
parts.answer: q = 0, so ΔU = W. Because the internal energy falls, W is negative: the gas does work on its surroundings.
parts.working: 1 mark for q = 0; 1 mark for W = ΔU (negative) so the gas does work.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the work done on the gas during this expansion.
parts.answer: -125 J (the gas does 125 J of work)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, using the kinetic model, why the temperature falls when the gas does work on its surroundings.
parts.answer: The gas molecules lose kinetic energy when they collide with and push the moving piston (which gains kinetic energy), so the average kinetic energy and hence the temperature fall.
parts.working: 1 mark for molecules losing kinetic energy; 1 mark for temperature ∝ average kinetic energy.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the kinetic model to show that the internal energy of N monatomic molecules of an ideal gas at temperature T is U = (3/2)NkT, where k is the Boltzmann constant.
parts.answer: The mean kinetic energy of one molecule is (3/2)kT, so the total internal energy (kinetic energy only, for an ideal gas) is N × (3/2)kT = (3/2)NkT.
parts.working: 1 mark for mean KE per molecule (3/2)kT; 1 mark for multiplying by N.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gas contains 3.0 × 10²³ molecules at 350 K. Calculate its internal energy. Take k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. Show that this equals (3/2)nRT with n = N/N_A, N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the increase in internal energy when the temperature rises to 400 K.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A container holds 0.30 mol of argon and 0.20 mol of helium, both behaving as ideal monatomic gases, at 310 K. State one assumption about the gas molecules that you need to make.
parts.answer: The molecules are point masses with no intermolecular forces, so their internal energy is all kinetic energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the internal energy of the mixture depends only on the total amount of gas and its temperature, not on the type of gas.
parts.answer: For each monatomic ideal gas, U = (3/2)nRT and the mean kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2)kT, which is the same for all gases at a given T. The total U is therefore (3/2)(n_total)RT, with no dependence on molar mass.
parts.working: 1 mark for mean kinetic energy depends only on T; 1 mark for total depends on n total only.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total internal energy of the mixture.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A balloon containing an ideal monatomic gas at 290 K expands at a constant atmospheric pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa from 2.0 m³ to 2.6 m³ as it absorbs 150 kJ of thermal energy from sunlight. Calculate the work done by the gas.
parts.working: W done by gas = pΔV = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 0.6 = 60000 J = 60 kJ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the change in internal energy of the gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The gas contains n mol, where n = pV/RT at the start. Calculate n and the rise in temperature of the gas.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the molar heat capacities at constant pressure C_p and at constant volume C_v of an ideal gas satisfy C_p = C_v + R. Use the first law with q = C_pΔT at constant pressure, the change in internal energy ΔU = C_vΔT, and W = −pΔV = −RΔT for one mole.
parts.answer: At constant p: q = ΔU − W = C_vΔT + pΔV = C_vΔT + RΔT, so C_p = C_v + R.
parts.working: 1 mark for q = ΔU − W at constant pressure; 1 mark for pΔV = RΔT for one mole; 1 mark for C_p = C_v + R.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For a monatomic ideal gas, C_v = (3/2)R. Calculate C_v and C_p in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
parts.answer: C_v ≈ 12.47 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; C_p ≈ 20.78 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the ratio C_p/C_v.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sample of 0.50 mol of an ideal monatomic gas must have its internal energy increased by 500 J. Calculate the temperature rise needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gas is heated at constant volume to achieve this change. State the thermal energy supplied.
parts.working: At constant volume W = 0, so q = ΔU = 500 J.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Instead, the gas is heated at constant pressure through the same temperature rise. Calculate the thermal energy supplied, and explain the difference from (b).
parts.working: q = 2.5nRΔT = 2.5 × 0.50 × 8.31 × 80.2 = 833 J. The extra 333 J is the work done by the gas (pΔV) as it expands against the constant pressure. 1 mark for q = ΔU + pΔV = 2.5nRΔT; 1 mark for 833 J; 1 mark for the extra energy as work done by the gas.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A heater of power 250 W runs for 90 s. Only 80 % of the energy reaches a gas of 20 mol of monatomic ideal gas held by a piston at constant pressure 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Calculate the thermal energy supplied to the gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The piston moves so that the volume of the gas increases by 0.040 m³. Calculate the work done by the gas.
parts.working: W done by gas = pΔV = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 0.040 = 4000 J.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rise in temperature of the gas. Take R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

practice.subtopic: Internal energy & first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rigid sealed container holds 0.40 mol of ideal monatomic gas at 290 K. Show that doubling the pressure at constant volume doubles the absolute temperature.
parts.answer: pV = nRT with V and n constant gives p ∝ T, so p₂/p₁ = 2 means T₂ = 2T₁ = 580 K.
parts.working: 1 mark for p ∝ T at constant V and n; 1 mark for T₂ = 580 K.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the increase in internal energy of the gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the values of q and W for this change, with their signs, and justify them.
parts.working: At constant volume no work is done, so W = 0 and q = ΔU; thermal energy must be supplied, so q is positive.
