practice.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg travels around a flat roundabout in Islamabad at a constant speed of 12 m s⁻¹ along a circular path of radius 25 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the centripetal acceleration of the car.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the resultant force on the car and state its direction.
parts.answer: 6910 N towards the centre of the roundabout
parts.working: F = ma = 1200 × 5.76 = 6910 N (A1); towards the centre (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what provides this force.
parts.answer: Friction between the tyres and the road
parts.working: B1: (sideways) friction of road on tyres.

practice.stem: A ball on a string moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle on a smooth horizontal table, the other end of the string being fixed to a peg at the centre.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the ball is accelerating even though its speed is constant.
parts.answer: Its direction of motion (velocity) changes continuously; acceleration is rate of change of velocity.
parts.working: B1: velocity is a vector / direction changes; B1: change in velocity means acceleration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction of the resultant force on the ball and explain why this force does no work on the ball.
parts.answer: Towards the centre of the circle; it is always perpendicular to the velocity, so there is no displacement in the direction of the force.
parts.working: B1: towards centre; B1: force perpendicular to motion → no work done, so kinetic energy (speed) constant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The string breaks. Describe the subsequent path of the ball, as seen from above.
parts.answer: A straight line along the tangent to the circle at the point of release.
parts.working: B1: tangential straight line (no resultant horizontal force).

practice.stem: A ball of mass 0.25 kg is whirled in a vertical circle on a light string of length 0.80 m. At the top of the circle its speed is 4.0 m s⁻¹. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the tension in the string when the ball is at the top of the circle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum speed at the top for the string to remain taut.

practice.stem: The drum of a washing machine has radius 0.25 m and spins at 1200 revolutions per minute during the spin cycle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the drum in rad s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the centripetal force needed to keep a 0.10 kg piece of wet cloth moving with the drum wall.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why water leaves the clothes through the holes in the drum wall.
parts.answer: The drum wall pushes the clothes towards the centre, but where there is a hole there is no force on the water, so it continues in a straight line (tangentially) out through the hole.
parts.working: B1: water needs a centripetal force to stay in the circle; B1: at the holes no force acts on it, so it moves off along a tangent.

practice.stem: An athlete swings a hammer of mass 7.26 kg on a wire so that it moves in a circle of radius 1.9 m. Just before release the speed of the hammer is 25 m s⁻¹. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the tension in the wire just before release. Assume the hammer moves in a horizontal circle and ignore its weight.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the centripetal acceleration of the hammer and compare it with g.
parts.working: a = v²/r = 329 m s⁻² (A1); ratio a/g ≈ 34 (A1).

practice.stem: The Moon moves around the Earth in an approximately circular orbit of radius 3.84 × 10⁸ m with a period of 27.3 days. The mass of the Moon is 7.35 × 10²² kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Moon is accelerating even though its speed is constant.
parts.answer: Its velocity is continually changing because its direction of motion changes; a change in velocity is an acceleration (directed towards the centre).
parts.working: B1 direction changes so velocity changes; B1 acceleration = rate of change of velocity, towards the Earth

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the centripetal acceleration of the Moon.
parts.working: C1 ω = 2π/T with T = 2.36 × 10⁶ s; M1 a = rω²; A1 2.72 × 10⁻³ m s⁻²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the centripetal force on the Moon.

practice.stem: In a simple model of the hydrogen atom, the electron moves in a circle of radius 5.29 × 10⁻¹¹ m around the proton at a speed of 2.19 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. Mass of electron = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the centripetal acceleration of the electron.
parts.working: C1 a = v²/r; A1 9.07 × 10²² m s⁻²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the centripetal force on the electron and state what provides it.
parts.answer: 8.26 × 10⁻⁸ N; the electric attraction of the proton

practice.stem: A cyclist and bicycle, of total mass 85 kg, ride round a flat (unbanked) circular track of radius 20 m at a constant speed of 9.0 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the centripetal force needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what provides this force.
parts.answer: Friction between the tyres and the track (acting towards the centre).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The cyclist doubles her speed on the same circle. State the factor by which the required force changes.

practice.stem: A car of mass 1300 kg goes round a flat bend of radius 45 m on a wet road. The largest sideways friction force that the road can provide is 6.5 kN.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the greatest speed at which the car can go round the bend without skidding.
parts.working: M1 friction provides centripetal force: 6500 = 1300v²/45; A1 v² = 225; A1 v = 15 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the path of the car if it goes faster than this speed.
parts.answer: It moves along a curve of larger radius, sliding outwards towards the outside of the bend (not radially outwards).

practice.stem: A car of mass 1100 kg drives at a constant speed of 20 m s⁻¹ through a dip in a road. At the bottom of the dip the road is part of a vertical circle of radius 40 m. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the normal contact force of the road on the car at the lowest point.
parts.working: M1 N − mg = mv²/r; C1 mv²/r = 1.10 × 10⁴ N; A1 N = 2.18 × 10⁴ N

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a passenger feels heavier at the bottom of the dip, and calculate the ratio (seat force) ÷ (passenger's weight).
parts.answer: The seat must push up with more than the weight to provide the upward centripetal force; ratio = 2.02
parts.working: B1 resultant must be upwards towards centre; A1 2.02

practice.stem: A section of a racing track is a horizontal circular arc of radius 80 m, banked at 15° to the horizontal. A car of mass m travels round it. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: By considering the vertical and horizontal components of the normal contact force N, show that the speed at which no friction is needed is given by v² = rg tan θ.
parts.answer: N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = mv²/r; dividing gives tan θ = v²/(rg).
parts.working: B1: N cos θ = mg (no vertical acceleration); B1: N sin θ = mv²/r (provides centripetal force); B1: divide to obtain v² = rg tan θ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate this speed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what additional force is needed if the car travels faster than this speed, and state its direction.
parts.answer: Friction acting down the slope (towards the centre side), to provide the extra centripetal force.
parts.working: B1: N sin θ alone is too small to give mv²/r; B1: friction needed, acting down the banking (parallel to surface).

practice.stem: A large Ferris wheel at a funfair has radius 20 m and turns at a constant rate, making one revolution every 60 s. A passenger of mass 60 kg sits in a seat that stays upright. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the centripetal acceleration of the passenger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the contact force of the seat on the passenger at the top and at the bottom of the wheel.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the passenger feels lighter at the top.
parts.answer: The seat pushes up with a force less than her weight because part of her weight provides the centripetal force.
parts.working: B1: contact force (felt as weight) is less than mg at the top.

practice.stem: In a 'well of death' show at a fair in Pakistan, a motorcyclist rides around the inside of a vertical cylindrical wooden wall of radius 5.0 m, moving in a horizontal circle. The total mass of rider and motorcycle is 250 kg and the speed is 15 m s⁻¹. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the normal contact force of the wall on the motorcycle and rider.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the size of the frictional force on the tyres and explain why it has this value.
parts.working: B1: there is no vertical acceleration, so friction (upwards) balances weight; B1: 250 × 9.81 = 2450 N.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The maximum frictional force available is 0.60 times the normal contact force. Calculate the minimum speed at which the rider can go round without sliding down.

practice.stem: A passenger aircraft of mass 5.0 × 10⁴ kg flies at a constant speed of 120 m s⁻¹ and turns in a horizontal circle of radius 2.0 km by banking its wings. The lift force acts perpendicular to the wings. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the lift force allows the aircraft to turn in a horizontal circle.
parts.answer: When banked, the lift (perpendicular to the wings) is tilted; its vertical component balances the weight and its horizontal component provides the centripetal force.
parts.working: B1: vertical component of lift = weight; B1: horizontal component of lift towards centre = mv²/r.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the angle of bank.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the lift force.

practice.stem: A small coin is placed on a horizontal turntable 8.0 cm from its centre. The speed of rotation is increased slowly; the coin starts to slide when the turntable reaches 45 revolutions per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the centripetal acceleration of the coin just before it slides.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the maximum frictional force on the coin as a fraction of its weight.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The turntable is now set to 33 revolutions per minute. Calculate the greatest distance from the centre at which the coin can be placed without sliding.
parts.working: Same maximum acceleration: r = a/ω² (M1) with ω = 3.46 rad s⁻¹ → r = 0.149 m (A1).

practice.stem: A laboratory centrifuge in a hospital spins blood samples. A sample is 9.0 cm from the axis and must have a centripetal acceleration of 3000g, where g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express this as revolutions per minute.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the resultant force needed on 2.0 g of material in the tube at this radius.

practice.stem: A roller-coaster car runs round the inside of a vertical circular loop of radius 8.0 m. Friction and air resistance can be ignored; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why there is a minimum speed at the top of the loop for the car to stay in contact with the track.
parts.answer: At the top both the weight and the contact force of the track act towards the centre. The contact force cannot be negative, so the smallest possible centripetal force is the weight alone: mg = mv²/r. If the car is slower, its weight is more than the centripetal force needed, so it falls inside the circle and leaves the track.
parts.working: B1 at least weight must be the centripetal force; B1 if v smaller, mv²/r < mg so the car falls inwards (loses contact)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum speed at the top of the loop.
parts.working: C1 mg = mv²/r; A1 v = √(gr) = 8.86 m s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: The car starts from rest. Calculate the minimum height of the starting point above the bottom of the loop.
parts.working: M1 mgh = mg(2r) + ½mv² with v² = gr; A1 h = 2.5r = 20 m

practice.stem: A student of mass 70 kg stands on bathroom scales on the equator. Treat the Earth as a sphere of radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m that rotates once every 24.0 hours. g = 9.81 m s⁻² (the gravitational field strength without rotation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the centripetal acceleration of the student due to the Earth's rotation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the scales read less than the student's weight mg, and calculate the reading.
parts.answer: The resultant force (mg − N) must provide the centripetal force towards the Earth's centre, so N < mg; reading = 684 N
parts.working: B1 mg − N = mω²r (resultant towards centre); C1 mω²r = 2.36 N; A1 N = 686.7 − 2.36 = 684 N

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the length of a day, in hours, for which the scales on the equator would read zero.

practice.stem: On a curved section of railway track of radius 900 m, the outer rail is raised so that a train travelling at 25 m s⁻¹ needs no sideways force from the rails. The distance between the rails is 1.676 m. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that for a track banked at angle θ the condition is tan θ = v²/(rg).
parts.answer: Normal reaction N: vertical component N cos θ = mg; horizontal component N sin θ = mv²/r; dividing gives tan θ = v²/(rg).
parts.working: B1 N cos θ = mg; B1 N sin θ = mv²/r and divide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the angle of banking.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how much higher the outer rail is than the inner rail.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A slow goods train uses the same curve at 12 m s⁻¹. State which rail the wheel flanges press against.

practice.stem: A puck of mass 0.20 kg slides on a horizontal frictionless table in a circle of radius 0.50 m. It is attached to a light string that passes through a small smooth hole at the centre of the circle and supports a hanging mass of 0.50 kg, which stays at rest. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the puck.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time for one revolution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The radius is changed to 0.25 m with the same hanging mass. Calculate the new speed needed for the hanging mass to stay at rest.

practice.stem:
A student attaches a 0.20 kg mass to a force sensor on a rotating arm so that the mass moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.50 m. She records the centripetal force F for different speeds v.
v / m s⁻¹: 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0
F / N: 0.41, 0.89, 1.61, 2.48, 3.62

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the graph you would plot to obtain a straight line through the origin, and explain why.
parts.answer: F against v²; since F = (m/r)v², the graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient m/r.
parts.working: B1 F against v²; B1 gradient = m/r

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the gradient of this graph.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the gradient to determine the mass and compare it with the known value.
parts.working: M1 m = gradient × r; A1 0.20 kg, consistent

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the speed may be difficult to measure accurately and one improvement.
parts.answer: Timing a revolution by eye has reaction-time error – time many revolutions or use a light gate / video analysis.

practice.stem: A small metal bob of mass 0.15 kg hangs from a light string 1.2 m long. It moves in a horizontal circle at constant speed so that the string makes an angle of 30° with the vertical (a conical pendulum). g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the tension in the string.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the bob.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time for one revolution.

practice.stem: A car of mass 900 kg drives over a humpbacked bridge whose top is a vertical circular arc of radius 30 m. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the normal contact force on the car at the top of the bridge when its speed is 12 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the maximum speed at which the car can cross the top of the bridge without losing contact with the road.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the driver finds it harder to steer and brake near the top of the bridge at high speed.
parts.answer: The normal contact force is reduced, so the maximum friction between tyres and road is reduced.
parts.working: B1: normal force smaller at higher speed; B1: friction (grip) depends on the normal force, so less force available for steering/braking.

practice.stem: A ball of mass 0.20 kg on a light inextensible string of length 0.70 m is swung in a vertical circle. At the lowest point its speed is 6.0 m s⁻¹. Air resistance is negligible; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use conservation of energy to calculate the speed of the ball at the top of the circle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the tension in the string at the top and at the bottom of the circle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where in the circle the string is most likely to break, with a reason.
parts.answer: At the bottom, where the tension is greatest.
parts.working: B1: at the bottom — weight acts away from the centre so tension must supply mg + mv²/r and speed is greatest.

practice.stem:
A student investigates circular motion with a rubber bung of mass m tied to a string. The string passes through a vertical glass tube held in the hand and a mass of 0.100 kg hangs from its lower end, so the tension in the string is F = 0.981 N. The bung is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius r and the period T is measured:
r = 0.300 m, T = 0.49 s
r = 0.400 m, T = 0.58 s
r = 0.500 m, T = 0.62 s
r = 0.600 m, T = 0.69 s
r = 0.700 m, T = 0.76 s
r = 0.800 m, T = 0.79 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that T² = (4π²m/F) r, where F is the tension in the string.
parts.answer: F = mω²r and ω = 2π/T, so F = 4π²mr/T², giving T² = (4π²m/F)r.
parts.working: M1: F = mrω² with ω = 2π/T; A1: rearrangement shown.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate T² for each reading.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The best-fit straight line through the origin of a graph of T² against r has gradient 0.798 s² m⁻¹. Determine the mass of the bung.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the tension in the string may not equal the weight of the hanging mass, and explain one way to reduce the uncertainty in T.
parts.answer: Friction between string and tube; string not exactly horizontal; time 10 revolutions and repeat.
parts.working: B1 each for any two: friction at the tube; string not horizontal (only a component of tension is horizontal / r measured to the top of the tube is not the true radius); mass of string. B1: time 10 or 20 revolutions and divide; repeat and average; video with frame-by-frame timing.

practice.stem: In a 'chair-o-plane' fairground ride, each chair hangs from a chain 5.0 m long attached to the rim of a rotating frame, 4.0 m from the vertical axis. When the ride turns at a constant rate, each chain makes an angle of 35° with the vertical. A chair and rider have a total mass of 70 kg. Ignore the mass of the chain; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the radius of the circle in which the rider moves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the tension in the chain.
parts.working: M1 T cos 35° = mg; A1 838 N

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the rider and the period of rotation of the ride.
parts.working: M1 T sin 35° = mv²/r so v² = rg tan 35°; A1 v = 6.87 m s⁻¹; A1 period = 2πr/v = 6.28 s

parts.label: d
parts.text: State and explain whether an empty chair hangs at the same angle.
parts.answer: Yes – tan θ = v²/(rg) does not depend on mass (at the same radius and angular speed).

practice.stem: A boy of mass 60 kg swings across a stream on a rope of length 5.0 m tied to a branch. He starts from rest with the rope taut at 40° to the vertical and swings down through the lowest point. The rope can withstand a tension of 900 N. Ignore air resistance and treat the boy as a point mass; g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the boy at the lowest point.
parts.working: C1 height fallen h = 5.0(1 − cos 40°) = 1.17 m; A1 v = √(2gh) = 4.79 m s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the tension in the rope at the lowest point and state whether the rope breaks.
parts.answer: 864 N; the rope does not break

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the tension is greatest at the lowest point of the swing.
parts.answer: There the speed is greatest and the whole weight acts directly away from the centre, so T = mg + mv²/r is largest.
parts.working: B1 maximum speed and T must balance all of mg as well as provide mv²/r

parts.label: d
parts.text: Show that, for a starting angle θ, the tension at the lowest point is mg(3 − 2 cos θ), and calculate the largest starting angle for which the rope does not break.
parts.working: M1 v² = 2gL(1 − cos θ) so mv²/L = 2mg(1 − cos θ); M1 T = mg + 2mg(1 − cos θ) = mg(3 − 2 cos θ); A1 900 = 588.6(3 − 2 cos θ) → cos θ = 0.735, θ = 42.7°

practice.stem: A stunt pilot of mass 75 kg flies a vertical circular loop of radius 600 m. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: At the bottom of the loop the speed is 150 m s⁻¹. Calculate the force of the seat on the pilot and express it as a multiple of the pilot's weight.
parts.working: M1 N − mg = mv²/r; A1 N = 3.55 × 10³ N; A1 4.82 mg

parts.label: b
parts.text: At the top of the loop the speed is 120 m s⁻¹. Calculate the force of the seat on the pilot and state its direction.
parts.working: M1 N + mg = mv²/r; A1 1.06 × 10³ N downwards

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed at the top below which the pilot would need a seat belt to stay in the seat.

practice.stem: A design for a space station is a large ring of radius 120 m that rotates about its central axis to give 'artificial gravity'. Astronauts stand on the inside surface of the outer wall. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed needed for the centripetal acceleration at the outer wall to be 9.81 m s⁻².
parts.working: C1 a = rω²; A1 ω = 0.286 rad s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the period of rotation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: An astronaut is 1.80 m tall. Calculate the percentage difference between the centripetal acceleration at her feet and at her head, and explain why a larger ring is better.
parts.answer: 1.5%; for a larger radius the fractional difference (and the required ω) is smaller, so the effect is less noticeable
parts.working: M1 a ∝ r so difference = 1.80/120; A1 1.5 %; B1 larger r → smaller difference / slower rotation

practice.stem: A small ball moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle on the smooth inside surface of a hemispherical bowl of radius 0.30 m. The circle is 0.10 m above the lowest point of the bowl. g = 9.81 m s⁻².

parts.label: a
parts.text: The normal contact force on the ball acts towards the centre of the hemisphere. Calculate the angle between this force and the vertical.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the radius of the horizontal circle.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the ball and its period of revolution.
parts.working: M1 N cos θ = mg, N sin θ = mv²/r → v² = rg tan θ; A1 v = 1.57 m s⁻¹; A1 period 0.897 s

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the radian.
parts.answer: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert 270° to radians.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A point on a circle of radius 0.35 m moves through an angle of 2.4 rad. Calculate the length of arc travelled.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A ceiling fan has blades of length 0.60 m measured from the axis and rotates at 180 revolutions per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the blades.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of a blade tip.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the angular speed and the linear speed of a point halfway along a blade compare with those of the tip.
parts.answer: Same angular speed; half the linear speed.
parts.working: B1: ω same for all points on a rigid blade; B1: v = ωr so half.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A large clock on a clock tower has hands that move steadily.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the minute hand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the hour hand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The minute hand is 1.2 m long. Calculate the speed of its tip.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the angle, in radians, that the hour hand turns through between 12:00 and 16:30.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A wind turbine at a wind farm near Jhimpir, Sindh, has blades 40 m long and turns at 15 revolutions per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the rotor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of a blade tip.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time for the rotor to turn through 1.0 rad.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: The bob of a simple pendulum of length 0.80 m moves along an arc of length 0.12 m from its lowest point to one end of its swing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle swung through, in radians.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert this angle to degrees.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage difference between θ in radians and sin θ, and comment on the result.
parts.answer: 0.37%; for small angles sin θ ≈ θ (in radians)
parts.working: sin 0.15 = 0.1494 (M1); difference = 0.37% of θ, so small-angle approximation is good (A1).

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Express one complete revolution in radians.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert 45° into radians.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Convert 0.50 rad into degrees.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A point on a wheel of radius 0.40 m turns through 0.50 rad. Calculate the distance it moves along its circular path.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A record turntable rotates at 33⅓ revolutions per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the turntable.
parts.working: C1 f = 0.5556 s⁻¹; A1 ω = 2πf = 3.49 rad s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of a point on the record 14.5 cm from the centre.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the angular speed of a point 5.0 cm from the centre compares with your answer to (a).
parts.working: B1 all points on a rigid rotating object have the same ω

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A car's wheels, of radius 0.30 m, roll without slipping. At one moment each wheel turns with an angular speed of 85 rad s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the car in m s⁻¹ and in km h⁻¹.
parts.working: A1 v = rω = 25.5 m s⁻¹; A1 91.8 km h⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of revolutions the wheel makes each second.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: The lamp at the top of a lighthouse rotates steadily, making one revolution every 10 s. Its narrow beam sweeps across the sea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the beam.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the angle, in degrees, through which the beam turns in 1.5 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed at which the patch of light moves across a ship 2.0 km away.
parts.working: C1 v = rω; A1 1.26 × 10³ m s⁻¹

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A spin bowler releases a cricket ball of radius 3.6 cm spinning at 25 revolutions per second about an axis through its centre.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the ball.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of a point on the seam, at the ball's surface, relative to the centre of the ball.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the angle the ball turns through, in radians, during a flight time of 0.60 s.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: The Earth (radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m) rotates once on its axis in 24 hours. Treat it as a sphere.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the Earth about its axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of a point on the equator due to this rotation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Karachi is at latitude 24.9° N. Calculate the speed of a building in Karachi due to the Earth's rotation.
parts.working: Radius of its circle = R cos 24.9° (M1); v = ωR cos 24.9° = 420 m s⁻¹ (A1).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the angular speed of the building in Karachi compared with a point on the equator.
parts.working: B1: every point on the Earth turns through 2π in the same time.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A car travels at a constant 30 m s⁻¹ on the motorway. Its wheels have a diameter of 0.62 m and roll without slipping.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the wheel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of revolutions per minute.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for one revolution.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define angular speed.
parts.answer: The angle swept out per unit time by the radius (rate of change of angle).
parts.working: B1: rate of change of angular displacement (angle in radians per unit time).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the definition of the radian, show that the speed v of an object moving in a circle of radius r with angular speed ω is v = rω.
parts.answer: In time Δt the angle is Δθ = ωΔt; arc length s = rΔθ; v = s/Δt = rω.
parts.working: M1: s = rθ (radian definition); A1: divide by time: v = rΔθ/Δt = rω.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A point on the rim of a potter's wheel of radius 0.18 m makes 2.5 revolutions per second. Calculate its speed.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A cyclist turns the front chain-wheel (radius 0.10 m) at 1.5 revolutions per second. The chain connects it to a rear sprocket of radius 0.040 m fixed to the rear wheel. The bicycle does not skid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the chain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the rear sprocket.
parts.working: Chain speed same at both sprockets (M1); ω = 0.942/0.040 = 23.6 rad s⁻¹ (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The rear wheel, radius 0.34 m, turns with the rear sprocket. Calculate the speed of the bicycle.
parts.working: Same ω as sprocket (M1); v = 23.6 × 0.34 = 8.01 m s⁻¹ (A1).

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A child sits 2.5 m from the centre of a playground roundabout that makes 6 complete revolutions in 50 s at a steady rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the roundabout.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the child.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the angle the child turns through in 3.0 s, in radians and in degrees.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A potter in Multan shapes clay on a wheel. Clay at the edge of the wheel, 0.18 m from the axis, moves at 2.4 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the wheel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of revolutions per minute.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the angle turned in 0.50 s and the number of revolutions this represents.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: The Sun has a diameter of 1.39 × 10⁹ m and is 1.50 × 10¹¹ m from the Earth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle, in radians, that the Sun's diameter subtends at the Earth. Explain why the arc formula can be used.
parts.answer: 9.27 × 10⁻³ rad; the angle is so small that the diameter is very nearly equal to an arc of radius 1.50 × 10¹¹ m
parts.working: A1 θ = s/r = 9.27 × 10⁻³ rad; B1 small angle – straight diameter ≈ arc

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert this angle to degrees.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Because of the Earth's rotation, the Sun appears to move across the sky at 2π rad per 24 h. Calculate the time it takes to move through its own diameter, in minutes.
parts.working: C1 ω = 4.36 × 10⁻³ rad min⁻¹; A1 t = θ/ω = 2.12 min

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: The Earth orbits the Sun in a path that is approximately a circle of radius 1.50 × 10¹¹ m, taking 365.25 days for one orbit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the Earth in its orbit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the orbital speed of the Earth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the angle, in degrees, through which the Earth moves round its orbit in one day.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: During a delivery, a cricket bowler's straight arm rotates about the shoulder through an angle of 200° in 0.12 s at an approximately constant rate. The distance from the shoulder to the ball is 0.75 m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the arm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the ball relative to the shoulder at release, in m s⁻¹ and km h⁻¹.
parts.working: A1 v = rω = 21.8 m s⁻¹; A1 79 km h⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why fast bowlers also run up to the crease before bowling.
parts.answer: The ball's speed relative to the ground is the run-up speed plus its speed relative to the shoulder.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A merry-go-round turns at a constant rate. Horse A is 3.0 m from the axis and horse B is 4.5 m from the axis. Horse B travels 85 m in 1.0 minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the merry-go-round.
parts.working: C1 v_B = 1.42 m s⁻¹; A1 ω = v/r = 0.315 rad s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the period of rotation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the ratio (speed of B) ÷ (speed of A) and explain your answer.
parts.answer: 1.5; both have the same ω, and v = rω
parts.working: A1 1.5; B1 same angular speed so v ∝ r

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: The rotor blades of a helicopter are 5.3 m long, measured from the axis. To avoid shock waves, the speed of the blade tips relative to the helicopter must stay below 90% of the speed of sound, 330 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum angular speed of the rotor.
parts.working: C1 v = 297 m s⁻¹; A1 ω = v/r = 56.0 rad s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert this to revolutions per minute.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the tip speed relative to the air is larger on one side of the helicopter when it flies forwards.
parts.answer: On the side where the blade moves forwards, the helicopter's forward velocity adds to the tip speed.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem:
A student marks a point on a turntable and uses video analysis to measure the angle θ turned through after time t.
t / s: 0, 0.50, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00
θ / rad: 0, 1.62, 3.10, 4.75, 6.27

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the data show that the angular speed is approximately constant.
parts.answer: Equal time intervals give approximately equal increases in θ (≈ 1.5–1.65 rad per 0.50 s); θ ∝ t.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the angular speed from a best-fit line (or the overall change).
parts.working: M1 gradient of θ–t graph; A1 3.1 rad s⁻¹

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the rotation rate in revolutions per minute.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the increases in θ are not exactly equal.
parts.answer: Uncertainty in locating the marked point / angle on each video frame (or slight speed variation).

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: On an athletics track the inside lane (lane 1) running line is a semicircular bend of radius 36.5 m. Each lane outward adds 1.22 m to the radius, so lane 8 is 7 lanes out. A runner in lane 1 runs round the bend at a constant speed of 9.0 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the runner in lane 1 about the centre of the bend.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A runner in lane 8 stays level with the lane-1 runner (on the same radius line) throughout the bend. Calculate the speed needed in lane 8.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each bend is a semicircle. Calculate how much further a runner in lane 8 travels round one bend than a runner in lane 1, and hence explain why starting positions are staggered.
parts.working: Δs = πΔr = π × 8.54 = 26.8 m (M1 A1); stagger makes all lanes the same total distance.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A computer hard disc spins at 7200 revolutions per minute. The read head is over a track 3.0 cm from the axis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the disc surface under the head.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each bit of data occupies 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m along the track. Calculate the time for one bit to pass under the head.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The head moves to a track at radius 0.015 m. State and explain the effect on the rate at which bits pass the head if bits are the same length.
parts.answer: The rate halves, because the linear speed v = ωr halves at the same angular speed.
parts.working: B1: ω unchanged; B1: v ∝ r, so half the speed → half the bit rate (time per bit doubles).

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: An electric motor in a flour mill turns a small pulley of radius 2.5 cm at 1450 revolutions per minute. A belt that does not slip connects it to a larger pulley of radius 10.0 cm on the machine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the belt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rotation rate of the machine pulley in revolutions per minute.
parts.working: Belt speed same, so ω ∝ 1/r (M1): 1450 × 2.5/10.0 = 362.5 ≈ 363 rev min⁻¹ (A1; accept 362).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the centripetal acceleration of a small piece of belt as it passes round the motor pulley.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A fan with three identical, equally spaced blades is lit by a stroboscope flashing 25 times per second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the fan appears stationary when it turns at certain speeds.
parts.answer: Between flashes each blade moves exactly to the position of a blade (the same or another) at the previous flash, so every flash shows the same pattern.
parts.working: B1: between flashes the fan turns through a multiple of 120° (the angle between blades); B1: so the image looks identical at each flash.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the lowest angular speed of the fan for which it appears stationary.
parts.working: Turns 1/3 rev in 1/25 s (M1) → f = 25/3 = 8.33 rev s⁻¹ → ω = 52.4 rad s⁻¹ (A1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the next higher rotation frequency, in revolutions per second, at which the fan appears stationary.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: The minute hand and the hour hand of a clock are both pointing at 12 at exactly 12:00.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle, in radians, through which (i) the minute hand and (ii) the hour hand turn in 20 minutes.
parts.working: A1 minute hand: 2π/3 = 2.09 rad; A1 hour hand: 2π/36 = 0.175 rad

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time after 12:00 when the hands are next exactly on top of each other. Give your answer in minutes.
parts.working: M1 the minute hand must gain 2π rad on the hour hand; M1 t = 2π/(ω_m − ω_h) with ω_m = 2π/3600 and ω_h = 2π/43 200 rad s⁻¹; A1 3927 s = 65.45 min

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the angle between the hands at 3:30, in degrees.
parts.working: A1 hour hand at 105°, minute hand at 180°: 75°

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: Two runners start together from the same point on a circular track of radius 50 m. Runner A runs at a steady 5.0 m s⁻¹ and runner B at a steady 4.0 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of each runner.
parts.answer: A: 0.10 rad s⁻¹; B: 0.080 rad s⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: They run in opposite directions. Calculate the time until they first meet.
parts.working: M1 together they cover 2π rad: (ω_A + ω_B)t = 2π; A1 34.9 s

parts.label: c
parts.text: Instead they run in the same direction. Calculate the time until A first overtakes B, and the distance A has run by then.

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: A bicycle travels along a level road at a steady 6.0 m s⁻¹. Its wheels have radius 0.34 m and roll without slipping.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of each wheel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Relative to the bicycle frame, every point on the rim moves at the same speed. State this speed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the speed relative to the road of (i) the point of the tyre touching the road and (ii) the point at the top of the wheel. Explain your answers.
parts.answer: (i) 0 (ii) 12 m s⁻¹; the rim velocity relative to the frame (6.0 m s⁻¹) adds to the bicycle's velocity (6.0 m s⁻¹) at the top and cancels it at the bottom
parts.working: B1 bottom 0; B1 top 12 m s⁻¹; B1 vector addition of rim velocity and frame velocity

practice.subtopic: Kinematics of circular motion (radian, angular speed)
practice.stem: In an experiment to measure the speed of light, a plane mirror rotates at 500 revolutions per second. Light reflected from the rotating mirror travels to a fixed mirror 3.0 km away and back to the rotating mirror. Speed of light = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time for the light to travel to the fixed mirror and back.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the angle through which the rotating mirror turns in this time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When a mirror turns through an angle θ, a reflected ray turns through 2θ. Calculate the angle between the returning reflected beam and its original direction, in degrees.
